en: The Bodhisattva Stage within the *Yogācārabhūmi*: The Foundation of the Yoga Practice (Book 1)
The Chapter on the Spiritual Lineage (Gotra-paṭala) (Chapter 1.1).
Om! Homage to the Buddha!
These ten factors conduce to the inclusion of the Mahāyāna, the path of the bodhisattva together with its fruit.
What are the ten?
They are: the basis, the mark, the faction, the resolute intention, the dwelling, the rebirth, the adoption, the stage, the conduct, and the foundation.
The summary verse:
Support, gender, factions, resolute intention, and dwellings; rebirth, adoption, stages, conduct, and finally, the foundation.
In that regard, what is the basis?
Here, the bodhisattva’s own lineage, the first production of the thought of awakening, and all the factors conducive to awakening are called the basis.
For what reason?

In this regard, a bodhisattva, relying upon the lineage (*gotra*), becomes established and capable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Therefore, by virtue of its commonality, the lineage is called the "support" (*ādhāra*).

In this regard, a bodhisattva, relying upon and established in the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), applies himself to generosity, as well as to ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Alternatively, he applies himself to the perfections, to the accumulation of merit, to the accumulation of knowledge, and to all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Therefore, the first production of the thought of awakening is called the support for the application of the bodhisattva’s conduct.
In this regard, a bodhisattva, relying upon and established in that very application of the bodhisattva conduct, fulfills unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, that application of the bodhisattva conduct is called the basis for the fulfillment of his great enlightenment. A person who abides in the absence of a lineage (agotra), lacking the spiritual lineage, is incapable of fulfilling unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, even if they have generated the thought of enlightenment and rely upon effort.

Therefore, by this method, it should be understood that even for a bodhisattva who has not yet generated the thought [of awakening] and has not yet engaged in the practice of the bodhisattva conduct, the lineage (*gotra*) is the foundation.

Furthermore, if one who abides in the lineage does not generate the thought [of awakening] and does not apply himself to the practices of awakening, he will not quickly realize awakening; however, it should be understood that through the opposite of these conditions, he realizes it quickly.
Furthermore, this lineage is called the "support";
it is also called the "sustenance," the "cause," the "basis," the "proximate cause," the "forerunner," and the "abode.
Just as it is with the lineage, so it is with the first production of the thought of awakening and all the conduct of a bodhisattva.
In that regard, what is the lineage (*gotra*)?
In brief, the lineage is of two kinds:
that which exists by nature (*prakṛtistha*) and that which is acquired through effort (*samudānīta*).

In this regard, the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra*) is that specific excellence of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana-viśeṣa*) belonging to bodhisattvas; it has been transmitted through succession, is beginningless, and is obtained by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Therein, the acquired lineage (*samudānīta-gotra*) is that which is obtained through the prior cultivation of roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
In this context, both types [of lineage] are intended.
Furthermore, that lineage is also called the "seed" (bīja),
and it is also called the "element" (dhātu) and the "nature" (prakṛti).
Furthermore, that which has not yet realized its fruit is subtle and exists without the fruit;
that which has realized its fruit is gross and exists together with the fruit.

Indeed, for those bodhisattvas who are endowed with that lineage, having transcended all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and let alone other sentient beings—an unsurpassed distinction is to be understood.
For what reason?
Briefly stated, there are these two purifications:
purification from the obscuration of afflictions and purification from the obscuration of the knowable.

In that regard, the lineage of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is purified through the purification of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but not through the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The bodhisattva lineage, however, is purified both through the purification of the afflictive obscurations and through the purification of the cognitive obscurations. Therefore, it is said to be preeminent and unsurpassed.
Furthermore, the distinction of a bodhisattva from śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should be understood through four aspects.
What are these four?
They are: that which is made by way of faculties, that which is made by way of practice, that which is made by way of skillfulness, and that which is made by way of the fruit.
In this regard, the distinction made by way of the faculties is as follows:
by their very nature, a bodhisattva possesses sharp faculties,
a pratyekabuddha possesses middling faculties, and a śrāvaka possesses dull faculties.
In this regard, this is the distinction made by way of practice:
the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha are practiced for their own benefit;

the Bodhisattva, however, is practiced for his own benefit as well as for the benefit of others—for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
In this regard, the distinction made by way of skill is as follows:

the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha cultivate skill in the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, the possible and the impossible, and the [Four] Truths; whereas the Bodhisattva cultivates skill in those and in all other branches of knowledge.
In this regard, the distinction made by way of the result is as follows:
The śrāvaka realizes the fruit of śrāvaka-enlightenment;
the pratyekabuddha realizes pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; the bodhisattva realizes the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
(Dutt 3) These six are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva regarding the perfections,
by which others recognize him as "this one is a bodhisattva."

The characteristic of the lineage for the perfection of generosity, and the characteristic of the lineage for the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom:
therein, this is the characteristic of the lineage for a bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity.
Here, a bodhisattva is by nature itself one who delights in giving.

When objects to be given are available, he is constantly and continuously disposed to share them with others; he gives with a joyful heart and not with a dejected mind. He is one who practices sharing even from what is small, and he bestows his gift with clarity.
He does not disparage others; he feels shame for his own failure to give, and he speaks in praise of giving to others.
He encourages them toward generosity;
upon seeing a donor, he becomes joyful and glad at heart;
and toward his teachers, elders, those worthy of offerings, and those deserving of honor, he rises and offers them a seat.

Whether asked or unasked, he provides instruction in the proper method regarding various duties of sentient beings that leads to no misfortune in this world or the next. To those beings terrified by fear of kings, thieves, enemies, water, and so forth,
he grants fearlessness and protects them according to his ability from that manifold, extensive, and fierce danger.
He does not misappropriate wealth entrusted to his hand by others;
having received a debt from others, he does not deceive them nor does he misappropriate it;
he does not defraud or deceive his own heirs.

He perfectly awakens the deluded and perverted mind regarding various types of articles— such as gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, silver, emeralds, musāragalva, rubies, and right-spiraling conchs— so that he may not be deceived by anything else;
how much less, then, would he himself deceive him?
By nature, he is inclined toward magnificent enjoyments;
his mind inclines toward all magnificent enjoyments and possessions,
and he is devoted to magnificent enterprises rather than to those that are meager or of limited scope.
And there are these calamities in the world, namely: the calamity of women and the calamity of intoxicants.
He very quickly attains detachment from such vices as the addiction to gambling, and the addiction to watching actors, dancers, jesters, mimes, and the like;
he manifests a sense of shame and dread of blame, and even when obtaining vast wealth, he does not become excessively greedy, much less so over a small amount.
These and other similar qualities should be understood as the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*):
In this case, a bodhisattva is by nature endowed with bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are mild, unwholesome, yet not excessively fierce or excessively harmful to sentient beings.
Even after committing a sinful deed, he very quickly attains remorse;
feeling shame for it, he practices [virtue], not born of delight.
He is by nature one who does not harm sentient beings with hands, clods of earth, sticks, weapons, or the like;
he is naturally affectionate and beloved by sentient beings.
Furthermore, toward those worthy of honor, he attends at the proper times with salutations, prostrations, rising from his seat, joining his palms, and respectful conduct.
He is generous;
he is urbane and compliant with the minds of others;
he is preceded by a smile, with an open countenance, free from frowns, and is the first to speak.

He is grateful and mindful of favors toward sentient beings who have helped him; and toward sentient beings who seek his aid, he maintains straightforwardness and does not deceive them with guile or hypocrisy.
He acquires wealth through righteous means and without violence, not through unrighteous means;
by his very nature he desires to perform meritorious deeds,
and he even engages in the meritorious activities of others, let alone his own.
Furthermore, he is excessively afflicted by the suffering of others—namely, by seeing or hearing of their execution, imprisonment, mutilation, beating, reviling, or threatening.
He values the undertaking of the Dharma and values the future life;
he perceives danger even in the slightest fault, let alone in a great one.

And he becomes a helper in the affairs and duties of others—namely, in agriculture, commerce, cattle-rearing, royal service, writing, calculation, accounting, reckoning, and sealing; in pleasing a master, pleasing a family, pleasing the royal court, and pleasing friends and enemies; and in the acquisition, protection, storage, investment, expenditure, and distribution of enjoyments, as well as in marriages, betrothals, feasting, and communal eating—in such matters pertaining to the activities of sentient beings.

He acts as a companion; he does not join in quarrels, disputes, conflicts, or arguments, nor in activities that cause harm to others— those things which lead to misfortune, disadvantage, and suffering for both oneself and others—
and he restrains them from what should not be done, namely, from the ten evil, unwholesome actions.
He becomes subject to others and subservient to others;
because of his equal patience and virtue, having abandoned his own business, he is employed by others in their own affairs according to their will.

He possesses a moist heart and a gentle mind; he does not long maintain a state of malice or resentment, but rather at that very moment his mind turns toward amiability. He values truth and does not deceive others with false speech.
He takes no pleasure in causing dissension among friends, nor does he do so.
He does not impulsively chatter that which is incoherent, meaningless, or purposeless.

He speaks kindly and avoids harshness toward others, even toward his own servants and attendants, let alone others; he is fond of the virtues of others and is one who proclaims the true qualities of others.
These and similar traits should be understood as the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

Here, a bodhisattva, by his very nature, having received harm from others, does not manifest a mind of resentment, nor does he resort to retaliation. And when being conciliated, he quickly accepts the conciliation.
He does not harbor stubbornness, nor does he carry a long-standing intention of enmity.
These and other such qualities should be understood as the signs of the lineage for a bodhisattva’s perfection of patience.
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage for a bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor:
In this regard, a bodhisattva is by nature industrious;
rising early and retiring late, he does not excessively indulge in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, or the pleasure of lying on his side.
And when a task has arisen, having overcome the lack of desire to act and laziness through careful reflection, he applies himself to the accomplishment of that task.

In the undertaking of all tasks, he possesses firm resolve; without having accomplished them or attained them entirely, he does not relax his vigor nor fall into despondency midway. Furthermore, regarding sublime and supreme goals, he does not allow his mind to shrink, nor does he disparage himself.
Thinking, "I am capable and have the strength to master these," he becomes inspired with enthusiasm;

he is heroic when entering a great assembly, or when engaging in offensive or defensive action against adversaries, or in other difficult tasks and great undertakings that lead to meaningful results, for he does not fall into excessive weariness even in such cases, much less in minor ones.
Thus, these and similar qualities should be understood as the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) for a bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage for a bodhisattva’s perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*):
here, a bodhisattva by nature possesses little distraction when contemplating the meaning of the teachings (*dharmārtha*).

Having seen or heard of forest retreats, wilderness hermitages, and remote lodgings— frequented by those seeking seclusion from people, free from evil, and conducive to solitary meditation— he generates an intense longing for that renunciation and solitude, thinking, "How happy is that state of going forth and withdrawal!"
By nature, he has weak afflictions (*kleśa*), weak hindrances (*nivaraṇa*), and weak inner corruption (*dausthulya*).
When he has gone into seclusion and is reflecting upon his own welfare, evil and improper thoughts do not excessively disturb his mind, nor do they remain by taking possession of it.
Even toward the side of enemies, he very quickly establishes a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*), let alone toward the side of friends or neutral persons.
Upon hearing of or seeing the suffering of sentient beings who are afflicted by various miseries, he gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
And for the sake of removing the suffering of those beings, he exerts himself according to his ability and according to his strength.
By nature, he desires their welfare and desires their happiness.
He is steadfast in the face of calamities—whether in the misfortune of kinsmen, the loss of enjoyments, execution, imprisonment, or exile—and in other such adversities.
He is intelligent, capable of grasping, retaining, and discerning the teachings (*dharmas*), and is endowed with the power of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Thus, he is able to remember what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago, and he is able to cause others to remember as well.
Thus, these and similar qualities should be understood as the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*):
here, a bodhisattva is endowed with innate wisdom (*sahajā prajñā*) for the sake of entering into all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) that are to be known.
He is not dull-witted, nor is he sluggish; he is by nature free from delusion.
Furthermore, regarding various points of heedlessness and their abstention, he possesses the power of analytical discernment.
These and other similar qualities should be understood as the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom.
These should be understood as the coarse, inferential signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva.
However, regarding the determination of the ultimate reality, only the Blessed Buddhas are those who see it directly.
Furthermore, because that lineage of bodhisattvas is by its very nature endowed with virtues, auspicious, excellent, and possessed of pure qualities.

Therefore, for the sake of attaining the state of a Tathāgata—which is difficult to realize, supreme, inconceivable, immovable, and unsurpassed—one applies oneself by way of its causal basis; otherwise, one does not.

And a bodhisattva is naturally endowed with these pure qualities only so long as he is not afflicted by the four secondary defilements that are contrary to those pure qualities, whether in their entirety or in part.
When he is afflicted by defilements, he then no longer appears amidst these pure dharmas,
and at times he is reborn in the states of woe.

Even when a bodhisattva is reborn in the miserable states, it should be understood that there is a great distinction based on their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) compared to other beings born in those miserable states.
In this case, the bodhisattva is reborn in the miserable states only very rarely after a long period of time.
Once reborn there, he is quickly liberated from the miserable states;

moreover, he does not experience such intense suffering of the miserable states as do other beings born in those states. Touched by that slight painful sensation, he gives rise to an exceedingly great sense of spiritual urgency.

And toward those beings who have been reborn there and are suffering, he acquires a mind of compassion; that is to say, by means of that very lineage, he acquires a mind of compassion toward those beings reborn there in suffering, being impelled by that very lineage and by the cause of the Buddha’s great compassion.
In this manner, the distinction of a bodhisattva born in the states of woe from other beings born in those states of woe should be understood.
In that regard, what are the four secondary afflictions of a bodhisattva that are antagonistic to the white dharmas?

First, for one who was previously negligent, there is the intensity of afflictions and the protracted nature of afflictions due to the habituation to afflictions; this is the first secondary affliction.
The second secondary affliction is the reliance upon evil friends by one who is deluded and unwholesome.
The third secondary affliction is the lack of autonomy and the confusion of mind experienced by one who is overwhelmed by teachers, husbands, kings, thieves, adversaries, and the like.
The fourth secondary affliction is the preoccupation with livelihood for one who lacks the necessary requisites.
For four reasons, even a bodhisattva endowed with such a lineage is unable to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What are these four?
In this case, from the very beginning, a bodhisattva does not obtain a spiritual friend—a Buddha or a bodhisattva—who teaches the path to enlightenment without error.
This is the first cause.
Furthermore, even after having found a spiritual friend, a bodhisattva grasps things erroneously and trains erroneously in the bodhisattva trainings;
this is the second cause.

Furthermore, although a bodhisattva has obtained a virtuous friend and is training unerringly in the bodhisattva trainings, he becomes lax in his application and indolent, not being endowed with intense and continuous vigor;
this is the third cause.
Furthermore, although a bodhisattva has obtained a virtuous friend and is training unerringly in the bodhisattva trainings...

And in that application, although one has initiated vigor, one's faculties remain unripened and the equipment for awakening remains incomplete due to not having practiced the factors conducive to awakening for a long period;
this is the fourth cause.
When the lineage exists, there is a failure to attain awakening due to the deficiency of its causes;
however, through their presence, attainment occurs.
But when the lineage is absent, it should be understood that there is an absolute and total non-attainment of awakening in every respect.
The first chapter, on the lineage, in the section on the basis within the Bodhisattvabhūmi, is completed.
(Dutt 8) Chapter 1.2:
The Generation of the Thought of Enlightenment.

Here, the first generation of the thought of enlightenment by a bodhisattva is the primary correct aspiration among all the correct aspirations of a bodhisattva; it encompasses all other correct aspirations.
Therefore, from the very beginning, that has the nature of right resolve (*samyak-praṇidhāna*).
Indeed, when that bodhisattva resolves his mind toward awakening, he forms such a mental intention and speaks these words:

"O, may I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; may I act for the benefit of all sentient beings and establish them in ultimate, final nirvāṇa and in the knowledge of a Tathāgata."
Thus, seeking both his own enlightenment and the welfare of sentient beings, he generates the thought of awakening;
therefore, that generation of the thought of awakening has the form of aspiration.
Indeed, having taken that enlightenment and the welfare of sentient beings as its object, that generation of the thought of awakening aspires to them, and not without an object.
Therefore, that production of the thought of enlightenment has awakening as its object and the welfare of sentient beings as its object.

Furthermore, because it is the precursor for gathering all the roots of virtue conducive to awakening, that production of the thought of enlightenment is virtuous, endowed with the quality of supreme skill,
auspicious, supremely auspicious, excellent, supremely excellent, and contrary to all misconduct of body, speech, and mind based upon all sentient beings.

And whatever other wholesome right aspirations there may be regarding mundane or supramundane matters, this right aspiration of a bodhisattva— namely, the first production of the thought of awakening— is the foremost and unsurpassed among them all.
Thus, this first production of the thought of awakening should be understood by way of its essential nature.
It should be understood as having five characteristics: by way of its aspect, its object, its qualities, and its excellence.
Upon the very arising of that thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the bodhisattva has entered the unsurpassed Great Vehicle of awakening;
he comes to be reckoned as a "bodhisattva," that is to say, according to the method of conventional linguistic usage.
Therefore, that production of the thought of enlightenment is comprised within "entry.
And having produced that thought, a bodhisattva gradually attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, but not without having produced it.
Therefore, that production of the thought is the root of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
And toward suffering sentient beings, that compassionate bodhisattva, with the intention of providing protection, generates that thought;
therefore, that generation of the thought is the outflow of compassion (*karuṇā-niṣyanda*).

Relying upon and established in that generation of the thought, the bodhisattva applies himself to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*), to the performance of the welfare of sentient beings, and to the training of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, that production of the thought of enlightenment is the basis for the bodhisattva training.
Thus, this first production of the thought of enlightenment should be understood in terms of its inclusion, its root, its outflow, and its basis.
Furthermore, that first production of the thought of enlightenment by a bodhisattva is, in brief, of two kinds.
There is that which leads to liberation and that which does not lead to liberation.
In this context, that which leads to liberation is what, once arisen, continues indefinitely and never turns back;
whereas that which does not lead to liberation is what, once arisen, does not continue indefinitely but turns back again.
Furthermore, the turning back of that production of the thought of awakening is also twofold:
absolute and non-absolute.
Among these, the absolute is when the thought, once turned back, does not arise again for the sake of awakening.
Furthermore, that which is non-ultimate is when the mind, having turned back, arises again and again for the sake of enlightenment.
Indeed, the arising of that mind should be understood by means of four conditions, four causes, and four powers.
What are the four conditions?

In this case, a son of good family or a daughter of good family sees the inconceivable and most wonderful miracle and power of a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva, or hears of it from someone who has trust; having seen or heard it, it occurs to them:
"Ah, how great is the majesty of this awakening (bodhi), for one who stands in or has entered upon it possesses such power as this!"

When such a miracle is seen or heard, one takes that very sight or hearing of power as the dominant condition and, being inclined toward great enlightenment, generates the mind set on great enlightenment.
This is the first condition for the arising of the mind.

He does not indeed see or hear of such power; rather, he hears the true Dharma concerning unsurpassed enlightenment as the Bodhisattvapiṭaka is being taught. Having heard it, he gains deep faith, and with that faith, making the hearing of the true Dharma his primary influence, he becomes intent upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata and generates the resolve to attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This is the second condition for the arising of the resolve.
He does not merely hear the Dharma; rather, the bodhisattva perceives that the disappearance of the true Dharma (*saddharmāntardhāni*) is imminent.
Having seen this, he thinks: "Alas! The endurance of the true Dharma of the bodhisattvas leads to the removal of suffering for immeasurable beings.
What if I were to generate the resolve for the long endurance of the true Dharma of the bodhisattvas, namely, for the sake of eliminating the suffering of these very beings?"
Making the upholding of the true Dharma itself his primary motive, he resolves his mind toward the attainment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, being himself resolved upon that wisdom.
This is the third condition for the arising of the mind.

He does not merely see the disappearance of the true Dharma approaching; rather, in the final age, at the end of time, he sees the physical bases of sentient beings belonging to that inferior final age, namely, those defiled by ten secondary afflictions.

That is to say, having seen those who abound in delusion, who abound in lack of shame and lack of dread of blame, who abound in envy and avarice, who abound in suffering, who abound in depravity, who abound in afflictions, who abound in misconduct, who abound in negligence, who abound in laziness,
and who abound in lack of faith, he further reflects as follows:
"Alas! This great age of defilement has arrived.

In such a corrupted time as this, it is not easy even to give rise to the thought of the inferior enlightenment of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha, let alone that of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, I too shall first give rise to that thought, so that others, following my example, might also give rise to it."

Thus, at the time of death, making the rarity of generating the thought of awakening the predominant factor, one who is resolutely intent upon great awakening generates the thought of great awakening.
This is the fourth condition for the arising of the thought.
What are the four causes?
The perfection of the spiritual lineage (*gotrasaṃpad*) is the first cause for the arising of the bodhisattva’s mind;
being sustained by Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the second cause for the arising of the mind;
and compassion toward sentient beings is the third cause for the arising of the bodhisattva’s mind.

Fearlessness toward the suffering of saṃsāra, as well as toward the suffering of difficult practices—even those that are long-lasting, diverse, intense, and continuous—is the fourth cause for the arising of the [awakening] mind.
In this regard, the excellence of the bodhisattva’s lineage (*gotrasaṃpad*) should be understood as being obtained through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The excellence of the bodhisattva’s spiritual friend (*mitrasaṃpad*) should be understood by way of four aspects.
In this case, from the very beginning, a bodhisattva’s friend is not dull-witted, is not of a sluggish nature, is wise, possesses discernment, and has not fallen into wrong views;
this is the first excellence of a friend. Furthermore, such a friend does not incite one toward negligence.
He does not provide him with any occasion for negligence;
this is the second excellence of a friend. Nor does he incite him toward misconduct, nor does he provide him with any opportunity for misconduct.

This is the third perfection of a friend: he does not dissuade him from superior qualities of faith, aspiration, undertaking, vigor, and skillful means, and instead incite him toward inferior qualities of faith, aspiration, undertaking, vigor, and skillful means— such as, for example,
dissuading him from the Mahāyāna and inciting him toward the Śrāvaka-yāna or the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or [dissuading him] from that which consists of cultivation.

Having discouraged them from those consisting of reflection, he discourages them from that which consists of reflection; having discouraged them from that which consists of hearing, he discourages them from that which consists of hearing; having discouraged them from the work of service, he discourages them from that which consists of ethical discipline; and having discouraged them from that which consists of generosity—without discouraging them from such superior qualities as these—he encourages them toward such inferior qualities as these.
This is the fourth perfection of friendship.
Through four aspects, a bodhisattva becomes abundant in compassion toward sentient beings.
There are world-systems among the infinite and boundless world-systems in the ten directions where suffering is not found;
yet that bodhisattva is reborn in a world-system where suffering is found, not in one where there is no suffering,
and he perceives others as touched, afflicted, and overwhelmed by some form of suffering.
He himself is touched, afflicted, and overwhelmed by one or another form of suffering;
furthermore, he perceives either another person or both himself and others as touched, afflicted, and overwhelmed by suffering that is long-lasting, diverse, intense, and continuous.

Thus, based on his own spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and by virtue of his natural goodness, compassion—whether weak, middling, or intense—arises in that bodhisattva through these four objective supports and bases, even without prior cultivation.
For four reasons, a bodhisattva, having placed compassion for sentient beings foremost, does not fear or tremble even before long-lasting, diverse, intense, and continuous suffering of saṃsāra,
let alone inferior suffering;
by nature he is courageous, steadfast, and powerful.
This is the first cause.
He is wise, habituated to correct contemplation, and possessed of the power of analytical discernment;
this is the second cause.
He is endowed with an intense resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
this is the third cause.
And he is endowed with an intense compassion toward sentient beings; this is the fourth cause.
What are the four powers?
They are the internal power, the external power, the causal power, and the power of application.
Among these, that inclination toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment which falls within one's own capacity is called the bodhisattva’s internal power for the arising of the thought of awakening.
The power of others (*parabala*) for the arising of the mind of a bodhisattva toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is said to be that which is produced by another’s influence.

This refers to the bodhisattva’s previous practice of wholesome qualities associated with the Mahāyāna, which now leads to the swift arising of the mind through merely seeing Buddhas and bodhisattvas, or merely hearing their praise, let alone through hearing the true Dharma.
Or, the power of the cause (*hetubala*) is said to be for the arising of the mind through the observation of [the Buddha’s] majestic power.

A Bodhisattva’s long-term cultivation of wholesome qualities in this present life—beginning with attending upon superior persons, hearing the true Dharma, and reflecting upon it—is called the power of application (*prayogabala*) for the arising of the mind.

In that regard, when a Bodhisattva relies upon the four conditions and the four causes, whether collectively or individually, if he relies upon both powers together—the internal power and the power of the cause—then [the mind arises].
In this way, that [mind] arises as firm, substantial, and immovable;
however, through the application of external forces and the force of [past] conditioning, that mind should be understood as having an unstable arising.
There are four causes for the turning back of a bodhisattva’s mind.
Which four?
He is not endowed with the spiritual lineage;
he is taken hold of by evil friends.
He possesses weak compassion toward sentient beings;
he is afraid of the long-lasting, diverse, intense, and uninterrupted sufferings of *saṃsāra*, and he becomes excessively terrified, alarmed, and falls into a state of dread.
These four causes for the turning back of the mind should be understood in detail as being the opposites of the four causes for the arising of the mind, as previously explained.
These two qualities of a bodhisattva who has firmly generated the initial thought of awakening are uncommon in the world and marvelous and extraordinary.
Which two?
He embraces all sentient beings as his own family.
Furthermore, he is not defiled by the fault of maintaining a household.
In this regard, the fault of maintaining a household consists of afflicted compliance and hostility resulting from the benefit or injury done to one's family.
And those two do not exist for the Bodhisattva.
These two noble intentions toward sentient beings proceed in a Bodhisattva who has firmly generated the first thought of enlightenment:
the intention for their welfare and the intention for their happiness.
In this context, the resolve for benefit (*hitādhyāśaya*) is the desire to cause [beings] to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states;
the resolve for happiness (*sukhādhyāśaya*) is the desire to provide those beings who are afflicted, unprotected, and without refuge with beneficial things that are free from defilement.
These two are the applications of a bodhisattva who has firmly generated the initial thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*).
There is the application of resolute intention (*adhyāśaya-prayoga*) and the application of practice (*pratipatti-prayoga*).
Among these, the application of resolute intention is the daily strengthening of that very same resolute intention for their welfare and happiness.

The application of practice is the daily application toward the ripening of the Buddha-qualities within oneself, and—relying precisely upon that application of resolute intention—the application toward bringing about welfare and happiness for sentient beings according to one's capacity and strength.
For a bodhisattva who has firmly generated the initial thought of awakening, there are these two great gateways for the influx of wholesome qualities:
the application for one's own benefit, which leads to the full realization of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and the application for the benefit of others, which leads to the liberation of all sentient beings from all suffering.

Just as there are two gateways for entry, so too are there two great accumulations of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) and two immeasurable aggregates of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharmaskandha*). [And so on.

These two are the preeminent acquisitions of wholesome qualities for a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (*prathamacittotpādika*), starting from that initial resolve (*prathamaṃ cittotpādam upādāya*), when compared with other acquisitions of wholesome qualities.
There is a distinction in the cause and a distinction in the fruit.
Indeed, this acquisition of virtue by a bodhisattva is the cause of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and that [enlightenment] is its fruit.
No other acquisition of virtue by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas is such, let alone that of other sentient beings.
Therefore, the acquisition of virtue by Bodhisattvas is superior to all other acquisitions of virtue, both in terms of its causal nature and its fruit.
There are these two benefits for the arising of the thought [of awakening] in a Bodhisattva who has firmly generated that initial thought:

from the very moment the thought arises, he becomes one worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*) for all sentient beings, one who is venerable, a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), and like a father to all creatures; and he effects the acquisition of merit that is indestructible.
In this regard, there is this merit that is invulnerable to harm,
endowed with which a bodhisattva is protected by a protection twice as great as that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

When this protection is constantly present, neither wild beasts, nor *yakṣas*, nor non-human beings, nor local spirits are able to cause any affliction, even when he is asleep, intoxicated, or heedless.
Furthermore, having undergone rebirth, this bodhisattva, by virtue of that accumulation of merit, becomes one who has little affliction and is naturally free from disease.
He is not touched by long-lasting or severe illness.

And when he exerts himself for the sake of sentient beings in deeds to be done for them—whether through body, speech, or in teaching the Dharma—his body does not become excessively exhausted, his mindfulness is not lost, and his mind is not impaired.

By their very nature, a bodhisattva established in the lineage (*gotrastha*) possesses mild corruption (*dausthulya*); however, once the thought of awakening has been generated, they possess an even greater degree of diminished corruption—namely, of both physical and mental corruption. Furthermore, even those mantra-words and vidyā-words that pacify the calamities, misfortunes, and portents of sentient beings—which fail to succeed when held by others—do become effective when held by them.

How much more so, then, those that have been accomplished? Furthermore, he is endowed with an excellence of patience and gentleness; he endures the injuries inflicted by others and does not inflict injury upon others.
Moreover, upon perceiving another being tormented by someone else, he is excessively pained;
his secondary afflictions—anger, envy, deceit, hypocrisy, and so forth—their force diminished, become weakened and only occasionally manifest, and they quickly vanish.

Furthermore, in whatever village or field he dwells, the evils of fear, terror, and famine, as well as calamities caused by non-human beings, do not arise if they have not yet arisen, and those that have already arisen are pacified.

Furthermore, if that bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening should at some time be reborn in the hells or in the states of woe, he is released from those hells much more quickly and to a greater degree; he experiences only very slight painful sensations and generates an even more intense sense of spiritual urgency toward those beings, for the sake of acquiring merit that is free from affliction and characterized by a mind of compassion.
A bodhisattva who has first generated the thought of awakening experiences many such benefits as these, arising from the acquisition of unassailable merit.
Thus ends the second chapter, "The Generation of the Thought," in the section on the Foundation within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 15) Chapter 1.3: On the Welfare of Oneself and Others.
What is the bodhisattva practice for those bodhisattvas who have thus generated the resolve?
In brief, the entirety of that in which bodhisattvas train, how they train, and what they train in—condensed into a single whole—is called the "bodhisattva conduct.
Furthermore, in what do bodhisattvas train?
They train in seven points.
What are the seven points?

They are: one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, the meaning of reality, spiritual power, the ripening of sentient beings, the ripening of one’s own buddha-qualities, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment as the seventh point.
Summary verse:
The welfare of oneself and others, the meaning of reality, power, the ripening of sentient beings and of one's own buddha-qualities, and seventhly, supreme enlightenment.
What is the welfare of oneself and others? In brief, the welfare of oneself and others should be understood as being of ten kinds:

that which is solitary, that which is connected with others, that which follows from benefit, that which follows from happiness, that which is comprised within the cause, that which is comprised within the fruit, that which pertains to this life, that which pertains to future lives, that which is ultimate, and that which is non-ultimate.

Among these, the solitary welfare of oneself and the welfare of others must be fully understood and abandoned by the bodhisattva, because they transcend the bodhisattva’s rule and are inconsistent with it.
And one should train in the supplementary [teachings].
In that regard, this is the purely selfish interest of a bodhisattva which must be fully understood and abandoned:
the pursuit and enjoyment of wealth by one who desires his own happiness.
Furthermore, for one who is stingy with the Dharma, it is the seeking and retaining of the teachings spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
For one desiring heaven, it is the undertaking and practice of ethical discipline, the arousal of vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom for the sake of heaven.
Or, for one who desires the fruits of worldly material gain, it is the worship of the shrines of the Tathāgata for the sake of worldly material gain.

Or, for one desiring gain, it is the proclamation of various false qualities for the sake of gain, as a cause for gain, as a means to produce gain, and for one's own benefit, in order to delude others.

Or, for one desiring to have service rendered to oneself, it is the gathering of a community through unrighteousness rather than through righteousness for the purpose of having service rendered to oneself.
Or, one causes sentient beings who are like slaves to others to be released from their state of slavery only so that they may become slaves to oneself.
Having liberated beings bound by fetters from those bonds, he himself binds them again for as long as it takes to accomplish his own purpose.
And he liberates from the fear of punishment and the like those beings who are terrified by the fear of punishment and the like from others, only so that he himself may seize that very fear.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva’s dwelling in happiness in the present life, when devoid of reflection on the welfare of beings, should be understood as a purely selfish aim.
Such categories as these are to be understood as the purely self-interested aims of a bodhisattva, which the bodhisattva, having fully understood them, must abandon.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva’s generosity, patience, and compassion—whether preceded by compassion, dedicated toward enlightenment, or aimed at [rebirth in] heaven—are to be understood as self-interest that is always connected with the welfare of others.
Excluding these aforementioned modes, all other forms of self-interest for bodhisattvas, being the opposite of these, are to be understood as entirely connected with the welfare of others.
In this regard, a bodhisattva, having fully understood it, must abandon this purely altruistic aim [of a bodhisattva]:

giving to one with perverted views or to one who holds a view of non-rebirth and sees no fruit; teaching the Dharma to others by one whose ethical discipline has lapsed and who lacks correct practice;
and for a bodhisattva skilled in turning back from meditative absorption, the application of the pure dharmas belonging to a lower level to one who has already transcended that lower level.
For instance, having dwelt in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), he emerges from that absorption and, having made a vow, is reborn wherever he desires within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Furthermore, for a Bodhisattva who has attained mastery, there is the performance of beneficial activity for various sentient beings through diverse emanations throughout the ten directions.

And for a Sage, a Tathāgata who has accomplished his own purpose, there is immeasurable beneficial activity toward immeasurable sentient beings by relying upon all the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma), such as the powers (bala) and the grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya).
That too should be understood as being solely for the sake of others.
In this regard, the former two kinds of exclusive benefit for others, as previously described, must be fully understood and abandoned by the bodhisattva;
however, he should train even more extensively in the other kind of exclusive benefit for others.
Setting aside these aforementioned modes and their opposites, all the altruistic aims of bodhisattvas are connected to their own self-interest;
in this regard, too, a bodhisattva must train.
What is the bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others that follows from welfare?
In brief, it should be understood as being of five aspects:
having the characteristic of being irreproachable, having the characteristic of being beneficial, pertaining to this life, pertaining to future lives, and pertaining to peace.
In that regard, whatever appropriation of the wholesome or accumulation of the wholesome a bodhisattva performs, whether small or great, for himself—

Or he causes another to do so; or, with respect to the accumulation of merit—whether small or great—he encourages, disciplines, settles, and establishes others in the gathering of wholesome qualities.
This should be understood as the faultless characteristic of a bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others, which is consequent upon welfare.

Whatever happiness a bodhisattva brings about— whether for himself or for others— that is free from affliction, whether it be the happiness of material requisites or the happiness of meditative absorption, this should be understood as the bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others characterized by assistance and associated with welfare.
There is a benefit for the bodhisattva’s own and others’ welfare that is beneficial in this life but not in the next.
It exists there but not here;
it exists both there and here;
it exists neither there nor here.
Furthermore, this fourfold benefit for oneself and others should be understood as corresponding respectively to the four ways of undertaking the Dharma (*dharmasamādāna*).
What are the four ways of undertaking the Dharma? There is a way of undertaking the Dharma that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future.
There is that which is suffering in the present but has a pleasant ripening in the future; there is that which is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant ripening in the future;
and there is that which is suffering in the present and has a painful ripening in the future.
The detailed analysis of these should be understood exactly as in the Sūtra.

In this regard, nirvāṇa, that which leads to the attainment of nirvāṇa, and the mundane and supramundane factors conducive to nirvāṇa— this, in brief, should be understood as the bodhisattva’s benefit-related, quiescent aim for self and others, which is preeminent and unsurpassed in all respects.
What is the bodhisattva’s pursuit of happiness for the benefit of self and others?
In brief, it should be understood as being comprised of five kinds of happiness.
In this regard, these are the five kinds of happiness:
There are five kinds of happiness: happiness as a cause, happiness as a feeling, happiness as an antidote to suffering, happiness from the cessation of feeling, and fifthly, invincible happiness.
Among these, the two factors belonging to the side of happiness are the faculty and the object.

Furthermore, whatever contact conducive to pleasant feeling arises with those as its cause, and whatever action has a desirable fruit—whether in this very life or in a future existence—all that, taken together and condensed into one, is called "happiness as a cause."
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.

With regard to the pacification of suffering, the experience that arises from these very three causes subsumed under causal happiness—which brings benefit to body and mind—is called "feeling-happiness.
Furthermore, in brief, it is of two kinds: with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
In that regard, that which is untainted (anāsrava) consists of the states of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The tainted (sāsrava), moreover, belongs to the three realms (traidhātuka), being associated with the desire, form, and formless realms.

Furthermore, all that which belongs to the three realms is, according to its application, sixfold through the division of the sense bases (āyatana): from that born of eye-contact up to that born of mind-contact.
Furthermore, that [feeling] is sixfold and twofold:
bodily and mental.
Among these, that associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness is bodily, while that associated with the mental consciousness is mental.

When various and manifold kinds of sufferings, such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, arise repeatedly, the cessation of those sufferings through their respective remedies—cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth—gives rise to a perception of pleasure in that very state of mere alleviation of suffering; this is called "pleasure as an antidote to suffering.
Furthermore, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāveditanirodhasamāpatti*) is called "the pleasure of the cutting off of feeling."
Furthermore, the happiness of being free from affliction should be understood, in brief, as having four aspects:
the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of tranquility, and the happiness of awakening.

For one who has gone forth from the home to the homeless life with perfect faith, it is called the "happiness of renunciation" because of liberation from the suffering of the various attachments of a householder.
Due to the seclusion resulting from the abandonment of sensual desires and evil, unwholesome states, the joy and bliss born of seclusion in the first *dhyāna* is called the "bliss of seclusion.
In the second and subsequent *dhyānas*, due to the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is called the "bliss of tranquility.

That bliss which arises from the absolute dissociation from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and from the realization of objects of knowledge as they truly are, is called the "bliss of awakening" (*saṃbodhi-sukha*).

In this regard, causal happiness is called "happiness" because it is a cause of happiness, but not by its own nature. Sensual happiness is happiness neither by way of being a cause nor by its own nature; rather, it is happiness merely through the subsiding of suffering, due to the removal of suffering. Counteractive happiness is neither by way of being a cause nor by its own nature; rather, it is happiness solely through the cessation of suffering, due to the alleviation of suffering.

The happiness of the severance of feeling is not [happiness] by way of being a cause, nor by its own nature, nor even from the removal of suffering; rather, whatever is felt, it is considered "suffering" in this context. It is called "happiness" because of the temporary subsiding of that ultimate suffering during one's dwelling. This final awakening-happiness, which is comprised within the happiness free from affliction, pertains to that very same ultimate [state] in the future as well.

There is happiness because of the ultimate subsiding of suffering, and because of the absolute cessation of the underlying corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the side of all afflictions that resides within the basis (*āśraya*) in this very life.

That which remains is the happiness free from affliction (*avyābādhya-sukha*); it should be understood as happiness free from affliction because it is conducive to that [ultimate state], belongs to its side, and brings it about.
In this regard, a bodhisattva should provide sentient beings only with that happiness which belongs to the side of benefit, and not that which belongs to the side of harm.

Furthermore, having thoroughly understood with correct wisdom that pleasure which belongs to the side of the unbeneficial as it truly is, one should dissuade sentient beings from it and strive, according to one's ability, to remove and take away that [pleasure].

Even that which is beneficial but accompanied by suffering should be provided by a bodhisattva—even at the cost of his own suffering and dejection—to sentient beings who do not desire it, by relying upon skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).

Furthermore, whatever may be harmful even when accompanied by happiness, that too must be removed and eliminated along with that happiness and mental ease for the sake of beings who desire pleasure, by relying on skillful means.
Why is that?
It is for their very happiness. (Dutt 19)
In the future, it should be understood as certain for sentient beings:
that which is the bringing about of benefit together with suffering, and the removal of harm together with happiness.
For this very reason, a bodhisattva who desires the welfare of sentient beings should be known as one who, in actual fact, also desires their happiness.
He who bestows benefit and bestows happiness should be known as such;
for indeed, benefit occupies the place of the cause and happiness occupies the place of the fruit.
Therefore, he should be understood as being truly accompanied by happiness toward sentient beings.

Whatever action follows from what is beneficial, and whatever action has a desirable fruit in both the present life and the future— being comprised of causal happiness, being an antidote to suffering, being the happiness of the cessation of feeling, and being the happiness free from affliction— a Bodhisattva should, with absolute certainty and without hesitation, bring all this about for the sake of sentient beings.
This [kind of giving] is indeed beneficial and blameless.

Regarding the feeling of pleasure comprised of the contact between the sense faculties and their objects—which constitutes causal happiness—the Bodhisattva should not provide that which leads to affliction, or that which is afflicted, blameworthy, unwholesome, or detrimental.

However, that which does not lead to affliction, or which is unafflicted, blameless, wholesome, and beneficial, the Bodhisattva should provide to sentient beings according to his ability and according to his strength.

Furthermore, one should act in exactly the same way oneself, train accordingly, and experience it for oneself; this should be understood as the bodhisattvas’ pursuit of their own and others' welfare, which follows from benefit and happiness.
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s pursuit of their own and others' welfare as comprised of cause and fruit?
In brief, it should be understood that there are three kinds of causes and likewise three kinds of fruits:
the ripening cause and the ripening fruit, the merit cause and the merit fruit, and the knowledge cause and the knowledge fruit.
What is ripening?
In brief, maturation (vipāka) is of eight kinds:
excellence of lifespan, excellence of complexion, excellence of lineage, excellence of sovereignty, authority in speech, great renown, human status, and eighthly, strength.
Longevity and long duration of life constitute the bodhisattva’s excellence of lifespan.
Beauty, loveliness, amiability, and excellence of complexion constitute the perfection of form. Rebirth in high families constitutes the perfection of lineage.
Great wealth, great influence, and a large retinue constitute the perfection of sovereignty.

Furthermore, he becomes trustworthy and reliable to sentient beings regarding whatever legal disputes arise; he is authoritative and worthy of being followed because he is free from deceit and fraud, such as cheating with scales or false measures of cotton.
He does not misappropriate deposited wealth and is non-deceptive.
On that account, his words are accepted by sentient beings.
This is called having speech that is worthy of being accepted.

Great fame and renown become celebrated for him in the world, namely with respect to his heroism, or vigor, or fortitude, or discernment, or skill, or good character, or his preeminent and superior proficiency in various fields of arts and crafts.
On that account, one becomes heavy [with dignity], worthy of being honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the great body of people;
this is called "greatness" (*maheśākhyatā*).
It is the state of being a man, endowed with the male faculty, and the condition of being human.
Having little affliction, being of a healthy constitution, and having great energy constitute the natural perfection of strength.
What is the ripening cause? Non-violence toward sentient beings and the intention of non-violence toward them are the causes for the perfection of longevity.
Giving light and pure clothing is the cause for the perfection of complexion.
Humility toward sentient beings is the cause for the perfection of virtue;
giving to those in need and to those lacking necessities is the cause for the perfection of sovereignty;
and the practice of truthful speech, free from slander, harshness, and frivolous chatter, is the cause for having one's words accepted with authority.
For one who possesses the aspiration to establish various virtues within oneself in the future, worship of the Three Jewels and worship of the guru is the cause for attaining great authority;
as is delight in the human state and aversion toward the female state,
due to perceiving the defects therein.
And the bringing about of human status for others occurs through two causes:

by means of dissuading women who are attached to their female state from that female state; and by means of liberating, in accordance with the Dharma, those men who have been seized and brought to the point of the destruction of their male organ. This is the cause of human status.

Performing service for sentient beings with the body, acting as their helper in whatever tasks arise according to one's power and strength, and providing— righteously and without violence— food, refreshments, gruel, drinks, aphrodisiacs, and stimulating foods and beverages to sentient beings, is the cause for the attainment of physical strength.
Thus, this eightfold cause should be understood as the cause for this eightfold ripening (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, this cause is nourished in brief by three reasons for the production of a ripening that is complete, nourished, and sublime.
What are these three reasons?
Purity of mind, purity of application, and purity of field.

Among these, purity of mind consists of: the pure intention resulting from the dedication of those roots of virtue toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment; the intense intention resulting from practicing with a profound, thick, and sublime clarity of faith; and the joy arising from seeing one's fellow practitioners of the Dharma.
And that which is the frequent application of sustained thought and investigation, day by day and moment by moment, in accordance with that very Dharma—
this is called purification of mind. In this regard, it is the long-term cultivation, the uninterrupted practice, and the skillful practice, even when others have not yet completed it.

Praising [others] for the sake of inducing them to undertake wholesome deeds, or again, praising them for the sake of encouraging those who have already undertaken them, as well as establishing and settling them in that very root of virtue—
this is called purity of application (*prayoga-śuddhi*).
In brief, the purification of the field should be understood as resulting from the correct accomplishment of the application and the establishment of that very correct application in its fruit.
In this regard, what is the fruit of maturation?

A Bodhisattva endowed with a full lifespan applies himself to the side of virtue for a long time and accumulates a vast store of roots of virtue, undertaking both his own welfare and the welfare of others.
This is the fruit of the perfection of lifespan:
a bodhisattva endowed with excellence of complexion becomes dear to the great body of people;
and because he is dear, he becomes worthy of being approached.

And because of that pleasing appearance and because he approaches them face-to-face, the great mass of people considers his words worthy of being heard and acted upon. This is to be understood as the fruit of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of physical form (*varṇasaṃpad*).
A Bodhisattva endowed with noble birth is esteemed by the great mass of people, and is both honored and praised.

Because he is esteemed, honored, and praised, whatever matter he encourages sentient beings toward, they—overwhelmed by his splendor—swiftly undertake it; they do not dispute it, nor do they act contrary to it.
This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s excellence of lineage.
A bodhisattva endowed with sovereign power gathers and matures sentient beings through generosity;
this should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s attainment of sovereign power.
A bodhisattva whose speech is authoritative gathers and matures sentient beings through pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency between words and deeds.
This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s authoritative speech:
a bodhisattva of great renown becomes a benefactor by acting as an assistant to sentient beings in their various tasks and duties.
Because of this benefit, sentient beings—whose minds are bound to him—obey his instructions very quickly, out of respect and gratitude, with honor and earnestness.
This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s great majesty (*maheśākhyatā*):

being a human being, the bodhisattva is endowed with the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) and becomes a vessel for all virtues, all resolute undertakings, and all investigations into the objects of knowledge. He is also confident and possesses unobstructed movement regarding approaching, conversing, dwelling together, sharing enjoyments, and staying in private with all sentient beings at all times. This is the fruit of the bodhisattva’s manhood (*puruṣatva*).
It should be understood that a bodhisattva endowed with power is untiring in the application of acquiring wholesome qualities and in the application of benefiting sentient beings;
he is one who has initiated vigor, possesses firm vigor, and is swift in the superknowledges.
This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of power.

Thus, this constitutes the eightfold fruit of the eightfold maturation of bodhisattvas, which is conducive and favorable for the benefit of sentient beings and for the arousal of the qualities of a Buddha.
Indeed, when a bodhisattva is established in this fruit of maturation, he himself becomes capable and competent to accomplish various and abundant aims for sentient beings.
Furthermore, those disciples of his become subject to his direction so that they may be acted upon according to his will—that is, with respect to the accomplishment of their own welfare.
For if this bodhisattva were himself competent, yet his disciples were not subject to his direction, [he would not be able to fulfill his purpose].
In this way, his performance of the welfare of others would not be abundant or skillful, such that he would be unable to accomplish the welfare of others.

Furthermore, if this bodhisattva himself were incapable and lacking in power, while those to be trained were capable of undertaking the accomplishment of their own welfare, even so the bodhisattva’s performance of the welfare of others would not be abundant or skillful, such that he would be unable to accomplish the welfare of others.

Therefore, when both are present and both perfections are attained, a bodhisattva’s performance of the welfare of sentient beings becomes abundant and skillful, by which he is able to accomplish the aims of others.
Being such as this, the bodhisattva quickly brings his own buddha-qualities to maturity and matures sentient beings in the three vehicles;
and he himself awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And he liberates those beings who are fully ripened.
Thus, by this method, because the eightfold fruit of maturation for Bodhisattvas conduces to the welfare and happiness of sentient beings,
that saṃsāra which is barren and purposeless for all other beings becomes for them both fruitful and of great significance.
In that regard, what is merit?
What is knowledge? Merit, in brief, is said to consist of three perfections.
The perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of patience [belong to the side of merit].
Furthermore, knowledge is one perfection, namely the perfection of wisdom.
The perfection of vigor and the perfection of meditative concentration should be understood as belonging to both the side of merit and the side of knowledge.
That vigor by relying upon which one gives gifts, undertakes or guards moral discipline, and cultivates the immeasurables such as loving-kindness—
this kind of vigor belongs to the side of merit. Furthermore,
that vigor by relying upon which one applies oneself to wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and [attains] skill in the aggregates...

Or he practices skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*), skill in the sense-bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*), skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*), and skill in what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
He contemplates suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path.

He discerns and examines, according to reality, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, blameworthy and blameless phenomena, inferior and superior phenomena, and phenomena that are black, white, or a mixture of both, all arisen through dependent origination.
This is called the energy belonging to the side of knowledge (*jñānapakṣya-vīrya*).
That meditation which, having relied upon it, one gives gifts, undertakes or guards moral discipline, and cultivates the immeasurables such as loving-kindness—
this kind of meditation belongs to the side of merit (*puṇyapakṣya-dhyāna*).

Furthermore, relying upon meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one applies oneself to the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; or, as previously described, one applies oneself to skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*). All of this should be stated in the same manner as was said regarding vigor (*vīrya*).
This is called the meditative absorption belonging to the side of knowledge (*jñāna-pakṣya-dhyāna*).
And this merit and knowledge, in brief, are of six kinds.
However, this should be understood as immeasurable according to each individual subdivision.
What is the cause of merit and knowledge?
In brief, three causes of merit and knowledge should be understood.
The desire for the acquisition, maintenance, and accumulation of merit and knowledge consists of favorable and non-disruptive conditions, as well as prior practice of merit and knowledge.
Among these, "non-disruptive conditions" refers to the non-occurrence and absence of erroneous conditions,
and the occurrence and presence of non-erroneous conditions.

In this regard, that which arises through association with a bad friend (*pāpamitra*), such as a distorted teaching of merit and knowledge, or through distorted mental attention (*manaskāra*), or through grasping things erroneously—
this is called the presence of distorted conditions. By contrast, the presence of non-distorted conditions in the white category (*śuklapakṣa*) should be understood as the opposite of this.
Furthermore, those obstacles to the attainment, maintenance, and increase of merit and wisdom,
as well as their avoidance and non-arising, are called the "non-deficient condition" for a bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom.
It should be understood that if there is a deficiency in even one of these three causes, neither merit nor wisdom will arise.
What is the fruit of merit and knowledge?
Relying upon merit, a bodhisattva wanders through cyclic existence unhurt and is not excessively oppressed by sufferings;
and he is able to perform the welfare and assistance of sentient beings according to his wish.

Relying upon knowledge, a bodhisattva correctly undertakes the accumulation of merit and not falsely, through the performance of various and immeasurable skillful means, until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus, this fruit of merit and knowledge should be understood briefly as being fourfold according to its application;
however, it is immeasurable due to the distinctions among its various types.

In this regard, whatever is maturation (*vipāka*), whatever is the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), and whatever is the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*)—all of this is based upon merit (*puṇya*) and originates from merit.

Furthermore, merit is based upon knowledge (*jñāna*) and originates from knowledge. Therefore, both of these are primary for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*). Merit is primary, while knowledge is unsurpassed. If either of these two—merit or knowledge—is lacking, this bodhisattva would not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Thus, this should be understood as the bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others, comprised of cause and fruit.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others pertaining to the present life? What is that pertaining to future lives?
The acquisition of enjoyments through human effort consisting of appropriate crafts and occupations,
as well as the moderate enjoyment of those very enjoyments once acquired,
[arise] from previous karma whose ripening has matured and yielded its desired fruit.
It is the enjoyment of the fruit in the present life;

and for a bodhisattva skilled in the withdrawal from meditative absorption, the reliance upon absorption in this very life for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life, and not for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others;

and that nirvana in the present life belonging to one who has become a Tathāgata; and those conditioned phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, which bring about the attainment of nirvana in the present life.
This is called the bodhisattva’s own benefit pertaining to the present life.
Just as it is for the bodhisattva, so too should the benefit of others be understood:
namely, those sentient beings who have been disciplined by the bodhisattva.
In this regard, it is the cultivation of causes— both in the present life and in future lives—

accompanied by suffering and accompanied by mental distress, through repeated careful deliberation, for the sake of attaining the perfection of enjoyments in the future within the desire realm, the perfection of the personal basis in the future, and rebirth in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) or the formless realms (*ārūpya*) in the future.

This should be understood as the bodhisattva’s welfare for future lives alone; whereas that which pertains to the present life consists of the cultivation of causes for the perfection of enjoyments and the physical body, accompanied by both pleasure and mental joy,
as well as the meditative attainments of the form and formless realms that do not lead to decline.
The welfare of oneself and others pertaining to the present life and the future life is to be understood.
What is the ultimate welfare of oneself and others?
And what is the non-ultimate?

In the desire realm, the perfection of enjoyments and the physical body, together with their causes and fruits, as well as the mundane purity of ordinary beings, together with its causes and fruits, constitute the non-ultimate benefit for oneself and others.
The absolute abandonment of all afflictions, the noble eightfold path, and whatever mundane wholesome dharmas have been attained by relying upon it—
this is called the ultimate benefit for oneself and others.
In this regard, the state of being ultimate and the state of being non-ultimate should be understood through three causes:
by way of intrinsic nature, by way of retrogression, and by way of the exhaustion of the enjoyment of the fruit.
Among these, nirvāṇa is ultimate by way of its intrinsic nature.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are indeed non-ultimate.

The Noble Eightfold Path is ultimate because it is not subject to decline and because its enjoyment of the fruit is inexhaustible. Other wholesome, contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are non-ultimate, due to their susceptibility to decline and the exhaustion of the enjoyment of their fruits.

Thus, this tenfold benefit for oneself and others of the bodhisattvas has been presented both concisely and in detail; therein bodhisattvas should train according to their capacity and according to their strength. There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
In the past and in the future as well, those who have trained or will train in the benefit for oneself and others—all of them do so within this very same tenfold benefit for oneself and others.
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
The third chapter, on the Benefit of Oneself and Others, in the section on Yoga within the Foundation of the Bodhisattva-bhūmi, is completed.
(Dutt 25) Chapter 1.4: The Chapter on the Meaning of Reality.
What is the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*)?
In brief, it is twofold:

the suchness (*bhūtatā*) of phenomena with respect to their mode of being as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), and the totality (*sarvatā*) of phenomena with respect to their extent of being (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
Thus, the reality of all phenomena—both their suchness and their totality—should be understood as the complete meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).
Furthermore, that meaning of reality is fourfold according to its different aspects:

that which is established by worldly consensus, that which is established by reasoning, that which is the domain of the knowledge purified of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and that which is the domain of the knowledge purified of the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

In this regard, for all worldly people, there is a uniformity of perception with respect to a given object through a cognition that has entered into conventional agreement, worldly convention, familiarity, and tradition—such as, for example, regarding earth: "This is indeed earth, not fire.
Just as it is with earth, so it is with fire, water, air, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and food.

Regarding drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments and their accessories, household utensils and furnishings, perfumes, garlands, and ointments, dancing, singing, and instrumental music, lighting, the attendance of women and men, and fields, shops, houses, and property—concerning pleasure and pain, one thinks: "This is suffering, not pleasure;
this is pleasure, not suffering."

In brief, that object which is the domain of certain conviction— such as "this is this," "this is not that," or "this is thus and not otherwise"— which is established by the conceptual constructions of all worldly people through conventionally transmitted designations, and which is grasped without having been reflected upon, weighed, or examined; this is called the reality established by worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhatattva*).
What is the reality established through reasoning?

It is that which is [known] by the wise who are learned in the meaning of reason, the discerning, the logicians (*tārkika*), and the investigators (*mīmāṃsaka*)— those who abide on the level encompassed by reasoning, possessing their own intuitive wisdom, belonging to the stage of ordinary persons, and following the practice of investigation based on direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture.

That which is established and settled by means of the reasoning that proves through logical proof— that object of knowledge which is the domain of well-known and well-ascertained cognition based upon valid means of knowledge—
is called reality established by reasoning.
What is the reality that is the domain of the knowledge purified of the obscuration of afflictions?

It is the objective domain of the uncontaminated knowledge of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the mundane knowledge that brings about the uncontaminated and the mundane knowledge obtained subsequent to the uncontaminated;
this is called the reality that is the domain of the knowledge purified of the obscuration of afflictions.
By means of that object of focus, knowledge is purified from the obscuration of afflictions,
and it abides in a state of non-obscuration for the future.
Therefore, reality is said to be the domain of the knowledge that purifies the obscuration of afflictions.
Furthermore, what is that reality?
It is the four noble truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
As one investigates and realizes these four noble truths, and once they have been realized, that knowledge arises.
