Furthermore, this realization of the truths for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas arises through the practice of seeing the non-existence of a person (pudgala) apart from the aggregates, by means of a wisdom associated with the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena produced through dependent origination; for they perceive only the aggregates and do not perceive a self as a distinct entity other than the aggregates.
What is reality as the objective domain of the knowledge that purifies the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocaratattva*)?
The obstruction of knowledge regarding the knowable is called "obscuration.

That objective domain and range of knowledge which is liberated from that cognitive obscuration should be understood as reality as the objective domain of the knowledge that purifies the cognitive obscuration.

What, then, is that? It is [the knowledge] belonging to Bodhisattvas and the Blessed Buddhas, which— having entered for the sake of penetrating the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and having become thoroughly purified—
concerns the ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena, and is equal to the object of non-conceptual knowledge regarding the intrinsic nature of designations and verbal expressions.

That which is the objective domain of gnosis is that supreme, unsurpassed suchness, which has reached the limit of the knowable; from it all correct investigations of phenomena turn back and do not proceed further.
Furthermore, that characteristic of reality should be understood as being manifested by non-duality from the perspective of its formal establishment.
Duality is said to be existence and non-existence. Therein, existence is that which is established as having the nature of conceptual designation,
and it is likewise long-standingly adhered to by the world.
It is the root of all the conceptual proliferations of the world,
such as "form," or "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness";
or "the eye," or "the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
Whether as "earth," or "water," or "fire," or "air";
or as "form," or "sound," or "odor," or "taste," or "the tangible";
or as "wholesome," or "unwholesome," or "indeterminate."
Whether it be arising, or passing away, or dependently originated;
whether it be the past, or the future, or the present;
or whether it be conditioned, or unconditioned.
This world and the other world;
both the sun and the moon;
and whatever has been seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought after, or even mentally pondered and reflected upon.
Or even as far as "nirvāṇa"—
this kind of intrinsic nature of phenomena, established through conventional discourse, is called the "existence" of the world.

In this context, "non-existence" refers to the fact that for the conceptual designation "this is form," and so on, up to the conceptual designation "this is nirvana," there is a lack of a real entity (*nirvastukatā*) and a lack of a sign (*nirnimittatā*). It is the total and complete non-existence and non-presence of the basis for conceptual designation,
depending upon which the conceptual designation proceeds.
This is called non-existence (*abhāva*).

Furthermore, that reality which is comprised of the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), being free from both the aforementioned existence and this non-existence—that is, free from both existence and non-existence—is non-dual (*advaya*).
That which is non-dual is the Middle Way, devoid of the two extremes.
It is called "unsurpassed.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the perfectly pure gnosis of the Blessed Buddhas resides in that reality;
whereas, on the other hand, the gnosis of the Bodhisattvas therein should be understood as being characterized by the path of training.
And that wisdom is the great means for a bodhisattva to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For what reason?

Because by means of that conviction in emptiness, while engaging in various births and wandering through cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) among sentient beings for the sake of ripening the qualities of a Buddha, the bodhisattva [perceives] that very cyclic existence...
He understands it as it truly is;
yet, he does not cause his mind to become weary of that cyclic existence through aspects such as its impermanence.
For if he did not understand cyclic existence as it truly is, he would be unable to maintain equanimity toward the mind regarding all afflictions, such as attachment, aversion, and delusion.

If he were to wander in *saṃsāra* with a defiled mind without practicing equanimity, then wandering with a defiled mind, he would neither bring the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) to maturity nor would he mature sentient beings.

Furthermore, if he were to cause his mind to feel revulsion toward *saṃsāra* through aspects such as impermanence and so forth, then the bodhisattva would very quickly enter final nirvāṇa (*parinirvāyāt*).
And by entering final nirvāṇa very quickly, the bodhisattva would likewise fail to mature either the Buddha-qualities or sentient beings.
How much less, then, will he fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
By means of that very same conviction in emptiness, the bodhisattva who applies himself does not fear nirvāṇa, nor does he long for nirvāṇa.
If that bodhisattva were to fear nirvāṇa, his equipment for nirvāṇa would not be fulfilled in the future, just as it is.

Furthermore, because his mind is terrified of it, he does not perceive the benefits of nirvāṇa; being devoid of the clarity and resolve that comes from seeing its virtues, such is the case for the bodhisattva.

If, however, that bodhisattva were to dwell frequently in the longing for nirvāṇa, he would quickly pass into final nirvāṇa. By passing into final nirvāṇa too quickly, he would neither ripen the qualities of a Buddha nor ripen sentient beings.
In this regard, there is the wandering in saṃsāra of one whose mind is afflicted due to not understanding saṃsāra as it truly is;
there is the premature cessation of one whose mind is weary of saṃsāra;
and there is the non-completion of the requisites for that [cessation] by one whose mind is terrified of nirvāṇa.
The rapid parinirvāṇa of one who dwells frequently in the longing for nirvāṇa should be understood as an improper method for a bodhisattva regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
whereas the wandering in saṃsāra by one who understands saṃsāra as it truly is and whose mind is undefiled is the proper method.
That which is the non-hasty attainment of nirvāṇa by one whose mind is not distressed by cyclic existence through its aspects such as impermanence;

that which is the fulfillment of the equipment for it by one whose mind is not terrified of nirvāṇa; and that which is the non-hasty attainment of nirvāṇa by one who perceives the qualities and benefits in nirvāṇa but has not reached an excessive longing for it—this is the great skillful means of a bodhisattva for the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And this very means is based upon that resolute conviction in supreme emptiness.
Therefore, that cultivation of resolute conviction in supreme emptiness is called the great means of the bodhisattva’s path of training for the sake of attaining the knowledge of a Tathāgata.
Indeed, by means of that knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena which has deeply penetrated far, that bodhisattva [realizes] the ineffable intrinsic nature.
Having known all phenomena as they truly are, he does not conceptualize anything at all; he perceives nothing other than the mere thing, which is mere suchness (*tathatā*).
Yet, it does not occur to him that "this is the mere thing" or "this is mere suchness. Rather, that bodhisattva courses in the ultimate object (*artha*).
Practicing in the ultimate sense, he perceives with wisdom all phenomena as being exactly equal to that suchness (*tathatā*) as they truly are.
Being one who sees equally and possesses an even mind in all things, he attains supreme equanimity.
Relying upon this, the bodhisattva, while applying himself to skill in all branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), does not turn back despite all exhaustion or the onset of any suffering.
Swiftly, with an untiring body and an untiring mind, he brings that skill to completion;
he attains the empowerment of great strength of mindfulness,
yet he does not become arrogant because of that skill.
He does not practice the "teacher's fist" with others;
his mind is unshrinking in all skills;
and he is energetic, with an unhindered course.

The practice of firm armor is such that, the more he encounters specific sufferings while wandering in saṃsāra, the more his enthusiasm for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment increases. The more he attains specific distinctions in physical stature, the more he becomes free from pride toward sentient beings. The more he attains specific distinctions in knowledge, the more he increasingly avoids censuring others, engaging in disputes, idle chatter, and the primary and secondary afflictions.
Having fully understood his conduct that has strayed from the proper way, he maintains equanimity toward it;
as he increases in virtues, he becomes one who conceals his goodness.
He does not seek to be known by others, nor does he seek gain or honor.
These and many other such benefits accrue to a bodhisattva who relies upon that knowledge—benefits that belong to the wings of enlightenment and are conducive to awakening.

Therefore, all those who have attained awakening, those who will attain it, and those who are attaining it now, do so by relying on this very knowledge, and not on any other, whether inferior or superior.

Thus, having ascended to the method of the non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*), the bodhisattva, possessing such great benefits, becomes one who has correctly practiced for the sake of maturing the Buddha-qualities within himself and for the sake of maturing the qualities of the three vehicles in others.
Furthermore, he becomes one who has correctly practiced in this way.
He becomes free from craving for enjoyments and for his own person;
and training in that state of freedom from craving, he does so for the sake of sentient beings alone, in order to relinquish enjoyments and his own person for the benefit of sentient beings.
Furthermore, he is restrained and well-restrained.

He trains in restraint of body, speech, and mind for the sake of a natural distaste for evil and a natural state of being auspicious and virtuous. He becomes patient toward all forms of injury and offensive conduct from others;
he trains in patience for the sake of mildness in anger and for the sake of not harming others.

He applies himself to all fields of knowledge and becomes skilled in them for the sake of eliminating the doubts of sentient beings, for the purpose of providing them with assistance, and for his own acquisition of the causes of omniscience.
His mind is inwardly established and well-composed;

he trains for the stability of the mind, for the purification of the four divine abodes, for sporting with the five supernormal powers, for the performance of the welfare of sentient beings, and for the dispelling of the weariness born from application to all forms of skillfulness.
And he becomes discerning, knowing the supreme reality;
he trains for the sake of knowing the supreme reality and for his own final nirvana in the future within the Mahāyāna.
Indeed, that bodhisattva, thus correctly applied, attends to virtuous beings with offerings, gains, and honor;
he attends to faulty beings with a supreme mind of compassion and a mind of pity,
and exerts himself to the best of his ability and strength for the sake of their abandoning faults.
He remains present toward harmful beings with a mind of loving-kindness;
and according to his ability and according to his strength, being free from deceit and free from guile, he provides them with benefit and happiness.

For the sake of abandoning the state of enmity arising from the fault of his own intention and application toward those harmful beings, he remains present toward beneficial beings with gratitude and with a return of assistance equal to or greater than what was received.
He fulfills his righteous aspirations according to his ability and according to his strength.
Even when he lacks the power, being requested, he demonstrates respect and exertion toward those various tasks and duties; he does not reject them once and for all.
"How can this person be persuaded that 'I am incapable, not that I am unwilling to act'?"—

this kind of correct application should be understood as belonging to a bodhisattva who has ascended to the method free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and relies upon the knowledge of supreme reality (*paramatattvajñāna*).
(Dutt 30)
In this regard, by what reasoning is the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpyasvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena to be understood?

This designation of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaprajñapti*) of phenomena—namely, "form," or "feeling," and so forth as before, up to finally "nirvāṇa"—should be known as mere designation (*prajñaptimātra*).
It is neither an intrinsic nature, nor is it something other than that [designation], nor is it a domain of speech; rather, it is beyond the scope of speech.
This being so, the intrinsic nature of phenomena does not exist in the manner that it is expressed;
yet, on the other hand, it is not the case that it does not exist at all.
Furthermore, while it does not exist in that way, it is not entirely non-existent in every respect.
How does it exist?
It exists as being free from the conceptual grasping that superimposes what is non-existent, and free from the conceptual grasping that denies what is real.
Furthermore, that ultimate intrinsic nature of all phenomena should be understood as the objective domain of non-conceptual gnosis alone.
If, moreover, those phenomena or that object were of the same nature as the verbal expression that operates upon them,
then there would be many various intrinsic natures for a single phenomenon or a single object.
For what reason?
For indeed, with respect to a single dharma and a single entity, many various designations and conventional expressions are made by means of numerous verbal expressions;
yet no fixed rule is observed among these many various designative statements such that identity,
consistingness, or intrinsic nature would belong to that dharma or that entity through one particular designative statement alone, and not through the other remaining designative statements.

Therefore, by means of all conceptual designations— whether complete or incomplete— there is no identity, no being composed of that, and no intrinsic nature of those [designations] in all phenomena and all entities. Furthermore, if phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) were to have the nature of conceptual designation as previously described,
then in that case, first there would be the entity and subsequently the metaphorical application of the conceptual designation according to one's preference.

Prior to the conventional application of the designation, when the conventional application of the designation has not yet been made, that phenomenon and its objective basis would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
If they were devoid of intrinsic nature, a designation lacking an objective basis would be untenable.
Furthermore, if the conventional application of the designation did not exist, it would be untenable for the phenomenon or the objective basis to have the designation as its intrinsic nature.
If, moreover, that dharma and that thing were of such a nature even prior to the application of conventional designation— that is, before the application of conventional designation had been made—

then, in that case, the cognition of "form" would arise with respect to the dharma designated as "form" and the thing designated as "form," even without that application of the conventional designation "form.
Yet, it does not so arise.
Therefore, by this reason and through this logic, the ineffable intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) should be understood.
Just as it is with form (*rūpa*), so too should feeling (*vedanā*) and the other phenomena as previously described be understood, up to and including the limit of *nirvāṇa*.
These two should be known as having strayed from this Dharma and Vinaya.

On the one hand, there is one who adheres through false superimposition to the intrinsic nature and specific characteristic of phenomena such as form— the entities such as form— which consist of the nature of conceptual-linguistic designation (*prajñaptivāda*). On the other hand, there is also one who, by denying that entity which is ultimately real because it is ineffable in its essence— namely, that which is the basis for the signs of conceptual-linguistic designation and the support for the signs of conceptual-linguistic designation— destroys it by asserting that "it does not exist at all in any way whatsoever."

First, those faults regarding the superimposition of what is non-existent have already been examined, laid bare, clarified, and revealed. It should be understood that by these faults, one becomes ruined and estranged from this Dharma and Vinaya through the superimposition of what is non-existent upon entities such as form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, it should be understood how a total nihilist (*sarvavaināśika*), who denies even the mere entity (*vastumātra*) within phenomena such as form, is likewise ruined.

It follows from this Dharma and Vinaya that I shall explain as follows: for one who denies the mere substance of phenomena such as form and so forth, neither reality nor designation is possible; both of these are untenable.
For example, it is only when the aggregates such as form exist that the designation "person" (pudgala) is tenable.
It is not [possible] when [the bases] do not exist;
for there can be no designation of a person (*pudgala*) that is devoid of a real entity (*nirvastuka*).
This being so, it is only when there is the mere entity of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) that the conventional designation and metaphorical usage of phenomena such as form are tenable.

It does not exist when there is no basis; for there can be no metaphorical application of a designation without a real entity. In that case, since the entity for the designation does not exist, the designation itself, being without a foundation, does not exist either.

Therefore, there are some who, having heard certain sutras associated with the Mahāyāna— sutras that are difficult to understand, profound, associated with emptiness, and expressed with an underlying intention (abhiprāya)—

fail to comprehend the meaning of what was spoken as it truly is; instead, they conceptualize it improperly and, by means of mere reasoning applied incorrectly, come to hold such views and speak as follows:
"All this is merely a designation, and this is the reality;
he who sees thus sees correctly.
Because for them there is no mere thing (*vastumātra*) that serves as the basis for designation, that very designation does not exist at all in any way whatsoever.
How much less, then, could mere designation be the reality?
Thus, by this line of reasoning, they have negated both reality and designation.
And because of this negation of both designation and reality, one should be known as a preeminent nihilist.
Being thus one who has lost [the path], he becomes one who is not to be spoken with and one who is not to be lived with by wise fellow-practitioners;
he ruins himself and brings ruin also to the world that follows his view.
And it was with reference to this that the Blessed One said: "It is better for some person here to have a view of a self than for some person to have a wrongly grasped emptiness. For what reason?
A being who holds a view of a self might merely be deluded regarding the object of knowledge, but he would not deny all objects of knowledge.
On that account, one would not be reborn in the states of woe;
nor would one deceive or mislead another who seeks the Dharma and seeks liberation from suffering,
but rather one would establish them in the Dharma and in truth.
Furthermore, one should not be lax regarding the precepts of training;
nor, by means of a wrongly grasped emptiness, should one become deluded regarding the object of knowledge,
or even deny all that is to be known.
On that account, one is reborn in the miserable states;
one may bring ruin to another who is righteous and seeks liberation from suffering;
and one becomes lax regarding the precepts of training.
One who denies such a reality as this has fallen away from this Dharma and Vinaya.
But how is emptiness wrongly grasped?
It is when any ascetic or brahmin does not accept that by which something is empty.
He does not even accept that which is empty;
this is called emptiness wrongly grasped in such a manner. For what reason?
For emptiness is logical because that by which something is empty does not exist,
and because that which is empty does exist.
However, if everything were non-existent, where, what, and by what would there be emptiness?
Nor is it logical for that very thing to be empty of itself;
therefore, emptiness is thus wrongly grasped.
But how, then, is emptiness rightly grasped?
And because one correctly perceives that whatever is not present in a certain place is empty of that,
and further, that whatever remains there truly exists as a reality,
this is called the entry into emptiness— being according to reality and non-erroneous.
For example, in a thing designated as "form" and so forth, as previously described, there exists no dharma whose essence consists of the conventional designation "form" and so on.
Therefore, that thing designated as "form" and so forth is empty of that essence consisting of the conventional designation "form" and so on.
What, then, remains there in that thing designated as "form" and so forth?
That is to say, it is the basis for designations such as "this is that very form" and so forth.
He understands both of these as they truly are: namely, the mere entity (*vastumātra*) which exists, and the mere designation (*prajñaptimātra*) upon that mere entity, which does not exist.
He does not superimpose what is non-existent; he does not deny what is existent; he does not add anything extra, nor does he diminish anything; he does not elevate, nor does he reject.
And one understands suchness as it truly is—the ineffable intrinsic nature—as it truly is.
This is called "emptiness well-grasped," which has been thoroughly penetrated by right wisdom.
This, first of all, is the conformable reasoning that establishes proof, by means of which the ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena is to be understood.
From authoritative scripture as well, it should be understood that all phenomena have an ineffable intrinsic nature;
as was stated by the Blessed One in the *Bhavasaṃkrānti-sūtra*, elucidating this very meaning through the singing of verses: (As quoted from Dutt, p. 33)
"For by whatever name each phenomenon is expressed, that [phenomenon] does not exist therein; for such is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena.
How, then, does this verse illuminate this very meaning?
The name of a phenomenon designated as "form" and so forth is such as "form" and so on.

By means of that name, "form" and so forth, those phenomena designated as "form" and so forth are expressed and conventionally designated—whether as "form," or "feeling," and so on in detail, up to "nirvāṇa.
In this regard, the phenomena designated as "form" and so forth do not themselves consist of the nature of form and so forth.
And among those [dharmas], no other dharma consisting of form and so forth exists.

Furthermore, that which is the existence of those dharmas designated as "form" and so forth by way of an ineffable object—this should be understood as their ultimate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-dharmatā*).
And it was said by the Blessed One in the *Arthavargīya*:
Whatever conventions there may be in the world, the Sage does not approach any of them;
for he does not resort to them, so by what means would he take them up? Not forming an attachment to what is seen or heard—how does this verse illuminate this very meaning?
The designations such as "form" and so forth, which apply to an entity designated as "form" and so on, are called conventionalities (*saṃvṛti*).
One does not approach those conventionalities by thinking that the entity has identity (*tādātmya*) with those designations.
For what reason?
Because he has no view characterized by superimposition or denial;
therefore, due to the absence of that view which manifests as perversion, he is called "one who does not adhere."
Being thus free from attachment, by what means would he grasp anything?

Without that view, and neither through superimposition nor through denial regarding that object, not grasping at it, he becomes one who possesses right vision; that which is seen by him is the "seen" (dṛṣṭa) with respect to the object of knowledge (jñeya).
That which is the oral tradition concerning the verbal expression of that very same object of knowledge is his "heard" (śruta).
Regarding that which has been seen or heard, he does not produce craving nor cause it to increase;
rather, by means of that very object, he abandons it and dwells in equanimity. In this way, he practices cultivation.
Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One concerning Saṃtha Kātyāyana: "In this case, Saṃtha, a bhikṣu does not meditate depending on earth; nor on water; nor on fire."
Nor wind;

nor the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, or neither-perception-nor-non-perception; nor this world, nor the other world, nor both the sun and the moon; nor what is seen, heard, thought, or cognized; nor what is attained, sought after, or mentally deliberated upon and reflected over.
He meditates without relying on any of that.
How does he meditate?
He meditates without relying on earth, and so on in detail until: he meditates without relying on anything at all.

In this case, friend, whatever perception of earth there is for a monk regarding the earth has been eliminated; likewise, the perception of water regarding water—and so on in detail until—whatever perception there is regarding everything has been eliminated.
A monk who meditates in this way does not meditate depending upon the earth, and so on in detail until he does not meditate depending upon "everything is everything."
The gods, together with Indra, Īśāna, and Prajāpati, pay homage from afar to a monk who meditates in this way:
"Homage to you, O noble among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
We do not understand what it is upon which you rely as you meditate. Thus they say.

Furthermore, how does this scriptural passage illuminate this very meaning? Regarding an entity designated as "earth" and so forth, the designation of a name and convention such as "earth" is called a "perception" (*saṃjñā*) of earth and so forth.
Moreover, that perception is both superimposing and negating with respect to the entity designated as "earth" and so forth.
It is superimposing insofar as it grasps the entity as having a nature consisting of that [designation].
The notion that grasps at the destruction of the ultimate reality of mere phenomena is called a nihilistic notion (*apavādikā saṃjñā*).
And that notion becomes eliminated for him;
"elimination" (*vibhava*) is said to mean abandonment (*prahāṇa*) or relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Therefore, even from scripture—that is, from the Tathāgata, the supreme authoritative source—it should be understood that all phenomena have an ineffable intrinsic nature.

If all phenomena thus possess an ineffable intrinsic nature, for what reason is verbal expression employed? For without verbal expression, that ineffable true nature of phenomena could not be communicated to others, nor could it be heard.
If there were neither speech nor hearing, that ineffable intrinsic nature could not even be known.
Therefore, speech is employed for the sake of hearing and knowing it.
Because immature beings do not fully understand that very suchness in this way, an eightfold conceptualization arises from that cause, which generates the three types of entities.
It is that which brings about the production of all sentient beings and the receptacle world.

Namely: the conceptualization of intrinsic nature, the conceptualization of specific qualities, the conceptualization of grasping at a composite whole, the conceptualization of "I," the conceptualization of "mine," the conceptualization of the pleasant, the conceptualization of the unpleasant, and the conceptualization that is the opposite of both.
Furthermore, of which three things does this eightfold conceptualization become the generator?

Namely, the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), the conceptualization of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*), and the conceptualization of grasping at a whole (*piṇḍagrāha-vikalpa*). These three conceptualizations generate the entity known as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, which serves as the basis for the proliferation of conceptualization (*vikalpa-prapañca-adhiṣṭhāna*) and the objective support for the proliferation of conceptualization (*vikalpa-prapañca-ālambana*).

Based upon a certain object, that conceptualization— which is grasped by names, notions, and expressions, and permeated by names, notions, and expressions— proliferating, ranges over that very same object in many ways and in numerous diverse forms.

Among these, the conceptualization of "I" and the conceptualization of "mine"— these two conceptualizations produce the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is the root of all other views, and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), which is the root of all other conceits.

In that regard, the conceptualization of the pleasant, the conceptualization of the unpleasant, and the conceptualization that is the opposite of both, give rise respectively to attachment, aversion, and delusion.

Thus, these eight kinds of conceptualization lead to the manifestation of this threefold entity: namely, the entity of proliferation which is the basis of conceptualization, and the view of a self-identity and the conceit "I am.
Among these, based upon the entity of proliferation and conceptualization, there arises the view of a self-identity and the conceit "I am."
Attachment, aversion, and delusion are based upon the view of a self-identity and the conceit "I am.
By means of these three factors, the entire side of worldly involvement for all people is explained without exception.
In that regard, what is the conceptualization of intrinsic nature?

The conceptualization regarding an object designated as "form" and so forth, such as "this is form," is called the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavikalpa*). What is the conceptualization of specific qualities (*viśeṣavikalpa*)?

Regarding that very object designated as "form" and so forth, there is the conceptualization based on its intrinsic nature through an immeasurable method of differentiation, such as: "this is material," "this is immaterial," "this is visible," "this is invisible," likewise "with resistance," "without resistance," "with outflows," "without outflows," "conditioned," "unconditioned," "wholesome," "unwholesome," "determinate," "indeterminate," "past," "future," or "present."

The conceptualization of an object as qualified by that [attribute] is called the conceptualization of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*). What is the conceptualization of grasping a whole (*piṇḍagrāha-vikalpa*)?

That which, with respect to that very entity designated as "form" and so forth, proceeds accompanied by the designations and conventions of "self," "sentient being," "living soul," and "creature"— arising from the cause of grasping at a composite in many aggregated phenomena— and which, with respect to houses, armies, forests, and so forth, as well as food, drink, vehicles, clothing, and so forth,
proceeds accompanied by those respective designations and conventions; [this is called the conventional designation].
This is called the conceptualization of grasping at a whole.
What is the conceptualization of "I" and "mine"?
It is that object which is with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and subject to grasping (*sopādānīya*), which has for a long time been familiarized and adhered to as a self or as belonging to a self.
Therefore, based on that familiarity with the lack of grasping and attachment, a false conceptualization arises in dependence upon an object that serves as the basis for one's own views;
this is called the conceptualization of "I" and "mine."
What is the conceptualization of the pleasant? It is the conceptualization that has as its object a beautiful and agreeable thing. What is the conceptualization of the unpleasant?

What is the conceptualization that has as its object things that are impure and unpleasant? It is the conceptualization that is the opposite of both the pleasant and the unpleasant. What is the conceptualization that is the opposite of both the pleasant and the unpleasant?
It is the conceptualization that has as its object things devoid of both the pure and the impure, and the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Briefly stated, these two are conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the entity that is both the basis and the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpādhiṣṭhāna-vikalpālambana-vastu*).
Both of these should be understood as being beginningless and mutually causal:
prior conceptual construction leads to the manifestation of the present entity that is the object of conceptual construction, and the present [entity]...
Furthermore, an object that has appeared as the focal point of conceptualization is the cause for the arising of a present conceptualization that takes it as its object;
therein lies the lack of full comprehension of conceptualization at present, which leads to the future arising of an object that serves as its focal point.
Furthermore, due to the occurrence of that [object], there necessarily arises the manifestation of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which has that as its basis and depends upon it.
And how, moreover, does the thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) of this conceptual construction come about?
It occurs through the four investigations and the fourfold thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).
What are the four investigations? They are the investigation of names, the investigation of things, [the investigation of intrinsic nature, and the investigation of specific characteristics].
And the investigation into the designation of intrinsic nature,
and the investigation into the designation of specific qualities.
Among these, the investigation into names is when a bodhisattva perceives within a name that it is merely a name.

Thus, seeing only the thing-in-itself within a thing is the investigation of the thing; seeing only the designation of intrinsic nature within the designation of intrinsic nature is the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature;
and seeing only the designation of specific difference within the designation of specific difference is the investigation of the designation of specific difference.
He perceives both the distinct and the conjoined characteristics of the name and the object;
he penetrates the designation of intrinsic nature and the designation of specific qualities which are based upon the conjunction of the name and the object.
What are the four thorough cognitions of reality as it is?

There is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) regarding the search for names, and the thorough knowledge of reality as it is regarding the search for things (*vastu*), the search for the designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti*), and the search for the designation of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-prajñapti*). What is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is regarding the search for names?

It is when that bodhisattva, having searched for the state of being merely a name within a name, thoroughly knows that very name as it truly is: "This name is established upon a thing solely for the purpose of a sign (*saṃjñā*)."
It is for the purpose of vision and for the purpose of conventional designation (*upacāra*).
If the name "form" were not established for the entity designated as "form" and so forth, no one would perceive that entity as "form.
Not perceiving it thus, one would not adhere to it through superimposition (*samāropa*).
One should not speak of non-attachment.
When one understands this thus according to reality,
this is called the thorough knowledge of reality resulting from the search for names.
What is the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, which arises from the search for things?

It is when a bodhisattva, having searched for the mere-thingness within a thing, perceives that thing—designated by such names as "form" and so forth—as being disconnected from all verbal expression and as ineffable.
This is the second thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, which arises from the search for things.

What is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is regarding the search for the designation of intrinsic nature? It is that by which a bodhisattva, having investigated the mere-ness of designation within the designation of intrinsic nature regarding an entity designated as "form" and so forth, penetrates and understands according to reality how that entity— which lacks that intrinsic nature— appears as having that intrinsic nature through such a designation of intrinsic nature.

For one who perceives its intrinsic nature as being like a magical creation, a reflection, an echo, an optical illusion, the moon in water, a dream, or a phantom— appearing yet not consisting of that [appearance]— this is the third thorough knowledge of reality as it is,
which has the extremely profound meaning as its domain.
What is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is that pertains to the investigation of specific designations?

And because the bodhisattva, having investigated the mere-ness of designation within the specific designation, perceives that specific designation in the entity designated as "form" and so forth by way of non-duality;
that entity is neither an existent nor a non-existent.
It is not an existent because it is not established by way of an expressible nature.
Furthermore, it is not non-existent, because it is established by way of an ineffable nature.
Thus, it is not material from the perspective of ultimate truth,
nor is it immaterial from the perspective of conventional truth, because there is a metaphorical designation of "form" therein.
Just as existence and non-existence, and the material and the immaterial,

so too all the various designations of specific conceptual constructs— such as the visible and the invisible— are to be understood in this very same manner. Thus, when one understands these specific conceptual constructs as they truly are through the sense of non-duality, [one realizes suchness].
This is called the thorough knowledge of reality as it is, which results from the investigation into the designation of specific distinctions.

In this regard, that eightfold false conceptualization of the foolish—which generates the three bases and brings about the world—proceeds due to the deficiency and non-occurrence of these four kinds of thorough knowledge of reality as it is; and from that false conceptualization, again, arises affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
From affliction comes the wandering in *saṃsāra*; from the wandering in *saṃsāra*, there proceeds the suffering associated with *saṃsāra*, such as birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.

And when a bodhisattva, relying upon the fourfold thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, has thoroughly understood those eight kinds of conceptual construction, then through that correct thorough knowledge in the present life, the basis for them and their objective support [are eliminated] in the future.
For one who has fallen into conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),

the manifestation of an entity does not occur. Because that [entity] does not arise and does not manifest, the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) which takes it as its object also does not manifest in the future.
Thus, the cessation of that conceptualization which possesses a basis should be understood as the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
And in this way, the cessation of conceptual proliferation should be understood as the Mahāyāna parinirvāṇa of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, in this very life, because his knowledge of the sphere of the supreme reality-meaning is purified, that bodhisattva attains mastery in all respects.
That is to say: in the manifestation of various emanations through the power of emanation; in the transformation of various things through the power of transformation;
and in the knowledge of all that is knowable, as well as in remaining for as long as intended.
And by virtue of his mastery over death, he passes away without external intervention. Having thus attained such sovereignty, he becomes the unsurpassed best among all sentient beings.
Furthermore, for that Bodhisattva who is thus masterful in all respects, five supreme benefits are to be understood.
He attains supreme tranquility of mind through the serenity of his dwelling, not through the subsiding of the afflictions;
and his knowledge and vision proceed unimpeded, pure, and purified regarding all fields of learning;
and he is untiring in wandering through cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings.
He penetrates all the intentional teachings (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) of the Tathāgatas,
and he cannot be turned back from his faith in the Mahāyāna because he does not rely on others.
Indeed, for these five kinds of benefits, one should understand that there are exactly five corresponding types of activity.

The supreme dwelling in happiness in the present life should be understood as the activity that brings about the benefit of mental tranquility for a bodhisattva who has dedicated himself to the practice for awakening, in order to eliminate physical and mental exhaustion from exertion.
The maturation of all the qualities of a buddha should be understood as the activity that brings about the benefit of unimpeded knowledge regarding all fields of learning.
The maturation of sentient beings should be understood as the activity resulting from the benefit of a bodhisattva’s lack of weariness with *saṃsāra*.

It consists in the dispelling of the doubts that arise one after another among those to be trained, the long-term drawing forth and preservation of the guide of the Dharma, and the thorough understanding, revelation, and removal of those counterfeits of the true Dharma that cause the teaching to disappear.
This should be understood as the function of the benefit of entering into all intentional speech (*sandhāyabhāṣita*).

Furthermore, this should be understood as the function of the benefit of being unsubduable and not depending on others: namely, the subduing of all adversaries, firmness of vigor, non-retrogression from one's vow, and being unsubduable due to not relying on others.
For in this way, whatever is to be done by a bodhisattva, it is all encompassed by these five functions of benefit.
Furthermore, what is that which is to be done?

It is unafflicted personal happiness, the maturation of the Buddha-qualities, the maturation of sentient beings, the upholding of the true Dharma, and the refutation of the arguments of opponents through unwavering resolve and ardent vigor.
In that regard, among the four meanings of reality, the first two should be known as inferior,
the third as middling,
and the fourth as supreme.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Foundation (*ādhāra-yogasthāna*), this is the fourth chapter: "The Meaning of Reality" (*tattvārtha-paṭala*).
(Dutt 40) Chapter 1.5: On Power.
In this regard, what is the power of the bodhisattvas?

In brief, for one who has attained mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the fulfillment of all aims through mere aspiration by relying on that mastery of concentration— belonging to one whose mind is pliant and well-cultivated— is called "noble power" (*ārya-prabhāva*). Furthermore, the great fruitfulness and great benefit of phenomena is called their "power" (*prabhāva*).
Due to the prior accumulation of a great mass of merit, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess an innate, marvelous, and wonderful nature.
This should be understood as another innate power of theirs.
Indeed, according to its various classifications, this power of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is fivefold.

The power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-prabhāva*), the power of the Dharma (*dharma-prabhāva*), innate power (*sahaja-prabhāva*), and common power shared with *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, as well as power not shared with them. Among these, the six supernormal knowledges— the domain of miraculous powers (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), knowledge of the minds of others (*cetaḥ-paryāya*), recollection of former abodes (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti*), vision of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapāda-darśana*), and the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*)— are called the power of supernormal knowledge.
In this context, the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom—are called "dharmas.
The power inherent in those dharmas is called the "majesty of the dharma" (*dharmaprabhāva*).
Among these, what is supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)?
In brief, it is of two kinds:
transformative (*pāriṇāmikī*) and emanated (*nairmāṇikī*).
Furthermore, each of these two is of many kinds according to the distinction of their types.
In that regard, what is the classification of the types of transformative supernatural power (*pāriṇāmikī ṛddhi*)?

It is as follows: shaking, blazing, pervading, manifesting, effecting transformation, going and coming, contracting, expanding, entering all forms and bodies, approaching those of one's own kind, appearing, and disappearing.

The exercise of mastery, the surpassing of the supernatural powers of others, the granting of eloquence, the granting of mindfulness, the granting of happiness, and the emission of rays— such categories as these are called transformative supernatural power (*pāriṇāmikī ṛddhi*).
Among these, there is "shaking."
In this case, a Tathāgata who has attained mastery over meditative concentration, or a Bodhisattva whose mind is pliant, causes even a monastery to tremble;

he causes even a house, a village, a city, a field, the realm of hell-beings, the realm of animals, the realm of hungry ghosts, the realm of humans, and the realm of gods to tremble; he causes even a world-system of four continents, a thousandfold world-system, a second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system, and even a third-order great thousandfold world-system to tremble.
He causes even a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand world-systems to tremble, up to immeasurable and incalculable trichiliocosm-megachiliocosm world-systems;
therein he produces blazing fire.
From the upper part of his body he blazes forth;
from the lower part of his body cool streams of water flow.
From the lower part of his body he blazes forth.
From the upper part of his body, streams of cool water flow forth;
he also enters the fire element and blazes forth with his entire body.

As his entire body blazes forth, various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, madder-colored, and crystal-colored—issue from his body. Therein lies the pervasion: just as that house is pervaded by this radiance, so too is the monastery, and as before, up to immeasurable and incalculable world-systems being pervaded by this radiance, just as described previously regarding the shaking.
In that regard, "clear vision" (vidarśana) is as follows:

when an assembly of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas has gathered while seated comfortably, the Tathāgata or a bodhisattva clearly reveals even the lower realms below.
He manifests gods and humans above;
he also manifests other buddha-fields,
and within them, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas— even beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
He reveals that buddha-field by whatever name it is designated, and he reveals the Tathāgata who resides in that buddha-field and bears whatever name he has;
he designates both that name of the buddha-field and that of the Tathāgata.
He demonstrates and explains what lies even closer than that, and what lies further beyond that, as much as he desires and for as long as he wishes;
therein lies the act of causing transformation.
If he resolves that earth be water, it becomes exactly so and not otherwise;
if he resolves that fire or wind [be something else], that too becomes exactly so and not otherwise. If he resolves that water be earth...
If he resolves that fire is earth,
or resolves that water is wind;
or if he resolves that wind is earth.
Water is resolved upon as fire;
all that becomes exactly so and not otherwise.

Just as there is no action of transformation into something else in the mutual transformation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), so it should be understood regarding visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
If he resolves that substances such as grass, leaves, cow dung, and clay are food, drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments, vessels, utensils, perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
or that stones, pebbles, potsherds, and the like are jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, and coral;
or, beginning with Himavat, the king of mountains, that all mountains are gold.
All that likewise becomes exactly so and not otherwise;
in the same way, he resolves that beings who are beautiful become ugly,
and those who are ugly become beautiful.
For those who are devoid of both, whether it be beauty, ugliness, or both;

just as with beauty and ugliness, so too with being maimed or unmaimed, being thin or fat, and so forth— whatever else exists that is different from its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) yet capable of being perceived, if one resolves upon it otherwise,
all that becomes exactly as one resolves.
Therein, as for coming and going:

he passes through walls, through mountains, and through ramparts with an unimpeded body; in detail, he approaches the Brahma-world and returns from it, and even upwards to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, or again horizontally as far as immeasurable and incalculable trichiliocosms.
He goes to and comes from world-systems either with his coarse body composed of the four great elements,
or he goes and comes with a speed like that of the mind, having resolved upon the distant as being near;
therein lies the contraction and expansion [of the body].
He condenses even Himavat, the king of mountains, into the size of a single atom;
he expands even a single atom into Himavat, the king of mountains.
Therein, regarding the entry of all forms and bodies:
in the presence of a vast and diverse assembly, he causes the physical form of villages, towns, grasslands, forests, lands, and mountains to enter his own body;
and that entire assembly perceives itself as having entered into that very body.
In that regard, there is the approach to a similar assembly:
he approaches an assembly of kṣatriyas;
having approached, his excellence of complexion becomes just like theirs.
Whatever their height and girth may be, such is his;
whatever their protection of the voice may be, such is his;
and whatever purpose they deliberate upon, that same purpose he deliberates upon.
Whatever matter they do not discuss with him, he likewise does not discuss that matter with them;
and having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse consistent with the Dharma, he vanishes.
Once he has vanished, they do not recognize him, wondering, "Who was this who vanished? Was it a god or a human?"

Just as with the assembly of kṣatriyas, so too [he approaches] the assemblies of brahmins, householders, and ascetics; the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trayastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin gods; and likewise the gods of Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, and Apramāṇaśubha.
[He goes] to the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Anabhrakas, the Puṇyaprasavas, the Bṛhatphalas, the Asaṃjñisattvas, the Abṛhas, the Atapas, the Sudṛśas, the Sudarśanas, and the Akaniṣṭhas;
therein he manifests and disappears.
In the presence of a great assembly, he makes himself invisible a hundred times, a thousand times, or even more than that;
and then, in that very same way, he displays and manifests his physical form once again.
This is the exercise of mastery therein.
Whatever the extent of the realm of sentient beings, he directs them all toward activities such as going, coming, and staying;
and if it occurs to him, "Let him go," then he goes; "Let him stay," then he stays.
When one says "come," it comes;
when one says "speak," it speaks.
In that regard, there is the overcoming of another's supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
The Tathāgata, having surpassed the exercise of supernatural power (*ṛddhy-abhisaṃskāra*) of all others possessing such powers, accomplishes everything according to his wish.

With the exception of a Tathāgata and a Bodhisattva of equal status who is bound to only one more birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*) or in his final existence (*carama-bhavika*), a Bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate goal surpasses the exercise of supernatural power of all others.

Setting aside other bodhisattvas who have entered superior stages and those of equal class, all other bodhisattvas surpass the miraculous power (*ṛddhi-abhisaṃskāra*) of all other possessors of supernatural powers;
therein lies the gift of eloquence (*pratibhāna-dāna*). When the [other's] eloquence is exhausted, he bestows eloquence upon them.
In that regard, the gift of mindfulness is to provide mindfulness when mindfulness regarding phenomena has been lost.
In that regard, the gift of happiness is as follows:

To those who hear the Dharma as he speaks, he provides such physical and mental assistance and the bliss of tranquility that they listen to the Dharma free from hindrances. This occurs through temporary application and not permanently; it pacifies imbalances of the elements, as well as afflictions caused by external attacks or unleashed by non-human beings.

In that regard, the emission of rays refers to a bodhisattva or a Tathāgata who, through supernatural power, emits from his body such rays as some of which, having gone to immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions, alleviate the hellish sufferings of beings in the hells.

To some, he goes to the noble beings dwelling in the celestial realms—the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas residing in their own abodes—and exhorts them to come here.
Likewise, he exhorts the bodhisattvas residing in other world-systems throughout the ten directions, in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems, to come here.
In brief, the Tathāgata, by means of immeasurable, incalculable, and diverse kinds of light rays, accomplishes manifold, immeasurable, and incalculable benefit for infinite sentient beings.
Furthermore, all these varieties of transformative supernatural power (*pāriṇāmikī ṛddhi*) should be understood as being individually immeasurable and incalculable when analyzed in detail.
The transformation (*pariṇāma*) of an existing entity that exists by its own nature into a different state is called "transformation.
Therefore, this is called transformative supernatural power.
In that regard, what is emanated supernatural power (*nairmāṇikī ṛddhi*)?
Briefly stated, it is an emanation that lacks a real basis.
That which is produced at will by the mind of emanation and succeeds is called emanated supernatural power.
And that [emanation] is of many kinds:
emanation of the body, emanation of speech, and emanation of objects.
Furthermore, that emanation of the body creates either a form similar to or dissimilar from oneself, or a form similar to or dissimilar from another.
Furthermore, that emanation of the body is similar or dissimilar to oneself and to others;
it creates the basis of the sense faculties (*indriyādhiṣṭhāna*) as being of the same class as the sense faculties (*indriyasabhāga*), but not the sense faculties themselves.
It also creates an emanation that resembles the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*).

For example, he creates at will everything similar to or distinct from external requisites— such as food, drink, and so forth, as well as jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, and so forth— which are comprised of form, odor, taste, and tangible objects. Furthermore, he creates many various kinds of forms resembling himself, in numerous diverse ways, having the appearance of gods, nāgas, [yakṣas], asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

The form of a human, the form of an animal, a hungry ghost, or a hell-being; the form of a śrāvaka, the form of a pratyekabuddha, the form of a bodhisattva, or the form of a tathāgata—if that bodhisattva is of such a nature, he creates an emanation of exactly that kind.
That emanation of his becomes identical to himself.
Otherwise, however, the transformation is dissimilar to oneself.
If one creates another who has become a deity by way of similarity, that transformation of his is similar to another;
if he creates by way of dissimilarity, it becomes dissimilar to another.
Just as it is with the state of a deity, so it should be understood up to the state of a Tathāgata.
In that regard, what is the emanation of many bodies?

Here, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva simultaneously benefits immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems throughout the ten directions by means of those emanations of various forms and colors.
Some emanations are sustained such that they continue even after the Bodhisattva or Tathāgata has passed away;
some emanations of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas exist merely for the purpose of manifesting to sentient beings and are like an illusion;
yet others are actual emanations of food, drink, vehicles, clothing, and so forth, as well as jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, and the like.
It is exactly thus and not otherwise;
by means of which wealth and requisites the function of wealth and requisites is performed.
This, first of all, is the emanation of the body and the emanation of objects.
Furthermore, the transformation of speech is endowed with a melodious quality;

it is possessed of a clear tone, and it may be connected to oneself, connected to others, or unconnected. It is comprised of the teaching of the Dharma and is comprised of the exhortation of those who are heedless. Among these, "melodious quality" is as follows:

The vocal utterance emanated by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is profound; it has the resonance of thunderclouds, resembles the pleasing voice of the kalaviṅka bird, and is heart-stirring, delightful, and captivating.
That emanated speech is urbane—beautiful, distinct, intelligible, worth hearing, not disagreeable, independent, and limitless.
In this regard, it possesses clarity of tone.

If a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva so desires, they can, with a perfectly full voice, make themselves understood by an assembly of various gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas— seated and gathered together— extending as far as the limit of a circle of assemblies reaching a hundred yojanas, whether they are seated far away or nearby; and if they so desire, they can make themselves heard by their voice throughout a thousandfold world-system of the Cūḍika type.
Whether it be a dvisāhasra or a trisāhasra world system, he makes himself known by his voice throughout immeasurable and incalculable world systems in the ten directions;
and from that sound, there issues forth the teaching of the Dharma in many varieties for the benefit of sentient beings.
In that regard, speech-emanation connected with oneself is that which one teaches the Dharma or exhorts the heedless by means of speech that one has emanated oneself.

Speech-emanation connected with another, however, is that which one teaches the Dharma or exhorts the heedless by means of speech emanated by another. Therein, speech-emanation unconnected [to a person] is that which issues forth as speech from space or from an emanation, rather than from a sentient being's mental continuum.
In that regard, the emanation of the teaching of the Dharma is that which serves to demonstrate logical reasoning for those who are deluded here and there.

The emanation of exhortation is that which, for those who are not deluded and have attained serene faith, generates a sense of shame regarding negligence when they are negligent, and inspires them toward non-negligence.
Such is this manifold kind of emanation.
In brief, it should be understood that there is the emanation of body, the emanation of speech, and the emanation of objects;
this is the supernatural power of emanation (*nairmāṇikī ṛddhi*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that even this is immeasurable and incalculable when distinguished by its various individual types.
Furthermore, these two kinds of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, in brief, accomplish two tasks:

either, having attracted sentient beings through the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), they cause them to enter the teaching of the Buddha; or, they provide manifold assistance to suffering sentient beings in many various ways.
In this regard, what is the knowledge of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
In this regard, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva first recollects his own former births by himself:

"Those beings were named such-and-such where I was born with such-and-such a name," and so forth; as described in detail in the sūtras, he recollects everything, including the bodies of sentient beings and other such details.
Just as he recollects them for himself, he likewise causes others to recollect them.
And he himself recollects others;

he himself recollects those bodies of beings who were his dwellings in the past, and he causes others to recollect them as well, in detail: "Those beings named so-and-so, where I myself was, having such-and-such a name," and so forth.
He likewise recollects all the former births of those beings exactly as he does his own in the present life.
He recollects even the subtlest thing— whatever was previously performed, whether little or much, having been intended beforehand and not forgotten—
and he recollects them even in their uninterrupted succession.

He recollects even that which was done in succession, uninterrupted by means of continuous moments, in whatever order it occurred; he recollects even that which is immeasurable and incalculable, for which a calculation could be made by means of counting eons, as well as that for which a calculation cannot be made by means of counting eons. In brief, his knowledge of former abodes proceeds unhindered wherever he desires, in whatever manner he desires, and for as long as he desires.
Such is the power of a Bodhisattva and a Tathāgata, comprised of their recollection of former abodes.

By means of that knowledge of recollecting former abodes, he reveals various and manifold Jātaka tales of his previous lives and his conduct as a Bodhisattva, for the purpose of generating faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One, and for the purpose of inspiring reverence in sentient beings.
And [he teaches] narratives connected with past lives (*pūrvayoga*), beginning with the ripening of the results of the karma of sentient beings;

he destroys the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) in those sentient beings who hold such a view—for example, among those who speculate about the past (*pūrvāntakalpaka*), those who advocate eternalism (*śāśvatavādin*), or those who maintain partial eternalism (*ekatya-śāśvatika*).
What is the divine ear-knowledge (*divya-śrotra-jñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?

In this regard, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva, with the divine ear, hears divine and human sounds— whether noble or ignoble, loud or faint, distinct or indistinct, created or uncreated— whether situated far or near. Among these, "divine sounds" refers to those of beings born as high as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
If he does not direct his attention beyond that, then even further beyond, he hears sounds in other world-systems above;
therein he hears human sounds,
as well as the sounds of beings born among animals throughout all four continents.
In that regard, noble sounds are those of the Buddhas,
the disciples of the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the Pratyekabuddhas;
or those heard from them as they proclaim [the Dharma] to other sentient beings.
That is to say, it consists of those who demonstrate, encourage, inspire, and gladden others with respect to the undertaking of wholesome qualities and the abandonment of unwholesome ones;

likewise, it includes the recitation, study, and definitive determination of the teachings by those with undefiled minds, as well as correct admonition, reminding, instruction, and exhortation— whatever else may be well-spoken, well-uttered, and endowed with meaningful purpose.

These are called noble sounds. Among them, the ignoble sounds are those of sentient beings consisting of false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter— whether belonging to those reborn below in the miserable states, or reborn above among the gods, or reborn horizontally among humans.
In that regard,

sounds are those such as the sounds of great assemblies of beings, or the sounds of those being tormented by various causes, crying out in distress, wailing, or shouting; or the sounds of thundering clouds, or the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and tabors.
Subtle sounds,
even down to the sounds of whispering into the ear;
and distinct sounds.
Those whose meaning is understood are indistinct sounds;
those whose meaning is not understood [are likewise].
For example, there are the mantras of the Drāmiḍas, and the sounds of wind, trees, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, jīvaṃjīvaka birds, and so forth; as well as the sounds produced by emanations,
which are fashioned through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) by those who have attained mastery over the mind.
Distant sounds:

excluding those sounds that issue forth in whatever village, field, or monastery the Tathāgata or a bodhisattva dwells, [he hears] all others, even those as far as immeasurable and incalculable world-systems.
What is the knowledge of death and rebirth belonging to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?

Here, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva, with the divine eye—purified and surpassing that of humans—beholds sentient beings at the time of death, as they are dying, in their beautiful or ugly forms, and whether low or exalted; he also beholds them born in the future limit.

Through the increase and subsequent maturation of the sense faculties, as they engage in various bodily movements—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—he sees and knows them even as they appear; he sees even the subtle. He sees whatever form is manifested, and whatever divine, translucent form there is, from the Avīci hell below up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven above.

If he applies his attention to seeing forms below or above, or in other world-systems, he sees all that belongs to the realm of form as far as immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the transverse directions;
finally, he sees those various Tathāgatas in their respective Buddha-fields, seated within diverse and vast circles of assemblies, teaching the Dharma.

In that regard, with the divine eye, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva, having seen the bodily conduct—whether auspicious or inauspicious—of beings in the ten directions, acts toward those beings as is appropriate and as is fitting; and with the divine ear, having heard their verbal conduct—whether auspicious or inauspicious—he acts toward those beings as is appropriate and as is fitting.
In this way, by means of the divine eye and the divine ear, a Bodhisattva or a Tathāgata performs his activity in brief.
In that regard, what is the knowledge of the mental dispositions (*cetaḥparyāya-jñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?

Here, a Bodhisattva or a Tathāgata knows the minds of sentient beings in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems throughout the ten directions—even a mind that is obsessed by afflictions (*kleśa-paryavasthita*), as well as one that is free from obsession by afflictions; they know a mind that is accompanied by the persistence of afflictions (*sānubandha*) and possessed of latent tendencies (*sānuśaya*), as well as one that is without the persistence of afflictions and without latent tendencies; and they know even a mind that is wrongly directed (*mithyā-praṇihita*).
For example, he knows the mind of a non-Buddhist, as well as a defiled mind characterized by worldly motives and even a mind that is correctly resolved.
By the opposite of these, he also knows an inferior mind—
such as that of all beings born in the desire realm, down to the beasts and birds.

He knows the middling mind, such as that of all beings born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu); he also knows the sublime mind, such as that of all beings born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). He knows the mind associated with pleasure, the mind associated with suffering, and the mind associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

By means of a single knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), one simultaneously knows, as it truly is, the mind that has arisen in a single sentient being—whatever it is, however it is, of whatever kind, and to whatever extent. By means of that very same single knowledge of others' minds, one also simultaneously knows, as it truly is, the minds that have arisen in many sentient beings—whatever they are, however they are, of whatever kind, and to whatever extent. Furthermore, this supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) serves for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to know the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings and to know their various inclinations (*nānādhimukti*).

It should be understood that its function is to bring about the correct application of various paths leading toward the city of Nirvana, according to what is appropriate, for the sake of knowing the diverse elements and temperaments [of beings]. In that regard, what is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
In this regard, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, the attainment of the destruction of the afflictions;
he knows whether the destruction of the outflows has been attained by himself or by others,
and he also understands, as it truly is, the means for attaining the destruction of the outflows for both himself and others.
Just as he understands skillful means as they truly are, so too he understands what is not a skillful means as it truly is.
He understands, as it truly is, the overestimation of others regarding the attainment of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*),
and he also understands the absence of such overestimation as it truly is.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva understands all of this, yet he does not personally realize the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Therefore, he does not personally realize that which is associated with outflows;
for this reason, the bodhisattva does not abandon contaminated things even at the cost of his life.
And therein he investigates impure objects without becoming defiled; this should be understood as his greatest among all powers.
Indeed, by that knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves are not defiled.
They point this out to others and destroy their conceit;
this is to be understood as his activity.
In that regard, what is the power of the Dharma?
The power of generosity, as well as the powers of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
this power of the dharmas such as generosity and the rest, in brief, should be understood through four aspects:
by the abandonment of opposing factors, by the ripening of the accumulations, by the benefiting of oneself and others, and by the yielding of fruit in the future.
While giving a gift, the bodhisattva abandons stinginess, which is the opposite of generosity;
that gift of his becomes a provision for his own enlightenment,
and through the means of attraction that is generosity, he brings sentient beings to maturity.
Before giving, one is well-disposed; while giving, one clarifies the mind;
and having given, one is free from regret.
By means of a joyful mind throughout these three times, one benefits oneself.
Furthermore, by removing the suffering of others—namely hunger, thirst, cold, heat, disease, the frustration of desires, fear, and pain—he provides supreme assistance.

Moreover, wherever he is reborn in the future, he becomes wealthy, possessing great enjoyments, a great faction, and a large retinue. This is the fourfold power of giving; there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
By undertaking the ethical discipline of restraint in body and speech, the bodhisattva abandons immorality, which is the opposite of ethical discipline.
This undertaking of ethical discipline becomes for him a provision for enlightenment;
and through the means of attraction consisting of consistency in purpose, he brings sentient beings to maturity.
Abandoning fear, transgression, and enmity caused by immorality, he benefits himself, sleeping in peace and waking in peace.
Likewise, for one who possesses ethical discipline, there arises freedom from remorse, joy, and so on, up to mental concentration;
in this way, he benefits himself.
Furthermore, by not harming sentient beings in any manner whatsoever, he bestows fearlessness upon them.
In this way, one also benefits others;
and on that account, after the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world among the gods.
Thus is the fourfold power of ethical discipline.
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this:
the patient bodhisattva abandons impatience, which is the opposite of patience;
and that patience of his becomes a provision for enlightenment.
And it is precisely through this common purpose that he brings sentient beings to maturity.
By protecting both himself and others from great fear through that patience, he benefits both himself and others.
On account of this, in the future, the bodhisattva will have little enmity, little dissension, and little suffering and mental distress.
In this very life, one dies without regret;
and with the breakup of the body, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods.
Thus, this is the fourfold power of patience; there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
A bodhisattva dwelling with initiated vigor abandons laziness, which is the opposite of vigor.
That vigor becomes the equipment for awakening and serves as its foundation;
furthermore, it brings sentient beings to maturity through the very quality of having a common purpose.

Having initiated vigor, dwelling in comfort and unmixed with evil, unwholesome states, and perceiving successive attainments of distinction from before to after, he sustains himself with joy and gladness;
being devoted to the side of the wholesome, he does not harm others by body or speech,
and he generates a desire for others to initiate vigor as well.
In this way, one also benefits others;
one becomes strong in causal power and delights in human effort for the sake of the future.
Thus, this is the fourfold power of vigor.
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.

When a bodhisattva enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), he abandons the afflictions that are the opposites of meditation—such as sensual desire, discursive thought, joy, pleasure, and perceptions of form—as well as the secondary afflictions.
Furthermore, this meditation of his becomes a provision for awakening and serves as its foundation.
And it is precisely through consistency of purpose that he brings sentient beings to maturity;
by dwelling in happiness in the present life, he benefits himself;
and by means of a mind that is calm, tranquil, and free from passion, being neither harmful nor agitated toward sentient beings, he benefits others as well.

The purification of knowledge, the purification of the manifestation of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and rebirth among the gods in the future are the fruits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Thus, this fourfold power of meditative concentration is neither exceeded nor surpassed;
the wise Bodhisattva abandons ignorance, which is the adversary of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, this wisdom of his becomes the equipment for enlightenment;
and he brings sentient beings to maturity through generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, and consistency between words and deeds.
He favors himself with a sublime joy and gladness associated with the correct realization of the objects of knowledge as they truly are;
and by teaching the method everywhere, he also favors sentient beings with benefit and happiness in both the present life and the future.
Furthermore, he correctly accomplishes the gathering of all roots of virtue through that [joy].

And in the future, one realizes the dissociation from both kinds of obscurations: the dissociation from the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the dissociation from the obscuration to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Thus, this is the fourfold power of wisdom; there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
This is called the power of the Dharma.
What is the innate power of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
It is the natural recollection of past births.

The endurance of long-term, diverse, intense, and continuous suffering for the sake of sentient beings without deliberation; rejoicing in the very suffering that accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings for their sake alone;
and remaining among the Tuṣita gods for as long as one's lifespan lasts after being reborn there.
Furthermore, there are three ways in which he surpasses the other sons of the gods born in Tuṣita: by his divine lifespan, his divine complexion, and his divine fame.
Upon entering his mother’s womb, the world-system is pervaded by a sublime radiance; and while fully conscious, he enters, remains within, and emerges from his mother’s womb, and is born.
Immediately upon birth, he takes seven steps upon the earth, unassisted by anyone.

And there is the act of speech, consisting of the utterance [of the Dharma] by one who has been born, and the performance of worship by noble gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas with divine garlands, musical instruments, incense, the waving of garments, and excellent, most preeminent offerings such as parasols, banners, and flags;
and there is the state of having a body well-marked by the thirty-two unsurpassed marks of a Great Man.
In his final existence and last birth, he is unassailable by all adversaries, even by the hosts of Māras, and by all forms of assault;
