and while seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), he conquers the entire army of Māra through loving-kindness (maitrī);
and in every one of his joints, he is endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
Even as a mere infant, being naturally skilled in his own right,
he very swiftly entered into all worldly arts and crafts;
and furthermore, without a teacher and entirely alone, he attained the perfect awakening of great enlightenment within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.
Brahmā Sahāmpati himself approached and requested him to teach the true Dharma in the world;
he experienced no sound even like that of a great thundercloud;
and there was a state of tranquility due to his non-emergence from meditative absorption.

Furthermore, even among the beasts and birds, and even down to the smallest of wild animals, there is the highest degree of trust in a bodhisattva; they approach him at all times and dwell near him according to their desire. Likewise, there is worship of the Tathāgata by animals, such as when a monkey presented a honeycomb without bees to the Tathāgata.
When that [honey] had been accepted by the Blessed One, the monkey, his mind filled with joy, was dismissed;
dancing, he waited for a cloud, thinking, "The Tathāgata will bathe, and I shall bathe him," directed solely toward the Blessed One.
And while the Bodhisattva or the Tathāgata stood at the foot of a tree, even though the shadows of all other trees slanted toward the east, the shadow of that particular tree did not leave his body.
For six years, even though Māra sought an opportunity against the Tathāgata who had attained perfect enlightenment, he found no such opening.
Furthermore, there was the constant and continuous presence of mindfulness accompanied by its appropriate form;
and for one thus mindful, there was the arising, the abiding, and the cessation of feelings, perceptions, and thoughts as they were clearly understood.
Likewise, the innate power of the Buddhas consists of both that which bestows favor through being seen and that which is comprised within the noble conduct and dwellings.
Regarding these, that which bestows favor through being seen is as follows:
for example, those who are insane or deranged regain their own minds upon seeing the Tathāgata.
Women with inverted fetuses have their fetuses turned to the normal position;
the blind regain their sight, and the deaf their hearing.
For those who are impassioned, the obsession of passion departs; for those who are hostile, the obsession of hatred; and for those who are deluded, the obsession of delusion.
Thus, this kind of innate power that provides assistance through vision should be understood.
In this regard, the innate power comprised within the noble conduct and dwelling is as follows:
for example, he prepares his lion’s posture for sleep on his right side.
And that bed of grass and leaves remains lying on one side;
the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, lies there undisturbed.
Furthermore, the wind does not blow his robe away from his body.
He walks with the gait of a lion; he also walks with the gait of a bull. He raises his right foot first.
Then he follows with his left foot;
and as he walks, the high ground becomes low,
and the low ground becomes high.
The ground is level like the palm of a hand,
free from stones, pebbles, and potsherds;
and with a mind inclined toward seclusion, he enters the village.
As he enters, low doorways become high for him;
when he takes his food, not even a single grain of boiled rice falls to the ground,
nor does any remain until he has taken the second mouthful.
He casts [them] away.
Such as these are the powers to be understood as comprised within the noble conduct and dwelling;
and at the time of his final nirvāṇa, there occurs a great earthquake, the falling of meteors, the blazing of the quarters, and the sounding of celestial drums in the sky.
That too is indeed the innate power of the Tathāgatas, not something produced by supernatural knowledges (*abhijñā*).
This is called the innate power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In that regard, what is the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas that is not shared with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?
And what is the common [nature]?
The uncommon nature, in brief, should be understood through three aspects:
by way of subtlety, by way of type, and by way of realm.

In this regard, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva understands, according to reality and with such subtlety, how the performance of purposeful action occurs for immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings through immeasurable and incalculable means of power;
and likewise, they are endowed in every way with the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the power of the Dharma, and innate power.
Thus it is by way of its modes;
all world-systems and all realms of sentient beings become the scope of his power.
Thus it is by way of its elements.
For a śrāvaka, however, the domain of his supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) is a two-thousandfold world system together with its realm of sentient beings;
for a pratyekabuddha, the entire three-thousandfold world system is the domain of his supernormal knowledges.
Why is that?
For they have set out for the sake of taming only their own single self,
and not that of all sentient beings;
therefore, for them, only a single realm constitutes the sphere of supreme power.
Excluding these specific modes, the other powers of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas should be understood as being shared with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

This being so, even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not possess superknowledges equal to those of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; how much less, then, can all gods, humans, non-Buddhist teachers, and ordinary worldlings do so?
Furthermore, whatever miraculous power of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is comprised of miracles of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), of mind-reading (*ādeśanā*), and of instruction (*anuśāsti*),

that too should be understood as being included, as appropriate, within the powers of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*)— specifically within the powers of the superknowledge of the range of supernatural power, of the superknowledge of the penetration of others' minds, and of the superknowledge of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).
This concludes the fifth chapter, "Power," in the section on the Foundation of Yoga within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 55) Chapter 1.6: On Ripening.
In this regard, what is ripening?
In brief, maturation should be understood through six aspects:

by way of its intrinsic nature, by way of the persons to be matured, by way of the different types of maturation, by way of the means of maturation, by way of the person who matures, and by way of the characteristics of the matured person.
In this regard, the nature of maturation is as follows:

when the seeds of wholesome phenomena exist, through the sequence of cultivating those wholesome phenomena, there arises a pliancy and fitness of body and mind that is conducive to the purification resulting from the abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obstructions; it is the culmination of right application, established in which one—whether having relied upon a Teacher or not—[attains the goal].

Or, he becomes capable and competent to realize immediately after [hearing] the Teacher either the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) or the abandonment of the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is just as when an ulcer has reached the point of ripeness for lancing and is immediately ready to be incised.
That is said to be "fully ripened.
Just as earthenware vessels such as jars, pots, and bowls are called "ripened" when they have reached their final state for use and are immediately fit for use;
or just as fruits such as mangoes and jackfruits are called "ripe" when they have reached their final state for consumption and are immediately fit for consumption.
In the same way, through the sequence of cultivating wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*), this culmination of correct application leads immediately to purification;
that is the nature of maturation (*paripāka*).
In that regard, the individuals (*pudgala*) to be matured are, in brief, fourfold.
One of śrāvaka lineage should be matured in the Śrāvaka vehicle;
one of pratyekabuddha lineage in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
and one of buddha lineage in the Mahāyāna.
Even a person who lacks the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) must be brought to maturity for the sake of proceeding to a happy rebirth;
thus, these four types of persons are to be matured by Bodhisattvas and the Blessed Buddhas in these four matters.
In this way, maturation should be understood from the perspective of the persons to be matured.
In that regard, what is the classification of ripening?
Briefly stated, ripening is of six kinds:
ripening of the faculties, ripening of the roots of virtue, ripening of knowledge, and ripening that is weak, middling, or superior.
In this context, the maturation of the faculties consists of the perfection of long life, physical beauty, noble lineage, sovereignty, authoritative speech, great renown, and human birth;

as well as great enthusiasm. Having attained this excellence of the fruit of the maturation of the basis, one becomes capable of applying oneself with arduous effort and possesses a mind free from weariness in the diligent pursuit of mastering all fields of knowledge.

What is the ripening of the roots of virtue? It is that, by virtue of being naturally possessed of little passion, one’s mind does not incline toward evil and unwholesome states by its very nature; one has weak hindrances, few discursive thoughts, and is upright and receptive to what is skillful.
What is the maturation of knowledge?
It is that one possesses mindfulness and intelligence, and is capable of understanding, grasping, retaining, and penetrating the meaning of teachings that are well-spoken and ill-spoken.
One is endowed with innate wisdom, by relying upon which one becomes fit and capable of completely and utterly liberating the mind from all afflictions.
In this regard, through the maturation of the faculties, one becomes liberated from the obscuration of ripening;
through the maturation of the roots of virtue, one becomes liberated from the obscuration of karma;
and through the maturation of knowledge, one becomes liberated from the obscuration of afflictions.
What is weak maturation?
Weak maturation occurs due to two causes:

because of practice for a short period of time, which is the cause for the maturation of the faculties, roots of virtue, and knowledge; and because of practicing with causes that are neither fully nourished nor inferior.
Intermediate maturation should be understood as occurring due to the deficiency of one of these two causes and the presence of the other.
Furthermore, superior maturation should be understood as occurring due to the non-deficiency of both of these two causes. In that regard, what is the means for maturation?

It should be understood as being of twenty-seven kinds: by way of the nourishment of the elements (*dhātu*); by way of the application of present conditions; by way of entry; by way of grasping delight; by way of initial setting forth; by way of non-initial setting forth; by way of distance from purity; by way of proximity to purity; by way of application (*prayoga*); by way of intention (*āśaya*); and by way of the gathering of material things (*āmiṣa*).

[It is] through the presentation of the Dharma; through attracting [beings] by means of supernatural power; through the teaching of the Dharma; through the proclamation of secret teachings; through the proclamation of revealed teachings; through mild application; through middling application; through intense application; through hearing; through reflection; through cultivation; through gathering [disciples]; through subduing [them]; through one's own initiative; through the request of others; and through both of these.
In that regard, what is the nourishment of the element (*dhātupuṣṭi*)?

It is the arising and persistence of the seeds of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*), which— relying on the natural excellence of the seeds of wholesome qualities— become increasingly and most fully nourished through the prior cultivation of wholesome qualities.
This is called the nourishment of the elements (*dhātupuṣṭi*).
In that regard, what is the application of present conditions?
The teaching of the Dharma without error regarding the present life, the correct apprehension of it therein,
and the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma as it truly is.
In that regard, through the prior cause consisting of the nourishment of the constituent elements (*dhātu*), the present maturation is brought about.
Through the application of present conditions, it should be understood that the present cause likewise brings about present maturation.
In this context, what is "entry"?
Making the attainment of faith the dominant factor, there is the undertaking of the training rules for the avoidance of misconduct by a householder,
or the undertaking of the training rules for the avoidance of sensual pleasures by one who has gone forth into the homeless life.
What is the grasping at delight?

Having attained the path that leads out of all suffering, which avoids the extremes of sensual pleasure and self-mortification, and having attained the pleasant path, one finds delight in the teaching within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
In this regard, what is the initial undertaking?

It is the very first entry [into the path] after having experienced spiritual urgency regarding those things that should inspire urgency, and having recognized the benefit in practicing for the sake of the right goal.
This alone is called the initial stage.
What is the non-initial stage?
It is the state of one who has entered [the path] and is currently undergoing maturation, having attained non-neglect by the Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas.
And regarding those states that have been opened up, it is the process of making them manifest again and again, leading to a state of progressive maturation.
In this context, what is the remoteness from purification?

It is when, due to either laziness or a deficiency of favorable conditions, one becomes capable of attaining purification only after a great and long period of time, through many transitions of future births or through the passage of many eons.
The proximity to purification should be understood as the opposite of this.
In that regard, what is application?

It is the constant practice of guarding the precepts, having developed an intense desire for the attainment of one’s own welfare, or having regard for the fear of falling into ruin in the next world, or the fear of ill-repute from others in this present life.
And acting with reverence.
In that regard, what is the intention?
It is the correct investigation of phenomena, which, by relying on receptivity, leads to being unshakable from this Dharma and Vinaya and [the desire] for the realization of others.
It is that unwavering state of faith regarding the Three Jewels and the attainment of one’s own goal, which arises from confidence and the estimation of their qualities.
What is the application of these [faiths]?

It is the provision of food, drink, and so forth, in every way and for all those who are destitute of food, drink, and so forth; and the provision of suitable food, drink, and so forth, for those who lack suitable food, drink, and so forth.
In that regard, what is the provision of the Dharma?
It is either the bestowing of the teachings by way of brief instruction, or the correct exposition of their meaning.
What is attraction through supernormal power?

It is the manifestation of the miracles of supernormal power by one possessing such power, out of compassion for sentient beings, whether for the sake of purifying their dispositions or as a dominant influence over them.
Having purified their application, or having seen or heard these miracles, these beings will attain purity of intention regarding the teaching and will apply themselves correctly.
With their minds won over by that miracle, they either attain purity of intention or apply themselves correctly.
In that regard, what is teaching?
It is the teaching of the true Dharma for one who is personally unable to attain their own goal, serving as an aid for correct practice;
and it is the teaching of the true Dharma conducive to swift superknowledge even for one who is capable.
In that regard, what is the teaching of the secret dharma?

It is the concealment of the extremely vast and profound meaning of the dharma for those beings of immature wisdom, and the teaching of the dharma through easy means of entry that are clear and accessible. What is the teaching of the revealed dharma?
It is the elucidation of extremely vast and profound points for those beings of broad wisdom who have easily entered the methods of the Buddha’s teaching.
In that regard, what is the weak application? It is that which is devoid of constant application and devoid of respectful application.
What is middling application? It is that which is devoid of either continuous application or respectful application;
thus, it is one that lacks either of these two types of application.
What is the superior application?
It is that which is conjoined with both types of application, conjoined with constant application, and conjoined with respectful application. In this context, what is "learning"?
What is reflection? It is the application of oneself to hearing, grasping, retaining, and reciting the teachings such as the sūtras, for one who is devoted to the Buddha’s word.
What is investigation?
It is the deliberation on the meaning, the discernment, and the ascertainment of one who delights in contemplating the teachings in seclusion.
What is cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?

It is the delight in the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), preceded by the correct discernment of the signs (*nimitta*) of tranquility, exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity.
What is gathering?
It is providing support for one whose mind is rightly free from worldly motives, according to the manner of a teacher and preceptor;

and it is various kinds of service, such as service consisting of attending to the sick, and service consisting of providing robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the ill in accordance with the Dharma.
The service of dispelling sorrow and regret, and the service of dispelling the afflictions— one should understand that various kinds of service such as these exist. What is restraint?

Having established for oneself the protection against internal defilements, one should provide a reminder regarding a lapse when the transgression is slight; a reprimand when the transgression is moderate;
and expulsion when the transgression is grave.
In that regard, whatever admonition and whatever reproval there may be, they are for the sake of the welfare and happiness of those very individuals as well as others.
Furthermore, whatever expulsion there may be for the purpose of subsequent reinstatement, that too is for the welfare and happiness of both them and others.
However, whatever expulsion there may be that is not subject to reinstatement, that is solely for the welfare and happiness of others.
For instance, when others commit transgressions that lead to their expulsion,
one resolves to ensure they do not transgress again;
how, then, does one bring others to maturity oneself?
And he teaches the conformable Dharma in order to raise [beings] up from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states;
he acts according to his words,
practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and follows its essential nature.
Because others would not say this to him:
"Since you yourself have not yet emerged from unwholesome states and are not established in wholesome states, why do you think that you should exhort, urge, and remind another in that regard?"
You yourself, first of all, must be urged by others, reminded, and exhorted. How does one entreat another?
It is toward one in whose presence beings have established an intense degree of affection and reverence.
Furthermore, one who is skilled in means and well-trained in the teaching of the Dharma requests [the Buddha] and exhorts him for the sake of maturation.
It should be understood that maturation is brought about by both of these together: one's own [exertion] and the request made by others.
By means of these twenty-seven types of methods for ripening, that perfection of the sixfold distinctions of ripening should be understood:
namely, the ripening of the faculties, the ripening of the roots of virtue, the ripening of knowledge, and the ripening that is weak, middling, and superior.
In this regard, who are the persons that bring about ripening?
In brief, six types of bodhisattvas, established in the six bodhisattva stages, bring sentient beings to maturity.
A bodhisattva established on the stage of conduct through aspiration is one who practices through aspiration (*adhimukticārī*).
A bodhisattva established on the stage of pure resolute intention is one whose resolute intention is pure;
a bodhisattva established on the stage of the practice of conduct is one who has entered upon the practice of conduct;
a bodhisattva established on the stage of certainty is one who has fallen into certainty.
A bodhisattva established on the stage of the practice of certain conduct is one who has entered the practice of certain conduct;

a bodhisattva established on the stage of reaching the culmination is one who has reached the culmination. In that regard, for individuals not established in a spiritual lineage (*agotra*), the maturation for proceeding to a happy rebirth is subject to repeated regression and must be performed again and again.
Furthermore, for those established in the spiritual lineage (*gotrastha*), maturation is irreversible and does not need to be performed again and again.
In that regard, what are the characteristics of a person who has reached maturation?
A *śrāvaka*, through the prior practice of wholesome deeds, when established in a state of weak maturation, possesses weak aspiration.
One whose practice is weak may even go to the states of woe, nor does he attain the fruit of the ascetic life in this present life, nor does he attain final nirvana in this present life.
However, when he is established in moderate ripening, he possesses moderate zeal and moderate practice, and he does not go to the states of woe.
In this very life, one attains the fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*),
yet one does not attain final nirvāṇa in this very life.
Established in the highest degree of maturation, one possesses the highest degree of aspiration and the highest degree of application, and one does not go to the states of woe (*apāya*).
One attains the fruit of asceticism in this very life, and one attains final nirvana in this very life. A pratyekabuddha is to be understood in the same way as a śrāvaka.
For what reason?
His path is of the same nature as that of the śrāvakas;
however, this is the distinction of the pratyekabuddha from the śrāvakas.

In his final existence, upon obtaining his final physical body, he— without a teacher and by the power of previous practice— cultivates the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening and, through the abandonment of all afflictions,
realizes arhatship; therefore, he is called a pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva abiding on the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) should be understood as having weak maturation; one who is pure in superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) on the stage of the practice of conduct (*caryāpratipattibhūmi*) has middling maturation;
and one who is fixed in the certainty of liberation (*niyāta*) and has reached the culmination has superior maturation.
In that regard, a bodhisattva established in the stage of weak ripening has weak aspiration and weak application, and he goes to the miserable realms;
he should be understood as being at the end of the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
He remains entirely disconnected from all the wholesome factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*), which are [otherwise] ardent, immovable, and perfectly pure.
A Bodhisattva at the stage of middling maturation possesses middling aspiration and middling application;
he does not go to the miserable realms, and he reaches the end of the second incalculable eon,
endowed with the refined and immovable wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment.
He becomes associated with what is thoroughly pure and dissociated from what is not.
A bodhisattva who has reached the stage of supreme maturation possesses supreme aspiration and supreme application.
Nor does he go to the miserable realms;
and by the end of the third incalculable eon,
he becomes endowed with the wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) that are refined, immovable, and perfectly pure.
In that regard, they are called "blazing" because they are by nature dense, radiant, characterized by exceedingly great fruit, and possessed of great benefits.
They are called "immovable" because they are irreversible, not subject to decline, and lead to further distinction.
They are called "utterly pure" because they are unsurpassed within the stage of a bodhisattva.
In this regard, there is ripening produced by material gifts, that born from attracting others through supernormal powers, that born from the proclamation of the secret Dharma,

that consisting of weak application, and that produced by mere hearing; this fivefold ripening remains only weak even after long-term practice of these dharmas, let alone after practice for such a short time.
By all other causes of maturation, however, the threefold method of maturation is to be understood:
through mild practice, mild maturation is to be understood; through middling [practice], middling [maturation]; and through intense [practice], intense maturation.
Furthermore, for each of those—mild, middling, and intense maturations—a threefold method is to be understood.
Of the weak [level], there is the weak-weak, the weak-medium, and the weak-strong;
of the medium, the medium-weak, the medium-medium, and the medium-strong;
and of the strong, the strong-weak, the strong-medium, and the strong-strong.
In this manner, by way of such successive subdivisions, the immeasurable variety of the ripening of sentient beings brought about by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is to be understood.

In that regard, through these aforementioned causes of ripening, a Bodhisattva brings about for himself— and for other sentient beings— the ripening of the faculties, the ripening of the roots of virtue, and the ripening of knowledge, whether they be weak, middling, or superior, for the sake of ripening his own Buddha-qualities.
This is for the sake of the departure via the three vehicles of other persons.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on Ripening, in the section on the Foundation within the Bodhisattva-bhūmi.
(Dutt 62) Chapter 1.7: The Chapter on Enlightenment.
In that regard, what is enlightenment?
In brief, awakening (bodhi) is said to consist of two kinds of abandonment and two kinds of knowledge.
Therein, the two kinds of abandonment are the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa) and the abandonment of the obscuration of the knowable (jñeyāvaraṇa).
Furthermore, the two kinds of knowledge are: that which is stainless due to the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions, and the knowledge that is free from the continuity of all afflictions.
Furthermore, due to the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there arises a knowledge that is unimpeded and unobstructed regarding all objects of knowledge.
Another formulation is that it is pure knowledge, omniscient knowledge, and unattached knowledge.

The complete uprooting of all afflictive latencies (*kleśa-vāsanā*) and the total abandonment of non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭā-avidyā*) is called unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
In this regard, that knowledge which results from the abandonment of all afflictions along with their latencies—both in every respect and absolutely—is called "pure" (*śuddha*).
That knowledge which operates unimpededly across all realms, all objects, all modes, and at all times is called "omniscience" (*sarvajñāna*).
In that regard, there are two realms: the world-realm and the realm of sentient beings.
In that regard, there are two kinds of entities.
There is the conditioned and the unconditioned.

Furthermore, regarding that very same conditioned and unconditioned entity, there is an immeasurable differentiation of types by way of the distinctions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), subsequent categories (*uttarajāti*), and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); by way of the distinctions of cause and fruit; and by way of the distinctions of realm (*dhātu*), destiny (*gati*), and the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
In this regard, time is threefold.
Past, future, and present—

this knowledge that pertains to all realms, all objects, all modes, and all times is called "omniscience" (*sarvajñāna*). In this context, "unimpeded knowledge" (*asaṅgajñāna*) refers to that knowledge which, by mere mental application, proceeds swiftly and without attachment, being established everywhere.
Furthermore, that knowledge does not arise from repeated mental effort, but rather it is bound to a single moment of effort.
Another formulation:

it consists of the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), as well as the Tathāgata’s absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
This is called unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this regard, there are these one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*):
the thirty-two marks of a great person (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), and the four purities in all their aspects (*sarvākārapariśuddhi*).

The ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three foundations of mindfulness, the three ways in which he needs no protection, great compassion, the quality of being incapable of confusion, the eradication of latent predispositions, and the knowledge of all aspects in their excellence.

The classification of these Buddha-qualities will be explained in the Chapter on the Foundation (*pratiṣṭhā-paṭala*). In this regard, this supreme enlightenment (*paramā bodhi*) is endowed with seven types of supremacy, by virtue of which it is called the highest among all forms of enlightenment.

What are the seven supremacies? They are: supremacy of basis (*āśraya-paramatā*), supremacy of practice (*pratipatti-paramatā*), supremacy of attainment (*sampatti-paramatā*), supremacy of knowledge (*jñāna-paramatā*), supremacy of power (*prabhāva-paramatā*), supremacy of abandonment (*prahāṇa-paramatā*), and supremacy of dwelling (*vihāra-paramatā*).
That the Tathāgata’s body is well-characterized by the thirty-two marks of a great person— this is called his excellence of physical basis (*āśraya-paramatā*).

That the Tathāgata has practiced for his own benefit, for the benefit of others, for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
This is called his supremacy of practice (*pratipatti-paramatā*).

That the Tathāgata is endowed with four unsurpassed and incomparable perfections— having practiced with perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-sampad*), perfection of view (*dṛṣṭi-sampad*), perfection of conduct (*ācāra-sampad*), and perfection of livelihood (*ājīva-sampad*)—
this is called his supremacy of perfection (*sampatti-paramatā*).

That the Tathāgata is endowed with the four unsurpassed and peerless analytical knowledges— namely, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*)—
this is called his supremacy of knowledge.
That the Tathāgata is endowed with the six unsurpassed and incomparable higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) as previously described—
this is called the Tathāgata’s supremacy of power (*prabhāva*).

Furthermore, that the Tathāgata is endowed with the abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), and with the unsurpassed and incomparable abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is called his supremacy of abandonment.
That the Tathāgata frequently dwells in the three unsurpassed and peerless abidings— the noble abiding, the divine abiding, and the Brahmā abiding—
this is called his supremacy of abiding.
In this context, the dwellings of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as the dwelling of the attainment of cessation, are called the noble dwellings (*ārya-vihāra*).

The four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are called the divine dwellings (*divya-vihāra*). The four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are called the brahma-dwellings (*brāhma-vihāra*).
Furthermore, from those three types of dwellings, there are four supreme dwellings by which Tathāgatas frequently abide:
from the noble dwelling, the dwelling of emptiness and the dwelling of the attainment of cessation;
and from the divine dwelling, the dwelling of the fourth dhyāna, which is immovable.

From among the sublime abidings, it is the abiding in compassion by which the Tathāgata, three times during the night and three times during the day—six times in a day and night—surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye: "Who is declining?
Who is progressing? Whose unarisen roots of merit shall I cause to be planted? And whom, in detail, shall I establish in the supreme fruit of arhatship?"
In this regard, by virtue of the supremacy of their basis, the Tathāgatas are called Great Beings;
by virtue of the supremacy of their practice, they are called the Greatly Compassionate Ones;
and by virtue of the supremacy of their accomplishment, they are called those of Great Virtue and Great Dharma.
Because of the supremacy of their knowledge, they are called those of great wisdom;
because of the supremacy of their power, they are called those of great supernormal knowledges;
because of the supremacy of their abandonment, they are called those of great liberation.
Because they abide in the supreme dwelling, they are said to dwell frequently in the great dwelling.
Furthermore, the qualities of those Tathāgatas are expressed in ten ways, and there is the recollection of their qualities.
What are these ten?

Thus, that Blessed One is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. In this context, he is called the Tathāgata because his speech is never otherwise than true.
He is an Arhat because he has attained all that is to be attained, because he is an unsurpassed field of merit, and because he is worthy of worship.
He is a Samyaksaṃbuddha because he has perfectly awakened to the dharmas according to reality and in the ultimate sense.

He is endowed with knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*) because he is perfectly accomplished in both the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and the side of tranquility (*śamatha*), as well as in the three types of knowledge and the conduct as described in the sūtras.
He is the Sugata because he has gone to the supreme excellence and will not return again.
He is the Knower of the World because he possesses knowledge in every aspect regarding the affliction and purification of both the realm of sentient beings and the realm of the world.
He is the Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men to be Tamed because he knows the supreme means for subduing the mind and because he appears as the one true person in the world.

Because it has become the eye; because it has become the reality of the nature of phenomena regarding the objects of knowledge; because it determines manifest objects; because it is the refuge for all objects; because it brings about the understanding of objects not yet understood;
because it cuts through doubt that has already arisen; because it reveals profound points; because it brings about complete purification;
because it is the root of all phenomena; because it leads [to them]; because it is the refuge for all suffering.
He teaches and points out the way of deliverance for gods and humans;
therefore, he is called the Teacher of gods and humans.

Because he has attained the complete and perfect awakening in every aspect regarding the mass of teachings that lead to welfare, the mass of teachings that do not lead to welfare, and the mass of teachings that lead neither to welfare nor to non-welfare—[he is the Teacher].
He is called "Buddha" because the Blessed One has utterly shattered the great battle against the entire host of Māras.
In that regard, even after many eons, the appearance of even a single Buddha may not occur;
yet within a single eon, the arising of many Buddhas does occur.
Furthermore, it should be understood that in those various immeasurable and incalculable world-systems throughout the ten directions, there is indeed the arising of immeasurable Buddhas.
For what reason?
Because there are immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattvas in the ten directions who have made their vows at the same time and have accomplished the same accumulations;
on whichever day, fortnight, month, or year one bodhisattva has resolved his mind upon awakening, on that very day, fortnight, month, or year, all of them have done so as well.

And just as one has exerted himself, striven, and endeavored, so have all. For indeed, in this very world-system, many hundreds of bodhisattvas are seen who have made their vows at the same time, who possess equal renunciation, equal patience, equal vigor, equal meditative concentration, and equal wisdom.
How much more so in the infinite and boundless world-systems in the ten directions!

There exist in the ten directions immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields, even trichiliocosm-megachiliocosms. Yet, there is no room for two Bodhisattvas who have equally perfected their accumulations to arise simultaneously in a single world-system or Buddha-field, let alone for immeasurable and incalculable numbers of them.
Furthermore, it is not logical that those with equal accumulations should arise sequentially one after another;
nor is it logical that there should be no arising at all for anyone.

Therefore, in the ten directions, within immeasurable and incalculable world-systems—some of which have been purified while others are empty of Tathāgatas—those Bodhisattvas with equal accumulations arise in various Buddha-fields.
Thus it should be understood.
By this reasoning, it is logical that there is an abundance of Buddhas in many world-systems;
however, the simultaneous arising of two Tathāgatas does not occur within a single Buddha-field.
For what reason?
Because for a long time, indeed, the Bodhisattva has cultivated this vow:
"May I alone be a leader in a world without a leader; may I be the guide of sentient beings, their liberator from all sufferings, and their bringer to final nirvana."
For one who thus cultivates such a long-term aspiration embraced by right practice, that very aspiration succeeds.
Furthermore, a single Tathāgata is capable of performing all the Buddha-activities within a single trichiliocosm great trichiliocosm Buddha-field;
therefore, the arising of a second Tathāgata would be entirely purposeless.
Furthermore, from the arising of a single Tathāgata in the world, the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings becomes more abundant and more effective.
Why is that?
Because it occurs to them: "In this entire world-system, there is only this one Tathāgata; there is no second."

Realizing that "whether he has departed on a journey through the countryside or has entered final nirvāṇa, there will be no second person in whose presence we may practice the holy life or hear the Dharma," they hasten with even more intense zeal and effort for the sake of dwelling in the holy life and hearing the true Dharma.
However, having perceived the multiplicity of Buddhas, they would not be in too great a hurry;
for in this way, through the arising of even a single Buddha, the accomplishment of one's own welfare becomes more abundant and more favorable.
In that regard, everything concerning all Buddhas is exactly equal and without distinction, with the exception of four points: lifespan, name, family, and physical stature.
Thus, the distinctiveness of the Buddhas arises from the decrease or increase of these four factors,
and not by any other means;
furthermore, a woman does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
For what reason?
Because, indeed, after the passing of the very first incalculable eon, the bodhisattva abandons the female state.

From the moment of sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, one never again becomes a woman. Furthermore, the entire female sex is by nature possessed of many afflictions and is characterized by poor wisdom;

and it is not possible for one whose mental continuum is naturally full of many afflictions and whose mental continuum is characterized by poor wisdom to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Thus, this unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*) should be understood as it truly is, both in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as previously described, and also in terms of its excellence (*parama*), its recollection through the description of its qualities (*guṇanirdeśānusmaraṇa*), its manifestation (*saṃbhava*), and its distinction (*viśeṣa*), all as previously described. Furthermore, this unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is indeed inconceivable (*acintya*) because it transcends the path of all logic (*sarvatarkamārgasamatikrāntatva*), and it is immeasurable and possesses an accumulation of incalculable qualities (*aprameyāsaṃkhyeyaguṇasamuditatva*). It is indeed unsurpassed for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas.
It leads to liberation;
therefore, this very awakening is the foremost, the most excellent, the best, and the most sublime.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, "Awakening," in the section on the Foundation within the *Yogasthāna* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 67) The Chapter on the Lineage of Power (Balagotrapaṭala), the first [chapter],
has thus been set forth, wherein a bodhisattva must train.
I shall now explain how one should further train. The summary verse:
Abundance of resolute belief, the search for the Dharma, and its teaching.
Practice, as well as correct instruction and admonition,
and finally, the action of body, speech, and mind accompanied by skillful means.
Here, from the very beginning, a bodhisattva who wishes to train in the bodhisattva precepts must be abundant in resolute conviction.
One who seeks the Dharma, teaches the Dharma, practices in accordance with the Dharma, provides correct instruction and admonition,
and abides in that correct instruction and admonition, must have their actions of body, speech, and mind embraced by skillful means.
And how does a bodhisattva become abundant in resolute conviction?
In this regard, a bodhisattva is endowed with a certainty and a delight preceded by faith and serene confidence regarding eight bases of resolute belief:
the Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; the qualities of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as it has been described;
the reality of the ultimate meaning as it has been described; and the various causes and fruits, which are appropriately categorized, non-erroneous, and to be attained.
"I am capable of attaining the goal.
Just as with the goal to be attained, so too regarding the means of attainment: "This is the means for attaining the goal that is to be reached.
In this context, the goal to be attained is, for example, unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarā bodhi*).
Furthermore, the means of attainment consists of all the paths of training for a bodhisattva.
Likewise, it is resolute belief (*adhimukti*) in that which is well-spoken, well-uttered, and well-proclaimed—namely, in the teachings such as the *sūtras*, *geyas*, *vyākaraṇas*, and so forth.
In this regard, within these eight bases of resolute belief, it should be understood that a bodhisattva’s abundance of resolute belief arises from two causes.
And through the frequent practice of resolute belief, and through the establishment of intense patience—
therein, when a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma, what does he seek?
How does he seek it?
For what purpose does he seek them?
In brief, a bodhisattva seeks both the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
he also seeks external treatises and worldly crafts and occupations.
Among those, that which is the *vaipulya* from within the twelvefold division of the word of the Buddha is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
the remainder should be understood as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
Furthermore, the external treatises are, in brief, of three kinds.
These are the treatises on logic, the treatises on grammar, and the treatises on medicine;
therein are various worldly arts and crafts of many kinds and numerous varieties,
such as the knowledge of the work of goldsmiths, blacksmiths, and jewelers.
These, which are comprised within all branches of knowledge, constitute the five fields of knowledge:
the inner science, the science of logic, the science of grammar, the science of medicine, and the science of arts and crafts.
It is these five fields of knowledge that a bodhisattva seeks to master.
In this way, all fields of knowledge have been sought by him.
Among those, the word of the Buddha is called the inner science (*adhyātma-śāstra*).
Furthermore, in how many aspects does that [inner science] proceed?
In this way, as far as worldly crafts and occupations are concerned, they proceed in various forms.
However, the word of the Buddha proceeds, in brief, in two forms:
the form that elucidates the correct relationship between cause and effect, and the form that elucidates that what has not been done does not perish and what has been done does not go unrewarded.
The science of logic (*hetuśāstra*) also has two aspects:
the aspect of elucidating the benefits of discourse intended to refute others, and the aspect of elucidating the benefits of liberation from the disputes of others.
The science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*) also has two aspects.
The science of medicine proceeds in four aspects: the aspect that elucidates the determination of the elements, forms, and causal factors; the aspect that elucidates the benefits of vocal refinement;
the aspect that elucidates skill regarding diseases; and [the aspect that elucidates skill regarding health].
The mode of elucidating skill regarding the origination of afflictions; the mode of elucidating skill regarding the abandonment of afflictions once they have arisen;
and the mode of elucidating skill regarding the non-arising of abandoned afflictions in the future.
Worldly knowledge of the crafts and occupations has the characteristic of fully demonstrating the completion of the tasks involved in performing one's respective craft or occupation.
And how does the word of the Buddha demonstrate cause and effect without error?

These ten causes should be understood as the non-erroneous establishment of causes that encompasses all causes, whether for affliction or for purification, and also for the occurrence of even those neutral things of worldly people, such as crops.
What are the ten causes?
The cause of conventional designation,
the cause of dependence,
and the cause of projection.
The cause of appropriation,
the cause of production,
the cause of attraction, and the cause of specific determination.
There are three types of causes: the cooperative cause, the opposing cause, and the non-opposing cause.
Among these, regarding all phenomena, there is the name; preceded by the name is the conceptualization, and preceded by the conceptualization is verbal expression.
This is called the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) for those phenomena.

In this regard, that in relation to which, that by way of which cause, there arises a desire for and an appropriation (*upādāna*) of a given thing—this is called its "relational cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
For example, the act of grasping is in relation to the hand and has the hand as its cause.
Action consisting of advancing and retreating depends upon and has as its cause the feet;
action consisting of contracting and extending the limbs depends upon and has as its cause the joints;
and the taking up and seeking of food and drink depends upon and has as its cause hunger and thirst.
In this manner, such categories of causes that follow immeasurable principles should be understood as the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*).
Among these, the seed is the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) of its own final fruit;
any condition other than the seed is the supporting cause (*parigraha-hetu*).

That very seed is the cause for the production of its own fruit. Furthermore, that fruit produced from the seed is the cause for the bringing forth (*āvāhaka-hetu*) of a subsequent fruit projected by the seed. The state of having various distinct causes of different types is the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyama-hetu*). Having condensed all these causes—the causal condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*), the sustaining cause (*parigraha-hetu*), the productive cause (*nirvṛtti-hetu*), the bringing-forth cause (*āvāhaka-hetu*), and the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyama-hetu*)—into a single unity...
It is called the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-hetu*).
A cause that creates an obstacle to arising is the obstructive cause (*virodha-hetu*);
the absence of such obstacles is the non-obstructive cause (*avirōdha-hetu*).
In that regard, contradiction is, in brief, of six kinds: contradiction of speech;
for example, when the scriptures of certain recluses and brahmins are internally inconsistent from beginning to end; and contradiction of reasoning.
The logical reasoning for establishing the object to be proven—that which is to be known—becomes untenable;
this constitutes a contradiction regarding origination.
For example, origination does not occur due to the deficiency of causal conditions and the presence of factors that obstruct origination.
Contradiction by coexistence is,
for example, as between light and darkness, passion and hatred, or pleasure and pain.
Contradiction by opposition is...
For example, there is the hostility between the snake and the mongoose, or between the cat and the mouse—those who are mutual adversaries and enemies.
There is also hostility consisting of the opposition between the discordant factor and its antidote;

for example, the cultivation of the foul (*aśubhabhāvanā*) and sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrībhāvanā*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇābhāvanā*) and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).

In this context, what is intended is precisely the contradiction to the arising of the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and all afflictions belonging to the three realms.
Furthermore, all these causes are subsumed under two types of causes.
By way of the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*) and the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*):
that seed which is both projective (*ākṣepaka*) and actualizing (*nirvartaka*) is the producing cause.
The remaining causes should be understood as the cause of means (*upāyahetu*).

There are four conditions (*pratyaya*): the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Among these, that which is the productive cause is the causal condition.
Furthermore, that which is the cause of means (upāyahetu) should be understood as the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya).
The immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) and the object condition (ālambanapratyaya), however, belong only to mental states and mental factors (cittacaitasika-dharma).
For it is in this way that mental states and mental factors arise and proceed, being sustained by the provision of space by those [factors] arisen previously and being sustained by an object.

Therefore, it should be understood that the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are subsumed by the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*).
In this regard, how do all mundane phenomena proceed by means of these ten causes?
And how does affliction (*saṃkleśa*) come about?
And what is purification?

Regarding those various crops counted as grains in the world, by which this world maintains its livelihood—whatever names, designations, and verbal expressions there are for them, such as barley, rice, wheat, sesame, mung beans, black gram, horse gram, and so forth; [that is purification].

This is the cause for their conventional usage, such as the worldly transactions involving [the thought]: "Let the barley be brought, let it be given, let it be ground, let it be stored," and so forth;

just as it is with barley, so it should be understood for the remaining [grains] as well. Hunger, thirst, and weakness depend upon the maintenance of the body and depend upon the relish of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Regarding these [objects], there occurs the state of desiring them, seeking them, taking hold of them, and enjoying them;
this is their causal condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*).
From whichever respective seed each particular crop emerges, that seed is its projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
The conditions such as earth and rain are the supporting causes (*parigraha-hetu*) for the manifestation of the sprout; that seed is the productive cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) of that sprout.
Indeed, the continuous series (*santāna*) consisting of the succession of sprout, stalk, and leaf is the inducing cause (*āvāhaka-hetu*) for the production of the grain and the ripening of the crop.
From a barley seed, there is the manifestation of a barley sprout and a barley crop, and not of anything else.
In this same way, it should be understood for the remaining [causes].
This is their cause of specific determination (*pratiniyamahetu*).

And all these causes, beginning with the cause of dependence (*apekṣāhetu*) and ending with the cause of specific determination, are the cooperative causes (*sahakārihetu*) for the production of the crop.
For that grain is not produced if any one of its causes is deficient;
therefore, that entire collection [of conditions] is called the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-hetu*).
Obstacles such as lightning strikes, crop diseases, and blights are the opposing causes (*virodha-hetu*).
The deficiency of those [factors] is not an obstacle; it is a cause of non-opposition.
Thus, these ten causes should be understood as applicable, according to the circumstances, to other worldly phenomena as well, such as the cultivation of grain.

In this regard, whatever constitutes the designation, conceptualization, and verbal expression of all dependent origination— namely, ignorance, formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth in detail up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair— this, first of all, is the cause for the conventional discourse regarding affliction (*saṃkleśa*).

The formations have ignorance as their condition, up to old age and death having birth as their condition; such is the scope of this conventional discourse. Furthermore, the engagement with these factors of existence (bhavāṅgas) depends upon the relishing of their objects. This is the "condition of dependence" for this affliction (*saṃkleśa*).

The seeds of the factors beginning with ignorance that exist here in the present life for one who has been born and come into being are the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*) for the birth, aging, and death of a future life.

Associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), and the momentum of previous habituation are the *parigraha-hetu* (appropriating causes) for the arising of ignorance and the other [links].
Each respective seed of ignorance and the others is the *nirvṛtti-hetu* (productive cause).

Furthermore, those [links] beginning with ignorance and ending with existence, through their successive succession of bringing forth each subsequent stage, are the *āvāhaka-hetu* (bringing-forth cause) of that birth, aging, and death belonging to another lifetime.
Others, beginning with ignorance and ending with becoming, together with their own specific energies, lead to rebirth in hell;
others lead to rebirth among animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or gods.
Such is the cause for the specific determination of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).

Taking the causal condition of dependence as the beginning, all these causes, culminating in the cause of specific determination, are called the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-hetu*). Furthermore, the opposing cause (*virodha-hetu*) for that defilement consists of the excellence of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-saṃpad*), the appearance of Buddhas, the teaching of the true Dharma,
attendance upon virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*), and the practice in accordance with the Dharma— all of these.
And there are the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*).
The cause of non-opposition is the deficiency or absence of these very factors as they have been enumerated.
Thus, by means of these ten causes, all affliction (*saṃkleśa*) of all sentient beings is to be understood.
In this regard, whatever designation, perception, and verbal expression there is concerning all factors on the side of purification, as well as regarding cessation and nirvāṇa—
this is the cause for the conventional discourse of purification.
Thus [are] these foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, up to the noble eightfold path.
And from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and so on in detail until: from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death.

Regarding such a conventional discourse as this, that which consists of the consideration of the defects of the formative forces, the seeking of purification, the grasping of purification, and the perfection of purification—this is its "consideration cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
Furthermore, for a person established in the lineage (*gotrastha*), the excellence of that lineage is the precursor for the attainment of *nirvāṇa* with remainder and without remainder.
This is the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*) of purification.
Associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, proper mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), and the prior maturation of the faculties are the sustaining causes (*parigrahahetu*).

Those seeds of the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*) which are comprised within the lineage (*gotra*) are the productive cause (*abhinirvṛttihetu*) for the actualization of those factors conducive to enlightenment.

Furthermore, those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*), which have arisen from their own seeds, are the sequential inducing causes for the two realms of nirvana— namely, that with a remainder of substrate (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and that without a remainder of substrate (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).

In this regard, that which is the lineage of the disciples (*śrāvakagotra*) conduces to final nirvana by means of the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*), and [likewise] the lineage of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddhagotra*).

The Mahāyāna lineage leads to parinirvāṇa by means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, while [the Mahāyāna lineage] leads to parinirvāṇa by means of the Mahāyāna; this is the cause of specific determination for purification.
That which is the cause of dependence belonging to the side of purification, and that which is the cause of specific determination up to this point, is called its "cooperative cause."

The lack of endowment with the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the non-arising of Buddhas, birth in an inopportune state (*akṣaṇa*), association with unworthy persons, hearing the false Dharma, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), and wrong practice constitute the cause of opposition.
The absence of deficiency regarding this very cause of opposition is called the cause of non-opposition.
In this context, that which is the cause of opposition belonging to the side of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) should be understood as the cause of purification (*vyavadāna*).

That which is a cause of opposition belonging to the side of purification should be seen as a cause of affliction. Thus, by means of these ten causes, there is affliction; and by means of these same ten, there is purification. This has been so in the past time and will be so in the future time, whether for the sake of affliction or for the sake of purification. Beyond these, or more than these, no other cause exists.
In that regard, what is the fruit?
Briefly stated, there are five fruits:

the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
The maturation of unwholesome dharmas ripens in the miserable realms; that of wholesome dharmas associated with outflows ripens in a happy rebirth.
This is their fruit of maturation.

Furthermore, that which arises from the practice of the unwholesome—the state of delighting in the unwholesome and the abundance of the unwholesome—or from the practice of the wholesome—the state of delighting in the wholesome and the abundance of the wholesome; or the conformity of a subsequent result to its similarity with prior karma—that is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*). The cessation of afflictions through the noble eightfold path is the disjunction-result (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Furthermore, the cessation of afflictions through the mundane path does not persist for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*);
therefore, that is not the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
On the other hand, there is that which occurs in this very life through some kind of human effort based on any particular craft or field of work.

Whether by means of agriculture, or commerce, or royal service, one brings about results such as crops or profits through writing, calculation, accounting, numbering, and sealing; this is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Furthermore, visual consciousness is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of the eye faculty.
In this way, up to the mental consciousness [is the result] of the mind-faculty; likewise, non-separation from the vital breaths is the result of the life-faculty. Thus it is for all the faculties.
Thus, it should be understood that the result produced by each of the twenty-two faculties through its own respective sovereignty is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Furthermore,
that sovereignty of the twenty-two faculties should be understood as it is set forth in the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.

In this way, having understood the word of the Buddha as a mode of correctly elucidating cause and effect, the bodhisattva gradually purifies and increases the lineage (*gotra*) through the cultivation of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*). Furthermore,
nothing that is unperformed or performed by another ever ripens for anyone.
Furthermore, actions performed by oneself do not perish even after hundreds of eons with respect to their yielding of fruit.

Thus, having understood as it truly is the Buddha’s teaching that clarifies the non-arrival of what was not done and the non-perishing of what was done, the bodhisattva gradually purifies and increases the lineage of the power of knowledge regarding the ownership of one's own actions (*karma-svakatā-jñānabala-gotra*).
In that regard, how does a bodhisattva seek out what has been heard?
Here, a bodhisattva seeks out the Dharma in well-spoken and well-uttered words by establishing intense reverence. In brief, such reverence for well-spoken words is established within him.

If that bodhisattva would enter even a ground made of iron, heated and blazing, with the utmost joy and reverence for the sake of hearing even a single well-spoken word— were he not to obtain the hearing of a well-spoken word otherwise—
how much more so for the sake of many well-spoken words?

Whatever love and respect a bodhisattva has for his own person and physical form does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor any number, fraction, calculation, or comparison, when set beside the subsequent love and respect he has for hearing well-spoken words— let alone the love and respect he has for all other bodily requisites such as food, drink, and so forth.
Having thus developed reverence for well-spoken words, while listening to them, he becomes untiring and insatiable.
He becomes faithful, overflowing with serene confidence, tender in his mental continuum, and upright in view.
Out of a desire for virtue and a desire for the Dharma, he approaches the Dharma-preacher with reverence, not with the intention of finding fault.

Not out of pride or arrogance, nor for the sake of seeking some minor virtue, nor for the purpose of self-exaltation; thinking, "I shall establish both myself and others in roots of virtue," and not for the sake of gain or honor—
he, being thus perfected in his approach, hears the Dharma without affliction and without distraction.
How does one listen without affliction?
One listens being free from the affliction of arrogance, free from the affliction of contempt, and free from the affliction of lethargy.
In this regard, one becomes free from the affliction of arrogance by means of six aspects.
By four aspects, one becomes free from the affliction of contempt;
by one aspect, one becomes free from the affliction of laxity.
One listens at the proper time, listening with respect, desiring to hear, without envy, complying, and not looking for faults.
By these six aspects, he is free from the affliction of pride:

having established respect for the Dharma, having established respect for the person who is a Dharma-preacher, not disparaging the Dharma, and not disparaging the person who is a Dharma-preacher; by these four aspects, he is free from the affliction of contempt.
He listens;
he listens without disparaging himself.
By this single mode, he listens free from the affliction of laxity.
In this way, the bodhisattva hears the Dharma without being afflicted.
In that regard, how does the bodhisattva hear the Dharma without distraction?
By means of five aspects.
With a mind intent on understanding, with a one-pointed mind, with ears attentive, and with a mind fully inclined, he listens to the Dharma, attending to it with his whole heart.
In this way, a bodhisattva seeks out what has been heard.
Why, then, does a bodhisattva seek out what has been heard?
First, the bodhisattva seeks the word of the Buddha for the sake of accomplishing the correct practice of the Dharma and for the sake of explaining it extensively to others.
The bodhisattva seeks the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) in order to understand, as they truly are, the poorly spoken and poorly expressed aspects of that very treatise.

A bodhisattva seeks the science of grammar for the sake of full comprehension and for the sake of refuting the arguments of others; in order to inspire faith in those who have no faith in this teaching and to increase the faith of those who already have it; and for the sake of generating self-confidence in himself regarding those who are devoted to refined speech by means of defining words and syllables along with their etymologies, and for the sake of entering into the conventional usage of various types of etymological explanations for a single meaning.
A bodhisattva seeks the science of medicine for the purpose of pacifying the various kinds of diseases of sentient beings and for the sake of benefiting the great mass of people.

A bodhisattva seeks worldly arts and crafts for the purpose of acquiring wealth with little difficulty for the benefit of sentient beings, for the purpose of generating great respect in sentient beings, and for the purpose of benefiting and gathering them through the sharing of knowledge of those crafts.
A bodhisattva investigates all these five fields of knowledge for the sake of fulfilling the great accumulation of wisdom for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
For one who does not train in all of these accordingly will not gradually attain the unobstructed knowledge of the omniscient one.
Thus, that which the bodhisattva investigates, how he investigates it, and for what purpose he investigates it have been explained.
In this regard, what does the bodhisattva teach to others,
how does he teach it,
and for what purpose does he teach it?
In that regard, he teaches exactly what he has sought;
and for whatever purpose he has sought it, for that very same purpose he teaches it to others. Furthermore, he teaches by means of two aspects.
He delivers discourse that is both conformable and pure.
In this regard, how does he deliver conformable discourse?
He teaches one who is established in a suitable deportment, and not in an unsuitable one.

One should not [teach] while seated on a higher seat to one who is not ill, nor to one with their head covered, nor to one walking in front; this should be understood in detail as it is stated in the Sūtra.
For what reason?
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas hold the Dharma in high esteem.
For when that is performed with respect to the Dharma, an intense reverence for the Dharma arises in others;
they become filled with respect for hearing it rather than being filled with contempt,
and he teaches it to everyone.
He teaches everything without interruption;
not being stingy with the Dharma, he does not maintain the "teacher's fist" regarding the teachings,
but explains the words and syllables in their proper sequence.
He analyzes the words and syllables as they were taught in their proper sequence according to their meaning.
He teaches the Dharma and its meaning as connected with the goal, not that which is disconnected from the goal.
He demonstrates what should be demonstrated; he encourages what should be encouraged; he inspires what should be inspired; and he gladdens what should be gladdened.
He delivers discourse consistent with direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture, and not that which is inconsistent with valid means of knowledge.

It is conducive to proceeding toward a happy rebirth, unconfused, easy to enter, and not obscure; it is connected with the four noble truths, and for every assembly, he delivers discourse to each assembly exactly as is appropriate for them.
In these fifteen ways, it should be understood that the discourse of Bodhisattvas toward sentient beings is compliant with all aims for the benefit of others.

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva conducts discourse by establishing a mind of loving-kindness toward those sentient beings who cause harm; he conducts discourse by establishing a mind of beneficial intent toward those sentient beings who engage in misconduct.

Having established a mind of compassion for the welfare and happiness of beings— whether they are happy or suffering, heedless or distressed— he engages in conversation; he does not, however, exalt himself by making the obsession of envy his primary motive,
nor does he disparage others.
And with a mind free from worldly desire, he teaches the Dharma to others without expecting gain, honor, or fame.
By these five aspects, a bodhisattva delivers a completely pure discourse.
In brief, these constitute twenty aspects.

At the proper time, with respect, in due order, continuous and coherent, gladdening, making [them] find pleasure, satisfying, encouraging, and not discouraging; appropriate, consistent, unconfused, and in accordance with the Dharma, according to the assembly; with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of welfare, and a mind of compassion; independent of gain, honor, and fame; not exalting oneself and not disparaging others.
In this way, the bodhisattva teaches the Dharma to others.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s practice in accordance with the Dharma?
In brief, it should be understood as fivefold:
the conformity with, the correct reflection upon, and the cultivation of those very dharmas as they have been sought and as they have been grasped, by means of body, speech, and mind;
and [the avoidance of] those dharmas for which the Blessed One has prohibited action by body, speech, and mind, and the performance of those for which he has permitted action by body.
The verbal, mental, and physical actions— namely, the avoidance, the cultivation, and the accomplishment of those very deeds of body,
speech, and mind— and the conformity of body, speech, and mind [to the teaching], is called the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).
In that regard, what is the right reflection (*samyak-cintanā*) of a bodhisattva?

In this case, a bodhisattva, having gone alone into seclusion and desiring to reflect upon, weigh, and examine the teachings as they have been heard, first avoids those matters that are inconceivable and then begins to reflect on the teachings; he reflects continuously and with earnest application,
not in a lax manner.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva is engaged in reflection, he investigates and penetrates some [teachings] through reasoning, while others he merely accepts with resolute conviction.
And while reflecting, he relies on the meaning and does not rely on the letter.
He understands, as they truly are, the timely instructions and the great instructions;
through his initial entry, he does not enter into discursive thought,
and having entered, he brings it to a state of essential core through repeated mental attention.
Avoiding the inconceivable, the bodhisattva does not fall into delusion or mental distraction.
Constantly and continuously engaged in diligent application, reflecting upon it, he understands and attains meanings previously unknown;
and having attained them, he does not let them perish nor does he forget them.
Furthermore, by investigating, entering into, and examining [the teachings] through reasoning, one does not rely on others.

Regarding those phenomena examined through reasoning, even while having some degree of conviction in them, one does not reject those profound phenomena into which one's own intellect does not penetrate, thinking:
"These phenomena are the domain of the Tathāgata; they are not within the domain of our intellect. Thus, one does not repudiate them.
Relying on the Dharma, the Bodhisattva avoids what is self-destructive, harmful, and blameworthy;
relying on the meaning and not on the letter, he penetrates all the intentional (sandhyāya) utterances of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Skilled in the provisional teachings (kālāpadeśa) and the great teachings (mahāpadeśa), the Bodhisattva cannot be moved or shaken from the true meaning by anyone in any way.
Entering into reflection from the very beginning, the bodhisattva attains a patience never attained before;
then, bringing that very attained patience to its core essence, the bodhisattva enters into cultivation.
By means of these eight aspects, a bodhisattva becomes one who has entered upon the practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti) that is comprised of reflection.
What is cultivation?
In brief, it should be understood as being fourfold.
[It consists of] calm abiding (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), the cultivation of calm abiding and insight, and delight in calm abiding and insight.
In that regard, what is calm abiding?
It is when a bodhisattva, because of having fully perfected the eightfold reflection, [abides] in the ineffable mere thing (*vastumātra*).

Having bound the mind to an object that is merely the thing-in-itself, by means of a perception and mental attention free from all conceptual proliferation and free from all mental wandering, he resolves upon all objects; he settles and stabilizes the mind within the signs of internal concentration, and so on in detail until he unifies it and brings it into samādhi.
This is called *śamatha*.

What is *vipaśyanā*? It is the mental attention to the signs of the phenomena as they were previously reflected upon, by means of that very same mental attention cultivated through *śamatha*; it is investigation, thorough investigation, and the thorough investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), extending in detail up to erudition and the range of wisdom (*prajñā*).
This is called insight (*vipaśyanā*).
What is the practice of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*)?
It is the continuous application and the respectful application toward calm abiding and insight.
What is delight in calm abiding and special insight?

It is the non-wavering of the mind toward those very signs of calm abiding and special insight; it is the state of being carried along by its own natural flow through volitional effort, characterized by gathering [the mind] and non-diffusion.
This is called delight in calm abiding and special insight.
In this regard, to whatever extent a bodhisattva practices calm abiding and insight, to that same extent does delight in calm abiding and insight become established.
To whatever extent delight in calm abiding and insight becomes established, to that same extent do calm abiding and insight become purified.
To whatever extent calm abiding becomes purified, to that same extent physical pliancy and mental pliancy reach a state of vast increase and expansion.

To the extent that insight (*vipaśyanā*) becomes purified, to that same extent the vision of knowledge (*jñānadarśana*) attains expansion, growth, and vastness. This is the entirety of what must be accomplished through cultivation: namely, that the functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) residing in the basis must be removed, and the vision of knowledge regarding all objects of knowledge must be purified.
All of this is accomplished by a bodhisattva through this fourfold cultivation which constitutes the activity of cultivation.
What is instruction?
In brief, it should be understood as being of eight kinds.
That is to say, whether by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or through long-term association, a bodhisattva— who wishes to provide instruction to others—
or another bodhisattva who instructs him, or even a Tathāgata, first searches for and knows the [student's] mind.
Having investigated the mind, one investigates and knows the faculties;
