He dispels the suffering caused by the obsession of sensual desire for those beings who are afflicted by the obsession of sensual desire;

he dispels the suffering caused by the obsessions of ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt, up to the suffering caused by the obsession of doubt, for those beings who are afflicted by them.

He dispels the thought of sensual desire in sentient beings who are suffering from the obsession with thoughts of sensual desire. Just as it is with thoughts of sensual desire, so too should one understand thoughts associated with ill-will, harmfulness, kin, country, and others, as well as thoughts associated with contempt and those associated with the rise of one’s own family, for the sake of those suffering from the pain of humiliation and defeat.
He dispels for sentient beings the suffering of being humiliated and defeated by others;
he dispels the suffering of fatigue and exhaustion for those weary from travel by providing places to stay and seats, and by massaging their limbs.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva, pointing out the right method to sentient beings, teaches the Dharma for the sake of abandoning misconduct by those beings who engage in misconduct, using words and phrases that are logical, coherent, conformable, appropriate, expedient, suitable, favorable, and which constitute the equipment of the limbs of the wise.
Furthermore, he teaches skillful means so that beings who engage in misconduct may abandon such conduct;

likewise, for beings who are miserly, so that they may abandon miserliness; and for those who are obstructed toward this teaching, so that they may acquire wealth with ease and correctly in this very life, and for the sake of protecting that wealth, as well as for the attainment of faith and the attainment of vision.

Through the purity of vision, for the sake of transcending the states of woe by the exhaustion of all fetters, and for the sake of transcending all suffering, the bodhisattva—manifesting gratitude toward those beings who have been helpful to him—upon seeing them, addresses them with respect, converses with them, and greets them, saying: "Come, welcome! by means of a cordial greeting.
He welcomes [the visitor] by offering a seat and a place to stay;
he attends to him with gifts and honors that are equal or superior, never with inferior ones.
Furthermore, he provides assistance in his tasks even without being asked, let alone when requested.

Just as with their duties, so too [they act] regarding sufferings: by teaching the right method, by protecting from fear, by dispelling the grief of those in calamity, by providing necessary resources, by giving support, by conforming to their thoughts, by gladdening them with genuine virtues, by restraining them with affectionate inner disposition, and by startling and winning them over through supernatural power (ṛddhi).
And so forth.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva is a protector of sentient beings who are afraid amidst their fears;
he protects beings even from the fear of small wild animals, from the fear of whirlpools and crocodiles, from the fear of kings, and from the fear of thieves.

Out of fear of adversaries, fear of one's master or sovereign, fear of lack of livelihood, fear of ill-repute, fear of timidity before an assembly, and even fear of non-human beings such as *vetāḍas*,
the bodhisattva further dispels the grief of sentient beings who are in distress, beginning with the loss of kinsmen; he dispels their sorrow even in the event of the death of a mother or father.

Even upon the death of sons and wives, or the death of female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, or the death of friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations, or even the death of teachers, preceptors, and those in the position of gurus, he dispels his grief. Furthermore, regarding the loss of enjoyments— should those enjoyments be seized by the king or by others—
he dispels his grief in that regard as well.
Or they are stolen by thieves;
or they are consumed by fire, swept away by water, or lost because of being poorly stored;
or undertakings poorly executed come to ruin.
Or they may come into possession of unpleasant heirs,
or they may be born as a ruinous member within their own family.
A bodhisattva correctly dispels the mild, moderate, or intense sorrow that arises in sentient beings due to the fact that their wealth has been brought to ruin through improper means. Furthermore,
by providing the necessary requisites to those who desire them, a bodhisattva gives food to those who seek food.
Drink for those who desire drink;
vehicles for those who desire vehicles;
clothing for those who desire clothing.
Ornaments to those who desire ornaments;
household utensils and implements to those who desire household utensils and implements; perfumes, garlands, and ointments to those who desire perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
He gives shelter to those seeking shelter and light to those seeking light.

Furthermore, by means of the virtue of embracing others, the bodhisattva, while providing for sentient beings through the method of gathering a following, first provides a refuge with a mind free from worldly desire, with a mind of compassion, and indeed with nothing but a mind of compassion.

Having placed them at the forefront, he then seeks on their behalf— through righteous means and what has been lawfully obtained— from faithful brahmins and householders, robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick. And with his own righteous robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he shares in common enjoyment and does not eat in secret.
He also provides, from time to time, the eightfold conformable instruction and correctly exhorts [the disciple] by means of the fivefold admonition;
this should be understood here in the same way as it was explained in the "Chapter on the Lineage of the Power of Admonition."

Furthermore, by means of the ethical discipline of conforming to the minds of sentient beings, the bodhisattva, while conforming to their minds, from the very beginning knows both the dispositions and the natures of those beings. Having known their dispositions and natures, he dwells together with those beings in whatever manner it is necessary to dwell with them,
and he conducts himself toward those beings in whatever manner it is necessary to conduct oneself toward them.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva desires to comply with the mind of a certain being, and perceives that through such a physical or verbal engagement with that person, suffering and mental distress would arise for them—
and if that suffering and distress would not lead to their emergence from an unwholesome state nor to their establishment in a wholesome state—
then the bodhisattva, having reflected upon this, diligently avoids and does not engage in that physical or verbal conduct.
If, however, he perceives that this suffering and mental distress would lead to withdrawing [the person] from an unwholesome state and establishing them in a wholesome state,
the bodhisattva does not comply; rather, having reflected, he attends to the minds of others— specifically out of compassion for others— for the sake of what [benefits] others.
When physical or verbal conduct gives rise to suffering and mental distress in others,
and that [conduct] does not lead to the turning away of those others from unwholesome states nor to their establishment in wholesome states,
the bodhisattva, having reflected upon it, withdraws that physical and verbal conduct in order to protect the minds of those others.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva observes that others— whether they be different individuals or both [himself and others]— are acting with deliberate intent to rise from an unwholesome state and establish themselves in a wholesome state, he does not conform to those physical or verbal behaviors; rather,
having established a mind of compassion toward those sentient beings, he acts accordingly.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva perceives that through his own physical and verbal conduct toward others suffering and mental distress arise, yet that physical and verbal conduct is neither embraced by the training precepts nor accompanied by the accumulations of merit and knowledge—
and that suffering and mental distress of others [arise] from an unwholesome state— this is to be understood as previously explained.
The bodhisattva withdraws that conduct of body and speech out of regard for the minds of others;
conversely, the opposite conduct should be understood as before.
Just as with suffering and mental distress, so too should pleasure and mental joy be understood in detail according to their respective applications.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva who conforms to the minds of others does not, while another person is still under the sway of an outburst of anger, speak even a word of praise in their presence—much less a word of disparagement—nor does he offer them consolation as long as that outburst has not subsided.
Moreover, a bodhisattva who conforms to the minds of others addresses and greets another person even if they do not address him; how much more so if that person is already addressing or greeting him?
A bodhisattva who conforms to the minds of others does not become agitated by others, nor does he intend to disparage them;
rather, out of compassion for them alone, he disparages them with tranquil faculties.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva who conforms to the minds of others does not mock another, nor does he deride them, nor does he cause them to feel embarrassed, nor does he instill remorse in them so that they dwell in unease.
Even when another has been censured or defeated, he does not urge them on by means of that point of defeat. When another has fallen into a low state, he does not proclaim his own exalted status.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva who conforms to the minds of others does not become a non-associate with others, nor an over-familiar associate, nor one who associates at the wrong time; nor does he disparage what is pleasing to them before their faces, nor praise what is unpleasing to them.
Nor does he place undue trust in those with whom he is not acquainted;
he does not become a constant beggar,
and even when receiving gifts, he knows the proper measure.

When invited to accept food, drink, and so forth, he does not refuse; or, being righteous, he provides a response that is consistent with the Dharma and reason. Furthermore, by means of the discipline of gladdening beings through their actual virtues, the bodhisattva causes them to rejoice, making them endowed with the quality of faith.

He gladdens those endowed with the quality of faith by discourse on the quality of faith; those endowed with the quality of ethical discipline by discourse on the quality of ethical discipline; those endowed with the quality of learning by discourse on the quality of learning; those endowed with the quality of generosity by discourse on the quality of generosity; and those endowed with the quality of wisdom by discourse on the quality of wisdom.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva restrains sentient beings through the discipline of restraint, he reprimands them for a minor offense or a minor transgression with a gentle internal disposition, being undisturbed, using mild censure.

He subjects a person of middling offense and middling transgression to a middling form of censure; he subjects a person of excessive offense and excessive transgression to an excessive form of censure. Just as it is with censure, so should the disciplinary action (daṇḍakarma) be understood.
A Bodhisattva, through a temporary application, [deals with] a mild or middling offense and mild or middling transgression for the sake of a renewed undertaking.

Out of a mind of compassion, for the sake of instructing them and others, he banishes those who have committed an excessive offense or transgression— banishing them so that they no longer dwell with him, do not share in the community, and are not readmitted even for the rest of their lives—
and he does this out of compassion for them alone.
Thinking, "Lest they should acquire a great deal of demerit within this teaching," and for the sake of instructing others out of a desire for their welfare,
the bodhisattva, wishing to cause beings who practice misconduct to be free from fear or to win them over by means of the power of supernatural transformations (ṛddhi), [acts accordingly].
He leads beings, one by one, to the states of woe—the hells, the great hells, the cold hells, and the individual hells—and shows them, saying:
"Behold, sirs, this kind of fierce, supremely bitter, and undesirable ripening of the fruit of misconduct committed and accumulated while in human form.
Upon seeing this, they become terrified, experience a sense of spiritual urgency, and desist from misconduct.

When certain beings, seated in the great assembly of the Bodhisattva, desire to make his speech unconvincing by means of challenging questions, the Bodhisattva— having conjured up Vajrapāṇi or some other yakṣa of magnificent appearance, great body, and great strength— frightens and terrifies them.
This was for the purpose of correctly answering the questions of those who had developed conviction and great respect on that account;
and it was for the purpose of disciplining that great multitude of people by means of that answer to their questions;
or else, by means of various miraculous transformations—such as becoming many after being one, becoming one after being many, or passing through walls...

Passing through mountains and walls with a body that meets no resistance, extending [his power] as far as the Brahma-world, bringing his body under control, displaying even the twin miracles (*yamakaprātihārya*), and entering the fire-element (*tejodhātu*), he further manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) not shared by the disciples; thus winning them over, satisfying them, and gladdening them, he inspired faith in those who lacked it.
He establishes those lacking faith in the perfection of faith;

those of immoral conduct in the perfection of morality; those of little learning in the perfection of learning; the stingy in the perfection of generosity; and the foolish in the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, the bodhisattva becomes endowed with the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings in every possible manner.
These constitute the three aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) of a bodhisattva, which are immeasurable aggregates of merit:

the aggregate of ethical discipline comprised of the morality of restraint (*saṃvaraśīla*), the aggregate of ethical discipline comprised of the morality of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhakaśīla*), and the aggregate of ethical discipline comprised of the morality of acting for the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyāśīla*).
In this regard, a bodhisattva who desires to train in the bodhisattva training within these three types of aggregates of ethical discipline [should proceed as follows].

Whether a householder or one who has gone forth, having made a vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, one should first prostrate at the feet of a fellow-practitioner bodhisattva— one who has likewise made the vow, who is wise, and capable of understanding the meaning of verbal communication— and having thus made a formal request, [say]: "Just as I am [to you]..."

"O son of noble family, I desire to receive the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline from you; therefore, out of compassion for us, you should please grant me a moment to listen and explain this without hindrance.
Having thus made the proper request, one should arrange the upper robe over one shoulder and [pay homage] to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present.

Having paid homage to the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who have entered the great stages and attained the power of great gnosis, and having brought their virtues before his mind, he generates a profound and intense clarity of heart; then, whatever small amount he requests, according to his capacity and the strength of his causal roots—

That wise bodhisattva, having placed an image of the Tathāgata before him—either kneeling with his knees on the ground or sitting in a squatting posture—and having paid full homage, should speak as follows:
"O son of good family, O venerable one, O Bhadanta, please grant me the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline.
Having said this, he should establish one-pointed mindfulness and cultivate clarity of mind; then, before long, for him...
Thinking, "The attainment of the immeasurable, unsurpassed, and great treasure of merit will come to pass," one should remain silent while reflecting on this very matter.
Furthermore, that wise Bodhisattva, with an undistracted mind, should address the Bodhisattva who has practiced accordingly while he is either standing or seated upon his seat, saying this:

"Listen, O son of good family [or] Dharma-brother named so-and-so: you are a bodhisattva who has made the vow for awakening. He should respond, "So be it. Furthermore, he should be addressed with these further words:

"Do you, O son of good family named [so-and-so], accept from me all the bodhisattva training precepts and the entire bodhisattva morality— the morality of restraint, the morality of gathering virtuous qualities, and the morality of acting for the welfare of sentient beings— those very precepts and that very morality which belonged to all bodhisattvas of the past?"
Those training rules and that ethical discipline which will belong to all future bodhisattvas;
those training rules and that ethical discipline which currently belong to all bodhisattvas in the ten directions;
and those training rules and that ethical discipline in which all past bodhisattvas have trained.
All bodhisattvas of the future will train in it;
all bodhisattvas of the present are training in it.
Therefore, one should declare: "I accept it."
In this manner, that wise bodhisattva should speak thus a second and a third time;
and that bodhisattva who is receiving [the gift], being asked, should likewise promise it up to three times.
For in this way, by that wise bodhisattva, for that bodhisattva who is the recipient, up to three times—

Having bestowed the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline and having received the formal pledge, while that bodhisattva who has accepted it has not yet risen, one should prostrate at the feet of all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas dwelling, remaining, and staying in the ten directions before that very image of the Tathāgata, perform the proper salutation, and announce as follows:
This Bodhisattva, named [Name], has accepted from me, a Bodhisattva named [Name], the undertaking of the Bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline even up to three times.
Therefore, I, [Name], declare myself as a witness for this Bodhisattva named [Name] before the supreme Noble Ones— who, though beyond my sight,
possess a non-deluded cognition of all sentient beings everywhere throughout the infinite and boundless world-systems in the ten directions.

The undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*) should be recited in this same way a second and a third time as well. Furthermore, immediately after the completion of the ritual action for undertaking the vow of ethical discipline, this is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*): or rather...

In the infinite and boundless world-systems throughout the ten directions, such a sign appears for the Tathāgatas and for the Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages, as they abide and maintain themselves,
by which they come to this thought:
When a bodhisattva has completed the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline,
those [buddhas] immediately direct their attention toward that bodhisattva;
and as they direct their attention, a vision of knowledge arises.
Through that knowledge and vision, they perceive things exactly as they truly are:
"In such a world system, a Bodhisattva named so-and-so has received the formal undertaking of the Bodhisattva’s vow of perfect ethical discipline from a Bodhisattva named so-and-so.
And they all regard this [Bodhisattva] with virtuous thoughts, feeling compassion for him as if he were their own son or brother.
Thus, for that bodhisattva who has been compassionately favored by a virtuous mind,
an even greater increase in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not a decline;
and those [bodhisattvas] should be understood as having accepted his announcement of the undertaking of that vow of ethical discipline.
And upon the completion of that ritual for undertaking the vow of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline, both of those bodhisattvas,

having performed a respectful salutation toward the Buddhas and bodhisattvas residing in the infinite and boundless world-systems throughout the ten directions, should rise after prostrating at their feet.

This undertaking of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*) is preeminent among all undertakings of ethical discipline; it is unsurpassed, endowed with an immeasurable mass of merit, originated from a supreme and virtuous mental disposition, and serves as the antidote for every form of misconduct toward all sentient beings.

The undertaking of this restraint of ethical discipline does not allow even a hundredth part of all the undertakings of the *prātimokṣa* restraints to approach it; nor even a thousandth part, nor any number, fraction, calculation, comparison, or likeness—
this being with respect to the acquisition of merit.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva, having thus established himself in the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline, should repeatedly reflect for himself: "This is appropriate for a bodhisattva to do; this is inappropriate for a bodhisattva to do," and from then on, he should carry out his actions accordingly and train in the precepts.

Having heard it with effort either from the Bodhisattva Sūtra Piṭaka or from this compendium (*mātṛkā*) of the Bodhisattva Sūtra Piṭaka, one should train in exactly that way. Furthermore, this undertaking of the vow of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) should not be received from all [teachers], even if they are learned;
a bodhisattva must not receive it from one who lacks faith.

Whoever, from the very beginning, would not have faith in, would not enter into, and would not resolve upon such an undertaking of the restraint of ethical discipline—for one who is greedy, overcome by greed, full of great desire, and discontented; for one whose morality is ruined, who shows no respect for the trainings, and is lax; for one who is wrathful, resentful, full of intolerance, and unable to endure the transgressions of others—[for such a person, this is not possible].

It is not for one who is indolent and lazy, who for the most part throughout day and night indulges in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of lying down, and who passes his time in socializing; nor for one whose mind is distracted, who is ultimately incapable of cultivating one-pointedness of a wholesome mind even for as long as it takes to milk a cow.

It is not for one who is dull-witted, nor for one of a deluded nature, nor for a bodhisattva whose mind is excessively withdrawn, nor for one who disparages the Bodhisattva Sūtra-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka-mātṛkā.

Furthermore, even after a bodhisattva has taken up and mastered this procedure for undertaking the vows, he must not suddenly proclaim or reveal it to those beings who are hostile toward the Bodhisattva Piṭaka or lack faith in it.
For what reason? Because,
having heard it and not being convinced, they would be obscured by a great veil of ignorance and would revile it.

And whoever slanders him becomes possessed of an immeasurable mass of demerit for as long as that bodhisattva, established in restraint, remains endowed with an immeasurable mass of merit— until he completely and utterly abandons that evil speech, that evil view, and those evil intentions.

And for a bodhisattva who desires to undertake the restraint of ethical discipline, those training precepts and bases of transgression for a bodhisattva which are declared in this *Mātṛkā* of the Bodhisattva Sūtra-piṭaka should be recited in his presence.
If, having reflected with intention and deliberated with wisdom, he exerts himself [to observe them], [he should undertake them].
A bodhisattva should not be known as steadfast by means of inciting others to take up vows, nor through rivalry with others;
rather, he himself should receive it and give it to the other according to this procedure for the undertaking of this restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*).
And for a bodhisattva thus established in the restraint of ethical discipline, there are four dharmas that constitute grounds for defeat (*pārājika*).
Which four?
For a Bodhisattva who is intent upon gain and honor, self-exaltation and disparagement of others constitute an offense involving defeat (*pārājika-sthānīya-dharma*).
Furthermore, when resources are available, due to a nature of greed, [to fail to give] to those who are suffering, miserable, helpless, without refuge, and who beg in a proper manner;

When [suitable recipients] have approached, the failure to give material gifts out of stinginess, and the failure to share the teachings with seekers who have properly approached due to envy regarding the Dharma, are points of defeat for a bodhisattva. Furthermore,
when a bodhisattva nourishes such an obsession with anger that he does not desist merely by uttering harsh words.
Overcome by anger, one strikes, harms, or oppresses sentient beings with the hand, a clod of earth, a staff, or a weapon;
and having harbored an intense intent of anger within, one does not accept, does not forgive, and does not relinquish the intent when others acknowledge their transgression.
This also is a dharma for a bodhisattva that constitutes a defeat.

To disparage the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; to delight in, illuminate, and establish what are counterfeits of the true Dharma; or, being oneself inclined toward such counterfeits of the true Dharma, to follow the example of others—these are the bodhisattva’s dharmas that constitute grounds for defeat. Thus, these are the four dharmas that constitute grounds for defeat.

If a bodhisattva commits even one of these [offenses], let alone all of them, he becomes incapable in this very life of accumulating and acquiring the vast equipment of a bodhisattva, and he becomes incapable in this very life of purifying his intention.
He is a counterfeit bodhisattva, but not a true bodhisattva.

Furthermore, due to mild or moderate obsession, a bodhisattva does not abandon the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline through the commission of these four offenses involving defeat.
However, he abandons it through the intensity of the outburst (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*).

For when a bodhisattva, due to the frequent occurrence of these four dharmas that constitute grounds for defeat, does not give rise to even a slight sense of shame or dread of blame, and instead takes pleasure in them; [then he has fallen].
And one delights in that;
one perceives its qualities therein.
This should be understood as the intensity of the outburst of the affliction.

However, a bodhisattva does not abandon the undertaking of the bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*) merely by once committing an act that constitutes a defeat (*pārājayika-sthānīya-dharma*), in the same way that a monk abandons the *prātimokṣa* restraint through the defeat dharmas. Furthermore,
even if he has abandoned the undertaking, a bodhisattva remains capable in this very life of re-undertaking the bodhisattva ethical discipline.
One does not become incapable [of the vow], such as a monk abiding in the *prātimokṣa* restraint who has committed a defeat (*pārājika*).
In brief, the relinquishment of the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s ethical restraint occurs for only two reasons:
through the abandonment of the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and through the repeated commission of an intense obsession with a factor equivalent to a defeat.
Furthermore, even when he has undergone a change of birth, the bodhisattva does not abandon his undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*).
Whether being reborn below, above, or across the horizontal directions, wherever he may arise, that bodhisattva has not relinquished his original aspiration (*praṇidhāna*),
nor has he committed an excessive outburst of the afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) corresponding to the points of defeat (*pārājika*).

However, a bodhisattva who has undergone a change of birth and whose mindfulness has been lost takes up the vows again and again for the purpose of awakening that mindfulness upon encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);
yet this is not a new undertaking.
In this way, one should understand the nature of an offense even for a bodhisattva established in the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*).
There is also non-offense, which may be afflicted or unafflicted, and mild, medium, or intense. Thus,

a bodhisattva established in the bodhisattva ethical discipline should, every day, [make offerings] before a Tathāgata or at a shrine dedicated to a Tathāgata, or before the Dharma or at a shrine dedicated to the Dharma— even if it is merely the Bodhisattva Sūtra Piṭaka existing in the form of a book.

In the *Mātṛkā* of the Bodhisattva Sūtra-piṭaka, or regarding the Saṅgha— that is, the community of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages throughout the ten directions— if one has not performed even a small or great act of worship toward them,
at the very least a single prostration with the body, or at the very least a single four-line verse concerning their qualities, directed toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha...

If one passes day and night with speech uttering even a single verse from the Gāthās, or even a single moment of serene faith preceded by mental recollection of the virtues of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, one becomes guilty of an offense and transgression.
If, however, one falls into this through lack of respect, laziness, or indolence, one has committed an afflicted offense.
If he commits an offense through a lapse of mindfulness, he has fallen into an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense for one whose mind is deranged;
there is no offense for one who has entered the stage of pure intention.

For instance, a bodhisattva of pure intention— just as a monk who has attained verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) constantly serves the Teacher by the very nature of things and honors him with supreme worship,
and likewise [serves] the Dharma and the Saṅgha—
a bodhisattva who indulges in great desire, lack of contentment, and greed for gain and honor that have arisen becomes guilty of an offense, transgresses his rule, and incurs an afflicted offense.

There is no offense for one who has generated the desire to abandon those [defilements] and exerts vigor, yet, by embracing their opposites, remains hindered by them; nor for one who, being naturally possessed of intense afflictions, is overwhelmed and thus repeatedly manifests them again and again. Furthermore, there is no offense if a bodhisattva, upon seeing a fellow practitioner who is senior, virtuous, and worthy of honor, fails to rise and offer his seat because he is gripped by pride, or possesses a mind of malice, or a mind of resentment.
When addressed by others, greeted with a welcome, or questioned, if one does not respond with an appropriate verbal reply—
being held back by pride, or having a mind of malice or resentment— one becomes guilty of an offense, incurs a transgression,
and falls into a defiled offense.

If one is not constrained by pride, nor possesses a mind of malice or resentment, but rather, due to indolence and laziness, has a neutral state of mind, or due to a lapse of mindfulness, one indeed incurs an offense and a transgression,
yet does not incur an afflicted offense. There is no offense, however, if one is severely ill or mentally deranged.
There is no offense if he is asleep and the other person approaches, speaks, converses, greets, or questions him while perceiving him to be awake.
There is no offense for one who is engaged in teaching the Dharma to others or in the definitive resolution of discussion.
There is no offense for one who is greeting others besides that person.
There is no offense for one who listens with attentive ears while others are teaching the Dharma, or during a discussion or a definitive resolution of a point.
There is no offense for one who protects against a lack of interest in a discourse on the Dharma and guards the mind of the preacher of the Dharma.
There is no offense for one who, by that means, tames and disciplines those beings, causing them to rise from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state.
[There is no offense]: there is no offense for one who observes a formal agreement made by the Saṃgha; there is no offense for one who observes the minds of a greater number of others.

When a bodhisattva is invited by others to a house, another monastery, or another residence for food, drink, clothing, or other requisites, if he does not go because he is overcome by pride, or possesses a mind of malice, or a mind of resentment, [there is no offense].

If he does not accept an invitation, he becomes guilty of an offense involving transgression; he incurs an afflicted offense. If he does not go because of indolence or laziness, he incurs a non-afflicted offense.
There is no offense if one is ill, lacks the physical strength, or is deranged in mind;
there is no offense if the location is remote or the path is dangerous;
there is no offense if one intends to subdue that person by such means, or intends to discipline them, desiring to raise them up from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state.
There is no offense if one has already made a prior commitment to another;

there is no offense for one who does not go in order to protect the continuity of the application to the side of the wholesome by avoiding interruptions in that application; and there is no offense for the sake of preventing the loss of hearing the Dharma and its meaning, which is unprecedented and conducive to welfare.
Just as it should be understood regarding the hearing of the Dharma and its meaning, so too should it be understood regarding the determination of discussion.
There is no offense if one has been invited with the intention of causing harassment. There is no offense if one protects against the hostile mind of many others.
There is no offense for one who observes the communal regulations of the Saṃgha.

When a bodhisattva receives from others various kinds of abundant and excellent wealth— such as gold, silver, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, and so forth— and, being displeased and with a mind of malice or resentment, does not accept it but rejects it, there is no offense.
If one neglects sentient beings, one becomes guilty of an offense and transgression, and incurs an afflicted offense. If one does not accept [a gift] due to indolence or laziness,
one becomes guilty of an offense and transgression, but does not incur an afflicted offense.
There is no offense for one whose mind is deranged;
there is no offense for one who perceives that the mind finds delight in accepting that gift;
and there is no offense for one who anticipates that remorse will arise in him later.
There is no offense for one who suspects a confusion regarding the gift;
there is no offense for a donor who suspects that [the recipient] is free from grasping, or who suspects that it would cause poverty or ruin for him on that account;
there is no offense for one who suspects that it belongs to the Saṅgha or to a stūpa.
There is no offense for one who suspects that what has been taken away by another would lead to his death, imprisonment, punishment, or public reproach. Furthermore,
there is no offense if a bodhisattva, out of a mind of malice, resentment, or being disturbed by envy, does not bestow the Dharma upon others who seek it.
One becomes guilty of an offense and transgresses; one incurs an afflicted offense.
If one does not give due to laziness or indolence, one becomes guilty of an offense and transgresses, but does not incur an afflicted offense.
There is no offense if the person is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) seeking for a vulnerability.
There is no offense if he is severely ill or mentally deranged;
there is no offense if, by that means, he intends to subdue him, intends to discipline him, or intends to raise him up from an unwholesome state and establish him in a wholesome state;
there is no offense if he himself has not yet entered into the Dharma.
There is no offense if he should accept [the gift] from one who is disrespectful, lacking reverence, and of improper conduct.

There is no offense if, by means of a sublime teaching of the Dharma or a thorough mastery of the Dharma, he perceives that a person of dull faculties would experience terror, false views, false attachments, injury, or harm.
There is no offense if he perceives that once it has fallen into the hands of such a person, the Dharma would be dispersed among others who are unfit vessels.

If a bodhisattva, harboring a mind of malice or a mind of resentment toward beings who are fierce or of immoral conduct, remains indifferent or acts [negligently] by making their fierceness and immorality the very pretext for doing so, he becomes guilty of an offense and a transgression; he incurs an afflicted offense. If he remains indifferent out of laziness and indolence, or acts [negligently] through the loss of mindfulness, he likewise incurs an offense.
He becomes guilty of an offense and transgresses the rule, yet he does not incur an afflicted offense.
Why is that?
Because for a virtuous Bodhisattva whose physical, vocal, and mental actions proceed with tranquility, there is no lack of a mind of compassion.
And there is the presence of a desire to act toward beings who are fierce, immoral, and abiding in the causes of suffering.
There is no offense for one whose mind is deranged.
There is no offense if, by that means, one intends to discipline them, as detailed previously.
There is no offense for one who protects the minds of many others;
there is no offense for one who protects the formal procedures of the Saṅgha.

Regarding that which the Blessed One has established in the Prātimokṣa Vinaya as a fault of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)—a Bodhisattva may commit it out of consideration for protecting the minds of others, for the sake of inspiring faith in beings who lack faith, and for the sake of increasing the faith of those who already possess it.
For the sake of further increase,
he practices the training there in common with the śrāvakas, without exception.
For what reason?

The śrāvakas, for their part, are intent primarily on their own welfare; they do not train in the precepts even for the sake of inspiring faith in those who lack it or increasing the faith of those who already possess it, without regard for others.
How much more so, then, must this be true for bodhisattvas, who are intent primarily on the welfare of others?

Furthermore, regarding those prohibitions established by the Blessed One for the Śrāvakas— concerning limited aims, limited activities, and dwelling with limited zeal— a Bodhisattva does not undertake a training identical to that of the Śrāvakas in those matters.
For what reason?

A śrāvaka who is intent upon his own welfare, indifferent to the welfare of others, and who—when undertaking the welfare of others—is of little purpose, of few duties, and dwells with little zeal, is fitting.
But a bodhisattva who is intent upon the welfare of others is not fitting if he is of little purpose, of few duties, and dwells with little zeal regarding the welfare of others.
For it is thus: a bodhisattva, when invited, should seek out hundreds or thousands of robes from unrelated brahmins and householders for the sake of others;
and having observed the strength and weakness of those beings, he should accept as much as is needed.
Just as it is with robes, so it is with bowls.
Just as they are to be sought, so too should they be woven by unrelated weavers using thread requested by oneself;
and for the sake of others, hundreds of silk rugs and hundreds of sitting mats should be provided;
even hundreds of thousands of millions of gold and silver coins should be accepted.

Regarding such matters as having few concerns, few duties, and dwelling with little zeal, a bodhisattva established in the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline who, out of a mind of malice or resentment toward sentient beings, has few concerns, few duties, and dwells with little zeal, becomes equal in training to the śrāvakas regarding that which is an offense by prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*). Such a bodhisattva incurs an offense, commits a transgression, and falls into an afflicted offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*).
Due to indolence and laziness, he becomes one who achieves little, performs few deeds, and dwells with little zeal;
he incurs an offense and a transgression, yet he falls into an unafflicted offense.

There are certain things that are naturally reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*) which a bodhisattva may practice through such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) that he remains without offense and generates great merit.

It is as when a bodhisattva sees a thief or a robber intent on killing many hundreds of living beings— great-souled śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas— for the sake of some small material gain, and engaged in performing many acts of immediate retribution;
having seen this, he further forms a thought in his mind as follows:

"Even if, by depriving this living being of life, I were to be reborn in the hells— let my rebirth in the hells be as it may— I must ensure that this sentient being, having committed an act of immediate retribution, does not end up destined for hell. With such an intention, the Bodhisattva, having recognized that the living being is possessed of a wholesome or neutral mind, feels a sense of revulsion [toward the act].
Out of a mind of compassion alone, with regard for their future welfare, he deprives them of life;
he incurs no offense and generates much merit.
This is as when a bodhisattva [deals with] those beings who are kings or royal ministers, who are exceedingly fierce toward sentient beings, merciless, and solely intent on harming others.

When he has the power to do so, he causes them to fall from that sovereignty, lordship, and dominion; for wherever they remain, on that basis they produce great demerit. With a mind of compassion and an intention for their welfare and happiness, the Bodhisattva seizes that property from those who are thieves and robbers who steal the belongings of others, having taken away abundant wealth belonging to the Saṅgha or to a Stūpa, and desiring to appropriate and enjoy it for themselves.
"Lest that enjoyment of their property by them lead to harm and disadvantage for a long time"—
making this very consideration, he seizes what belongs to the community (*saṃghika*) and delivers it to the stūpa, and what belongs to the stūpa (*staupika*) to the community;
and those who are attendants or monastery-keepers (*ārāmika*) misappropriate abundant property belonging to both the community and the stūpa through improper means.
If they themselves consume what belongs to an individual person,
the Bodhisattva, having reflected upon it, thinks: "May this karma not lead to their long-term misfortune and harm through such improper consumption."
Therefore, he causes [the person] to fall from that state of dominance.
In this manner, even though the bodhisattva takes what has not been given, he incurs no offense and generates much merit.

For instance, a householder bodhisattva might engage in sexual intercourse with a woman who is not under the protection of another, whose mind is bound to him, and who is distressed by the search for non-celibacy; he does so out of compassion, thinking:
"Lest she, having conceived a heart of malice, produce much demerit;

rather, may she become submissive in the application of roots of merit as desired, and in the abandonment of unwholesome roots. Thus, maintaining only a mind of compassion, he engages in the practice of non-celibate sexual intercourse.
Even in that case, he is not guilty of an offense and generates much merit;
however, for a bodhisattva who has gone forth and who wishes to preserve the integrity of the Śrāvaka teaching, the practice of unchaste conduct is in no way permissible.

For instance, for the sake of liberating many beings from death, for the sake of liberating them from bondage, and for the sake of protecting them from the severing of hands, feet, noses, or ears, or from the impairment of their eyes—
a falsehood which a bodhisattva would not knowingly utter even for the sake of his own life.
He speaks that [teaching] after having reflected for the sake of those beings.
Thus, in brief, by whatever means a bodhisattva perceives only the welfare of beings and does not perceive what is not their welfare.
He himself possesses a mind free from worldly desire;
and having set aside his perception with the sole motive of wishing for the welfare of sentient beings, he speaks words to the contrary while remaining mindful and clearly conscious.
While speaking thus, he incurs no offense.
And he produces much merit;

for instance, when there are sentient beings who are under the influence of non-virtuous friends, the bodhisattva speaks words intended to cause separation from those non-virtuous friends to the best of his power and ability.

He becomes one who delights in causing dissension among the assembly, yet he does so out of a mind of compassion, thinking: "May these beings not suffer harm and disadvantage for a long time through association with evil friends.
By this method, even while creating a breach between friends, the bodhisattva remains free from transgression.
And he produces much merit;

for instance, when a bodhisattva reproaches with harsh and sharp speech those beings who walk on a wrong path or act unjustly, it is solely by that means for the purpose of causing them to rise from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state.
In this way, a bodhisattva who speaks harshly incurs no offense and generates much merit,

provided that it is for the sake of sentient beings who are devoted to dance, song, and instrumental music, or who are devoted to talk concerning kings, thieves, food, drink, prostitutes, streets, and the like.

And by means of dance, song, and instrumental music, as well as various conversations associated with frivolous talk (*sambhinnapralāpa*), he— out of a compassionate disposition— delights beings, wins them over,

brings them to a state of submissiveness and obedience, and having raised them from unwholesome states, establishes them in wholesome states. In this way, even a bodhisattva who engages in frivolous talk incurs no offense.
And he produces much merit.
A bodhisattva does not tolerate arisen hypocrisy, flattery, hinting, belittling, the desire to obtain gain by means of gain, or those qualities that constitute wrong livelihood;
he does not delight in them.
If one does not dispel [the affliction],
one becomes guilty of an offense involving transgression and incurs an afflicted offense.

There is no offense, however, for one who has generated the desire to dispel it and has exerted effort, yet the affliction continues to manifest because the mind is overwhelmed by the abundance of defilements.
A bodhisattva, with a mind seized by restlessness, being unpacified and not delighting in pacification, laughs loudly, plays, and makes a clamorous noise; he manifests agitation and levity,
desiring to make others laugh and desiring to entertain them.

And having made such a condition, one becomes guilty of an offense and commits a transgression; through loss of mindfulness, one incurs an afflicted offense, whereas through [mere] forgetfulness, one incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense for one who has developed the desire to dispel that [distraction], as previously stated.
There is no offense if one intends to dispel the malice arisen in others by means of that [method].
There is no offense if one wishes to dispel grief that has arisen in others.
There is no offense for the sake of gathering in those who are of such a nature or who delight in such things, or for the sake of preserving their affection, or for the purpose of conforming to them.

There is no offense for the purpose of demonstrating a state of pleasantness, inner purity, and clarity to others who have conceived resentment toward a bodhisattva, or who have conceived malice and aversion.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva should hold such a view and speak thus: "A bodhisattva should not dwell delighting in nirvāṇa;
rather, he should dwell with his face turned away from nirvāṇa.
He should not fear the afflictions and secondary afflictions, nor should he entirely withdraw his mind from them."
For it is thus: a bodhisattva must fully realize awakening while wandering through cyclic existence for three incalculable eons.
[If he fails to do so,] he becomes guilty of an offense, he transgresses, and he incurs an afflicted offense.
Why is that?

Just as a śrāvaka must cultivate delight in nirvāṇa and cause the mind to be repelled by the afflictions and secondary afflictions, so too a bodhisattva must cultivate delight in nirvāṇa with a hundred thousand times ten millionfold greater intensity and develop a repulsion toward the afflictions and secondary afflictions for the mind.
For in this way, while the śrāvaka is engaged for his own sake, the bodhisattva is engaged for the sake of all sentient beings.

Therefore, he must cultivate the practice of non-affliction of mind such that, even though he is not yet an arhat, he may move about amidst tainted objects while endowed with a non-affliction superior to theirs.
A bodhisattva does not protect against or avoid the unpleasant sound of his own untrustworthy speech, nor infamy and ill repute, when these concern a factual matter.
He becomes guilty of an offense and transgresses; he incurs an afflicted offense.
If he does not avoid [the matter] when it concerns an unreal fact, he becomes guilty of an offense and transgresses; he incurs a non-afflicted offense.
There is no offense if the other person is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika),
or if anyone else is similarly obstinate.
There is no offense if an ill-repute should arise on account of one’s going forth, one’s mendicant life, or one’s practice of wholesome conduct.

There is no offense if one should utter it while overcome by anger or with a perverted mind. However, if a bodhisattva perceives that a certain harsh application or sharp application would be for the benefit of sentient beings, yet does not carry out that application because of a desire to protect them from mental distress,
he becomes guilty of an offense and transgression.
He incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense if he perceives a minor benefit pertaining to the present life, while seeing that it would cause great mental distress as a consequence;
or if a bodhisattva, when reviled by others, reviles them in return.
When provoked to anger, he returns the provocation;
when struck, he strikes back;
when reviled, he reviles in return.

He becomes guilty of an offense, incurs transgression, and falls into a defiled offense: if a bodhisattva, having committed a transgression against others or being suspected of such a transgression, with a mind of malice and held fast by pride, does not grant a suitable apology but remains indifferent,
he becomes guilty of an offense, incurs transgression, and falls into a defiled offense.

If, due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, one does not grant a formal reconciliation, one becomes guilty of an offense and incurs transgression; yet this is an unafflicted offense. There is no offense if, by that means, one intends to subdue or discipline [the person], desiring to turn them away from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state.
There is no offense if he is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
There is no offense if he desires to receive a formal admonition for engaging in improper or blameworthy conduct.
There is no offense if he is by nature quarrelsome and prone to creating legal disputes (adhikaraṇika).
If, while being conciliated, he should become even more angry and hostile,

there is no offense if he perceives that the other person is by nature patient and free from malice, and thus refrains from conciliation because it would cause excessive distress to the other regarding the transgression.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva, with a mind of resentment and an intent to harm others, refuses to grant conciliation according to the Dharma and in an equitable manner to others who have come to him for a dispute and are seeking to be reconciled, [there is an offense].
He does not accept it;
he becomes guilty of an offense, an infraction, and incurs an afflicted offense.
If, however, he does not accept it not out of a mind of malice, but because of a disposition toward intolerance, [he incurs an unafflicted offense].
One incurs an afflicted offense.

There is no offense if one desires to subdue another by that means; all should be understood as previously stated. There is no offense if one should offer a conciliatory reconciliation (saṃjñapti) that is contrary to the Dharma or unjust.

If a bodhisattva harbors, maintains, and tolerates an arisen intent toward anger in others, he becomes guilty of an offense, he transgresses, and he incurs an afflicted offense. There is no offense, however, for one who has generated the desire to abandon that [anger], as previously described.
(Dutt 118) If a bodhisattva, being dominated by a craving for attendance and service, leads a group with a mind attached to worldly gain,
he becomes guilty of an offense, he commits a transgression, and he incurs an afflicted offense.
There is no offense for one who accepts service and attendance with a mind free from worldly desire.

However, if a bodhisattva, having given rise to laziness and indolence, indulges at an improper time and to an immoderate degree in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, or the pleasure of lying on one's side, he becomes guilty of an offense and a transgression; he incurs an afflicted offense.
There is no offense if one is severely ill or lacks the physical strength;
there is no offense for one exhausted by travel;
and there is no offense for one who has generated the desire to abandon that [fault], as should be understood from the previous cases.
If a bodhisattva, with a mind full of attachment, passes the time in socializing,
he commits an offense, he transgresses, and he incurs an afflicted offense;
he passes the time with a distracted mind.
One incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense if another person recites it,
and one listens for a moment with mindfulness established through compliance with that other person.

There is no offense for one who has merely asked out of curiosity, or for one who, having been asked, merely provides an illustration in response. However, if a bodhisattva, desiring to settle the mind by means of mental stability, does not approach and request instruction because of a mind of malice or being constrained by pride, he becomes guilty of an offense, he transgresses, and he incurs an afflicted offense.
One incurs an offense that is non-afflicted due to laziness or indolence.
There is no offense if one is ill or lacks the necessary strength.
There is no offense if one should converse with someone who would give perverted instruction.
There is no offense if he himself is very learned and capable of concentrating the mind,
and if he has already completed what was to be done by way of instruction.
Furthermore, there is no offense if a bodhisattva, having given rise to the hindrance of sensual desire, tolerates it rather than dispelling it.

One becomes guilty of an offense, transgressing with a defiled mind. There is no offense for one who has generated the desire to abandon it and is striving, yet whose conduct proceeds because the mind is overwhelmed by the intensity of the affliction.
As it is with sensual desire, so it should be understood for ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and doubt.
If a bodhisattva relishes meditative absorption and perceives excellence in that relishing of absorption,
he commits an offense; he is guilty of a transgression and incurs an afflicted offense.
There is no offense for one who has generated the desire to abandon that [fault], as previously described.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva should hold such a view and speak thus: "A bodhisattva should not listen to the Dharma associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor should he take it up, nor should he train therein."

"What is the use for a bodhisattva of hearing or grasping the teachings associated with the śrāvakas? What purpose is there in training therein?"— if one thinks thus, one becomes guilty of an offense, one commits a transgression, and incurs an afflicted offense.
For indeed, a bodhisattva should apply himself even to the treatises of the non-Buddhists, let alone to the word of the Buddha.
There is no offense in doing so for one who is single-mindedly devoted to that [non-Buddhist system] in order to turn them away from it.

If a bodhisattva, while the Bodhisattvapiṭaka exists, fails to apply himself to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and instead completely neglects the Bodhisattvapiṭaka to apply himself to the Śrāvakapiṭaka, [there is an offense].

He becomes one who has committed an offense, one who has transgressed, and incurs an afflicted offense: if a bodhisattva, while the word of the Buddha exists, does not apply himself to the word of the Buddha but instead applies himself to the treatises of non-Buddhists or external sciences,
he becomes one who has committed an offense, one who has transgressed, and incurs an afflicted offense.
There is no offense for one who possesses superior intelligence, who is capable of rapid comprehension, capable of not forgetting even after a long time,

capable of reflecting upon and penetrating the meaning, who is endowed with an unshakable intellect regarding the Buddha’s word that is accompanied by investigation through reasoning, and who practices daily in the Buddha’s word twice as much as that [amount of time].

Even so, if a bodhisattva, while not transgressing the prescribed rule, applies himself to skill in the treatises of the non-Buddhists and external sciences with a sense of delight, and engages in them with pleasure rather than practicing them like bitter medicine,
he becomes guilty of an offense, incurs a transgression, and falls into an afflicted offense.

Having heard profound points in the Bodhisattvapiṭaka— points that are supremely profound concerning either the meaning of reality or the majestic power of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— a bodhisattva, lacking resolute faith, slanders them, saying:
"These are not connected with the goal, not connected with the Dharma, not spoken by the Tathāgata, and do not lead to the welfare and happiness of sentient beings."
He becomes guilty of an offense, transgressing with a defiled fault,
whether by his own improper mental attention or by following the lead of others while disparaging [the teaching].
Indeed, it happens that upon hearing profound and supremely profound points, a Bodhisattva’s mind lacks resolute conviction.
In this regard, a faithful and honest bodhisattva should train himself thus:
"It would not be fitting for me—who am blind and sightless, and who must proceed solely by means of the Tathāgata’s eye—to reject what was spoken by the Tathāgata with intentional meaning.
In this way, that bodhisattva establishes himself as one who is ignorant.
Furthermore, one perceives the Tathāgata himself as being non-remote with respect to those Buddha-dharmas;
in this way, one becomes correctly practiced.
There is no offense for one who lacks resolute faith, provided they do not reject [the teachings].
If a bodhisattva, with a mind motivated by worldly gain or with a mind of resentment, exalts himself and disparages others in the presence of others, he commits an offense;
he is at fault and incurs an afflicted transgression.
There is no offense for one who desires to overcome non-Buddhist teachers or who desires the stability of the Teaching.
There is no offense for one who, by that very means, desires to discipline that same person, as detailed previously.
There is no offense for the purpose of inspiring faith in those who lack it, or for increasing the faith of those who already possess it.

A bodhisattva commits an offense if, being gripped by pride, with a mind of malice or resentment, he does not approach to listen to the Dharma or to engage in discussion and determination regarding the Dharma.
He becomes guilty of an offense and transgresses; he incurs an afflicted offense.
If he does not approach [the preceptor] due to indolence or laziness, he incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense for one who does not perceive it;
there is no offense if one is ill or lacks the capacity; there is no offense if one suspects the teaching to be erroneous;

there is no offense for one who wishes to protect the mind of the Dharma-preacher; and there is no offense for one who recognizes a discourse that has been heard repeatedly, mastered, and understood in its meaning.
There is no offense if one is learned, a retainer of what has been heard, and an accumulator of what has been heard.
There is no offense for one who is continuously established in mental focus on the object of meditation, being devoted to the accomplishment of the bodhisattva samādhis.
There is no offense for one whose wisdom is exceedingly dull, who grasps the Dharma slowly, retains it slowly, and stabilizes the mind upon the object of meditation slowly.

If a bodhisattva intentionally treats a person who is a Dharma-preacher with contempt, fails to honor them, mocks them, or derides them; and if he relies on the letter rather than relying on the meaning, he becomes guilty of an offense, a transgression, and incurs an afflicted offense.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva established in the vow who, with a mind of malice or resentment, does not act as a helper in the affairs of sentient beings [incurs an offense].

Whether it be in going to or returning from a journey, in the performance of right occupations, in the protection of wealth, in the restoration of what has been broken, or in festivals or meritorious deeds— whenever he goes while being incapable of performing those duties,
he becomes guilty of an offense, incurs a transgression, and falls into a defiled offense.
If, due to indolence or laziness, one does not provide assistance,
one incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense if one is ill or lacks the strength;
there is no offense if one is unable to perform the task oneself and the petitioner has someone else to rely upon;
there is no offense if the task would result in harm or be contrary to the Dharma.
There is no offense if, by that means, one wishes to discipline [the person], as detailed previously;
there is no offense if another has already previously undertaken [the task];
there is no offense if one requests another who is capable.
There is no offense if one is correctly engaged in the side of wholesome qualities without interruption.
There is no offense if one is naturally slow-witted and applies oneself slowly, as previously described.
There is no offense for one who desires to protect the minds of many others.
There is no offense for one who wishes to preserve a communal rule of the Saṅgha.
However, if a bodhisattva, upon encountering a sentient being who is sick or afflicted by disease, does not provide nursing or service with a mind of malice or resentment, he commits an offense;
he transgresses and incurs an afflicted offense.
If one does not act due to indolence or laziness,
one incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense if one is oneself ill or lacks the physical strength [to act].
There is no offense if one requests another who is capable and favorable [to perform the task].
There is no offense if one is ill and has a protector or a refuge.
There is no offense if one is afflicted by a chronic illness that is merely palliative.
There is no offense for one who is devoted to a vast and continuous course of wholesome practice, for the purpose of protecting that wholesome practice from interruption.
There is no offense for one whose wisdom is exceedingly dull, who recites the Dharma slowly, retains it slowly, and slowly composes the mind in concentration upon the object.
There is no offense if one has previously committed oneself to another [engagement].
Just as one attends to the sick,
so too should one understand the assistance rendered to remove the suffering of those who are suffering.

When a bodhisattva sees beings engaged in improper conduct regarding matters pertaining to this life or the next, he does not provide instruction on the right method or the right path with a mind of malice or resentment.
He becomes one who has committed an offense and transgressed; he incurs an afflicted offense. If, out of laziness or indolence, he does not point it out, he incurs a non-afflicted offense.
There is no offense if one is personally ignorant or lacks the capability;
there is no offense if one requests another who is capable;
there is no offense if that very person is themselves capable.
There is no offense if he is already sustained by another spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
There is no offense if, by that means, he intends to discipline him—as detailed previously.

There is no offense in the case of one for whom reasoned instruction should be given, but who possesses a mind of malice, is difficult to speak to, grasps things erroneously, is devoid of affection and respect, and is of a stubborn nature.
If a bodhisattva is ungrateful and unappreciative toward sentient beings who have been helpful, and with a mind of malice does not respond with a corresponding act of service in return,
he commits an offense; he transgresses and incurs an afflicted offense.
If one does not attend to it due to indolence or laziness,
one incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense for one who is making an effort but is incapable or lacks the necessary strength.
There is no offense if, as previously stated, he desires to discipline them by that means.
There is no offense if that very person does not accept the return of a favor.
A bodhisattva who, with a mind of malice, does not dispel the arisen grief of sentient beings who are suffering the loss of kinsmen or wealth.
He becomes guilty of an offense and transgresses the rule; he incurs an afflicted offense if he does not dispel [the thought] due to indolence and laziness.
He incurs an unafflicted offense [if he does not dispel it for other reasons].
As before, it should be understood that there is no offense in cases such as those beginning with failing to provide assistance in duties.
However, if a bodhisattva, when properly requested by those seeking food, drink, or other types of requisites, does not give them because of a mind of malice or a mind of resentment,
he becomes guilty of an offense, incurs transgression, and falls into an afflicted state.
If one does not grant [the request] due to indolence, laziness, or negligence,
one incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense when wealth and possessions are non-existent or unavailable.
There is no offense if one is asked for an improper or unwholesome object.
There is no offense if, by that means, one wishes to subdue or discipline [the requester] as previously described.
There is no offense if one protects against what is detrimental to the king. There is no offense if one protects the formal agreement (*kriyākāra*) of the Saṃgha.
A bodhisattva, having established an assembly, does not from time to time correctly exhort or correctly instruct them;

nor does he, with a mind of malice, seek in accordance with the Dharma robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick from faithful brahmins and householders who might obstruct their welfare.
He becomes guilty of an offense and incurs transgression; he falls into an afflicted offense.
[If, out of indolence, laziness, or negligence, he does not exhort, does not instruct, and does not seek [to help], he falls into a non-afflicted offense.
There is no offense if, by that means, he intends to subdue or intends to discipline [the person], as previously stated.
There is no offense for one who observes the formal agreement (kriyākāra) of the Saṃgha;
there is no offense if one is ill and incapable of exertion;
there is no offense if one requests another who is capable [to do so].
There is no offense if the assembly has acquired great merit;
or if he himself is capable of seeking out robes and other requisites;
or if what was to be accomplished through instruction and admonition has already been accomplished for them.
There is no offense if one who was formerly a member of a non-Buddhist sect has entered [the order] by means of stealing the Dharma,
and he is of a nature incapable of being disciplined.
If a bodhisattva, with a mind of malice, does not comply with the wishes of others,
he commits an offense, he transgresses, and incurs an afflicted offense.
If he does not comply due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, he incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense if what is intended by others would be unwholesome for them.
There is no offense if one is ill and incapable of exertion.
There is no offense if one is observing a communal regulation of the Saṃgha.
There is no offense if what is intended by him would be beneficial, yet it would be unintended and unbeneficial for a much greater number of others.
There is no offense if he is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who is to be subdued. There is no offense if, as before, he desires to tame or discipline [the person] by that means.
If a bodhisattva, with a mind of malice, does not proclaim the actual virtues of others, does not speak their true praise, or does not express approval for well-spoken words,
he commits an offense and transgresses;
he incurs an afflicted offense.
If one does not speak due to laziness, indolence, or negligence, one incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense if one considers the person to be naturally of few desires and acts solely out of a desire to protect that quality.
There is no offense if one is ill or lacks the physical strength.
There is no offense if, by that means, one intends to subdue or discipline [the person], as previously stated.

There is no offense for one who protects a formal agreement (*kriyākāra*) pertaining to the Saṃgha. There is no offense for one who considers that, on account of that [agreement], there would arise affliction, pride, arrogance, or harm, and who acts for the sake of avoiding those things.
There is no offense if the qualities are counterfeits of virtue rather than genuine;
if the well-spoken words are counterfeits of the well-spoken rather than authentic;
or if [the person] is a non-Buddhist who is to be refuted.
There is no offense for one who is waiting for the conclusion of the discourse.
A bodhisattva who, with a defiled mind, does not reprimand sentient beings who deserve reprimand, or who deserve punishment or banishment;
or who, even if he reprimands them, does not instruct them with the appropriate disciplinary action.
If he instructs him but does not expel him,
he becomes guilty of an offense involving transgression;
he incurs an afflicted offense.
If, due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, one does not cause [the person] to feel dejected nor expel them, yet does not incur an afflicted state of mind, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who overlooks someone who is incurable, who is unfit for conversation, who is abusive, or who is full of hostility.
There is no offense for one who is waiting for the right time.
There is no offense for one who observes [the situation] with the intent of preventing quarrels, strife, contention, and disputes arising from that cause.
There is no offense for one who observes with the intent of averting concealment or causing a schism.
There is no offense if those beings were not deceitful, but were endowed with intense shame and dread of blame, such that they would very quickly restore themselves to rectitude.

A bodhisattva, though endowed with the power of various miraculous transformations, does not terrify those beings who are to be terrified, nor does he win over those beings who are to be won over, nor does he [by means of supernatural power] avoid what has been given in faith.
He becomes guilty of an offense and transgresses the rule; he incurs an unafflicted offense.
There is no offense in cases where sentient beings are for the most part deeply attached—such as non-Buddhist heretics who possess wrong views that revile the noble ones.

Furthermore, it should be understood that there is no offense in all such cases when there is excessive mental derangement, or when one is overwhelmed by painful sensations, or when one has not yet formally undertaken the vows.

Thus, these training precepts (*śikṣāpada*) of the bodhisattvas, which have arisen from specific circumstances, were taught by the Blessed One in various scattered discourses (*sūtrānta*). Having been undertaken with reference to the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of acting for the benefit of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā-śīla*), they are here set forth in their entirety within this *Mātṛkā* of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. A bodhisattva who has developed a sense of urgency should apply themselves to training in these, maintaining the highest reverence toward them.

Having formally undertaken the vow of restraint from another, one must, from the very beginning, possess a desire for training that is perfectly pure—a resolve for awakening, a resolve for the welfare of sentient beings—and a sense of reverence so as not to transgress. Furthermore, should one transgress, one must restore oneself through remediation in accordance with the Dharma.
All such transgressions by a bodhisattva should be understood as being comprised within the category of "wrongdoing" (*duṣkṛta*).
It should be confessed in the presence of anyone belonging to either the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Mahāyāna who is capable of understanding and receiving that verbal communication.
If a bodhisattva has committed an offense involving a defeat (pārājika-sthānīya-dharma) through an intense degree of obsession (adhimātra-paryavasthāna), his vow is thereby relinquished;
it must be taken up once again, even twice.

If he has fallen into a middling state of obsession, he should confess that misdeed (*duṣkṛta*) before three persons, or even more than that. Having first announced the matter, he should sit down before them and speak as follows: "Pay attention, Venerable One! I, a bodhisattva named so-and-so, have committed a misdeed, an offense against the bodhisattva discipline, regarding the matter as it has been announced."
The remainder should be stated exactly as it is for a monk confessing his *duṣkṛta* offenses.

It should be understood that for an offense involving a *pārājika*-like dharma committed with a mild degree of obsession (*paryavasthāna*), as well as for other offenses, confession is to be made before only a single person.
Furthermore, if no suitable person is available before whom one might confess, the bodhisattva should, out of sincere intention, generate the resolve never to commit them again.
Furthermore, a restraint must be undertaken for the future. In this way, he who has emerged from that offense should be addressed. This also constitutes the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow.
If a person endowed with those qualities is not present, then the bodhisattva should himself undertake the vow of the bodhisattva ethical discipline in the presence of an image of the Tathāgata;
and furthermore, it should be undertaken in this manner:
having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder...
Having placed his right knee upon the ground, or remaining in a squatting position before [the assembly], he should speak as follows:

"I, who am named so-and-so, inform all the Tathāgatas in the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages. In their presence, I undertake all the training precepts of a Bodhisattva and the entire morality of a Bodhisattva, namely, the morality of restraint."
The morality of gathering virtuous qualities and the morality of acting for the benefit of sentient beings, in which all bodhisattvas of the past have trained,
in which all bodhisattvas of the future will train, and in which all bodhisattvas currently existing in the ten directions are training at present.
This should be stated a second and a third time as well.
Having spoken thus, one should rise.
All that remains, however, is to be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, there is no offense for a bodhisattva on the path of offenses that is without remainder.

Furthermore, regarding what was said by the Blessed One—that for the most part a bodhisattva’s transgression should be understood as arising from hatred and not from passion—the intended meaning there should be seen as follows:

whatever a bodhisattva undertakes, having made affection for sentient beings and love for sentient beings the primary motive, all that is the duty of a bodhisattva. It is not a non-duty; and it is not logical for a transgression to occur when one is performing what is one's duty.
However, a bodhisattva who harbors hatred toward sentient beings acts neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others;
this is not the duty of a bodhisattva. For one who performs such an improper act, an offense is appropriate.
Furthermore, the mild, medium, and intense degrees of a bodhisattva’s transgressions are to be understood as they are set forth in the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.

Moreover, a bodhisattva who is devoted to training in his own discipline dwells in comfort, endowed with three kinds of perfection: perfection of application, perfection of intention, and [perfection of result].
And by the perfection of prior causes.
In that regard, what is the perfection of application?
It is when a bodhisattva practices the precepts without flaw, possesses completely pure conduct of body, speech, and mind, does not repeatedly commit offenses, and reveals his misdeeds.
This is called the perfection of application.
What is the perfection of intention?
It is when one has gone forth with the intention for the Dharma, not with the intention for a livelihood.
He becomes one who seeks great enlightenment, not one who does not seek it;
he seeks the state of a recluse and nirvana, not that which is contrary to them.
