Being thus a seeker, he dwells neither indolent, nor lacking in vigor, nor devoid of effort; he is not defiled by evil, unwholesome states—those things which are afflictive, leading to rebirth, accompanied by fever, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to the future.
[It is] by those subject to birth, old age, and death;
this is called the perfection of intention (*āśaya-saṃpat*).
What is the perfection of prior causes?

It is when a bodhisattva, having performed meritorious deeds and established roots of virtue in previous births, is such that he himself is not deprived of the requisites of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick; and he is likewise capable of sharing these with others.
Thus, this should be understood as the bodhisattva’s perfection of prior causes.
A bodhisattva who is endowed with these three perfections and is engaged in training within the Vinaya dwells in a state of easeful contact.
Conversely, it should be understood that one who is endowed with the three failures, being the opposite of these, dwells in a state of painful contact.
This, then, is called the bodhisattva’s entire morality (*sarvaśīla*) in both its concise and detailed forms, pertaining to the side of the laity and the side of those who have gone forth.
Furthermore, the divisions of this very same entire morality should be understood as the other [categories], such as the morality that is difficult to practice (*duṣkaraśīla*) and so forth.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality that is difficult to practice?
That should be understood as being threefold.

When a bodhisattva who possesses great wealth and dwells in great sovereignty and power renounces those enjoyments and renounces that great sovereignty and power to undertake the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*), this is called the bodhisattva’s difficult ethical discipline (*duṣkaraśīla*).

Furthermore, even when fallen into hardship, a bodhisattva who has undertaken the ethical discipline does not breach that undertaking of the vows of ethical discipline even while losing his life; how much less would he ever violate it? This is called the bodhisattva’s second difficult practice of ethical discipline.

In such and such a way, the bodhisattva remains vigilant and established in mindfulness regarding all modes of conduct, dwellings, and mental attentions, so that throughout his entire life he does not incur even the slightest transgression, nor does he falter in his ethical discipline (*śīla*), much less a grave one. This is called the bodhisattva’s third difficult ethical discipline.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality that faces all directions?
It should be understood as fourfold:
undertaken morality, natural morality, practiced morality, and morality endowed with skillful means.

In that regard, "undertaken morality" refers to that by which the threefold undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline has been performed— namely, the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of acting for the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā-śīla*).

In that regard, "natural morality" (*prakṛti-śīla*) is that in which, for a bodhisattva established in the lineage (*gotra*), pure physical and vocal actions proceed simply by virtue of the natural goodness of their mental continuum.
In this regard, "habituated morality" refers to that bodhisattva by whom the threefold morality as previously described was practiced in former births.
By virtue of the empowerment of those past causes, he does not at all delight in the practice of evil.
He recoils from evil; he delights in the practice of wholesome conduct;
he yearns for nothing but the practice of wholesome conduct.

In this regard, ethical discipline endowed with skillful means is that virtuous physical and vocal action which proceeds toward sentient beings by relying upon the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Among these, what is the ethical discipline of a bodhisattva as a true person (*satpuruṣa*)?
It should be understood as being fivefold.
In this regard, a bodhisattva is himself virtuous and encourages others to undertake virtue.
Of virtue...
And he speaks in praise;
seeing one who shares the same Dharma, he becomes joyful;
and having fallen into an offense, he remedies it according to the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality of all aspects?
It should be understood as being of thirteen types, consisting of six types and seven types condensed together;
it is dedicated toward great enlightenment.
It is "clear" because it is embraced by extensive precepts;
it is a "basis for blameless joy" because it avoids the two extremes of devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification;
and it is "continuous" because one does not renounce the training even for the duration of one's life.
It is firm because it cannot be overcome or taken away by any gain, honor, heterodox doctrines, afflictions, or secondary afflictions;
and it is conjoined with the ornament of ethical discipline (*śīlālaṅkāra*).
The ornament of ethical discipline should be understood as, for example, the abstention from taking life and so forth, as described in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
The morality of abstention;
the morality of engagement, because it gathers what is wholesome and accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings;
and the protective morality, because it guards both the morality of engagement and the morality of abstention.
Ethical discipline that results in the maturation of the marks of a great person; that which results in the maturation of higher mental training;
and that which results in the maturation of a desirable rebirth.
And there is that which results in maturation (*vaipākya*). In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality concerning those who are distressed and those who seek [help]?
It should be understood as being of eight kinds.

In this regard, a bodhisattva reflects to himself in this way: "Just as I am desirous of life, let no one deprive me of life; let no one take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, utter slander, harsh words, or idle chatter; nor let them harm me with undesirable and injurious contacts, such as being struck by hands or clods of earth."
"May they treat me with kindness"—if those others were to treat me otherwise than that, for me who desires this, it would cause me distress and it would be unpleasant to me.
Just as we desire that others should not deprive us of life, and so on in detail, up to not treating us with harmful contacts; [so do I desire the same for others].

If I were to treat those who have such needs in a contrary manner, they would be frustrated, and that would be unpleasant for them. Since that which is unpleasant to myself and others is something I myself dislike, why should I treat others with it?
Having reflected thus, the bodhisattva does not treat others with the eight kinds of unpleasant conduct, even for the sake of his own life.
This is called the bodhisattva’s eightfold morality for those who seek relief from distress.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality that brings happiness in this life and the next? It should be understood as being of nine kinds.
In this regard, a bodhisattva prohibits sentient beings from those things that ought to be prohibited, permits them in those things that ought to be permitted,
and gathers to himself those sentient beings who ought to be gathered.
He restrains those beings who are to be restrained.
In that regard, whatever pure action of body and speech the bodhisattva carries out—
this, first of all, is the fourfold ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Furthermore, there is another fivefold morality: that accompanied by generosity, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
When these are condensed together into a single whole, they constitute morality in nine aspects.
And this leads to the happiness of both that bodhisattva and others, in both the present life and future lives.
Therefore, it is said that this brings happiness both here and hereafter.
In that regard, what is the pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of a bodhisattva?
It should be understood as being of ten kinds.
From the very beginning, it is well-grasped because it is undertaken out of a desire for the ascetic life and awakening, not for the sake of a livelihood.
It is not too lax because of the absence of sluggish remorse when a transgression occurs. It is not too overbearing because of the absence of misplaced remorse.

It becomes free from laziness by not indulging in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining on one's side, or the pleasure of lying down, and by application to the side of virtue day and night;
it is embraced by heedfulness by practicing the five factors of heedfulness as previously described.
It is rightly directed because it is free from craving for gain and honor, and because one does not undertake the practice of celibacy with the aspiration to become a deity.

It is embraced by the perfection of conduct through the complete excellence of physical and verbal behavior in the postures, duties, and application to the side of wholesome qualities. It is embraced by the perfection of livelihood through the avoidance of all faults that produce wrong livelihood, such as hypocrisy and the like.
It is free from the two extremes because it avoids devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasures and to self-mortification;
it leads to liberation because it is free from all the views of the non-Buddhist heretics;
and it is a morality that does not fall away from its undertaking because Bodhisattvas do not allow it to become breached or corrupted.
This tenfold morality of the bodhisattvas is called "pure.

This is the great aggregate of morality of the bodhisattva, which gives rise to the fruit of great enlightenment; relying upon this, the bodhisattva, having fulfilled the perfection of morality, awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And as long as he has not yet attained full awakening, while training in this immeasurable aggregate of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline, he obtains five benefits:
he is attended by the Buddhas;
he dies established in great joy.

And upon the dissolution of the body, he is reborn there among those bodhisattvas who are his equals or superiors in ethical discipline, who are his peers, his fellow practitioners of the Dharma, and his spiritual friends.
He becomes endowed with an immeasurable mass of merit that fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline.
Both in this life and in future lives, he attains natural ethical discipline and becomes one whose very essence is ethical discipline.
All this morality, as previously described—consisting of nine aspects beginning with natural morality (*svabhāva-śīla*)—should be understood as being subsumed under three types of morality:

the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of acting for the benefit of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā-śīla*).
Furthermore, these three types of morality briefly perform three functions for the bodhisattva.
The morality of restraint conduces to the stability of the mind;
the morality of gathering virtuous qualities conduces to the maturation of one's own Buddha-qualities;
and the morality of acting for the benefit of sentient beings conduces to the maturation of sentient beings.
And this is all that must be accomplished by a bodhisattva, namely:
the stability of the mind for dwelling in happiness in the present life;
and, with body and mind untiring, the ripening of the qualities of a Buddha and the ripening of sentient beings.
The bodhisattva’s ethical discipline is of this extent;
the benefit of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline is of this extent;
the purpose of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline is of this extent—there is nothing beyond this and nothing more than this.
In this, the bodhisattvas of the past who desired great enlightenment have trained;
those of the future will also train; and those of the present, throughout the infinite and boundless ten directions, are likewise training.
The tenth chapter on ethical discipline (*śīla-paṭala*) within the section on the Foundation of Yoga in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, concerning how [bodhisattvas] train in the world-systems.
(Dutt 130)
The summary for the Chapter on Patience (Kṣāntipaṭala), the eleventh,
should be understood as being the same as that in the Chapter on Ethical Discipline (Śīlapaṭala).
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience by nature?

That which is the endurance of harm from others— whether by relying on the power of analytical discernment or by one's very nature— the endurance of all [harm], the endurance of everything, and that endurance with a mind free of worldly desire and through pure compassion alone:
this, in brief, should be understood as the essential nature of a bodhisattva’s patience.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s all-inclusive patience?
It should be understood as being twofold:
that which relies on the side of householders and that which relies on the side of those who have gone forth.
Furthermore, although it relies on both sides, it should be understood as threefold:
patience in enduring the injuries of others,
and patience in accepting suffering.
[This includes] the patience of conviction through reflection on the Dharma.
In that regard, how does a bodhisattva endure and tolerate harm inflicted by others?
Here, when a bodhisattva is confronted with suffering born of harm from others—whether it be intense, continuous, varied, or long-lasting—he trains himself in this way:
This is my own fault of past actions,
whereby I myself experience such a fruit of suffering for unwholesome karma committed by my own hand;
and I have no desire for suffering.
Moreover, this lack of patience will become a cause of suffering for me even in the future;
thus, I would be adopting and abiding in a state that is a cause of suffering.
Or rather, by means of that which is undesirable to myself, I would be joining myself to myself.
Therefore, it would be an injury to myself alone,
and not so much to others;
for by their very nature, all these conditioned phenomena within the continuums of both self and others are of the very essence of suffering.

First of all, those who are ignorant are intent on inflicting further suffering upon us who are already suffering by our very nature. But for us, being wise, it would not be fitting that we too should inflict further suffering upon others who are already suffering by their very nature. Furthermore, even for the Śrāvakas who are devoted solely to their own welfare, impatience—which produces suffering for both oneself and others—is not appropriate.
How much more so for us, who are already dedicated to the welfare of others!

Having reflected thus, that bodhisattva cultivates five kinds of perceptions and endures all injuries from sentient beings—whether they be friends, enemies, or neutral parties; inferior, equal, or superior; happy or suffering; and possessed of virtues or faults.
What are the five perceptions? They are: the perception of former-life friends, the perception that follows mere phenomena, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of suffering.
And [the perception of them as] those to be cherished. Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of friends toward sentient beings who have done him harm?
Here, the bodhisattva trains himself in this way:

There is no being whose form is easily found who, after the passing of a long period of time, has not previously in other births been my mother or father, brother or sister, teacher or preceptor, guru or one in the position of a guru.
As he attends to this with wise reflection, the perception of them as adversaries vanishes regarding those beings who have done him harm, and the perception of them as friends becomes established.
Relying on that perception of them as friends, he endures and forgives their injuries.
And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of sentient beings who cause harm as being merely phenomena (*dharma-mātra*)?
Here, the bodhisattva trains himself in this way:
This is merely conditioned formations, merely phenomena, dependent upon conditions.

Herein there is no self, no sentient being, no soul, and no person who could revile, resent, strike, mock, or reproach; nor is there anyone else who is reviled, resented, struck, mocked, or reproached.
As he attends to this in such a systematic manner, the perception of a "sentient being" disappears,
and the perception of "mere phenomena" remains. Having determined and established that perception of mere phenomena, he endures and forgives all injuries from others.
And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of impermanence toward sentient beings who have done him harm?
Here, a bodhisattva trains himself thus:
"Whatever sentient beings have been born and have come into existence, all of them are impermanent and subject to death."
And this is the ultimate way of taking life: namely, depriving one of life.

Since sentient beings are by nature subject to death and impermanent, it would be unbecoming for a wise person even to give rise to a defiled thought toward them, let alone strike them with a hand, a clod of earth, or a staff.
Or rather, he might even deprive them all of life entirely;
as he attends to this with proper reflection (*yoniśo manasikāra*), the perception of permanence and solidity is abandoned,
and the perception of impermanence and lack of solidity becomes established.
Relying even upon that perception of impermanence and worthlessness, he endures and forgives all injuries.
And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of suffering toward sentient beings who cause him harm?
In this case, a bodhisattva considers even those sentient beings who abide in great prosperity through three [perceptions].

He perceives them as being pursued by the three types of suffering—the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*)—let alone those already situated in misfortune.
Seeing this, he trains himself thus:
"In this way, we must strive to remove the suffering of sentient beings who are constantly beset by suffering, and not to bring further suffering upon them."
As he attends to this in such a systematic manner (*yoniśas*), the perception of pleasure is abandoned and the perception of suffering arises.
Relying upon that perception of suffering, he endures and forgives all injuries inflicted by others.
And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of others as his own kin toward sentient beings who cause him harm?
In this regard, a bodhisattva trains himself thus:
"Indeed, by me, while generating the mind for enlightenment, all sentient beings have been embraced as my own kin;
I must accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings."

It would not be fitting for me, who have thus taken up all sentient beings [as my own], to bring about their very misfortune and harm by failing to endure their offenses. As he reflects in this way, his perception of others as "other" toward those beings who have done him harm is abandoned,
and the perception of them as "one's own" becomes established.
Relying on that perception of [others] as protectors, he endures and forgives all injuries from others.
What is patience?
It is that which does not become angry and does not retaliate.
Nor does it carry any latent tendency;
this is called patience.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience of enduring suffering?

In this regard, a bodhisattva trains himself thus: "Indeed, in the past, while engaged in the pursuit of sensual pleasures and seeking after them, I— having reflected upon how sensual pleasures are by nature suffering because they are the cause of suffering— accepted, endured, and experienced many intense sufferings for the sake of those sensual pleasures."
"Engaged as I was in agriculture, trade, and royal service,
I thus rendered those efforts fruitless and underwent great suffering for the sake of mere pain, having failed to discern the fault of ignorance.

Now, however, as I am engaged in wholesome deeds that bring about true happiness, it would be appropriate for me to deliberately accept the endurance of a suffering a hundred thousand times ten million times greater than that."
How much more so for that which is inferior to it?
Thus, applying himself to awakening while reflecting properly (*yoniśo manasikurvan*), the bodhisattva endures suffering pertaining to all things.
What is suffering pertaining to all things?
In brief, that should be understood as having eight aspects:

the basis of reliance, the basis of worldly conditions, the basis of postures, the basis of embracing the Dharma, the basis of the conduct of begging for alms, the basis of the fatigue of application, the basis of acting for the welfare of sentient beings, and the basis of duties to be performed.
There are four supports,
relying upon which there is the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
That is to say: robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

When a bodhisattva receives these things—whether they are coarse, meager, received with disrespect, or obtained slowly—he does not become despondent, nor does he feel alarmed, nor does he slacken his vigor on that account.
Relying upon this basis, he thus endures suffering.
There are nine worldly conditions (*loka-dharma*):

lack of gain, ill-repute, censure, suffering, the destruction of that which is subject to destruction, the exhaustion of that which is subject to exhaustion, the aging of that which is subject to aging, the illness of that which is subject to illness, and the death of that which is subject to death.

The suffering that arises from the occurrence and manifestation of these worldly conditions, whether collectively or individually, is called "that which has the worldly conditions as its basis" (*loka-dharmādhiṣṭhāna*).
Even when touched by that, the bodhisattva does not slacken his vigor on that account; rather, having reflected, he maintains it, endures it, and practices the four postures:
walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

In that regard, a bodhisattva, purifying the mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting by day or night, endures the suffering born of fatigue on that account; however, he does not lie down on his side at an improper time on a couch, a stool, a bed of grass, or a bed of leaves.
There are seven kinds of embracing the Dharma.

It consists of: rendering service and worship to the Three Jewels; rendering service and worship to the guru; the taking up of the teachings; the detailed teaching to others of those teachings already taken up; the practice of recitation in detail with a clear voice; and, when alone and in seclusion, correct reflection, deliberation, and investigation, as well as the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) comprised within the mental engagement of yoga.
When a bodhisattva exerts himself in this sevenfold grasping of the Dharma, whatever suffering arises, he endures it;
yet, on that account, he does not relax his vigor.
The mendicant’s livelihood should also be understood as being sevenfold.

The acceptance of deformity consists in the removal of the marks of a householder by means of shaving the head and beard and so forth; the acceptance of discoloration consists in wearing disfigured and discolored garments;
and the performance of unconventional conduct consists in dwelling under constraints regarding all worldly activities.
A livelihood dependent on others, consisting in maintaining one's existence by means of what is obtained from others for one who has abandoned occupations such as agriculture;
and the seeking of robes and so forth from others for as long as life lasts, characterized by not hoarding or consuming what has been obtained.
For as long as life lasts... (Dutt 134)

The practice of restraint regarding human sensual pleasures is by way of abstaining from unchaste sexual intercourse; and the practice of restraint regarding human amusements and games for as long as life lasts is by way of abstaining from witnessing performances such as those of actors, dancers, jesters, and mimes,
and by way of abstaining from laughing, playing, sporting, and diverting oneself with friends, companions, and associates.
A bodhisattva endures whatever suffering arises from resorting to such a difficult and constrained livelihood of begging for alms;

yet, on that account, he does not relax his vigor. Furthermore, even when a bodhisattva is devoted to the side of the wholesome, as to the physical fatigue and mental distress arising from the cause of that exertion, the bodhisattva does not—on that account—[relax his] vigor.
He sustains [them]. However, the activity for the benefit of sentient beings should be understood as being of eleven types, as previously described.
On that account, the bodhisattva also endures the suffering that has arisen.
And on that account, he does not slacken his vigor.
This refers to what must be done by one who has gone forth, such as the work concerning robes and the alms-bowl;
whereas for a householder, it refers to such things as proper agriculture, commerce, and service to the king.
For that reason, the bodhisattva endures suffering;
yet, for that reason, he does not slacken his vigor.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva is touched by any kind of suffering, he applies himself even more to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He does not fail to apply himself; once applied, he does not turn back;
and he applies himself with a mind free from dejection and undefiled by affliction.
This is called his patience in enduring suffering.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience consisting of resolute belief through the contemplation of the Dharma?
Here, by means of an intellect that has thoroughly investigated and correctly discerned the Dharma, [the bodhisattva abides] in the eightfold basis of resolute belief.
Resolute belief becomes well-established regarding the qualities of the Jewels, the meaning of reality, the great power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
the cause, the fruit, the goal to be attained, the means for its attainment by oneself, and the sphere of the knowable. Furthermore,
that resolute belief becomes well-established through two causes.

And through long-term cultivation and through the attainment of perfectly pure knowledge— this patience of the bodhisattvas relies upon two factors. Based upon this, the detailed classification of the bodhisattvas' "difficult patiences" and so forth is to be understood.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience that is difficult to practice?
It should be seen as being of three kinds:
here, a bodhisattva endures harm from weak sentient beings.
This is the first difficult patience: being powerful oneself, one practices patience. This is the second difficult patience.
To endure a superior and excessive injury from beings who are inferior in terms of birth and lineage—
this is the third patience that is difficult to practice.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience directed toward all quarters?
It should be understood as fourfold:
here, a bodhisattva endures harm even from a friend, and likewise from an enemy and from a neutral person.
And he endures those three types of persons—whether inferior, equal, or superior.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience of a true person (*satpuruṣakṣānti*)?
It should be understood as being fivefold.
In this regard, from the very beginning, a bodhisattva perceives the advantages in patience. A patient person becomes one who, in the future, has little enmity and little dissension.
He becomes abundant in happiness and mental gladness;
he dies without regret;
and after the dissolution of the body, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world among the gods.
Thus, seeing these benefits in this way,
he himself becomes patient and encourages others to undertake patience.
He speaks in praise of forbearance;
and seeing a person who is forbearing, he becomes glad at heart and filled with joy.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s forbearance in all its forms?
That [patience] should be understood as being of thirteen kinds when the sixfold and sevenfold types are condensed together.
Here, a bodhisattva, having recognized that impatience leads to undesirable maturation, practices patience even out of fear;
and toward sentient beings, possessing a mind of compassion, a mind of pity, and a mind of affection, he practices patience even out of love.
One who possesses intense aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and desires to fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) endures even for the sake of a causal motive.
Furthermore, the Blessed One has stated that those who have gone forth are endowed with the power of patience.

Therefore, by this reasoning as well, it is not appropriate for one who has gone forth and has undertaken the precepts to lack patience; thus, one endures even on account of the formal undertaking of the Dharma.
Abiding in the perfection of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and in the prior practice of patience, he is patient by nature;

furthermore, having realized that all phenomena are devoid of a sentient being (*niḥsattva*) and seeing only the ineffable nature of phenomena (*nirabhilāpya-dharmamātra*), he is patient even through the contemplation of the Dharma (*dharmanidhyāna*);
and he is patient with every form of harm.
He is patient toward all;
he is patient in every place;
and he is patient at all times, whether in private or in the presence of a great multitude.
Whether in the forenoon, at midday, or in the afternoon; whether by night or by day; whether regarding the past, the future, or the present; whether he is ill or healthy;
whether he has fallen or has risen—he endures with his body through non-violence, and he endures with his speech through the non-utterance of unpleasant words.

One endures even with the mind through being unshakable and by not harboring a defiled intention. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience toward those who are distressed or seeking something?
It should be understood as being of eight kinds.
The patience of enduring the importunities of suffering beggars;
the patience of refraining from malice toward fierce beings who commit excessive evil deeds by relying on the Dharma and great compassion;
[and the patience] toward those of immoral conduct who have gone forth [into the religious life].
Patience consisting in the absence of malice based on the great compassion for the Dharma;
and patience consisting in endurance through effort in five aspects:
for one who exerts oneself to remove the suffering of suffering beings, who seeks the teachings, and who practices in accordance with the Dharma.
The endurance of one who, having practiced them himself, extensively elucidates those very same dharmas to others, and who acts as a true companion in the affairs and duties of sentient beings—
this is called the eightfold patience of one who seeks to dispel the suffering of others.
By means of patience, one avoids that which would cause beings to suffer,
and one provides for those who have need;
therein, what is the bodhisattva’s patience that brings happiness in this world and the next?
That should be seen as being of nine kinds:
here, a bodhisattva dwelling heedfully in virtuous qualities becomes patient;
he becomes patient with cold and heat, hunger and thirst, the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind and sun, and the touch of creeping reptiles.
He becomes capable of enduring the exhaustion, fatigue, and distress of body and mind born of exertion.

With compassion for sentient beings toward the sufferings of old age, sickness, death, and so forth that fall within cyclic existence placed foremost, the patient bodhisattva dwells, unmixed with others, in a state of contact with happiness in this very life.
He lives having undertaken the causes of happiness for this life, free from evil and unwholesome states;
and he also lives having undertaken the causes of happiness for others.
Furthermore, one practices for the sake of the happiness of others both in the present life and in future lives;
therefore, this patience is called "patience that brings happiness here and hereafter.
In that regard, what is the pure patience of a bodhisattva?
It should be understood as being of ten kinds:
here, when a bodhisattva receives harm, injury, or transgression from others, he neither inflicts a counter-harm nor becomes angry in his mind.
Nor does he harbor an antagonistic intent;

rather, he is intent on being helpful. Just as he was before, so too afterwards, he does not overlook an injury through the performance of a beneficial act. Toward those who have done him harm, he himself offers an apology, and he does not seek an apology from others after having caused them distress.
He accepts it thinking, "May he become weary.
Having made this very condition, with respect to intolerance he becomes endowed with intense shame and dread of blame;
with respect to patience he becomes endowed with intense love and reverence for the Teacher.
Beginning with non-harming toward sentient beings, he comes to possess an intense disposition of compassion for them;
or, having abandoned in every way all factors associated with the lack of patience, he becomes free from passion for the realm of desire.
In these ten ways, the purity and stainlessness of a bodhisattva’s patience is to be understood.

Thus, by relying upon this patience— which begins with natural patience (*svabhāva-kṣānti*) and culminates in pure patience (*viśuddha-kṣānti*), which is vast, immeasurable, and results in the arising of great enlightenment— the bodhisattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on Patience, in the section on the Foundation within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 138) The Chapter on Vigor (Vīryapaṭala).
The summary (uddāna) is to be understood as before.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s essential vigor?

It is the bodhisattva’s mental enthusiasm for the gathering of immeasurable wholesome qualities and for acting for the benefit of sentient beings; as well as the activity of body, speech, and mind that arises from that [enthusiasm], which is ardent, uninterrupted, and unerring.
This should be understood as the nature of a bodhisattva’s vigor.
In that regard, what is a bodhisattva’s all-inclusive vigor?
Briefly, it should be understood as being of two kinds.
It relies on both the side of householders and the side of those who have gone forth.
Furthermore, that which relies on both sides should be understood as being threefold:
the vigor of armor, the vigor of gathering virtuous qualities, and the vigor of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
In this regard, this is the armor-like vigor of a bodhisattva:
here, even before the actual application of the undertaking of vigor, a bodhisattva first dons the armor with such enthusiasm of mind as follows:
"Even if I must dwell in the hells for days and nights equal to a thousand great eons for the sake of liberating a single sentient being from suffering..."

May I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in a period of time increased a hundred thousand million billion times over the duration it takes for Bodhisattvas to awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment while dwelling in other realms of existence;
nevertheless, I shall exert myself with such resolve.
I would not apply myself for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
nor would I rely upon applied diligence—
let alone in a shorter time or with less suffering.
This is the armor-like vigor of a bodhisattva.
Any bodhisattva who would produce even a mere inclination or a mere clarity of faith toward such armor-like vigor of bodhisattvas—
that bodhisattva, being steadfast, will nourish the element for the undertaking of immeasurable vigor for the sake of awakening.

How much more so for a bodhisattva who is already endowed with such armor-like vigor; for that bodhisattva, for the sake of awakening and for the benefit of sentient beings, there is no task whatsoever to be performed that is difficult, nor would there be any contraction of mind or difficulty in performing it.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ vigor for gathering wholesome qualities?

It is the vigor applied to the perfection of generosity for the sake of accomplishing the perfection of generosity; it is the vigor applied to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, up to the accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, that [stability] should be understood briefly as being of seven aspects:
it is *acala* (immovable), because it cannot be shaken by any conceptual constructions, discursive thoughts, afflictions, secondary afflictions, opposing disputants, or the touch of suffering;
and it is *gāḍha* (firm), because it involves application with earnest respect.

It is immeasurable because it is present as the attainment of all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). It is applied with skillful means (*upāya*) because it follows the non-erroneous path toward the goal to be attained and because of its penetration of equality.
It is right effort (*samyag-vīrya*) because it is directed toward the attainment of the goal to be attained that is associated with the welfare of others.
It is "continuous" because of its constant application;
it is "free from pride" because one does not become elated by that exertion of vigor.

Thus, through these seven aspects, the application of the exertion of vigor for the gathering of wholesome qualities leads Bodhisattvas to the swift fulfillment of the perfections and the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It proceeds thus:
since diligence alone is the primary and most excellent cause for the full realization of all wholesome qualities that produce awakening, and nothing else is so,
therefore the Tathāgatas declare that diligence leads to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Furthermore, the vigor of bodhisattvas for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings should be understood as being of eleven types,
just as it was described in the Chapter on Ethical Discipline (*Śīla-paṭala*);
that which was associated with ethical discipline there should now be spoken of here in relation to vigor.
This is the distinction.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s difficult diligence?
It should be understood as being of three kinds.

When a bodhisattva, continuously refraining from the perception of robes, the perception of alms-food, the perception of bedding and seats, and even the perception of a self, applies himself with uninterrupted cultivation toward virtuous qualities,
this is the bodhisattva’s first difficult exertion.
Furthermore, by means of such an undertaking of vigor, the bodhisattva remains applied at all times until the casting off of his commonality of rebirth (*nikāyasabhāga*).
This is the second difficult vigor of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva is endowed with a vigor that is characterized by the quality of penetrating equality, which is neither too slack nor too over-exerted, which is unerring, and which is connected with the goal.
This should be understood as the third difficult exertion of a bodhisattva.
Indeed, the power of this difficult exertion of bodhisattvas should be understood as having compassion for sentient beings and wisdom as its causes of integration.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing exertion?
That should be understood as fourfold:
that which abandons afflicted phenomena, that which gathers pure phenomena, that which purifies karma, and that which increases wisdom.

Among these, the bodhisattva’s vigor that abandons afflicted phenomena is for the non-arising of unarisen fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and obsessions, and for the abandonment of those already arisen.
In that regard, the bodhisattva’s vigor that attracts white dharmas is the vigor for the arising of wholesome dharmas not yet arisen,
and the vigor for the stability, non-forgetfulness, increase, and expansion of those already arisen.

In that regard, a bodhisattva’s vigor that purifies action is that which leads to the purification and integration of the three types of action— wholesome bodily action, vocal action, and mental action. Therein, a bodhisattva’s vigor that increases wisdom is that which conduces to the attainment and further growth of the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s vigor of a true person (*satpuruṣavīrya*)?
It should be understood as being of five kinds:
it is "unabandoned," because there is no abandonment of aspiration or application in any way whatsoever.
It is "not deficient" because it is augmented by a vigor that is equal to or greater than what was undertaken;
it is "unshrinking" because the mind is neither constricted nor despondent due to the exertion of undertaking a fervent, long-term, and uninterrupted vigor;
and it is "unmistaken" because it is embraced by means that are conducive to the goal.
And the intense application of the bodhisattvas' vigor is for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas' vigor in all its forms?
It should be understood as being of thirteen forms, by condensing together six forms and seven forms.
Uninterrupted vigor is characterized by constant application;
honored vigor is characterized by skillful application;
and natural vigor is characterized by the sustaining power of the cause of previous vigor.
There is the effort of application (*prāyogika-vīrya*), by virtue of applying oneself to the side of the wholesome through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*);

unshakable effort (*akopya-vīrya*), by virtue of being unshakable by any contact with suffering and by not falling into a state of alteration; and the effort of non-contentment (*asaṃtuṣṭi-vīrya*), by virtue of not being satisfied with the attainment of merely small or inferior distinctions. This, then, is the sixfold effort in all its aspects, endowed with which a bodhisattva is one who has initiated effort, who possesses stamina, who is vigorous, who is enthusiastic, whose prowess is firm, and who does not cast off the burden.
It is said [to be applied] "to wholesome qualities.

Furthermore, the sevenfold vigor of a bodhisattva accompanied by aspiration consists of: (1) vigor that repeatedly increases the intense aspiration and vow for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; (2) vigor of a bodhisattva endowed with equanimity through whichever [of the four immeasurables];...

It is that vigor by which a bodhisattva, whose mind is unafflicted and not overwhelmed by primary or secondary afflictions, comes to abide with an even mind regarding wholesome qualities. Furthermore, there is the superior vigor of a bodhisattva whose mind is afflicted or overwhelmed by any secondary affliction; it is like one whose head is on fire, applied for the sake of abandoning that secondary affliction.
Vigor:
the vigor of seeking is that of a bodhisattva through the pursuit of all fields of knowledge;

the vigor of training is that of a bodhisattva through the accomplishment of the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*) regarding those very teachings thus sought, as is appropriate and fitting.
The bodhisattva’s vigor for accomplishing the welfare of others should be understood as being of eleven kinds, as previously described.
The seventh vigor of the bodhisattva is that which serves to protect one’s own correct application and to restore, in accordance with the Dharma, whatever has gone astray.
Thus, this thirteenfold vigor of a bodhisattva is called "vigor in all its aspects.
The vigor of bodhisattvas that seeks to remove obstacles and the vigor that brings happiness in this life and the next should be viewed as being like patience.
In this regard, however, there is this distinction:
That which is patience (*kṣānti*) in that context should here be called vigor (*vīrya*) and enthusiasm (*abhyutsāha*).
Among these, what is the bodhisattva’s pure vigor?
It should be understood, in brief, as being of ten kinds.

It is appropriate, practiced, unremitting, well-grasped, applied at the proper time, endowed with penetration of the signs, undepressed, unadverse, balanced, and dedicated toward great enlightenment. In this regard, whatever secondary affliction (upakleśa) a bodhisattva is excessively oppressed by, he resorts to a corresponding antidote for the abandonment of that very secondary affliction.
One cultivates the meditation on the foul as the antidote to sensual desire;
loving-kindness as the antidote to ill-will;
and specific conditionality—dependent origination—as the antidote to delusion.
One cultivates mindfulness of breathing as the antidote to discursive thought,
and the analysis of the elements as the antidote to pride;
this kind of effort is called the bodhisattva’s appropriate effort.
In this case, a bodhisattva is not endowed with the vigor of a beginner— that is, of one who is just starting out—
for the sake of mental stability through instruction and admonition; rather,
he is one whose application is practiced and whose application is well-cultivated.
This is called the bodhisattva’s practiced vigor.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva does not yet possess practiced application regarding the stability of the mind within instruction and admonition;
rather, that bodhisattva is still a beginner, yet he is one whose application in that practice is unremitting through his constant and respectful application.
This is called the "unflagging vigor" of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva initiates vigor for the sake of mental stability—whether from the presence of a teacher or by himself—through the acquisition of the power of great learning and through non-erroneous comprehension;
this is called the "well-grasped vigor" of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva, thus grasping things without error, cultivates calm abiding at the time for calm abiding, restrains the mind at the time for exertion, and cultivates equanimity at the time for equanimity.
This is called his energy applied at the proper time.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva acts continuously and with reverence for the sake of discerning, not forgetting, and penetrating the signs of tranquility, exertion, and equanimity, as well as the signs for remaining in and emerging from meditative concentration.
Thus, this is called the bodhisattva’s vigor that penetrates signs.

Furthermore, having heard the instructions on the undertaking of vigor for bodhisattvas—which are supremely sublime, supremely profound, inconceivable, and immeasurable—the bodhisattva does not disparage himself, nor is his mind dejected;
nor does he become satisfied with a mere trifling or inferior attainment of excellence.
He does not turn back nor does he fail to exert himself;
this is called the "unflagging vigor" of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, from time to time, the bodhisattva maintains guardedness of the sense-faculties, moderation in eating, and [vigilance] during the first and last watches of the night.
He lives having undertaken the requisites for concentration— such as being devoted to wakefulness and dwelling with clear comprehension—
and he applies himself to them.
He exerts effort everywhere in a way that is unerring and connected with the true goal.
This is called the bodhisattva’s undistorted vigor.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva undertakes a vigor that is neither too slack nor too over-exerted;
it is balanced and effective, and he applies himself with equal respect to all tasks that are to be undertaken.
This is called the bodhisattva’s even vigor.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva dedicates all undertakings of vigor toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, this is called the bodhisattva’s correctly dedicated vigor.
Thus, the vigor of bodhisattvas—beginning with vigor of essential nature and ending with pure vigor—has great enlightenment as its fruit.
Relying upon which, bodhisattvas, having fulfilled the perfection of vigor, have awakened, will awaken, and are awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter on Vigor, within the section on the Foundation in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 143) The summary verse (*uddāna*) for the Chapter on Meditative Concentration (*Dhyānapaṭala*, Chapter 1.13) is to be understood as previously stated.
In this regard, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of bodhisattvas?

It is the mundane or supramundane wholesome one-pointedness of mind and mental stability of bodhisattvas, preceded by hearing and reflecting upon the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; it belongs to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*), or the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*), or is the path that proceeds with both joined together (*yuganaddhavāhin*).
Or, it may belong to both sides;

this should be understood as the intrinsic nature of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of bodhisattvas. In that regard, what is the "all-inclusive meditative concentration" (*sarvadhyāna*) of bodhisattvas?
That should be understood as being of two kinds:
mundane and supramundane.
Furthermore, it should be known as being of three kinds according to their respective applications.

There is the meditation for dwelling in happiness in the present life, the meditation for bringing forth the qualities of a bodhisattva’s samādhis, and the meditation for performing the welfare of sentient beings.

Among these, that which is the meditation of bodhisattvas— devoid of all conceptual construction, generating physical and mental pliancy, supremely tranquil, free from conceit, untasted by attachment, and devoid of all signs— is [the first].
This should be understood as their dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

In that regard, the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of bodhisattvas conduces to the production of various, inconceivable, and immeasurable concentrations (*samādhi*) comprised within the lineage of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
Even the names of those concentrations are unknown to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone how they could enter them.

Furthermore, that which conduces to the realization of qualities shared with Śrāvakas— such as the Bodhisattva’s liberations (*vimokṣa*), spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), absence of strife (*araṇā*), and knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*)—
this should be understood as the Bodhisattva’s meditation for the realization of the qualities of meditative concentration.
Regarding the activity for the benefit of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva’s meditation should be understood as having eleven aspects, as previously described.
Relying upon which meditation, a bodhisattva becomes a companion to sentient beings in their purposeful activities that bring about benefit;
he removes suffering and instructs those who are suffering in the proper method.
Grateful and appreciative of what has been done for him, he returns favors to those who have helped him;
he protects them from fears and dispels the grief of those in distress.
He provides necessities for those who lack them;
he properly leads his assembly;
and he conforms to their minds.
He gladdens them with their actual qualities and restrains them correctly;
and by means of his supernatural power, he both terrifies and wins them over.
Thus, all of this, condensed into one, is called the "all-inclusive meditative absorption" (*sarvadhyāna*) of the bodhisattvas;
there is nothing beyond this, nor anything more than this.
In that regard, what is the "difficult meditative absorption" (*duṣkaradhyāna*) of the bodhisattvas?
That should be understood as being threefold:

when bodhisattvas, having dwelt in sublime, diverse, well-mastered, and accomplished meditative abidings, voluntarily turn away from that supreme bliss of meditation and, through deliberate reflection, out of compassion for sentient beings, engage in extensive activities for their benefit.
Observing the ripening of the welfare of sentient beings, they take birth in the desire realm;
this should be understood as the first difficult meditation of the bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, it is when a bodhisattva, relying upon meditation, brings forth immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable bodhisattva samādhis that transcend the entire domain of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This should be understood as the second difficult meditation of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, that a bodhisattva, relying upon meditation, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
this should be understood as the third difficult meditation of a bodhisattva.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s meditation that faces all directions?
It should be understood as fourfold:
with applied thought and sustained thought; born of seclusion and born of concentration; accompanied by joy; and accompanied by equanimity and pleasant happiness.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s meditation of the true person (*satpuruṣadhyāna*)?
It should be understood as fivefold:
that which is untasted, and those accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s meditation of all aspects?
It should be understood as being thirteenfold, by condensing the six types and the seven types into one.

These are: wholesome meditation; neutral meditation for the purpose of creating emanations; meditation belonging to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*); and meditation belonging to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).

There is meditation for the sake of correctly contemplating one's own and others' welfare; meditation for the production of the qualities of the powers of the superknowledges; meditation having names as its object, meditation having meanings as its object, meditation having the signs of tranquility as its object, meditation having the signs of exertion as its object, and meditation having the signs of equanimity as its object; and meditation for dwelling in happiness in the present life and for performing the welfare of others.
Thus, this thirteenfold meditation of the bodhisattvas is called "meditation in all its aspects.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s meditation for those who are distressed and seeking aid?
That should be understood as being of eight kinds.
Meditation that serves as the basis for mantras which pacify afflictions such as poison, thunderbolts, irregular fevers, spirits, and planetary influences;
meditation for the complete alleviation of various diseases arising from an imbalance of the bodily elements;
and meditation that brings forth rain when times of famine and great distress have arrived.
It is the meditation that provides complete protection from various fears caused by humans and non-humans, whether occurring on water or on land;
likewise, it is the meditation for providing food and drink to those who have entered forest wildernesses and are destitute of food and drink.
There is meditation for the purpose of providing resources to those disciples who are destitute of them;
meditation for the purpose of correctly awakening beings who are heedless in the ten directions;
and meditation for the purpose of correctly performing the various tasks of beings as they arise.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s meditative absorption that brings happiness in this world and the next?
It should be understood as being of nine kinds:
the meditative absorption for the sake of disciplining sentient beings through the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
Meditation for the sake of disciplining sentient beings through the miracle of mind-reading and the miracle of instruction;
meditation that reveals the states of woe to those who commit evil deeds;
and meditation for the purpose of bestowing eloquence upon sentient beings whose eloquence has been lost.
There is meditative concentration for the restoration of mindfulness in sentient beings who have lost their mindfulness;
there is meditative concentration for the systematic arrangement of unerring treatises, poetry, and manuals, so that the true Dharma may endure for a long time;

and [there is meditative concentration] regarding worldly arts and crafts that are conducive to welfare and beneficial to sentient beings, such as writing, calculation, accounting, numeration, and sealing.
There is the meditative concentration that brings about various and manifold articles and utensils, such as beds, stools, umbrellas, and sandals;
and there is the meditative concentration that emits rays of light for the sake of alleviating the sufferings of those beings born in the states of woe at that particular time.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s pure meditative concentration?
That should be understood as tenfold:
meditation purified by mundane purity, which is untasted;
and meditation purified by supramundane purity, which is undefiled.
Dhyāna is pure through purity of preparation; it is pure through purity of the fundamental state; it is pure through purity that is superior even to the excellence of the fundamental state.
Dhyāna is pure through purity of mastery over entering, remaining, and emerging.

Furthermore, dhyāna is pure through purity of mastery over re-establishing concentration after withdrawing from dhyāna; it is pure through purity of mastery over the miraculous transformations of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
Dhyāna is purified through the purity of departing from all views;
and dhyāna is purified through the purity of abandoning the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.
This dhyāna of the bodhisattvas is immeasurable and has great enlightenment as its fruit, relying upon which bodhisattvas [fulfill] the perfection of dhyāna.
Having fulfilled [the requirements], they have awakened, will awaken, and are awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on Meditation, in the Foundation, the first stage of yoga, within the Bodhisattvabhūmi.
(Dutt 146)
The summary verse (*uddāna*) for the Chapter on Wisdom (Chapter 1.14) is to be understood as before.
In that regard, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a bodhisattva’s wisdom?

And that discernment of phenomena which proceeds by taking as its object the five fields of knowledge— the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), and the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*)— which functions for the sake of entering into all that is to be known and has already entered into all that is to be known:
this is to be understood as the intrinsic nature of the wisdom of bodhisattvas.
In that regard, what is the complete wisdom of bodhisattvas?
It should be understood as being twofold:
mundane and supramundane.
Furthermore, that [wisdom] should be understood briefly as threefold:
for the sake of awakening to and penetrating the reality of the knowable;
for the sake of exercising skill in the five fields of knowledge and the three collections as previously described; and for the sake of performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings.

That which, concerning the ineffable selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) of the bodhisattvas, is the wisdom directed toward the awakening to the truths, or at the time of awakening to the truths, or subsequent to the full realization of the truths; which is characterized by supreme tranquility, non-conceptual,

free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), conforming to the equality of all phenomena, entered into the great general characteristic (*mahāsāmānyalakṣaṇa*), reaching the limit of the knowable, and [free from] the two extremes of superimposition and denial.

Because it is free from [the extremes], this wisdom of the bodhisattvas, which follows the middle way, should be understood as that which leads to the realization and penetration of reality. Skillfulness in the five fields of knowledge should be understood in detail as previously explained, namely, as in the "Chapter on Powers and Lineages."
Furthermore, there are three aggregates of phenomena: the aggregate of phenomena associated with benefit,
the aggregate of phenomena associated with harm,
and the aggregate of phenomena associated with neither benefit nor harm.
Thus, the mastery of wisdom (*prajñā*) in these eight points fulfills the great, unsurpassed accumulation of knowledge for the sake of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, the performance of the welfare of sentient beings should be understood as being of exactly eleven types, as previously described;
that wisdom which pertains to those very same points should be understood as the wisdom for the performance of the welfare of sentient beings.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s difficult wisdom?
It should be seen as threefold: it is difficult for the sake of knowing the profound selflessness of phenomena;
it is difficult for the sake of knowing the means for disciplining sentient beings.
And for the sake of unobstructed knowledge regarding all that is to be known, it is supremely difficult to perform.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s wisdom that faces in all directions?
That [wisdom] should be understood as fourfold:
wisdom consisting of hearing and wisdom consisting of reflection, based upon the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
and wisdom comprised by the power of analytical discernment, which, through such discernment, conforms to what is to be done by a bodhisattva and desists from what is not to be done.
And it is the immeasurable wisdom belonging to the stage of meditative concentration, which is comprised by the power of cultivation.
In that regard, what is the wisdom of a true person belonging to a bodhisattva who is a true person?
It should be seen as being of five kinds.

It is the wisdom arisen from hearing the true Dharma, accompanied by correct mental attention directed toward one's own inner realization, which is certain regarding the welfare of both oneself and others, and is the wisdom that abandons the afflictions.
There is another formulation:
it is subtle, because it enters into the objects of knowledge through their mode of being as they truly are.
It is *nipuṇā* (subtle) because it enters into the knowable in its full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatayā*).
It is *sahajā* (innate) because it has been brought about by the prior accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*).

It is *āgamopetā* (endowed with scripture) because it involves the grasping and retaining of the meaning of the Dharma as proclaimed by the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*).
Endowed with realization, it begins from the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*) and extends up to the attainment of the final stage (*niṣṭhāgamanabhūmi*).
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s wisdom in all its aspects?
It should be understood as being of thirteen kinds, by condensing together six kinds and seven kinds into one.
Regarding the truths, there is the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path;
at the culmination, there is the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
This, first of all, is the sixfold wisdom.

Furthermore, there are seven kinds: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of the superknowledges (*abhijñājñāna*), knowledge of characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñāna*), knowledge preceded by the ten powers (*daśabalapūrvaṅgama-jñāna*), and the knowledge of reasoning (*yuktijñāna*) regarding the four types of reasoning.
Among these, what is the Bodhisattva’s wisdom that seeks to provide for others?
It should be understood as being eightfold.
The bodhisattva’s analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) begins with the knowledge of the synonyms of phenomena;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) begins with the knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena;
and the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) begins with the knowledge of the etymological definitions of phenomena.
The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) concerns the distinctions among the categories and terms of phenomena;
it is the bodhisattva’s wisdom for the purpose of refuting all opposing disputants,
and the wisdom for establishing and maintaining the system of one's own doctrine.
Wisdom for the purpose of correctly managing the household and for the prosperity of the family;
and that wisdom of the bodhisattva which is certain regarding royal policy and worldly conventions—
among these, what is the bodhisattva’s wisdom that brings happiness in this life and the next?
That [wisdom] should be seen as ninefold:
wisdom that is both well-purified and well-established in the inner science;
and wisdom that is well-purified but not established in the science of logic, the science of grammar, the science of medicine, and the science of worldly arts and crafts.
And relying upon that very same fivefold knowledge which is well-purified, there is the wisdom of a bodhisattva that respectively demonstrates,
instigates, inspires, and gladdens other disciples who are deluded, negligent, disheartened, and those who are correctly practicing. In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s purified wisdom?
In brief, it should be understood as being of ten kinds:

it is twofold with respect to the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*), because of the apprehension of the meaning of reality by way of its full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and by way of its mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*);
and it is twofold with respect to the meaning of phenomenal activity (*pravṛttyartha*), because of the apprehension [of it] by way of the correct cause and by way of the fruit.
Regarding the meaning of grasping (*upādāna*), there are two kinds [of wisdom] through the thorough knowledge of error and non-error as they truly are;
regarding the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*), there are two kinds through the thorough knowledge of all that is to be done and not to be done as they truly are.
Thus, this fivefold and ten-part wisdom of the bodhisattvas should be understood as pure by means of supreme purity.

Thus, this well-determined and immeasurable wisdom of the bodhisattvas has great enlightenment as its fruit; relying upon it, bodhisattvas fulfill the perfection of wisdom and awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Indeed, this should be understood as a concise summary of the six perfections taught by the Blessed One in various scattered discourses.

In whatever sutra spoken by the Tathāgata the perfection of giving, up to the perfection of wisdom, appears either in brief statement or in detailed explanation, it should be subsumed under giving that is intrinsic in nature, up to giving that is pure;
and its inclusion should be understood according to what is appropriate.

In this way, the entry into and the inclusion of the other [perfections], beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*) and ending with wisdom (*prajñā*), as they have been described, should be understood according to their respective applications.

Furthermore, all those immeasurable birth stories (*jātaka*) of the Tathāgatas concerning their bodhisattva conduct and lives, which are connected to difficult practices (*duṣkaracaryā*), should be understood as being connected to generosity (*dāna*) and concerning generosity.
Just as it is with generosity, so too for ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration—all [those stories] connected to wisdom should be understood as concerning wisdom.
Some [teachings] should be understood as concerning generosity alone, some as concerning everything up to wisdom alone, some as a combination of two, some as a combination of three,

some as a combination of four, some as a combination of five, and some as concerning all six perfections. Bodhisattvas who fully realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening through these six perfections are called "great oceans of pure dharmas" and "great seas of pure dharmas."
They are called great jewel-lakes that are the cause for the complete perfection of all aspects of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, for this immeasurable accumulation of the equipment of merit and wisdom, there is no fruit more appropriate than unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, on Wisdom, in the section on the Foundation within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 149) (Chapter 1.15) The summary verse (*uddāna*) for the Section on the Bases of Social Integration (*saṃgrahavastupaṭala*) should be understood as before.
In this regard, what is the intrinsic nature of the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas?
Here, a bodhisattva utters toward sentient beings speech that is pleasing, truthful, consistent with the Dharma, and endowed with meaning.
This, in brief, is the intrinsic nature of the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s all-inclusive pleasant speech?
It should be understood as being threefold.
Here, it is the bodhisattva’s agreeable speech by which the bodhisattva, free from a frown, is the first to speak.

With a bright facial complexion, preceded by a smiling countenance, he greets beings in various ways— by inquiring after their well-being and prosperity, or by inquiring about the equilibrium of their bodily elements, or by inquiring whether their days and nights have been pleasant, or by saying "Come, welcome"— thus conforming to worldly custom and the conduct of a city-dweller.

And there is the speech of a bodhisattva that is gladdening— the speech by which a bodhisattva, having seen an increase in sons, an increase in wives, an increase in kinsmen, an increase in wealth, or an increase in grain, gladdens those beings who have not themselves perceived their own increase;
or else, he gladdens them through an increase in faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

Furthermore, whatever speech of a bodhisattva is associated with the teaching of the Dharma endowed with qualities of every kind, which is constantly and continuously present for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, and which acts as a benefactor through supreme assistance—
all these various types should be understood as the loving speech of bodhisattvas.
In that regard, what is the concise summary of all the loving speech of bodhisattvas?
That [speech] should be understood as twofold:
that which conforms to worldly conduct and that which conforms to the correct teaching of the Dharma.
Among these, both the speech that causes mutual greeting and the speech that causes joy should be known as conforming to worldly conduct.
In this regard, that speech which is beneficial and presented as the supreme benefit should be understood as the kindness of correctly teaching the Dharma.
Among these, what is the bodhisattva’s difficult-to-practice pleasant speech?
It should be seen as being of three kinds.

When a bodhisattva, having reflected with a mind that is perfectly pure and free from defilement, utters words that are conciliatory, gladdening, or beneficial toward murderers, adversaries, and enemies—
this is to be understood as the bodhisattva’s first difficult practice of pleasant speech.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva, without becoming weary toward beings who are extremely deluded and of dull faculties,

deliberately delivers a discourse on the Dharma and, accepting weariness, causes them to grasp the principle, the Dharma, and what is wholesome— this should be known as the second difficult-to-practice kind of pleasant speech of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva, with a mind free from malice and a mind free from resentment, utters words that are conciliatory, gladdening, and beneficial toward beings who are deceitful, fraudulent, those who deceive teachers, preceptors, gurus, and those worthy of offerings, and those who have entered upon wrong paths—
this should be understood as the bodhisattva’s third difficult practice of pleasant speech.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing pleasant speech?
It should be understood as fourfold:
the teaching of the Dharma for the sake of abandoning the hindrances, for proceeding to a happy rebirth, and for what must be done beforehand.
For one whose hindrances have departed and whose mind is healthy, there is the teaching of the Dharma that is most excellent and connected with the Four Noble Truths;
and for the sake of correctly exhorting heedless beings— both householders and those who have gone forth— so as to rouse them from heedless conduct and establish them in heedful conduct,
there is the teaching of the Dharma consisting of the performance of discussion and definitive resolution for the purpose of removing whatever doubts may arise.
In that regard, what is the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas who are true persons?
It should be understood as being of five kinds.

Here, bodhisattvas who have become [bodhisattvas] and those who have become Tathāgatas teach the Dharma to those to be trained only with its cause, with its renunciation, with its refuge, with its exertion, and with its miracle.
In appropriate cases, they prescribe the training rules (śikṣāpada) together with their origin stories;
therefore, their Dharma is possessed of its causal basis.
Furthermore, for those who have undertaken the training and committed an offense, they prescribe the means of recovery from that offense.
Therefore, this Dharma is possessed of an escape.
They prescribe a practice within this Dharma and Vinaya that is unerring and comprised of the four reliances;
therefore, their Dharma is possessed of reliances.
They fully reveal the path that leads out of all suffering and is irreversible;
therefore, their Dharma possesses prowess.
And by means of the three miracles, they make their entire teaching fruitful.
Therefore, their Dharma is accompanied by miraculous power (*saprātihārya*).
In this regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ agreeable speech (*priyavāditā*) in all its forms?
It should be understood as being of thirteen types, by condensing the sixfold and sevenfold categories together.
Kind speech consists in granting permission regarding those things that should be permitted,
and in prohibiting those things that should be prohibited;
it is kind speech that elucidates the various methods for understanding the teachings.
It reveals the non-erroneous characteristics of phenomena; it reveals the non-erroneous etymological definitions of phenomena;
it reveals the distinctions between the various types of categories of phenomena.
Pleasant speech;
pleasant speech that is welcoming; pleasant speech that is gladdening.
It is pleasant speech that consists of having little concern for others regarding all their requisites, and having little concern when all their tasks have been properly accomplished;
it is pleasant speech that provides consolation to those who are afraid amidst various fears;
and it is pleasant speech comprised of instruction in the proper method.

Loving speech consists of exhortation, admonition, and censure for the purpose of raising [beings] from unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states—based on what is rightly seen, heard, or suspected.

Loving speech is also that which is brought forth by requesting another who is capable [of the task]. This thirteen-fold loving speech of the bodhisattvas should be understood as comprising all its aspects.
In that regard, what is the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas directed toward those who are distressed and seeking help?
It should be understood as being of eight kinds:
it is the speech of a bodhisattva based upon the fourfold purity of speech regarding eight types of purposeful transactions.
This is called the agreeable speech of Bodhisattvas directed toward those who seek relief from distress.
In this regard, there is this fourfold purity of speech:
abstaining from false speech.
Abstaining from malicious speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter;
herein lie these eight noble modes of discourse:
speaking of what was seen as having been seen, and speaking of what was heard, thought, or cognized as having been heard, thought, or cognized.
To speak of what has not been seen as not seen; to speak of what has not been heard, not thought, or not cognized as not heard, not thought, or not cognized.
In that regard, what is the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas that brings happiness in this world and the next?
That should be seen as ninefold:
pleasant speech for the sake of abandoning grief over calamities involving kinsmen;
pleasant speech for the sake of abandoning grief over calamities involving wealth; and pleasant speech for the sake of abandoning grief over calamities involving health.
Affectionate speech is for the sake of abandoning failures in ethical discipline and abandoning failures in view.
It is that affectionate speech which is the teaching of the true Dharma for the sake of perfection in ethical discipline, perfection in view, perfection in conduct, and perfection in livelihood.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s pure affectionate speech?
It should be seen as being of twenty kinds.
Furthermore, that teaching of the Dharma through twenty aspects is to be understood as previously explained,
namely, in the *Balagotra-paṭala*.

In this regard, beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) is to be understood in detail in exactly the same way as pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*). Furthermore, I shall describe another form of beneficial conduct that is even more distinguished than this.
For, by means of this pleasant speech in all its varieties, the bodhisattva practices it in various situations for the sake of approaching sentient beings.
In that regard, what is the nature of the beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) of bodhisattvas?

It is when, having established a mind of compassion toward those beings who have been shown the proper method through such pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), one engages in beneficial conduct regarding the trainings and in practice according to the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapraticaryā*) as appropriate, with a mind free from worldly motives (*nirāmiṣa*).
The exhortation by means of the mind, the training, the settling, and the establishing— this is, in brief, the explanation of the intrinsic nature of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
In that regard, what is the all-inclusive beneficial conduct of the bodhisattvas?
It should be understood as twofold:
the ripening of sentient beings who are not yet matured,
and the liberation of sentient beings who have been ripened.
