Furthermore, that single greatness of full attainment should be understood as corresponding to the fruit of these six.
These eight factors conduce to the summary of the entire Mahāyāna:
the teaching of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka,
and within that very Bodhisattvapiṭaka, the revelation of the true meaning of all phenomena.
Within that very Bodhisattvapiṭaka, there is the revelation of the inconceivable and most sublime power of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
and there is the proper hearing of it,
and the cultivation of the resolute intention preceded by proper reflection upon it.
The entry into the modes of cultivation is preceded by the approach with resolute intention;
the perfection of the fruit of cultivation is preceded by the entry into the modes of cultivation;
and the ultimate deliverance results from that very perfection of the fruit of cultivation.
For it is by training in this way that bodhisattvas fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Who, then, are those bodhisattvas who, training in this way, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
In brief, they should be known as tenfold.
One who abides in the lineage;
one who has entered [the path];
one whose intention is impure.
One of pure intention;
one who is not yet matured;
one who is matured.
One who has not fallen into certainty,
one who has fallen into certainty,
and one bound by a single birth.
And there is the one in their final existence.
Among these, the bodhisattva established in the lineage, while training, generates the thought of awakening;
he is said to be "one who has entered."
Furthermore, as long as that very same person who has descended [into the path] has not yet entered the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*), they are called one of impure intention;
but once entered, they become one of pure intention.
Again, as long as that very same one of pure intention has not yet entered the stage of reaching the ultimate end (*niṣṭhāgamanabhūmi*), they are called immature.
Once he has entered [the stage], he becomes matured.
Furthermore, as long as he is not yet matured, or as long as he has not entered the stage of certain or uncertain conduct (*niyatāniyatācaryābhūmi*), he is said to be "uncertain" (*aniyata*).
Once he has entered [the path], he becomes fixed;
furthermore, that very person is of two types when fully matured:
one who is bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), after which birth he will realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
And one who is in their final existence attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment while remaining in that very birth.
In this regard, ten types of bodhisattvas have been described, beginning from their spiritual lineage up to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
For those who train in the bodhisattva trainings, there exists no training higher than these.
Regarding where they should train, how they should train, and the fact that there is no bodhisattva superior to these aforementioned bodhisattvas who trains in the bodhisattva trainings—
furthermore, for all these bodhisattvas without distinction, one should know that these are their derivative names belonging to such a category:

namely, *bodhisattva*, *mahāsattva*, *dhīmān* (the wise one), *uttamadyutiḥ* (of supreme splendor), *jinaputraḥ* (son of the Victor), *jinādhāraḥ* (support of the Victor), *vijetā* (the conqueror), *jināṅkuraḥ* (sprout of the Victor), *vikrāntaḥ* (the valiant), *paramāryaḥ* (supremely noble), *sārthavāhaḥ* (caravan leader), *mahāyaśaḥ* (of great fame), *kṛpāluḥ* (compassionate), and *mahāpuṇyaḥ* (of great merit).
"An Īśvara and a righteous one.

Furthermore, among the infinite bodhisattvas in the endless and boundless world-systems in the ten directions, it should be understood that there are immeasurable individual attainments of conceptualization.
In that regard, those bodhisattvas who abide in the claim "we are bodhisattvas" but do not correctly practice the bodhisattva trainings should be understood as counterfeit bodhisattvas.
However,
those who abide in the vow "We are Bodhisattvas" and who train correctly in the Bodhisattva trainings— these should be known as true Bodhisattvas.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Qualities of Bodhisattvas, in the section on the Foundation within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The Section on the Yoga of the Foundation is completed.
The Section on the Yoga of the Dharma Following the Foundation (Book 2).
(Dutt 207)
The Chapter on the Marks of a Bodhisattva (Chapter 2.1).
Summary verse: Essential nature, the basis, the fruit and its benefits, the sequence, and the summary.
There are these five marks of a bodhisattva who has become such; endowed with which, a bodhisattva is reckoned as a "bodhisattva.
What are the five?
Compassion, pleasant speech, fortitude, open-handedness, and the ability to unravel the intentional meaning of profound teachings.
Furthermore, these five factors are to be understood through five aspects:
by way of intrinsic nature, basis, fruit and benefit, sequence, and summary.
Among these, the intrinsic nature of compassion is twofold.
It consists of that which pertains to intention and that which pertains to practice.

Therein, the intention pertaining to the welfare [of beings] and the intention pertaining to their happiness is called the Bodhisattva’s compassion toward sentient beings. As for that which pertains to practice, whatever intention the Bodhisattva has toward sentient beings, he provides that very thing through body or speech according to his ability and according to his strength.
In that regard, the nature of pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*) should be understood as speech that is, as previously stated, gladdening, consoling, and beneficial,
just as described in the "Chapter on the Means of Attraction" (*saṃgrahavastu-paṭala*).
Furthermore, the strength of a bodhisattva that consists of courage (*sattva*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and lack of dejection (*alīnatva*) is called the nature of heroism (*vairya-svabhāva*).
In this regard, that which is the bodhisattva’s magnanimous generosity or unafflicted generosity should be understood as the essential nature of open-handedness. Furthermore,

the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the correct, applied knowledge for their actualization should be understood as the essential nature of the bodhisattvas’ unraveling of the intentional meaning of profound teachings.
In that regard, there are five bases for compassion.

What are the five? They are: suffering beings, those who engage in misconduct, the heedless, those who have entered upon wrong practice, and those in whom the latent tendencies of the afflictions persist.
Starting from the beings in the hells, for certain other beings, painful sensations persist as a continuous stream established within their mental continuum;
these beings are said to be "suffering.
On the other hand, there are those who, while not necessarily suffering, nevertheless frequently engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
And they dwell there, finding delight in such forms.
These beings are called "practitioners of misconduct," namely those such as sheep-butchers, pig-butchers, poultry-farmers, and so forth.

On the other hand, there are those who are not necessarily suffering nor practitioners of misconduct, but rather who indulge in sensual pleasures with attachment, dwelling devoted to watching actors, dancers, jesters, and performers, intent on self-indulgence.
These beings are called "negligent," such as certain individuals who indulge in sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, those who are not necessarily suffering, nor practitioners of misconduct, nor even negligent, but who—relying on a failure of view—have set out for liberation from suffering;
these beings are called "wrongly resolved," such as those who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, have gone forth into a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.

Furthermore, those beings who are not necessarily suffering—in detail, up to those who have not practiced wrongly—but who are either fully bound or partially bound by the afflictions (*kleśa*), these beings are said to be "underlyingly afflicted" (*anuśayita*) by the afflictions. This includes both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who are correctly applied [to the path] and those who are virtuous, as well as those in training (*śaikṣa*). To this extent is the basis of the Bodhisattvas' compassion.
The basis by which and the object by which compassion proceeds—
there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
These five are the bases for the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas.
What are the five? They are:
correct addressing, correct gladdening, correct consolation, correct invitation, and instruction in the proper method.
Furthermore, their respective distinctions should be understood.
As stated in the *Saṃgrahavastupaṭala*:
"Through these five bases and these objects of focus, the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas proceeds;
there is nothing beyond this, nor anything more than this."
These five bases of a bodhisattva’s perseverance (vairya) are to be known.
What are the five?

It should be understood that the very same five aspects through which the acquisition of firm strength (dhṛtibalādhānatā) of bodhisattvas was described in the Chapter on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment (bodhipakṣapaṭala) are themselves the bases of a bodhisattva’s perseverance.
By means of those bases and those objects, a bodhisattva’s fortitude proceeds;
there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
There are these five bases for a bodhisattva’s open-handedness.
What are the five? They are: constant giving, joyful giving, respectful giving, unafflicted giving, and non-reliant giving.
Furthermore, their detailed classification should be understood as it is in the Chapter on Generosity (*Dānapaṭala*).
Through these bases and these objects, the open-handedness of bodhisattvas proceeds.
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
These five are the bases for a bodhisattva’s unraveling of the intentional terminology regarding profound meanings.
What are the five?
Those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata which are profound and reveal the profound, connected with emptiness, characterized by specific conditionality,
and in accordance with dependent origination—
this is the first basis.
Furthermore, in the Vinaya, there is skill regarding offenses and skill regarding the emergence from offenses;
this is the second basis.
Furthermore, in the Mātṛkā, there is the non-erroneous establishment of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).
This is the third basis:
the elucidation of the meaning of the signs of the Dharma that are intentional and concealed.
This is the fourth basis.
And the differentiation of the methods for the definitions of the meaning of all phenomena—
this is the fifth basis.
By means of this basis and by means of this object, the bodhisattvas' capacity to unravel the profound intentional meanings proceeds.
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this:
compassion on the part of a bodhisattva toward sentient beings, from the very beginning, leads to the abandonment of enmity.
Thus compassionate, the bodhisattva applies himself to all activities for the benefit of sentient beings with an undaunted mind.
And he does not grow weary in that practice;
his abiding frequently in compassion leads to faultless happiness in the present life and to the benefit of others.
Furthermore, whatever benefits of loving-kindness were spoken of by the Blessed One—such as poison and weapons not affecting his body—and so forth, these also accrue to him.
All of these should be understood as belonging to the compassionate bodhisattva;
thus, this should be seen as the fruit and benefit of the compassion of bodhisattvas.
A bodhisattva who speaks kindly abandons in this present life four types of verbal faults: lying, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
And this speech of his proceeds for the sake of benefiting himself and for the sake of benefiting others.
In this very life and in the future, the bodhisattva who speaks kindly becomes one whose words are accepted and whose words are heeded.
This should be understood as the benefit resulting from the bodhisattva’s pleasant speech.
The steadfast bodhisattva, in this very life, becomes entirely free from all sloth and indolence and possesses a joyful mind;
he undertakes the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline and,
having done so, does not become despondent.
Through patience, one favors both oneself and others;
and in the future, regarding the undertaking of all bodhisattva activities, one becomes by nature firm in one's exertion and does not turn back without having accomplished them.
Thus, these should be understood as the fruits and benefits of the bodhisattvas' fortitude;
likewise, the fruits and benefits of open-handedness and the unraveling of the intentional meaning of profound doctrines should be understood,
just as they are described in the "Chapter on Power" regarding the power of generosity and the power of wisdom.
This is the benefit of the fruit for these Bodhisattvas who possess discernment.
What, then, is their sequence?
First, a Bodhisattva favors sentient beings out of compassion and becomes concerned for them, desiring their welfare.
Then, having raised them up from unwholesome states and established them in wholesome states, he speaks of the proper method, causes them to grasp it, and instructs them.

Furthermore, regarding those beings who have thus entered [the path], as well as the misconduct of beings and the various types of objectives that are obscured by afflictions, he becomes capable of enduring their friction;
this is because he does not abandon beings, whether they abide in correct practice or in misconduct.

Thus, that steadfast one ripens some beings through the gathering of material goods (*āmiṣa*), some through the gathering of the Dharma, and some through both of these—the gathering of the Dharma and the gathering of material goods.
This should be understood as the sequence of these five marks of a bodhisattva.
These five marks of a bodhisattva are the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Among these six perfections, which mark of a bodhisattva is subsumed by which perfection?
Compassion is subsumed by the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Affability is subsumed by the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Courage is subsumed by the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of wisdom.
Open-handedness is subsumed by the perfection of generosity alone.

The unraveling of the intentional meaning of profound matters is subsumed by the perfection of meditative concentration and the perfection of wisdom. Thus, these five marks of a bodhisattva are to be understood through five transformations.
They should be understood by way of their intrinsic nature, their basis, their fruits and benefits, their sequence, and their summary.
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Characteristics of a Bodhisattva," in the section on Yoga within the *Ādhārānudharma* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 211)
The Chapter on the Wings (Pakṣapaṭalam), Second [Chapter]: Summary Verse.
Well-performed action, skillfulness, favoring others, and finally, dedication.
Whether abiding in the state of a householder or in the state of one who has gone forth, it should be understood that there are, in brief, four qualities of a bodhisattva.
Training in these, whether as a householder or one who has gone forth, a bodhisattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What are the four?
These are: well-performed action, skillfulness, benefiting others, and dedication.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s well-performed action?
It is acting with certainty regarding the perfections, acting with expertise, acting constantly, and acting irreproachably.
And how does a bodhisattva become one who acts with certainty regarding giving?
Here, when a gift is available and a petitioner has properly approached—whether he be a wrongdoer or a benefactor, virtuous or flawed—the bodhisattva necessarily gives.
No one at all in the world—whether human or non-human, ascetic or brahmin—is able to cause his mind of generosity to waver, even by means of a legitimate argument.
And how does a bodhisattva become one who acts with skill regarding generosity?
In this regard, when a gift is available and a petitioner has properly approached, the bodhisattva gives everything;
there is nothing whatsoever that he would not relinquish for the sake of sentient beings, even his own internal things, let alone external ones.
And how is a bodhisattva one who acts constantly with regard to giving?
Here, a bodhisattva, never becoming weary of giving, gives at all times, continuously and perpetually, whatever gift arises.
And how is a bodhisattva one who acts irreproachably with regard to giving?
In this regard, a bodhisattva avoids that afflicted giving which was described in the "Chapter on Giving" and bestows unafflicted giving.
In this way, a bodhisattva is one who acts well with respect to giving;
and just as it is with giving, so it is with the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
This should be understood according to the appropriate application.
These very four modes are: acting with certainty, acting with skill, acting constantly, and acting irreproachably.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s skillfulness?
In brief, that skill in means should be understood as being of ten kinds: skill in means for removing the hostility of hostile beings;
skill in means for introducing those who are neutral; skill in means for maturing those who have been introduced; and skill in means for liberating those who have been matured;
as well as skill in all worldly treatises.
Skill in reflecting upon lapses in the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline; skill in right aspiration;
and skill in the Śrāvaka vehicle, skill in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and skill in the Mahāyāna.
It should be understood that the detailed classification of all these skills, as appropriate, occurs within this very Bodhisattva stage, just as previously described.
Furthermore, these ten skillful means of a bodhisattva perform five functions.
By means of the first four skillful means, the bodhisattva establishes sentient beings in their own welfare.
Through skillfulness in all worldly treatises, the bodhisattva overcomes all the doctrines of others.
Through skill in reflecting upon lapses in the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline, a bodhisattva either does not incur an offense,
or if one is incurred, remedies it according to the Dharma; thus,
he brings about a thoroughly purified undertaking of the vow of ethical discipline.

Through skill in right aspiration, a bodhisattva attains the fulfillment of all intended aims in the future. Through three types of skill, a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma according to [the needs of] those who possess various lineages, faculties, and inclinations,
and points out the appropriate reasoning.
In this way, through these ten types of skillfulness, a bodhisattva performs five tasks;
by means of these five tasks, all his duties are brought to completion,
concerning both welfare in the present life and in future lives.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s assistance to others?

Here, relying upon the four means of attraction— generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency of purpose— the bodhisattva brings about both benefit and happiness for certain beings.
[He also bestows benefit and happiness.
This is a brief explanation of the bodhisattvas' assistance to others;
the detailed explanation, moreover, should be understood as before, namely, in the chapter on the welfare of oneself and others.
(Dutt 213) In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dedication?
Here, a bodhisattva, by virtue of having performed his duties well, dedicates whatever roots of merit have been accumulated through these three gateways.
With skillfulness and through the favoring of others, he dedicates all that— past, future, and present— with a profound essence of serene faith toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
He does not expect any other fruit or ripening of that root of virtue, nor anything other than unexcelled, perfect enlightenment itself.

Whatever rules of training for bodhisattvas, whether householders or those who have gone forth, have been taught by the Blessed One—all of them should be understood to be included within these very four: well-performed action, skillfulness, benefiting others, and dedication.

Therefore, for a bodhisattva who thus performs actions well, who is skilled, who is engaged in benefiting others, and who practices dedication, awakening—which is otherwise difficult to reach and difficult to attain—becomes near, very near.
It should be understood that whatever bodhisattvas, whether householders or those who have gone forth, are training in the past, future, and present time-epochs,
have awakened, will awaken, and are awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
All of them [attain this] by means of these very four qualities; there is nothing beyond this and nothing more than this.
Thus, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, a bodhisattva who is correctly applied to these four qualities becomes a true bodhisattva.
Moreover, one should understand that there is a very great distinction and a very great difference between a householder bodhisattva and a bodhisattva who has gone forth into homelessness.
For a bodhisattva who has gone forth is, from the very beginning, liberated from the fault of attachment to a family consisting of mother, father, children, wife, and so forth.
Furthermore, it should be understood that a householder is not liberated;

whereas a renunciant bodhisattva is liberated from the afflictions of attachment and the sufferings of toil—such as agriculture, commerce, and service to kings—for the sake of that very same possession.
It should be understood, however, that the householder is not liberated.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who has gone forth is able to practice a celibate life that is entirely pure, whereas a bodhisattva who remains a householder is not.
Moreover, a bodhisattva who has gone forth quickly attains direct knowledge (*abhijñā*) regarding all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*).
Whatever wholesome practice he undertakes, in each and every instance he very swiftly reaches its consummation.
But it is not so for a householder bodhisattva.
Furthermore, because a renunciant bodhisattva abides in the vows and restraints of others, his words become authoritative; but it is not so for a householder bodhisattva.
By means of such qualities as these, one should understand that there is a very great difference between the householder and the renunciant Bodhisattva.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the Side, in the section on the Application of Yoga concerning the Dharma Following the Foundation in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The Chapter on Superior Intention (Adhyāśayapaṭala). Summary Verse:
The affection of the wise toward all sentient beings is indeed sevenfold.
Among those, fifteen are intentions; ten are considered to be performers of the task.
A sevenfold affection toward sentient beings arises among bodhisattvas, endowed with which bodhisattvas are said to possess a virtuous intention (*kalyāṇāśaya*) and a supremely virtuous intention.
What is this sevenfold affection?
It is: fearlessness, propriety, lack of weariness, being unasked, non-material, extensive, and impartial.
For a bodhisattva does not become affectionate out of fear of anyone;
rather, he conducts himself toward them with compliant actions of body, speech, and mind that are pleasing and conducive to their welfare and happiness.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva’s affection for sentient beings never proceeds in a manner devoid of skillful means, such as by inciting them toward what is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, improper conduct, or toward what is inappropriate.
And thus a bodhisattva is affectionate toward sentient beings in such a way that he does not grow weary of all his undertakings for their sake.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva is affectionate toward sentient beings even without being asked; he is not affectionate only when requested by someone.

He is affectionate with a mind free from worldly motives (*nirāmiṣa*), not while expecting a reciprocal benefit from others or hoping for a desirable karmic maturation in the future; thus, he is one whose affection is without cause (*niṣkāraṇavatsala*).
The bodhisattva possesses affection for sentient beings;
moreover, that affection of the bodhisattva toward sentient beings is vast and not limited.
It is so vast that even when receiving every kind of harm from these sentient beings, the bodhisattva does not abandon them, though he may indeed act in ways that are unpleasant to himself.
However, he does not, by any means, desire evil deeds for others.

Furthermore, this very characteristic of the Bodhisattvas' affection (*vātsalya*), which is endowed with such qualities, is equal toward all sentient beings and is not merely partial to a limited portion of the realm of beings (*sattvadhātu*).
Thus, Bodhisattvas who are endowed with this sevenfold affection are called those of "virtuous intention" (*kalyāṇāśaya*) and "supremely virtuous intention."

(Dutt 215) In this regard, that resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), realization, and certainty concerning the Buddha-dharmas which is preceded by faith and preceded by the investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*) on the part of a bodhisattva is called "resolute intention" (*adhyāśaya*).
Furthermore, those resolute intentions of a bodhisattva should be understood, in brief, as being fifteenfold.
Which are the fifteen? They are:

the supreme intention, the virtuous intention, the intention regarding the perfections, the intention regarding the meaning of reality, the intention regarding power, the intention for benefit, the intention for happiness, the liberated intention, the firm intention, the non-deceptive intention, the impure intention, the pure intention, and the perfectly pure intention.
There is the restrained intention and the innate intention.
Among these, the resolute intention that a bodhisattva has toward the Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—is called the supreme intention.
The resolute intention regarding the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline and vows is called the conduct-intention.

The resolute intention for the full realization of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom is called the "intention regarding the perfections" (*pāramitā-āśaya*).

The resolute intention regarding the selflessness of phenomena and persons, the ultimate truth, and the profound suchness of phenomena is called the "intention regarding the meaning of reality" (*tattvārtha-āśaya*).
The resolute intention regarding the inconceivable power of the superknowledges of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or their innate power, is called the "intention regarding power" (*prabhāva-āśaya*).

The desire to bring about the welfare of sentient beings is called the "intent for benefit" (*hitāśaya*). The desire to bring about assistance for sentient beings is called the "intent for happiness" (*sukhāśaya*).
The state of having a mind free from worldly motives toward sentient beings, and a mind unattached even to desirable karmic results, is called the "liberated intent" (*vinirmuktāśaya*).
The state of one-pointedness of mind directed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is called the firm resolve (*dṛḍhāśaya*).

The resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) accompanied by non-erroneous knowledge regarding the means for the welfare of sentient beings and the means for enlightenment is called the non-deceptive resolve (*avisaṃvādanāśaya*).
That superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) of bodhisattvas throughout the entire stage of the excellence of resolute conviction is called the impure resolve (*aśuddhāśaya*).
Starting from the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*) up to the stage of certain conduct (*niyatacaryābhūmi*), the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) of bodhisattvas is called "pure intention.

On the stage of reaching the culmination (*niṣṭhāgamanabhūmi*), the superior intention of bodhisattvas is called "thoroughly pure intention" (*suśuddhāśaya*). In that regard, whatever is impure intention is itself called "restrained intention" (*nigṛhītāśaya*) because it must be attended to through analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*).

Furthermore, that resolve which is pure and thoroughly purified is called the "innate resolve" (*sahaja-adhyāśaya*), because by its very nature it consists of that [resolve] and is firmly established within the basis [of the person].
Thus, by means of these fifteen virtuous resolves pertaining to all the stages, bodhisattvas briefly perform ten tasks.
What are the ten?
With a supreme intention, they perform every form of jewel-offering, which is the foremost among all the accumulations for enlightenment;
with a virtuous intention, they undertake the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline and do not intentionally commit an offense even for the sake of their lives.
Having fallen [into transgressions], they confess them with the utmost haste.

With the intention of the perfections (*pāramitā*), through the continuous cultivation of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*), they abide in heedfulness and abide in supreme heedfulness. With the resolute intention toward the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha-adhyāśaya*), they wander through cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings with minds free from affliction.

They possess an resolute intention that is never separated from nirvāṇa; through their resolute intention regarding spiritual power, they manifest a profound and intense clarity of faith toward the Teaching;
and regarding cultivation, they dwell frequently with a sense of it being the essence and with a born longing for it.
But they are not satisfied merely with what has been heard or merely with reflection;
rather, with a disposition for benefit, a disposition for happiness, and a disposition for liberation, they apply themselves to every form of activity for the sake of sentient beings,
and having so applied themselves, they do not become weary.
With firm resolve, they dwell with ardent vigor and expansive vigor in their undertakings; their application is neither lax nor interrupted.
Through the resolute intention of non-deceptiveness, they quickly attain supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) in the realization of various wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*).
They do not find satisfaction in a mere slight, inferior, or low attainment of distinction;
rather, with a resolute intention that has been mastered, they draw forth the innate resolute intention (*sahajāśaya*).

Furthermore, by means of this innate resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), they swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. In that regard, whatever resolute intentions of bodhisattvas have been described, designated, and revealed by the Blessed One in various contexts— all of them should be understood as being subsumed within these very fifteen resolute intentions.

Therefore, those bodhisattvas in the past, future, and present times who have awakened, will awaken, and are awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through noble resolute intentions— all of them do so by means of these very fifteen resolute intentions.
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
Thus, these fifteen resolute intentions (*adhyāśaya*) of a bodhisattva bring great fruit and benefit;
therefore, by relying upon them, a bodhisattva shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Thus ends the third chapter, "The Chapter on Superior Intention," within the section on Yoga concerning the Dharma that Follows the Foundation in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 217) Chapter 2.4: The Chapter on Abodes.
The summary verse:
Lineage, as well as resolute belief; the Joyful [ground], higher ethics, and higher mind;
three [grounds] of wisdom, two signless [grounds], with effort and without effort.
And there would be the analytical knowledges and the supreme, highest dwelling of a Tathāgata.

Thus, based on the perfection of their lineage, for those bodhisattvas who train in the aforementioned bodhisattva training, who are seen to manifest the aforementioned marks of a bodhisattva, who are correctly engaged in the applications conducive to the side of a bodhisattva,
and who purify the aforementioned superior intentions of a bodhisattva, there are, in brief, twelve bodhisattva dwellings.
It should be understood that all the practices of a bodhisattva are subsumed within these bodhisattva dwellings,
as well as the thirteenth, the dwelling of a Tathāgata, which is his unsurpassed dwelling of perfect awakening.
In that regard, what are the twelve bodhisattva dwellings?
[The dwelling of the lineage;
the dwelling of conduct through resolute belief;
the dwelling of great joy.
The three dwellings are: the dwelling in higher ethics, the dwelling in higher mind, and the dwelling in higher wisdom.
It is associated with the factors conducive to enlightenment,
associated with the truths,
and associated with the progression and cessation of dependent origination.

Thus, regarding that by which a bodhisattva perceives reality and that reality which is perceived— due to the ignorance of that reality, suffering proceeds for sentient beings, and through the knowledge of it, suffering no longer proceeds—
for the bodhisattva who investigates this with wisdom through three gateways, there arise three abidings in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñavihāra*).

The dwelling that is signless (*nirnimitta*) involves volitional effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*), is shared with others (*sābhāga*), and proceeds by means of a path that is uninterrupted; the dwelling that is signless involves no volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and proceeds by means of a path that is effortless (*anābhoga*).
Then there is the dwelling of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvidvihāra*), and finally the supreme, perfected dwelling of the bodhisattva.

These are the twelve kinds of bodhisattva abodes of the bodhisattvas; by means of these abodes, there is a complete inclusion of all their abodes and a complete inclusion of all bodhisattva practices. [This is] the Tathāgata’s [teaching]. (Dutt 218)

Furthermore, regarding the dwelling: that which is the dwelling of one who has fully awakened to enlightenment after having transcended all bodhisattva dwellings is the dwelling of the Tathāgata. A complete exposition of this final dwelling will occur in the final section on the application of the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā-yoga-sthāna*).
As for the twelve bodhisattva dwellings, I shall now explain them according to their established arrangement.
And what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the lineage?
How does a bodhisattva dwelling in the lineage abide?

Here, a bodhisattva dwelling in the lineage, by virtue of having a naturally auspicious continuum, is by nature endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva and the wholesome dharmas worthy of a bodhisattva.
When that [unwholesome state] manifests,
he is seen to engage in that wholesome [counteraction] through his very nature of goodness, not by means of forced effort;
rather, through discernment, he becomes restrained and composed.
A bodhisattva dwelling in the lineage is the bearer of the seeds of all the qualities of a Buddha;
all the seeds of all the qualities of a Buddha exist within his personal existence and within his basis.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva dwelling in the lineage is free from gross defilements.
He is incapable of manifesting such an outburst of affliction by which,
being obsessed, he would commit one of the deeds of immediate retribution or sever his roots of virtue.

Whatever rule has been indicated for one established in the lineage (*gotrastha*) in the Chapter on Lineage (*gotrapaṭala*), that should be understood in detail as pertaining to the bodhisattva dwelling in the lineage (*gotravihārin*).
This is called the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the lineage (*gotravihāra*).
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*)?

Here, any bodhisattva practice whatsoever undertaken by a bodhisattva who, starting from the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*), has not yet purified his high resolve (*aśuddhādhyāśaya*), is called his stage of practice through resolute belief.

In that context, a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*) exists merely as a cause for all the other eleven bodhisattva stages and for the stage of the Tathāgata, by way of grasping the cause.
However, by that [bodhisattva], no other bodhisattva dwelling has been undertaken, attained, or purified;
how much less, then, the dwelling of a Tathāgata?
But by a bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryā-vihāra*), all bodhisattva dwellings as well as the dwelling of a Tathāgata have been undertaken.
However, they have not yet been attained nor purified;
rather, that very dwelling of the stage of practice through resolute belief has been attained,
and he has now set out for its purification.

When the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryāvihāra*) is purified, one attains the stage of joy (*pramuditavihāra*), which has already been previously initiated, and one proceeds toward its very purification. When the stage of joy is purified, one attains the stage of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīlavihāra*), which has already been previously initiated.
And he becomes one who has entered into practice for the sake of the purification of that very [state].
In this way, it should be understood in detail up until the supreme, perfectly accomplished bodhisattva dwelling.

When the supreme, perfectly accomplished bodhisattva dwelling is completely purified, immediately thereafter, the simultaneous attainment and purification of the previously initiated dwelling of a Tathāgata should be understood.
This should be understood as the distinction of the Tathāgata’s dwelling from the dwellings of the bodhisattvas.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling of joy?
It is the dwelling of a bodhisattva whose intention is pure.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*)?
It is the dwelling of one who is endowed with natural ethical discipline (*prakṛti-śīla*) by reason of the purity of their resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*).
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling of higher mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*)?
The dwelling in higher morality is that dwelling which consists of mundane meditations, concentrations, and attainments, having purity as its cause.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the factors conducive to enlightenment?

It is that which, relying upon a concentration that serves as the basis for the purification of mundane knowledge, [engages] with the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the applications of mindfulness, for the sake of awakening to the truths.
The dwelling of discernment.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling of higher wisdom associated with the truths?
It is the dwelling in the awakening to the truths as they truly are, based upon the discernment of the factors conducive to enlightenment.

In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the progression and cessation of dependent origination? It is that dwelling which, having made the very awakening to the truths its sovereign, is characterized by the investigation of the progression of suffering along with its causes due to ignorance of those truths, and is characterized by the investigation of the cessation of suffering along with its causes due to knowledge of those truths.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ signless dwelling with application and effort?

It is the dwelling accompanied by the cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom regarding the suchness of all phenomena, which— having made those same three types of dwellings in higher wisdom its sovereign— is continuous and uninterrupted through application and effort.
In that regard, what is the signless dwelling (*nirnimitta-vihāra*) of Bodhisattvas that is without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and without exertion (*anābhoga*)?
It is the dwelling that follows the path which flows without interruption or interval by its own natural force, due to the extensive cultivation of that very same previous signless dwelling.
In that regard, what is the Bodhisattvas’ dwelling of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid-vihāra*)?

It is the dwelling of one who, relying on that very same perfectly pure and immovable concentration of wisdom (*prajñāsamādhi*), has attained the vastness of great intelligence (*mahāmati*) and engages in the investigation of the synonyms, meanings, etymologies, and distinctions of phenomena (*dharma*), beginning with the unsurpassed excellence of explaining the Dharma to others.
In this regard, what is the supreme dwelling of a bodhisattva?

Established in this state, the bodhisattva has reached the culmination of the bodhisattva path; having attained the great dharma-consecration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he is either bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) or is in his final existence (*caramabhavika*).
Immediately following this dwelling, having awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he performs all the activities of a Buddha.

In that regard, while dwelling in the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukticaryāvihāra*), the bodhisattva practices the cultivation of a bodhisattva in a limited way, in an interrupted way, and in an uncertain way, due to the loss of what has been gained. In the stage of joy (*pramuditavihāra*), however, the bodhisattva practices that very same cultivation of a bodhisattva extensively, uninterruptedly, and with certainty, because there is no loss of what has been attained.
Just as it is in the stage of joy, so it is up to the three stages of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñavihāra*).
From the first signless dwelling up to the supreme bodhisattva dwelling, a bodhisattva becomes one who practices immeasurably, flawlessly, and with certainty in the cultivation of a bodhisattva.
In that regard, it should be understood that the commencement of the bodhisattva’s signless cultivation occurs in the dwelling of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).

It should be understood that the acquisition of that bodhisattva cultivation of the signless occurs during the stage of Great Joy (*pramuditā*) and during the stages of higher morality, higher mind, and higher wisdom.

Its full realization should be understood to occur in the first signless stage (*animitta-vihāra*), and its purification in the second signless stage. Furthermore, it should be understood that the experience of the fruit of that very same bodhisattva cultivation of the signless occurs in the stage of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and in the supreme stage (*parama-vihāra*).
What are the aspects, what are the marks, and what are the signs of a bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of practice through resolute belief?
A bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of practice through resolute belief possesses the power of analytical reflection;
having reflected with wisdom, he applies himself to the practical applications of a bodhisattva’s duties.
But he does not, by nature or through being composed of that,
possess a firm, stable, and irreversible cultivation of the bodhisattva path;

and as it is with cultivation, so it is with the fruit of cultivation— the various analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), superknowledges (*abhijñā*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Furthermore, he has not transcended five fears:
the fear of lack of livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of miserable rebirths, and the fear of timidity in assemblies.
And he applies himself to the welfare of sentient beings through analytical reflection, rather than out of natural compassion or affection.
At times he behaves wrongly toward sentient beings through body, speech, or mind; at times he becomes attached even to sense objects;
and at times he is seen to be preoccupied with the acquisition of requisites.
He becomes one who follows through faith in others— the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—

but he does not yet personally know reality for himself; that is to say, regarding the Tathāgata, or the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, or the meaning of reality, or the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or the cause, or the fruit, or that which is to be attained.
Whether it be the goal, the means of attainment, or the sphere of activity,
he is endowed with only limited knowledge derived from hearing and reflection, not with immeasurable knowledge; moreover,
even that [limited knowledge] is occasionally forgotten by him.
He is subject to forgetfulness,
and he is endowed with a bodhisattva’s path that is difficult and slow in its direct knowledge;
nor does he possess an intense aspiration for great enlightenment.
He is neither one whose vigor is ardent nor one whose serene confidence is deeply established;
and he becomes forgetful in three respects:
first, regarding objects—whether pleasant or unpleasant—consisting of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, due to occasional perversion of the mind.
Upon being reborn in various different states of existence, one forgets previous states of self;
and regarding the teachings that have been pointed out and mastered, one occasionally forgets what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.
Thus, in these three instances, one becomes one whose mindfulness is lost.
At times he becomes wise, capable of receiving, retaining, and penetrating the meaning of the teachings; at other times he is not so;
at times he possesses mindfulness.
At times, he is of a forgetful nature; he does not possess knowledge of the appropriate means for disciplining sentient beings,
nor does he possess knowledge of the means for accomplishing the qualities of a Buddha for himself.
And he teaches the Dharma to others by force,
or applies instruction and admonition;
yet that which is applied by him through force is not done with knowledge of things as they truly are.
At one time it is barren, and at another time it is fruitful,
depending on the accidental success of its aims— like arrows shot in the night. And at one time, even a thought that has been generated toward great enlightenment, they abandon.
At times, he turns away from or fails to persevere in undertaking the ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) of a bodhisattva;
at other times, even while engaged in working for the welfare of sentient beings, he becomes weary midway and withdraws from that application of working for their welfare.
Furthermore, by nature he desires his own happiness, yet through analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyā*), he desires the happiness of others.
He is frequently aware of the lapses of a bodhisattva, yet he does not— despite such awareness— completely abandon them by repeatedly committing those same lapses and transgressions. Furthermore,
at times he remains susceptible to being led away from this Dharma and Vinaya of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
At times, having heard a profound and sublime teaching of the Dharma, he becomes terrified;
his mind experiences agitation, perplexity, and doubt.
Furthermore, he becomes entirely devoid of the manifestation of great compassion toward sentient beings.
And he is present for the sake of bringing about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings only to a limited extent;
he does not train in all the bodhisattva trainings as they have been described in their vast and immeasurable fullness,
nor is he endowed with all the bodhisattva marks as they have been described in their complete perfection.
Nor is he seen to be perfected in all the applications of the factors conducive to enlightenment as they have been described;
he considers himself far from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and his resolute intention is not directed toward nirvana in the same way that it is toward wandering in saṃsāra.
He is not yet endowed with the refined, immovable, and wholesome factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*).
These and other such signs, marks, and aspects should be understood as belonging to a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).

It should be understood that for a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief who possesses the lowest degree of receptivity (*mṛdvī kṣānti*), these aforementioned aspects, signs, and marks are present in their highest degree.
It should be understood that for one abiding in medium patience, there is a state of mediocrity.

For a bodhisattva abiding in superior patience, it should be understood that these aspects, signs, and marks have become mild and attenuated. Furthermore, for one abiding in precisely that superior patience, immediately following the complete abandonment of these aspects, signs, and marks, it should be understood that the bodhisattva enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*) by way of attainment.

For this Bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of the Joyous (*pramuditā*), all those qualities that were described for one dwelling in the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā*) do not exist in any way whatsoever.
Conversely, all qualities belonging to the side of purity (*śukla-pakṣya*) are present;
endowed with these, the Bodhisattva is said to be "one of pure intention" (*śuddhāśaya*).
Furthermore, although a bodhisattva abiding even in the stage of practice through aspiration possesses a progressively increasing purity of resolve by means of weak, medium, and intense application,
this is not called "purity of superior intention.
Why is that?
For that resolve proceeds as it is defiled by these various kinds of secondary afflictions;

however, for a bodhisattva established in the Stage of Joyful Abiding (*pramuditavihāra*), because all these secondary afflictions of resolve have been abandoned, a pure resolve proceeds, free from secondary afflictions.
In this regard, what are the aspects, what are the marks, and what are the signs to be known of a bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of Joyful Abiding?

In this regard, a bodhisattva, having first entered the stage of the Joyful (*pramuditavihāra*) from the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryāvihāra*), abandons that previous bodhisattva vow for unexcelled perfect enlightenment— which, because awakening had not been thoroughly penetrated and the means for awakening were not thoroughly penetrated, was for the most part dependent on others and not firmly established— and generates another, new bodhisattva vow that is well-ascertained in six ways and personally realized within himself regarding all phenomena.
All that transcends other vows for merit; it is incomparable and possesses a fruit that is not shared [with others].
It is both mundane and yet transcends the entire sphere of the world.
Because it follows from the protection of all sentient beings from suffering, it is not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Even when that vow has arisen for only a single moment, the nature of phenomena (dharmaprakṛti) is such that it yields immeasurable, pure, and desirable fruits for Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, that vow is unchanging and inexhaustible;
once attained, no means whatsoever can be found by which its decline or alteration could occur.
And that which pertains to distinction reaches the ultimate limit;
it culminates in great enlightenment.
Furthermore, this well-ascertained vow of a bodhisattva is called the "arising of the thought" (*cittotpāda*).
Furthermore, this production of the thought of awakening (cittotpāda) of a bodhisattva should be understood, in brief, through four aspects.
What are these four?
First of all, what kind of bodhisattvas produce that thought?
With what as its object does it arise?
Of what kind is it, what are its characteristics, and by what nature does it arise?
And once that mind has arisen, what benefit is there?
Thus, that production of the thought of awakening (cittotpāda) should be understood through these four aspects.

In this regard, that thought arises in those bodhisattvas who dwell in the stage of practice through resolute belief (adhimukticaryā-vihāra), who have well-accumulated roots of virtue in all their forms, and who, in brief, have correctly emerged from the bodhisattva conduct;

[it arises for the sake of] the future, perfect and swift fulfillment of all the equipment for awakening (bodhisambhāra), the perfect fulfillment of all the activities for the benefit of sentient beings performed by a bodhisattva, and unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

In brief, the bodhicitta of those bodhisattvas arises by taking as its object the complete fulfillment of all aspects of all buddha-qualities and the complete fulfillment of the performance of the activities of a buddha;

it is correct, swift, conducive to all aspects of the entire equipment for enlightenment, conducive to all aspects of the bodhisattva’s duties toward all sentient beings, and conducive to the attainment of the self-arisen gnosis of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

That mind arises as being conducive to performing the buddha-activities in all their aspects. Through the arising of that mind, the bodhisattva transcends the stage of the foolish bodhisattvas who are ordinary worldlings and enters the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*niyāma*).
He is born into the family of the Tathāgata;
he becomes the legitimate son of the Tathāgata;
he is destined for perfect enlightenment and is fixed within the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
Having become thus and attained verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*), he becomes abundant in joy;
he is free from agitation, violence, and anger,
and [is intent upon] every form of the bodhisattva’s activity for the benefit of sentient beings and every form of the fulfillment of the accumulations for enlightenment.
Taking as his object, through a pure resolute intention, awakening in all its aspects, the qualities of a Buddha, and the performance of a Buddha’s deeds;
becoming convinced of them, entering into them, seeing that he is conformable to the swift attainment of these dharmas, and realizing it for himself, he becomes full of great joy.

I am endowed with wholesome, sublime, and peerless qualities— connected with renunciation, free from worldly motives, and beneficial to body and mind— consisting of a joy that is fervent and unshakable;
I have drawn near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and my resolute intention toward great awakening is purified.
"And all my fears have departed.
For this reason as well, he becomes full of great joy;
for indeed, the five fears of that bodhisattva who has generated a mind that is well-ascertained are abandoned.
For one whose knowledge of selflessness is well-cultivated, the notion of a self does not arise at all;
how much less, then, could there be in such a person attachment to a self or attachment to requisites?
Consequently, he has no fear for his livelihood.
Nor does he expect anything from others;
rather, he has this desire:
"I myself must provide for all the needs of these sentient beings."
Therefore, he has no fear of ill repute.
And because he is free from the view of a self, the perception of a self does not arise in him;
therefore, he has no fear of death.
He becomes certain that after his death, in the future, he will inevitably encounter Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
therefore, he has no fear of the miserable realms.
Furthermore, he perceives no one in the entire world who is equal to himself in terms of their resolute intention (*āśaya*).
"How much more so, then, anything superior?
Thus, he has no fear of timidity before an assembly.
Having thus become free from all fear, free from terror regarding any profound teaching, and free from the arrogance and haughtiness of superiority;

Free from hatred toward all injuries and hostile actions committed by others, and free from delight in all worldly material things, he— by means of an intention that is unimpaired due to being undefiled and unsurpassed due to being refined— exerts every form of bodhisattva vigor in this very life for the attainment of all wholesome qualities, having made faith its sovereign and its precursor.

Furthermore, regarding those ten great vows previously specified in the Chapter on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment, having brought them forth in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditavihāra*) by virtue of the purity of his intention, he makes the first great vow for the sake of worshipping the Supreme Being, the Worthy Recipient, the Teacher, and the Lord of Dharma;
the second for the sake of upholding the sublime True Dharma taught by Him; and the third for the sake of setting in motion the True Dharma in successive order.
The third is for the sake of practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva in accordance with that; the fourth is for the sake of maturing those beings who are vessels for it;
the fifth is for the sake of approaching the buddha-fields to behold, attend upon, and hear the true Dharma from the Tathāgatas;
the sixth is for the sake of purifying one’s own buddha-field; and the seventh is for the sake of never being separated from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas in all births.

Together with the bodhisattvas, he brings forth the eighth great vow for the sake of having a single intention and application; the ninth for the sake of making the welfare of all sentient beings fruitful; and the tenth for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and for performing the deeds of a Buddha. Furthermore, through these very great vows, there shall be—successively, until the end of the realm of sentient beings and like the non-interruption of the world’s phenomena—in birth after birth, until reaching the limit of enlightenment, no departure, no forgetting, and no separation.
"May it be so"—thus he correctly directs his mind.
It should be understood that the former is the aspiration regarding the object to be aspired for, while the latter is the act of aspiring.
Taking these very great aspirations as primary, there arise for that bodhisattva hundreds of thousands of incalculable sets of ten correct aspirations.

For one who thus possesses such aspirations for the future and has initiated vigor in the present life, ten qualities that purify the stages lead to the purification of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
He places deep faith in all the Buddha-qualities.
And as he perceives, through the principle of dependent origination, that the entire mass of suffering of sentient beings arises [from causes], compassion arises in him.
Loving-kindness is the vision that "I must liberate these beings from this entire mass of suffering";

it is the disregard for oneself by one who intends to protect all from suffering; and for one who disregards oneself, it is the relinquishing of internal and external things for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, for the sake of those very same sentient beings, there is indefatigability in seeking after mundane and supramundane dharmas;
and for one who is indefatigable, there is knowledge of the treatises (*śāstrajñatā*) through the purity of attaining the knowledge of all treatises;

and for one who knows the treatises, there is knowledge of the world (*lokajñatā*) through practicing toward inferior, middling, and superior sentient beings in accordance with what is appropriate and fitting.
In those very applications, there is a sense of shame and dread of blame beginning with the practice regarding time, occasion, measure, and so forth;
and in those very applications, there is the maintenance of strength through steadfastness by way of non-retrogression;
and there is the honoring and attending upon the Tathāgata through both gain and respectful service.
These ten qualities lead to the purification of one's dwelling;

namely: faith, compassion, loving-kindness, renunciation, indefatigability, knowledge of the treatises, knowledge of the world, a sense of shame and dread of blame, the acquisition of the power of fortitude, and the worship and service of the Tathāgata.
And that bodhisattva, having undertaken these dharmas, abides in them and cultivates them extensively.

Furthermore, from the presence of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, he thoroughly investigates all aspects of the qualities and defects of the path regarding the other nine bodhisattva dwellings, beginning with the higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
Having mastered those superknowledges (*abhijñā*), his path is not easily lost; he has well grasped the signs of the modes [of practice], their attainment, and their natural outflows (*niṣyanda*).
And having personally traversed all the stages of dwelling, he realizes great awakening and leads the caravan of great beings across the wilderness path of saṃsāra.
Those modes by which he enters are the "modes"; that entry is the "acquisition.
For one who has entered, the accomplishment and realization of the great fruits and benefits should be understood as the "outflow" (niṣyanda).
For him who is established in this dwelling, many Buddhas come into the range of his coarse vision for two reasons:
those whom he has heard of in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*,
and those toward whom he has formed a resolute conviction with his mind.
"There are Tathāgatas of various names in world-systems of various names throughout the ten directions. With a mind accompanied by coarse faith, he prays to see them;
and for one who is thus disposed, it indeed succeeds.
That supplication is one cause;
and he thus directs his mind:
"May my birth be there, where the Buddha has appeared."
For one who has become thus, that vow indeed succeeds.

Having seen those Tathāgatas in this way— through the vision of sublime faith and through the empowerment of the strength of his vow— he offers every form of worship and the provision of comforts according to his ability and power, and he performs honors for the Saṅgha.
And from those Tathāgatas, he hears the Dharma, takes it up, and retains it; he accomplishes it through practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti);
and he dedicates all those roots of merit toward great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
And he brings sentient beings to maturity through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
By these three causes of purification, those roots of virtue become purified to a greater degree:
by means of honoring and supporting the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; and by means of bringing sentient beings to maturity through the means of attraction.
And by dedicating the roots of virtue toward awakening for as long as many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons—
just as gold remaining in its natural state becomes increasingly purified the more it is cast into the fire by a skilled smith,
even so do those roots of virtue of this bodhisattva whose intention is pure become increasingly purified through those causes of purification.
Abiding there by way of rebirth, he for the most part becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) in birth after birth, the sovereign of Jambudvīpa;
free from all stains of avarice, he is a lord for the sake of disciplining the avarice of sentient beings.

Whatever action is undertaken by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*), all of that is never separated from the mental orientations (*manaskāra*) toward the jewels and the realization of enlightenment in all its aspects.

Desiring, "May I become the foremost of all sentient beings and the refuge for all their goals," he exerts such vigor that, having renounced all home, wife, and enjoyments, he goes forth into the teaching of the Tathāgata and, in a single moment, an instant, or a brief duration, [attains] a hundred bodhisattva samādhis.
He enters [into meditative absorption].
With the divine eye, he sees a hundred Tathāgatas in various Buddha-fields;
he also knows their emanations and empowerments, as well as the empowerments of the Bodhisattvas.
He causes a hundred world-systems to tremble;
likewise, he traverses them with his body and, having pervaded them with his radiance, displays them to others.
He ripens a hundred beings to be trained by means of a hundred emanations;
desiring it, he maintains his presence for even a hundred eons;
and through the vision of knowledge, he penetrates a hundred eons of the past and the future.
He thoroughly investigates hundreds of dharma-doors, such as those concerning the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

He emanates hundreds of bodies, and from each body he displays a retinue of a hundred bodhisattvas. Beyond this, it should be understood that through the power of their vows, the immeasurable manifestations of supernatural power (*prabhāva-vikurvaṇā*) of the bodhisattvas occur in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditavihāra*).
They abide [in this state]. For they possess the power of aspiration; by means of their specific aspirations, they manifest transformations.
It is not easy to calculate the number of their perfect aspirations, even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.

Thus, this Bodhisattvas’ stage of the Joyful (pramuditā-vihāra) should be understood as well-determined and characterized by four aspects: from the production of the thought of enlightenment; from the accomplishment of right vows and the exertion of vigor; from the purification of the stage and the mastery of the other stages; and from the purification of the roots of virtue, its rebirth, and its power—this being the summary description.

Furthermore, as for the detailed exposition, it is exactly as in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, beginning with the exposition of the *Pramuditā* (Joyful) stage. Those ten bodhisattva stages which are in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* should be understood here, in this Bodhisattvapiṭaka, as the ten bodhisattva abodes (*bodhisattvavihāra*) presented in the summary (*mātṛkā*), starting from the *pramuditavihāra* up to the *paramavihāra*, in their respective order.
In this context, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*) in the sense of being a domain for the Bodhisattvas;
furthermore, it is called a "dwelling" (*vihāra*) in the sense of a place of enjoyment and residence.
In that regard, what are the aspects, what are the marks, and what are the signs of the Bodhisattvas' dwelling in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*) that should be known?
In this regard, a bodhisattva has previously, in the stage of the Joyous (*pramuditā-vihāra*), attained purity of intention through a tenfold mental disposition:
the superior intention of not deceiving any teacher, preceptor, or one worthy of offerings; [and so forth].
The intention to dwell in harmony with fellow bodhisattvas through gentleness;
the intention to overcome all afflictions, secondary afflictions, and the deeds of Māra by gaining mastery over one’s own mind;
the intention to perceive defects in all conditioned phenomena; and the intention to perceive the benefits in nirvāṇa.
The intention for the continuous cultivation of the wholesome factors conducive to awakening;
the intention for seclusion in order to be favorable to that very cultivation;
and the intention of being indifferent toward all worldly pleasures, status, gain, and honor.
Having abandoned the Hīnayāna, there is the intention to realize the Mahāyāna and the intention to accomplish every benefit for all sentient beings.
Thus, these ten right intentions arise within that mind;
by means of them, his intention is said to be pure.
And because these very dispositions are predominant and perfected, the bodhisattva enters and ascends to the second dwelling, that of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).
In this dwelling of higher ethical discipline, he becomes one whose nature is ethical discipline;
he does not commit even the slightest misconduct comprised within the paths of wrong action.
How much more so for those that are middling or superior!
Furthermore, he is naturally seen to be fully established in the ten paths of wholesome action.

Being thus naturally virtuous, through his wisdom he understands, as it truly is, the establishment of the causal attainment and the manifestation of results regarding the performance of afflicted and unafflicted paths of action within the realms of miserable destinies, happy destinies, and the vehicles.
He understands those actions as they truly are in terms of their results of maturation (*vipāka*) and their results of natural outflow (*niṣyanda*).
He himself is seen to be engaged in the abandonment of unwholesome actions and the undertaking of wholesome actions;
he desires to encourage others toward that very same path, and he does so encourage them, [regarding those] corrupted by the fault of practicing uneven actions.

Compassionately regarding the entire realm of sentient beings without distinction— whether experiencing prosperity or adversity— as being ultimately suffering and situated in calamity through various forms of misfortune, he attains an abundance of compassion and reflects upon them.

For him who is established in this dwelling of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), the vision of the Buddhas and the purification of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) are to be understood as previously described.
In this regard, there is this distinction:
just as that very gold, when treated with green vitriol by a skilled smith, becomes even more purified the more it is cast into the fire,
so too should the purification of the roots of virtue of this bodhisattva be understood.
And in this dwelling, through the entry into the perfection of the pure mental disposition, one becomes by birth a universal monarch over the four continents;
and for the most part, and in great measure, one turns sentient beings away from immorality and unwholesome courses of action,
and establishes them in the wholesome courses of action.
Its power, moreover, should be understood as ten times greater than the previous one.
Such is the bodhisattvas' dwelling in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*),
by virtue of natural morality, by the removal of the stains of misconduct in all its forms, and by the penetration of the knowledge of the causes and fruits of all aspects of the paths of action.

It should be understood through a summary explanation in terms of: the desire to cause others to undertake virtuous actions; the attainment of an abundance of compassion; the contemplation of the suffering and calamities born of the karma of the realm of sentient beings; the purification of the roots of virtue; rebirth; and power.

Furthermore, as for the detailed explanation, it is just as stated in the *Sūtra*, such as in the *Daśabhūmika* regarding the Vimalā Bhūmi, which is called the "Stainless Ground" because it is free from the stain of immoral conduct (*dauḥśīlya*).
Because it is free from the stain of immorality, it is called the "abiding in higher morality.
That which is the stainless stage therein should be understood as the abiding in higher morality.
In that regard, what are the aspects, what are the marks, and what are the signs of the bodhisattvas' abiding in higher mind?
In this regard, a bodhisattva has previously, while in the dwelling of higher morality (*adhiśīla-vihāra*), attended to, cultivated, and realized those ten pure intentions (*śuddhāśaya*).

By means of ten other aspects, because those mental attentions regarding the intention of the mind have reached a state of intensity and perfection, he transcends the dwelling of higher morality and enters the dwelling of higher mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*).
This occurs through the mental attention: "My intention of mind is purified by way of the ten aspects."
By the mental attention: "I am incapable of falling away from that tenfold pure intention";
by the mental attention: "My mind does not enter into any phenomena associated with outflows or tainted by outflows, but abides in aversion toward them";
and by the mental attention: "My consciousness is established in the cultivation of their antidotes."

By means of the mental attention: "I am incapable of falling back again from this counteractive state"; by means of the mental attention: "Being thus possessed of a firm counteractive state, I am incapable of being overcome by all those tainted phenomena that are subject to outflows, nor by any Māras";
and by means of the mental attention: "My mind proceeds without shrinking back regarding all the qualities of a Buddha."
With the mental orientation that "I have no distress regarding any of the practices of difficult deeds";
with the mental orientation that "my mind is resolutely inclined toward the Mahāyāna alone, and not toward any other Hīnayānas";
and with the mental orientation that "my mind delights in performing what is beneficial for all sentient beings."
By means of these ten mental dispositions and attentions, he enters [the state of concentration].
Abiding in the dwelling of higher mind, the bodhisattva reviles all conditioned phenomena through various modes of their disadvantages and causes the mind to become weary of them.
He perceives the benefits in the wisdom of a Buddha through various forms of benefit;
having conceived a longing for it with an intense flavor of aspiration,
he beholds the realm of sentient beings as suffering through various modes of suffering.
And toward those beings, he maintains a mind of equanimity and a mind that relies upon their welfare;
he is heedful regarding all conditioned phenomena and possesses fervent vigor for the sake of awakening.
Possessing an intention of vast compassion toward sentient beings,
he perceives that the very means for liberating those beings from ultimate suffering is the knowledge that is unobstructed by all afflictions.

Furthermore, for the realization of that liberation, he perceives wisdom as the antidote to the activity of all conceptual constructions and the arising of defilements within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
And for the sake of accomplishing that light of knowledge, he perceives perfect enlightenment;
and he perceives that the accomplishment of meditative absorption, concentration, and attainment is preceded by hearing the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and has hearing as its primary cause.
Having perceived this, he applies himself with great exertion of vigor to the search for what has been heard.
For the sake of hearing the true Dharma, there is no wealth, no requisite, and no internal or external thing that he does not relinquish;
there is no service to his teachers that he does not undertake;
and there is no continuity [of effort] that he does not accept.
There is no bodily affliction that he would not accept;
he becomes more delighted by hearing a single four-line verse than by a great heap of jewels filling the three-thousandfold world system.
He becomes even more delighted by hearing a single word of the Dharma brought forth by the Perfectly Enlightened One, which purifies the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Not by the attainment of the exalted states of being Śakra, Māra, Brahmā, a world-protector, or a universal monarch;
if someone were to say this to him:
"In this way, I shall [attain] this verse of Dharma brought forth by the Perfectly Enlightened One, which purifies all the conduct of a bodhisattva."
"I shall cause them to hear it if you throw yourself into a great pit of fire and undergo great suffering.
Upon hearing this, he would think:

"For the sake of even a single verse of Dharma, as before, I am willing to cast myself from the Brahma-world into a pit of fire equal in size to the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, let alone into one that is inferior."
"We must seek the Buddha-dharmas even through dwelling in the sufferings of the hells, let alone through ordinary hardships.
Having sought the dharmas with such an exertion of vigor, he attends to them properly (*yoniśo manasikaroti*) in this way:
"I shall practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*), following the Buddha-dharmas, and not merely for the sake of purity in words and sounds."
Having understood this and relying upon that very learning, correctly taking the signs of phenomena as his object, he dwells having attained— secluded from sensual desires and so forth—
the first, second, third, and fourth worldly dhyānas, the four worldly formless attainments, the four immeasurables, and the five superknowledges.

Having dwelt extensively with them and having turned back from those meditative absorptions (dhyāna), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti), he is reborn by the power of his vow in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) wherever he perceives the welfare of sentient beings and the fulfillment of the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharma);
yet his rebirth does not occur through the power of those [meditative states] themselves.

Because he is free from passion for sense-pleasures, his bonds of desire are abandoned; because he turns away from the meditative absorptions, concentrations, and attainments, his bonds of existence are abandoned.
Even on the stage of practice through resolute belief, his bonds created by views have already been abandoned due to his prior resolute belief in the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*).
Furthermore, false attachment, aversion, and delusion do not arise in him at all.
His vision of the Buddha and the extensive purification of his roots of virtue are to be understood as previously described;
however, there is this distinction:
Just as that very gold, when held in the hands of a skilled smith, remains even when its impurities and dross have been removed, staying balanced and equal in weight;
in this way, his purification of the roots of virtue is to be understood.
And by way of rebirth, he mostly becomes Śakra, the lord of the gods.
He is skillful in turning sentient beings away from sensual desire.
Regarding its power, where a thousand was previously declared for the former dwelling, here it should be understood as a hundred thousand.

This is the bodhisattvas’ dwelling of higher mind (*adhicittavihāra*), by way of entering the perfection of mental attention and by way of the correct penetration of cyclic existence, the realm of sentient beings, and great awakening.
