It should be understood through a brief explanation by way of: the correct seeking of the means for liberating sentient beings from suffering; the seeking of the Dharma with great reverence; dwelling in the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*) and the accomplishment of worldly dhyāna, samādhi, meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); the turning away from those [worldly states] through aspiration; rebirth wherever one desires; the purification of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*); the manner of rebirth; and spiritual power.
The detailed exposition is as given in the *Sūtra*, specifically in the *Daśabhūmika* regarding the *Prabhākarī* stage (*bhūmi*).

Because this stage is characterized by the illumination of the light of the Dharma in the form of what has been heard and the illumination of the light of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "The Radiant" (*Prabhākarī*).
Based upon the internal purification of the mind, that radiance arises; therefore, that dwelling is called "Higher Mind" (*adhicitta*).
By the same meaning by which the stage is called "The Radiant" (*prabhākarī*), by that very meaning it should be understood as the "Abiding in Higher Mind" (*adhicittavihāra*).
In this regard, what is the Bodhisattvas' "Abiding in Higher Wisdom" (*adhiprajñavihāra*) associated with the factors conducive to enlightenment?

Here, a Bodhisattva has previously, while in the Abiding in Higher Mind, attained ten entries into the light of the Dharma (*dharmāloka-praveśa*) by making the pursuit of hearing [the teachings] his primary focus.
Because these [ten factors] are predominant and perfected, one transcends the dwelling in higher mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*) and enters the first dwelling in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*).
Furthermore, those ten entries into the light of the Dharma (*dharmāloka-praveśa*) should be understood according to the text of the Sūtra itself.
Moreover, that which is designated, that wherein it is designated, and that by which it is designated—these are equal, being the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
And that which possesses both affliction and purification—that by which [beings] are afflicted and purified;
that through connection with which they are afflicted; and that unsurpassed purity by which they are purified.
This should be understood as the summarized meaning of those expositions on the illumination of the Dharma.
Established in that dwelling,

he becomes endowed with the qualities that ripen knowledge— consisting of ten aspects as described in the sūtra— preceded by an indestructible intention, and thus he is born into the family of the Tathāgatas.
Because he has attained the dharmas that constitute that [state],

taking as his dominant influence the bodhisattva’s regard for all aspects, he cultivates the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, headed by the applications of mindfulness, exactly as described in the sūtras. As he cultivates those dharmas through the embrace of skillful means, even his most subtle view of a self-identity, his attachment to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and all mental fluctuations cease to manifest altogether.
They are abandoned.
Through their abandonment, he does not engage in any of those actions that have been disparaged by the Tathāgata in every way;
furthermore, he correctly follows all those actions that have been praised by the Tathāgata.
Having become such, his mind becomes to a great degree supple, soft, and workable; likewise, his mind becomes perfectly pure in its various aspects.
He becomes endowed with various wholesome qualities (*śukla-dharma*) that accord with his disposition, such as gratitude and thankfulness.
Furthermore, seeking out the practices that purify the higher stages, he attains the undertaking of great vigor (*mahāvīrya*).
On that account, his element of intention, resolute intention, and inclination becomes fulfilled;
and on that account, he becomes unshakable and immovable by any heretics, Māras, or adversaries of the teaching.
As before, the vision of the Buddha and the purification of the roots of virtue should be understood in detail.
In this regard, there is this distinction:
just as that very gold, when fashioned into an ornament by a skilled goldsmith, becomes unassailable by raw, unworked gold,
so too are the roots of virtue of this bodhisattva unassailable by the roots of virtue of other bodhisattvas who abide in the stages of ordinary beings (*bāla-vihāra*).
Just as a precious jewel that emits light cannot be outshone by other jewels,
and its radiance cannot be interrupted by any wind, water, or rain,
so too this bodhisattva cannot be surpassed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
His light of wisdom becomes unassailable by all Māras and adversaries;
and by virtue of his rebirth, he becomes Suyāma, the king of the gods,
skilled in turning sentient beings away from the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding its power, whereas it was declared to be a hundred-thousandfold in the previous dwelling, it should be understood that here it is declared to be ten-millionfold.

This is the Bodhisattvas’ dwelling of higher wisdom associated with the factors conducive to enlightenment. It is so called because of the attainment of the perfection of entering the light of the Dharma, because of the ripening of knowledge, and because of the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment.

Furthermore, it is through the abandonment of all agitations caused by attachment such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); through the avoidance of prohibited actions and the practice of permitted ones;

through the pliancy of mind resulting from those causes; through the abundance of qualities conducive thereto; through the undertaking of great vigor beginning with the pursuit of activities that purify the stages (*bhūmi*); and through the purification of the intention (*āśaya*), the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), and the inclination (*adhimukti*) resulting from those causes.

On account of that, it should be understood through a summary explanation in terms of being unassailable by any adversaries of the entire teaching, the purification of the roots of virtue, rebirth, and power.

Furthermore, the detailed explanation is as follows: in the *Daśabhūmika* [Sūtra], within the description of the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*) stage, the factors conducive to awakening become rays of knowledge on that stage, and the correct teaching of the Dharma produces the light that illuminates the world.
Therefore, that stage is called "The Radiant" (*arciṣmatī*).
And this very stage is here called the "Dwelling in Higher Wisdom that Produces the Illumination of the Wisdom Pertaining to the Factors of Enlightenment.
In that regard, what is the second dwelling in higher wisdom of the bodhisattvas, which is associated with the truths?

In this regard, a bodhisattva enters the second dwelling of higher wisdom because the ten equalities of pure intention, which were previously attained in the prior dwelling of higher wisdom, have now reached the stage of intensity and perfection.
These ten equalities of pure intention should be understood according to the text of the sūtra.
Buddhas are equal to Buddhas who are peerless;
they have transcended the realms of all other sentient beings,
and they are equal in those qualities by which they are so.
This should be understood as the summary meaning of the equality of those with purified intentions. Established in this dwelling,
and further aspiring to the excellence of knowledge, he understands the four truths as they truly are through ten aspects.
In terms of the text, everything should be understood exactly as it is in the sūtras.
This refers to that which is taught concerning the communication of others, the knowledge within oneself, and the basis for both;
and that which is taught by means of the sūtra, the vinaya, and the mātṛkā.

The summary meaning of that tenfold knowledge of the four noble truths should be understood as follows: how they are taught by way of the present nature of suffering, the production of future suffering from its cause, the non-arising of that [suffering] through the exhaustion of its cause, and the application of the means for its abandonment.
Being thus skilled in the truths, he thoroughly reviles the entire sphere of conditioned formations with wisdom.
He increases his compassionate intention toward the realm of sentient beings;
he correctly penetrates the false practices of foolish beings from the past limit to the future limit;
and for their liberation, he directs his mind toward the acquisition of the great equipment of merit and knowledge.
He brings to fulfillment that very intention,
being enriched by abundant and diverse qualities foremost among which are mindfulness, intelligence, and realization,
and is free from other mental engagements.
He brings sentient beings to maturity through various means of ripening.

Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings, he accomplishes all those worldly arts and crafts—such as writing, treatises, seals, and calculation—which benefit sentient beings, exactly as described in the sūtras;
this is done gradually for the purpose of establishing them in awakening, by way of conforming to worldly conventions and as a means to destroy poverty.

By pacifying afflictions brought about by humans and non-humans through the imbalance of the elements; by providing objects for blameless play and enjoyment to turn them away from attachment to worldly pleasures; by providing dwellings and requisites with little difficulty to those seeking them;

by protecting against calamities such as kings and thieves; by authorizing or prohibiting actions according to what is appropriate or inappropriate; and by enjoining the acquisition of auspicious things and the abandonment of inauspicious ones.
In this present life, by teaching the path to prosperity that is free from mutual malice and not erroneous regarding the future;
such, in brief, should be understood as the purpose of those fields of arts and crafts which benefit sentient beings.
All else is as before.
In this regard, there is this distinction:
just as that very same gold, when polished with musāragalva by a skilled goldsmith and set back in place, becomes incomparable and cannot be surpassed by other golds,
so too this bodhisattva becomes unsurpassable by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as by bodhisattvas residing on other stages.
Just as the radiance of the moon, the sun, and the stars cannot be obstructed by any whirlwinds and is carried along by all winds, being common to them,
even so the wisdom of this bodhisattva cannot be obstructed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
His worldly activities are common [to others],
yet by virtue of his rebirth, he becomes the divine king Saṃtuṣita;
he is skillful in turning back all non-Buddhist teachers.
Its power should be understood as numbering one hundred thousand times ten million according to its description.
This is the bodhisattvas' dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths,
by way of entering the perfection of the equality of pure intention, and by way of increasing the analytical investigation of skillful means regarding the truths.

It should be understood through a summary explanation by way of: the disparagement of all conditioned phenomena; the increase of compassion; the application of vows for the accumulation of the equipment of merit and knowledge for that purpose; the increase of qualities such as mindfulness, intelligence, and realization; the exertion in maturing sentient beings in every aspect with undistracted attention; the accomplishment of worldly arts and crafts; the purification of the roots of virtue; [the excellence of] rebirth; and [the excellence of] spiritual power.

Furthermore, in terms of detailed exposition, it is as follows: on the stage called Sudurjayā (Difficult to Conquer) in the *Daśabhūmika*, the certainty-knowledge regarding sentient beings is extremely difficult to conquer;
that is what is elucidated here.
Therefore, that stage is called Sudurjayā.
For that very reason, the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths should be understood [in this way].
In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ dwelling in higher wisdom associated with dependent origination?
Here, a bodhisattva has already previously attained ten equalities of phenomena within the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths.
These should be understood according to the text of the Sūtra. Because they are superior and complete, one enters this dwelling.

It is by means of the equality of signlessness regarding the ultimately existent intrinsic nature of all phenomena, and the equality of being without characteristics regarding the appearance of verbal expression and mental construction.

Because that very [reality] is without characteristics, there is the equality of being unarisen by itself; because it is unarisen from a cause, there is the equality of not having arisen from a cause; because it is neither self-arisen nor arisen from a cause, there is the equality of being absolutely quiescent from the beginning; because the knowledge that grasps existing entities is free from conceptual proliferation, there is the equality of the departure from the formative activities of grasping and abandoning;
and because of its dissociation from the afflictions, suffering, and defilements, there is the equality of the seclusion of the imagined nature of the knowable.

Through the equality of being like a magical illusion or a creation, and through the equality of the non-duality of existence and non-existence regarding the intrinsic nature that is the domain of non-conceptual knowledge—
this should be understood as the analytical explanation of the meaning of those ten equalities of phenomena.
Abiding in this dwelling, his compassion for sentient beings has increased, and he has given rise to an intense aspiration and longing for enlightenment.
He investigates and understands the arising and passing away of the worlds through the correct investigation of dependent origination in all its aspects.
Based upon his knowledge of dependent origination, the three gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—arise within him.
Consequently, for that reason, the notions of self, other, agent, and experiencer, as well as the notions of existence and non-existence, do not arise in him.

Thus, being skilled in the ultimate truth and concerned for sentient beings, he penetrates correctly [the nature of things]: conditioned phenomena proceed through the conjunction with afflictions and the assembly of conditions; they are inherently weak, devoid of self or what belongs to a self, and corrupted by manifold defects. They do not proceed without the conjunction with afflictions and the assembly of conditions.
Therefore, for the sake of protecting myself, I must disrupt both the conjunction with afflictions and the assembly of conditions.
And yet, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he does not pacify all conditioned phenomena in every respect.
For him who is thus endowed with wisdom and compassion, while in this dwelling, the perfection of wisdom dwelling called "Facing Unimpeded Knowledge" becomes manifest;
by means of which he engages in all worldly activities without being overcome by them.

That dwelling should be understood as being comprised by that conformable patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*)—the sharp patience of a bodhisattva on the seventh stage which has reached the culmination of preparatory practice.
Because he is oriented toward the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that faces unattached knowledge, he brings forth the conditions that bring about awakening;
yet, he does not dwell in association with worldly conditioned things.
He perceives tranquility in peace,
yet he does not abide therein.
For him who is thus followed by the knowledge of skillful means and wisdom, there manifest one million gateways to concentration, headed by the concentration on emptiness of entry.
Just as it is with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), so too should the concentrations on the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and the signless (*animitta*) be understood.
Through the manifestation of these, one’s intention becomes unshakable;
and through the teaching in all its aspects, one becomes incapable of being led astray by any Māras, non-Buddhists, teachers, or adversaries. The rest is as previously described.
In this regard, there is this distinction:

just as that very same gold, when set with a precious *vaidūrya* gem by a skilled goldsmith, becomes unassailable by all other types of gold, so too are the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) of this bodhisattva far more purified.
They become unassailable, as before.
Just as the light of the moon refreshes the bodies of sentient beings and its radiance becomes indestructible by the four circular whirlwinds,
so too does this Bodhisattva’s radiance of wisdom pacify the burning heat of the afflictions of all sentient beings.
And he becomes unassailable by all Māras and adversaries;
he becomes a well-fashioned king of the gods,
skillful in turning back all the pride of sentient beings.
Its power, too, should be understood as numbering one hundred thousand times ten million according to its enumeration.
This is the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with dependent origination,
both by way of entering into the perfection of the equality of phenomena and by way of the arising of the gateway to liberation through the awakening to dependent origination.

It should be understood through a summary explanation by way of: the non-occurrence of all false conceptions; the embracing of cyclic existence through skillful means; the orientation toward the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom that faces unattached gnosis; the attainment of immeasurable meditative absorptions; the attainment of an indestructible resolve; being unshakable from the teaching; the purification of the roots of virtue; [the manner of] rebirth; and [spiritual] power.
In detail, as described in the *Abhimukhī* stage:

because one who is oriented toward unimpeded knowledge is facing the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it is called "Facing" (*abhimukhī*). This dwelling should be understood by that very same meaning.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ signless dwelling that involves effort and application?

Here, in the immediately preceding dwelling of higher wisdom, the bodhisattva has attained through ten means and through wisdom the specific initiations of other paths— both those not shared with all sentient beings and those not shared with the entire world—
which have been brought forth.

Those for whom these qualities have become predominant and perfected enter the seventh dwelling; their detailed textual exposition should be understood exactly as it is in the Sūtra. This begins with the acquisition of merit that brings about worldly prosperity, and proceeds from the intention for the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.

Regarding enlightenment, beginning with the excellence and preeminence of the accumulation of merit and the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*), beginning with what is not shared with the *śrāvakas*, beginning with what is not shared with the *pratyekabuddhas*, beginning with the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), beginning with the world-realm (*loka-dhātu*), and beginning with the gnosis of the body, speech, and mind of a Tathāgata— thus, in brief, the meaning of the purpose for those specific undertakings of alternative paths, which are brought forth by skillful means and wisdom, should be understood.
Endowed with these, he penetrates the immeasurable and incalculable domain of the Tathāgatas.
And for the sake of its origination,

seeing that the origination of the immeasurable object of the Buddha's wisdom occurs through effortlessness (*anābhoga*), signlessness (*animitta*), and non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*), he applies himself continuously and without interruption in all postures, movements, dwellings, and mental attentions.

For him who has reached all stages, there is no disjunction from the path; in every moment of his mind, all the factors conducive to awakening, headed by the ten perfections, are fulfilled in an especially eminent way,
whereas in other dwellings they are not so.

In the first, the Stage of Joy, by means of the focal point of aspiration; in the second, by means of removing the stains of mental misconduct; in the third, by means of increasing aspiration and attaining the light of the Dharma; in the fourth, by means of entering the path; in the fifth, by means of entering worldly activities; and in the sixth, by means of entering the profound.
Furthermore, in this seventh dwelling, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are fulfilled by way of giving rise to all the qualities of a Buddha,

because this dwelling encompasses the fulfillment of the bodhisattva’s preparatory conduct and because it leads to the entry into the eighth dwelling, which is purified by the conduct of knowledge and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
For it is thus that the bodhisattva, immediately following this dwelling, enters the eighth dwelling, which is pure.
That dwelling is exclusively pure,
whereas these seven dwellings are mixed;
because they are preceded by the pure dwelling, they are undefiled.
Because it has not yet been fully attained, it should be described as falling within the accumulation of the defiled;
therefore, in this dwelling, all afflictions, headed by passion and the like, are abandoned.
Yet, it should be understood as neither defiled nor free from affliction, because [the afflictions] do not manifest and because there is a longing for the wisdom of a Buddha.
For one who has become thus, immeasurable physical, vocal, and mental actions proceed, purified by superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).

Those worldly crafts and sciences previously mentioned as being disparaged by the Tathāgata—which were brought forth in his fifth dwelling—are here brought to fulfillment; and he becomes esteemed as a master throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, with the exception of [the Buddhas].
Regarding the Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas who abide in the higher dwellings,
no one is equal to him in terms of intention and application;
furthermore, all the factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the meditative absorptions and so forth, become manifest before him.
By way of being oriented toward the aspects of cultivation, and not by way of abiding in the aspects of transcendence;
that is to say,
they become manifest by way of being oriented toward the aspects of cultivation, and not by way of abiding in the aspects of transcendence.
That is to say, as in the eighth stage;
thus engaged, he brings forth one million bodhisattva samādhis, headed by the samādhi of the well-ascertained object.
Through the attainment of these, he transcends the range of the samādhis of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Thus he dwells with body, speech, and mental action that are secluded from all afflictions, difficult to comprehend, and free from the movement of all conceptual constructions;
yet, out of regard for sentient beings, he does not abandon his application toward seeking further excellence.

For the sake of fulfilling awakening, his immeasurable body, speech, and mental action proceed, free from all signs, thoroughly purified, and illuminated by the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In this dwelling, by virtue of its being the object of his own wisdom, the Bodhisattva transcends the domain of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; however, in the other six dwellings, he does so by taking the Buddha-qualities as his objective support, and in the sixth dwelling, the Bodhisattva enters into cessation (*nirodha*).
In this [seventh] dwelling, moreover, he enters it at every moment.
And this is his most wonderful and inconceivable deed:
that while he dwells in the dwelling of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), he does not personally realize cessation (*nirodha*).

Making that very mastery of the application of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*) his dominant influence, he practices the bodhisattva conduct that is uncommon to all sentient beings—conduct that manifests in the world yet is not of its nature—just as described in the sutras.
The summary meaning of this, however, concerns the undertaking of meritorious deeds, the acquisition of a family and retinue, the initiation of the aspiration for specific types of rebirth,

dwelling in the three liberations, the training of those inclined toward the Lesser Vehicle through skillful means, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, and the aspiration for specific sensual delights.
Concerning the turning away from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the conformity with the minds of others, and the conformity with the great masses of people, the remainder is as before.
In this regard, however, there is this distinction:
it is just as that same gold, when polished with all kinds of precious gems by a skilled goldsmith, shines exceedingly.
And it becomes unsurpassable by other ornaments from Jambudvīpa;

likewise, these roots of virtue of his become more purified and unsurpassable by the roots of virtue of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as by the roots of virtue of bodhisattvas who abide in inferior states.
It is just as the light of the sun in Jambudvīpa mostly dries up moisture.
And it cannot be eclipsed by the radiance of anything else;
likewise, the radiance of this bodhisattva’s wisdom dries up the poisons of all the afflictions of sentient beings,
and it remains as before unassailable by the radiance of the knowledge of śrāvakas and others.
He becomes a sovereign king of the gods,
skilled in providing the realization of the disciples and solitary buddhas;
his power is to be understood through the description of hundreds of thousands of millions.

This is the signless dwelling with effort, characterized by the entry into the perfection of the specific undertaking of the path brought forth by skillful means and wisdom; by the continuous application toward the realization and penetration of the domain of the Tathāgatas; by the accomplishment of all factors conducive to awakening at every moment;
by the distinction between the afflicted and the unafflicted; and by the inclusion of the fulfillment of the conduct of application and the engagement in action through the purity of intention.

It should be understood through a brief exposition by way of: the fulfillment of all worldly arts, crafts, and activities; the attainment of immeasurable meditative absorptions (samādhis) uncommon to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation at every moment; the performance of worldly conduct uncommon to all sentient beings; the purification of the roots of virtue; [the manner of] rebirth; and [spiritual] power.
In detail, it is as before;
that is to say, on the *dūraṅgamā* stage,
it is called "Far-Reaching" because it is comprised of the fulfillment of the bodhisattva’s preparatory conduct (*prāyogikacaryā*).
And for that very reason, it should be understood as a "dwelling" (*vihāra*).
In this regard, what is the effortless, signless dwelling of the bodhisattvas?
Here, in the first immediately preceding dwelling, the bodhisattva has acquired a tenfold knowledge that enters into the ultimate reality of all phenomena.

With respect to the three times, as appropriate, beginning with their primordial non-arising, birthlessness, and lack of characteristics, and beginning with the impossibility of their being caused by anything other than themselves and their indestructibility; and with respect to the fact that, within a reality whose ultimate nature is inexpressible, that very nature— which appears through the mental construction of verbal expression— is non-existent both in terms of its characteristic and its causal status, yet proceeds and does not cease in the form of affliction.

And with regard to that ineffable reality which exists, [one considers] the equality of affliction at all times— beginning, middle, and end— caused by ignorance and false attachment; and, by means of the non-conceptual equality of correctly entering suchness, one begins the removal of those afflictions.
Because this ten-fold knowledge is superior and complete, he enters this eighth, perfectly pure dwelling.
Abiding here, he attains the most supreme and utterly pure bodhisattva-patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, what is that?
When this bodhisattva, having investigated all phenomena through the four investigations, understands them through the four types of thorough knowledge of reality as it is,
then, with all false conceptualizations and attachments removed, he perceives in this very life the conformity to the non-arising of all afflictions regarding all phenomena;

and he perceives their absolute, complete, and remainderless non-arising in the future, for those very phenomena which were previously produced from the causes of false conceptualizations and attachments.
Furthermore, those four investigations have been explained previously in the "Chapter on the Meaning of Reality" (*tattvārtha-paṭala*).

And the four thorough cognitions of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*) are not yet completely purified from the stage of the dwelling in conduct through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*) up to the dwelling that is signless with effort (*sābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*);
however, in this dwelling, they become completely purified.
Therefore, that bodhisattva is said to have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Through the attainment of that patience, he has reached the profound dwelling of a bodhisattva.
For him, those four defects that existed previously in the signless dwelling (*nirnimitta-vihāra*) are abandoned.
That effort involving deliberate application is abandoned;
furthermore, the eagerness for the higher pure dwelling is abandoned,
as is the eagerness regarding the capacity to perform the welfare of sentient beings in all its aspects.
It is abandoned;
and the manifestation of subtle perception is also abandoned.
Therefore, that dwelling is called "utterly pure."

And for him who delights in that profound dwelling, within that stream of the entrance to the Dharma, there is an immeasurable application of the activities of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and the knowledge of the gateways for accomplishing the exhortation and instigation by the Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, for one thus exhorted, the accomplishment of the knowledge of the differentiation of immeasurable bodies and the attainment of the ten masteries (*vaśitā*) should be understood in detail exactly as [described] in the sūtras.
Having attained mastery, he remains for as long as he desires;
or, with whatever mental abiding such as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) or liberations (*vimokṣa*), he wishes to dwell, in that he dwells.
By mere volition alone, all his requirements, such as food and other requisites, become perfectly provided.

He possesses the power to engage as he wishes in all arts and crafts; and regarding all actions leading to rebirth and all bases of rebirth, he has the power to take birth according to his desire; and he performs every miraculous feat exactly as he intends.
All his aspirations are fulfilled according to his wish;
whatever object he resolves upon in such a way, it becomes exactly so and not otherwise.
Furthermore, whatever object of knowledge he desires to know, he knows that too exactly as it is.
He also becomes one who obtains at will the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes,
and is skilled in the correct establishment of all phenomena.
For a bodhisattva who has thus attained mastery, the benefits resulting from that attainment of mastery beyond this point should be understood in detail exactly as they are set forth in the sūtra.
Having abandoned the coarse vision of the Buddha, one becomes constantly and continuously never separated from the vision of the Buddha.
The purification of the remaining roots of virtue should be understood according to the sūtra,
by means of the simile of precious gold and the simile of light.
The rebirth and the specific excellence of power of this bodhisattva in this dwelling should be understood exactly as described in the sūtra.
This is the effortless, signless dwelling;

it is so called because of the entry into the perfection of the knowledge that penetrates the ultimate reality, because of the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and because of the achievement of the profound bodhisattva dwelling that is free from all defects.

Birth should be understood through a brief description by way of the Buddhas' bestowal of the knowledge and superknowledges regarding the accomplishment of immeasurable gateways within the stream of the Dharma-gate; by way of entering the knowledge of the differentiation of immeasurable bodies; by way of the attainment of masteries; by way of experiencing the benefits of those masteries; by way of the purification of the roots of virtue; and by way of spiritual power.
In detail, as explained in the sūtras, for example, on the Immovable Stage (*acalā bhūmi*),
that mind proceeds upon that stage having mounted a path that flows effortlessly and immovably, due to the departure of former volitional formations (*pūrvakābhisaṃskāra*).
Therefore, that stage is called "the immovable.
For this very reason, this dwelling should be understood [in the same way].
In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas' dwelling of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
In this regard, the bodhisattva, being dissatisfied even with that profound dwelling and pursuing further excellence of knowledge,

understands as it truly is all the formative activities of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānābhisaṃskāra*) by which a bodhisattva must teach the Dharma to others in all its aspects, as well as the entire duty of proclaiming the Dharma; therein, this is the duty of proclaiming the Dharma:
Those who are afflicted and those who are purified amidst the dense movements of conceptual proliferation;
that by which they are afflicted and that by which they are purified;
and that which is affliction and purification itself.
That which is its uncertainty,
that which is its certainty,
and that which is both its certainty and its uncertainty.

His knowledge is in accordance with reality; and thus, for one who is skilled in teaching the Dharma and skilled in the task of exposition, there is the state of being a great Dharma-preacher in every respect— one who has attained immeasurable dhāraṇīs, who is skilled in the analysis of all components of vocal expression, who possesses inexhaustible eloquence,
and who is endowed with such power of retaining and grasping the Dharma.
By means of that speech which is brought forth through the Bodhisattva’s analytical knowledges;
while seated upon such a Dharma-seat;
in what place and for whom he teaches the Dharma; by how many modes; and being endowed with the power to inform, satisfy, and engage sentient beings.
All of that should be understood in detail exactly as it is set forth in the sūtra.
Furthermore, the specific excellence regarding the purification of the roots of virtue, rebirth, and spiritual power should also be understood exactly as it is set forth in the sūtra.

This is the bodhisattvas’ dwelling in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvidvihāra*), both by way of entering into contentment with peaceful liberation and by way of the knowledge of the mental formation involved in proclaiming the Dharma.

It should be understood through a summary explanation in terms of: knowledge of those duties; the attainment of the state of an inconceivable great Dharma-preacher; the purification of roots of virtue; rebirth; and power.
Furthermore, the detailed explanation is exactly as it appears in the sūtra.
Just as on the stage called Sādhumatī (the Good Intelligence),

that stage is called Sādhumatī because it has the function of proclaiming the Dharma through the Bodhisattva’s analytical knowledge and intelligence, which is purified by the intention for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings;
and for that same reason, this dwelling should also be understood in the same way.

In that regard, what is the supreme dwelling of the bodhisattvas? Here, in the dwelling of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), which is purified in every aspect, for the bodhisattva who is worthy of the sovereignty of Dharma and is near to the consecration of Dharma— due to the attainment of immeasurable samādhis such as the "Stainless" (*vimala*) and the performance of their functions, and due to the manifestation of the final samādhi, the consecration into the excellence of the knowledge of omniscience— this is the supreme dwelling.

[It is so] because they obtain seats, bodies, and retinues corresponding to all the Buddhas; because they receive the consecration of the omniscient knowledge in all its aspects through the going forth and returning of their own rays of light; because, once consecrated, they possess the knowledge of the Buddha-activities—the means for liberation and the gathering together of all those to be trained;

because they obtain immeasurable liberations, dhāraṇīs, and superknowledges; and because they establish the definitions and explanations of the great mindfulness and knowledge that have those [qualities] as their sovereign power.

The supreme dwelling should be understood through a concise description by way of the accomplishment of the great superknowledges (*mahābhijñā*) and the excellence of the purification of roots of virtue, rebirth, and power;
however, for a detailed description, it is exactly as set forth in the *Dharmameghā* Bodhisattva-bhūmi.

Having fulfilled the path of a bodhisattva and having perfectly completed the accumulations for enlightenment, that bodhisattva receives from the presence of the Tathāgatas, upon the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), the most sublime rain of the True Dharma, which is unbearable for all other sentient beings. Having become like a great cloud— whether not yet fully awakened to enlightenment or already fully awakened to it— he pacifies the dust of the afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings with the incomparable rain of the True Dharma.
Established on that ground, one causes the various crops of the roots of virtue to sprout, grow, and ripen;
therefore, that ground is called the "Cloud of Dharma" (dharmameghā).
For this very reason, it should be regarded as the supreme dwelling (vihāra).
Furthermore, those factors which have been definitively established in each successive dwelling do not exist at all in the preceding dwellings;
rather, because they are present only in a weak degree, they do not count as such.
It should be understood that the establishment of the attainment and perfection of the other, subsequent stages occurs precisely through the medium and superior degrees of those very same factors.

In this regard, each and every dwelling (vihāra) is attained and perfected over many hundreds of thousands of millions of great aeons (*mahākalpa*), or even more than that. Yet, all those dwellings are fully realized through three incalculable great aeons (*mahākalpāsaṃkhyeya*). Having transcended the dwelling of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukticaryā-vihāra*) during one incalculable great aeon, the dwelling of joy (*pramuditavihāra*) is attained;
and this is achieved by one who exerts effort with constancy, not by one who does not exert effort.

During the second incalculable great eon (*mahākalpāsaṃkhyeya*), having transcended the stages from the Joyful Abode (*pramuditavihāra*) up to the signless abode with effort (*sābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*), he attains the effortless signless abode (*anābhoga-nirnimitta*). And that is necessarily so; for that bodhisattva of pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*) exerts himself with certainty.

During the third incalculable great aeon (*mahākalpāsaṃkhyeya*), having transcended both effortless signlessness (*anābhoga-nirnimitta*) and the abiding in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid-vihāra*), one attains the supreme bodhisattva abiding.
In this regard, two incalculable aeons are to be understood.
Even that which is called a "great aeon" is termed "incalculable" because its duration is immeasurable when reckoned by means of days, nights, months, and half-months.

Furthermore, that number which transcends all calculation by means of the method of counting those very great eons (*mahākalpa*) is also called "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*). Enlightenment is attained through many incalculable eons according to the former [definition of] an incalculable eon; however, according to the latter, it is attained in no more than three incalculable eons.

It should be understood that while some who apply themselves with the highest degree of superior effort may turn back [the course of saṃsāra] for many intermediate kalpas, and others for as many as great kalpas, there is no one for whom an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*) of kalpas is turned back. Furthermore,

through these twelve bodhisattva dwellings over three incalculable eons, the corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) associated with the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and that associated with the hindrance to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned.

In that regard, it should be understood that within these three dwellings, there is the abandonment of the functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the side of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*). In the Dwelling of Great Joy (*pramudita-vihāra*), there is the total and complete abandonment, in terms of active manifestation, of the afflictions pertaining to the miserable realms;

and of the most intense portion of all afflictions pertaining to the side of the afflictions generally. In the Dwelling of the Signless without Effort (*anābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*), there is the abandonment of the afflictions that act as obstacles to the purity of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
It should be understood that for one belonging to the [Bodhisattva] side, there is the abandonment of all forms of functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) in every respect;
however, this refers to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of all afflictions.

Furthermore, in the supreme dwelling, it should be understood that there is the abandonment of all afflictions along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), proclivities (*anuśaya*), and obscurations (*āvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, for one entering that dwelling of the Tathāgata, it should be understood that there are three types of *dauṣṭhulya* belonging to the side of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):
that which resides in the bark, that which resides in the pith, and that which resides in the heartwood.
Among these, the abandonment of that which resides in the bark occurs in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditavihāra*).
In the effortless, signless dwelling of one who has reached the pith, there occurs the abandonment [of obscurations] within the Tathāgata-dwelling.

Furthermore, the state of knowledge consisting in the purification of all obscurations pertains to those three dwellings; for that abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, the other dwellings serve as the accumulations in their respective order.
In these thirteen dwellings, it should be understood that, in brief, there are eleven types of purity.
In the first, there is the purification of the lineage;
in the second, the purification of liberation through faith;
in the third, the purification of the resolute intention.
In the fourth, there is purity of ethical discipline;
in the fifth, purity of mind;
and in the sixth, seventh, and eighth, there is purity of the undertaking of right knowledge.
In the ninth [ground], there is the purity of the fulfillment of preparatory practice;
in the tenth, the purity of the realization of the knowledge of reality; in the eleventh, the purity of the analytical knowledges for the sake of correctly explaining that meaning to others;
and in the twelfth, the purity of the knowledge that penetrates all aspects of all objects of knowledge.
In the thirteenth stage, the Tathāgata abode, there is the purification of all afflictive and cognitive obstructions along with their latent predispositions (*savāsana*).
It should be understood that these thirteen abodes are subsumed by the eight factors previously mentioned that comprise the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the first and second abodes, [they belong to] one in whom faith has arisen and who has reached the stage of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The hearing and reflection upon the Bodhisattvapiṭaka;
in the third dwelling, the attainment of the resolute intention preceded by the acquisition of the modes of cultivation;
and in all the other dwellings up to the effortless signless state, the abundance of cultivation.
Thereafter, in the three bodhisattva dwellings comprised within the completely purified conduct, there is the accomplishment of the fruit of cultivation.
In the dwelling of a Tathāgata, absolute deliverance is to be understood.
Furthermore, the sequence of these twelve bodhisattva dwellings should be understood by analogy with the dwellings of a śrāvaka.

Just as the śrāvaka’s dwelling in his own lineage is understood, so should his first [dwelling] be known; just as his dwelling in the application for entering the certainty of correctness (*samyaktva-nyāmāvakrānti-prayoga-vihāra*) is, so is his second;
and just as his dwelling in the entry into certainty (*nyāmāvakrānti-vihāra*) is, so is his third dwelling.

Just as for one who has attained verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*), there is the dwelling in the higher training of ethics (*adhiśīla*) for the sake of the subsequent destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), so too is his fourth dwelling.
Just as for him, based on the higher training in ethics, there is the dwelling in the accomplishment of the training in the higher mind (*adhicitta*), so too is his fifth dwelling.

Just as for him there is the dwelling in the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) consisting of the knowledge of the truths as they have been realized, so too should his sixth, seventh, and eighth dwellings be understood.
Just as his dwelling in the application of the signless samādhi [occurs] when the object of knowledge has been well-investigated, so is this ninth dwelling;
just as his perfected signless dwelling [occurs], so is this tenth dwelling;
just as his dwelling in the bases of liberation occurs for him when he has emerged [from meditative absorption], so is this eleventh dwelling.
Just as his dwelling in arhatship is of every aspect, so too should his twelfth dwelling be understood.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on the dwellings, in the section on the yoga of the *ādhārānudharma* within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
And the second stage of yoga is completed.
The Third Book: The Stage of Yoga Consisting of the Culmination of the Foundation (Ādhāraniṣṭhāyogasthāna), Chapter 3.1:
The Section on Rebirth (Upapattipaṭala).

In brief, the rebirths of bodhisattvas are of five kinds; they are irreproachable in all places and in all dwellings for all bodhisattvas, and are for the sake of the welfare and happiness of other beings.
They are: the rebirth that pacifies calamities, the rebirth that conforms to those [beings], the rebirth of greatness, the rebirth of sovereignty, and the final rebirth.
Among these, what is the rebirth that pacifies calamities?

In this regard, during times of famine, hardship, and great wildernesses, a bodhisattva makes a vow and takes birth in the wombs of large fish and other such beings so that sentient beings may subsist with little difficulty. Having been born in vast physical forms, he satisfies the entire world with his own flesh.
Furthermore, among sentient beings afflicted by many diseases, he makes a vow and assumes the body of a perfected vidyādhara or a great physician in order to pacify those illnesses.
When sentient beings are severely afflicted by the calamities of foreign armies, he becomes a powerful ruler who, through righteousness, tranquility, and skillful means,

acts for the purpose of pacifying those foreign military threats; and toward sentient beings who are mutually hostile, his words become authoritative for the sake of establishing reconciliation and abandoning the intent of enmity.

When kings are engaged in punishing, imprisoning, and inflicting various tortures upon their subjects, he is reborn into such royal families in order to eliminate those very afflictions of sentient beings;
and he becomes a righteous king who has compassion for living beings.

Furthermore, out of compassion for those beings who hold wrong views, commit evil deeds, and are devoted to some particular temple of a deity, he appears in that very temple in order to cause them to abandon wrong views and misconduct.

This birth, preceded by compassion, should be understood as immeasurable due to the power of both aspiration and mastery; this is the detailed explanation regarding beings born in various diverse wombs, such as those in the animal realm. However, the summary explanation is as follows:
what is birth that conforms to and resembles them?
In this case, a bodhisattva— either by means of a formal vow or through the attainment of mastery— manifests among various beings born in the animal realm,
among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others who are mutually hostile and antagonistic, as well as among brahmins with wrong views and those who practice misconduct. (Dutt 248)

Among beings who are devoted to wrong livelihoods, likewise to sensual desires, excessively attached to them, and intent upon sense-pleasures, he is reborn in the same realm as those beings primarily for the sake of turning away from that fault.
Having become their leader, he does not practice those things which those beings habitually practice.
Whatever wholesome [quality] they do not practice, that he practices;
and for the sake of their practicing what is wholesome, he teaches them the Dharma.
Through that teaching of the Dharma and through that practice of what is dissimilar [to their faults], they turn away from those defects by means of that skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
This [birth] is also to be understood as being measurable by reasoning, as before.
In that regard, what is birth with greatness?

Here, a bodhisattva, by his very nature at the time of birth, brings about a maturation consisting of lifespan, complexion, lineage, sovereignty, and so forth, which is preeminent over the entire world.
And by that ripening, he performs the deeds as described in the "Chapter on the Welfare of Self and Others.
That birth of the bodhisattva should also be understood as immeasurable across those various modes of existence.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s birth through sovereign power?
That birth of a bodhisattva which has been described, beginning from the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), up to the tenth stage, is called his "birth through mastery" (*adhipattyopapatti*).

Beginning from lordship over Jambūdvīpa up to the state of Maheśvara, it extends beyond the Akaniṣṭha heaven and enters all spheres of rebirth, wherein only those bodhisattvas who have attained the supreme stage (*paramavihāra*) are born; for that [state] is produced by the sovereign power of their karma.
In that regard, what is the final birth of a bodhisattva?
It is that birth in which a bodhisattva, having fulfilled the accumulations for awakening, is born into either a family of priests or a royal family, realizes unsurpassed perfect awakening,
and performs all the activities of a Buddha.
This rebirth is called the final and last.

Whatever bodhisattvas have been born, will be born, or are being born in pure, auspicious, and virtuous rebirths throughout the past, future, and present time periods— all of them are born in these very five.
There is nothing beyond this, nor anything more than this, setting aside the births on the level of fools;
for these five types of birth are intended by wise bodhisattvas.
Indeed, these births have great enlightenment as their fruit.
Relying upon which, bodhisattvas swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus ends the first chapter, on "Birth," in the section on the Foundation within the *Yogasthāna* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 249)

The Chapter on Appropriation (Parigrahapaṭala). In this regard, it should be understood that, in brief, there are six kinds of correct appropriation by bodhisattvas throughout all the bodhisattva practices pertaining to the various stages of dwelling: the appropriation of all sentient beings at once; [the appropriation of them] gradually; [the appropriation of them] with a view toward their welfare in this life; [the appropriation of them] with a view toward their welfare in future lives; [the appropriation of them] with a view toward both their welfare in this life and in future lives; and the appropriation of them for the sake of their ultimate liberation. Among these, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is as follows: [it occurs] when a bodhisattva, having generated the mind of awakening for the first time, makes a vow regarding all sentient beings, saying, "I shall bring about the welfare of all sentient beings. This is called the appropriation of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, having entered the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), attains the realization of the equality of self and others. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva realizes that there is no distinction between self and others, and thus, since they do not even perceive a self, how could they perceive others? It is because of this realization of the equality of self and others that the bodhisattva appropriates all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, having attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), enters the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva has abandoned the two obstructions—the obstruction of afflictions and the obstruction to knowledge—and has thereby become free from the fear of saṃsāra. Since they have abandoned the fear of saṃsāra, they are able to appropriate all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, having attained the stage of the Tathāgata, becomes a Buddha. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva has perfected the cultivation of all roots of virtue and has fully realized all dharmas. Since they have fully realized all dharmas, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, having completed the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*) and fulfilled the accumulations of merit and wisdom, attains the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva has exhausted all the afflictions and secondary afflictions of themselves and others, and has attained the supreme, perfect enlightenment. Since they have attained the supreme, perfect enlightenment, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, having attained the power of mastery over all dharmas, turns the wheel of the Dharma. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva has attained the unimpeded power of mastery over all dharmas and is able to teach the Dharma according to the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings. Since they are able to teach the Dharma according to the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, having manifested the great parinirvāṇa, establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva manifests the great parinirvāṇa to lead sentient beings to abandon attachment to existence and to enter the path of liberation. Since they lead sentient beings to abandon attachment to existence and to enter the path of liberation, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their vows, manifests birth in the various realms of existence to mature sentient beings. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, by the power of their previous vows, manifests birth in the various realms of existence—whether in the hells, among animals, among hungry ghosts, among humans, or among gods—to mature sentient beings. Since they manifest birth in the various realms of existence to mature sentient beings, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their skillful means, manifests various forms of conduct to lead sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, through the power of their skillful means, manifests various forms of conduct—such as the conduct of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a householder—to lead sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha. Since they manifest various forms of conduct to lead sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their great compassion, manifests weeping and lamenting to lead sentient beings to generate the mind of awakening. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, out of great compassion, manifests weeping and lamenting to lead sentient beings to generate the mind of awakening. Since they manifest weeping and lamenting to lead sentient beings to generate the mind of awakening, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their wisdom, manifests the extinction of all phenomena to lead sentient beings to realize the emptiness of all dharmas. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, through the power of their wisdom, manifests the extinction of all phenomena to lead sentient beings to realize the emptiness of all dharmas. Since they manifest the extinction of all phenomena to lead sentient beings to realize the emptiness of all dharmas, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their miraculous transformations, displays various miraculous feats to lead sentient beings to develop faith and respect. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, through the power of their miraculous transformations, displays various miraculous feats—such as emitting light, shaking the earth, or transforming objects—to lead sentient beings to develop faith and respect. Since they display various miraculous feats to lead sentient beings to develop faith and respect, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their teaching, expounds the profound Dharma to lead sentient beings to penetrate the meaning of emptiness. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, through the power of their teaching, expounds the profound Dharma—such as the teachings on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—to lead sentient beings to penetrate the meaning of emptiness. Since they expound the profound Dharma to lead sentient beings to penetrate the meaning of emptiness, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their maturation, matures sentient beings in accordance with their capacities and dispositions. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, through the power of their maturation, matures sentient beings in accordance with their capacities and dispositions, leading them to enter the path of the Buddha. Since they mature sentient beings in accordance with their capacities and dispositions to lead them to enter the path of the Buddha, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their protection, protects sentient beings from all fears and calamities. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, through the power of their protection, protects sentient beings from all fears and calamities—such as the fear of fire, water, weapons, or robbers. Since they protect sentient beings from all fears and calamities, they are able to appropriately take hold of all sentient beings at once. Furthermore, the appropriation of all sentient beings at once is also to be understood as occurring when a bodhisattva, through the power of their service, serves sentient beings with body, speech, and mind. Why is that? Because at that time, the bodhisattva, through the power of their service, serves sentient beings with body, speech, and mind, providing them with food, clothing, medicine
Mastery-grasping,
appropriation-grasping,
and long-term grasping.
The final appropriation is not of long duration;
for at the very first production of the thought of awakening, the Bodhisattva has already appropriated the entire realm of sentient beings as his own family.

"I must, to the best of my power and strength, provide for them the introduction to all forms of welfare and happiness," and he acts accordingly. This is the bodhisattva’s simultaneous embracing of all sentient beings.

A bodhisattva has the notion of "possessive appropriation" regarding the circle of dependents—consisting of mother, father, children, wife, female and male slaves, laborers, servants, and retainers—when he is a master, and regarding the people of his realm when he is a king.
Furthermore, within that circle of dependents, he engages in activities appropriate to such possession and consistent with his nature as a bodhisattva;
moreover, by means of various skillful methods, he establishes his parents in roots of virtue.
From time to time, he performs acts of worship and service;
he is grateful and appreciative of what has been done for him;
and he complies with the wishes of his mother and father.
Having mastery over his wealth and possessions,
he provides his sons, wives, female and male servants, and others with proper food and clothing from time to time,
and he does not oppress them with excessive labor.
He forgives their transgressions,
provides proper nursing for those who are ill,
and establishes them in what is wholesome.
From time to time, he honors them with special gifts and kind words, and he does not regard them as mere male or female slaves;
rather, he protects them especially, even more so than himself.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has become a king over a realm of people, he governs the kingdom without punishment and without weapons.
He acquires wealth through righteous means and enjoys a kingdom inherited through his lineage;
he does not invade another kingdom by force or violence.
To the best of his ability and according to his strength, he restrains sentient beings from evil;
he becomes like a father to all creatures,
and he is disposed to share his wealth even with other beings, let alone with his own dependents.
He is free from malice and is a speaker of truth;
he avoids all oppression of sentient beings, such as killing, binding, punishing, mutilating, and beating.
In this regard, the proper guidance of a community is called a bodhisattva’s “acceptance through taking hold. He properly takes hold of an assembly for two reasons:
he takes hold of them with a mind free from worldly motives.
He applies himself correctly to his own welfare;
he does not lead others astray through wrong application.
And regarding all possessions, he maintains an even mind and does not fall into partiality.
He harbors no stinginess regarding the Dharma toward them, nor does he maintain the "teacher's fist" (withholding instruction).
He does not expect service or attendance from them;

rather, when they perform such service out of a desire for virtue, he does not prevent them, so that they may accumulate a store of merit. And when the time is right, he himself performs service and attendance for them.
He causes them to understand meanings that have not yet been understood, he brings to full purification those meanings already understood,
and he destroys every doubt as it arises.
He dispels remorse;
having penetrated profound points of meaning with wisdom, he elucidates them from time to time;
and he shares equally in their suffering and happiness.
For their sake, he applies himself with great effort for the sake of material goods from his own presence;
and from time to time, when they transgress, he becomes one who correctly reproves them,
and at the proper time, he becomes one who restrains them in accordance with the rule.

He does not neglect those who are ill or dejected in any way, but acts for the sake of alleviating their illness and removing their despondency. He does not despise those who are inferior in physical form, mindfulness, vigor, wisdom, and so forth.
And from time to time, having entered into their weariness, he teaches them the Dharma in a suitable manner.
From time to time, he provides them with correct instruction regarding their object of focus;
he is patient under pressure and remains unshakeable;
and he conducts himself with a mode of life and conduct that is equal to theirs, or even superior, but never inferior.
He is free from desire for gain and honor;
he is compassionate;
he is neither arrogant nor fickle; and he is perfected in conduct, view, behavior, and livelihood.
His facial complexion is bright;
he is free from frowning, amiable, sweet-spoken, the first to speak, and preceded by a smile.
He is also constantly and always diligent.
Regarding the side of wholesome qualities,
he is free from negligence and indolence;
likewise, it is for the sake of training the assembly and for his own attainment of excellence.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not gather an assembly at all times, nor does he never gather one,
nor does he do so in any other way.

In that regard, those beings who are established in a mild stage of maturation are said to be the Bodhisattva’s long-term acquisition, because they are capable of purification only after a long period of time. Those, however, who are established in a middling stage of maturation are said to be his short-term acquisition, because they are capable of purification before long.

Furthermore, those beings who are established in the highest degree of maturation are called the "final acquisitions" of a bodhisattva, because they possess the capacity for purification within that very lifetime.
Thus, this is the sixfold correct gathering of sentient beings by bodhisattvas;
through this gathering, bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present have gathered, will gather, or are gathering sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is nothing beyond this, nor is there anything more.
Thus, for those bodhisattvas who practice the correct way of embracing sentient beings, twelve kinds of narrow and difficult situations should be understood;
and in these, a bodhisattva must be discerning.

When beings are established in transgression, whether there is the infliction of harm upon them or the practice of equanimity toward them, it constitutes for the bodhisattva an encounter with difficulty and distress; likewise, the application of harsh means toward a being while protecting one's own intention from affliction constitutes an encounter with difficulty and distress.
When there is only a small amount of property to be given, yet many supplicants appear before one to beg, this constitutes falling into a state of distress and difficulty.

Furthermore, when various tasks for the sake of many sentient beings arise, and one is asked to act as their helper while being alone, this constitutes falling into a state of distress and difficulty.

Moreover, for one whose mind is rendered unworkable, the attainment of mundane meditative absorptions conducive to negligence, or birth in the world of the gods, constitutes falling into a state of distress and difficulty.

For one who seeks to act for the benefit of sentient beings, the inability to accomplish that benefit is an encounter with a narrow strait. To teach the Dharma to sentient beings who are deluded, deceitful, and stubborn—or to neglect them—is an encounter with a narrow strait.
Furthermore, to constantly perceive the defects of cyclic existence while yet not abandoning cyclic existence is an encounter with a narrow strait.
Death while one’s resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is impure and one’s mindfulness is lost is a state of distress and peril.
Furthermore, when one’s resolute intention is impure, being asked by others for a preeminent and most beloved object is a state of distress and peril.
And failing to provide instruction to, or remaining indifferent toward, sentient beings who hold diverse and conflicting views and diverse inclinations is a state of distress and peril.
Furthermore, one must practice constant vigilance while yet not abandoning all the afflictions (*kleśa*) in every respect; thus, a state of extreme confinement and difficulty is encountered.

When a bodhisattva has fallen into such confinement and difficulty, he should act accordingly by observing what is weighty and what is light in certain cases; in some instances, he should exercise discernment regarding individuals;
and in others, he should proceed by relying on fortitude and taking up the underlying cause.
One should also make right aspirations;
one should not allow the mind to wander toward anything whatsoever;
and in some cases, having established intense discernment, one must remain untiring and patient.
In some instances one must be equanimous;
in some instances one must exert vigor and act with ardent application;
in some instances one must be skillful in means.
Thus, the bodhisattva who is skilled in the correct antidotes does not despair even when confronted with all manner of constraints and difficulties, and he properly protects himself.
This concludes the second chapter, "On Appropriation," in the section on the Foundation within the *Yogasthāna* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
(Dutt 253)
The Chapter on the Grounds (Bhūmipaṭala): It should be understood that within these thirteen dwellings as they have been described, there are seven grounds to be known;
six of which are the grounds of the bodhisattvas.
One is the mixed stage of the Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata;
[the others are] the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi),
the stage of practice through resolute belief (adhimukticaryābhūmi), and the stage of pure superior intention (śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi).
The stage of practicing the conduct;
the stage of certainty;
the stage of certain conduct.
And the stage of reaching the culmination—these are the seven bodhisattva stages.
Among these, the last one is mixed;
therein, the two stages of the abiding in the lineage and the abiding in conduct through resolute conviction [are included].

The stage of joyful abiding is the level of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*). The two abidings of higher ethics and higher mind, along with the three abidings of higher wisdom, constitute the stage of practice and application (*caryāpratipatti-bhūmi*), which includes both the abiding of signlessness with effort (*sābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*) and the effortless abiding of signlessness (*anābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*). The latter is the level of certainty (*niyatā-bhūmi*).
On that stage, the bodhisattva has entered the third certainty.
The dwelling in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is the stage of certain conduct;
the supreme dwelling and the Tathāgata dwelling are the stages of reaching the ultimate consummation.
Furthermore, a subsequent explanation of the dwelling and the stage of the Tathāgata will be given in the chapter on the establishment of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharmapratiṣṭhāpaṭala*).

In that regard, how does a bodhisattva, when entering from the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) into the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi*), transcend the miserable states of existence (*apāya*)?

Here, the bodhisattva, relying upon the completely pure mundane meditative concentration (*laukikapariśuddhadhyāna*) while on the stage of practice through aspiration, has well accumulated the equipment for awakening (*susambhṛtabodhi*).

The equipment consists of cultivating compassion toward sentient beings through the one hundred and ten aspects previously specified, with undistracted attention. Through the sequence of that cultivation, he acquires such a disposition of compassion and a disposition of pity toward sentient beings,
by which, for the sake of sentient beings, he dwells in the lower realms as if they were his own home.

If even while dwelling among these very beings my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is fully realized, nevertheless, I am willing for the sake of removing the suffering of sentient beings. With that pure intention, he desires that all the karma of sentient beings leading to the miserable realms be his own maturation; and he makes a firm vow so that all unwholesome actions may never again be committed.
For him, that mundane, thoroughly purified meditative concentration, having been thus cultivated,
draws away from his basis the depravity belonging to the side of the afflictions that lead to the miserable states.

Because of its abandonment, before long, the basis of this bodhisattva undergoes a transformation for the sake of the absolute non-performance of evil karma leading to the miserable states and for the sake of not going to the miserable states.
To this extent, the bodhisattva has completely transcended all states of miserable rebirth;
having transcended the stage of conduct through resolute belief,
he has entered the stage of pure superior intention.

Furthermore, those ten qualities— faith and the rest— which were taught in the "Chapter on the Dwellings" as the purifiers of the dwellings, should also be understood here as the purifiers of the stages (*bhūmi*). Their systematic arrangement should be understood in terms of the opposition between the adverse factors and their antidotes.
The summarized meaning and the sequence should be understood. In this regard, there are these ten:
the factors that constitute the adversaries to these ten factors which purify the stages.
Those for which this [faith] is established as the antidote—what are these ten?
Not generating the thought of enlightenment at all, in any way, and not undertaking the training precepts of a bodhisattva: this is the factor that is the opposite of faith.
Faith is the antidote to that [lack of faith];
the intention to harm sentient beings is the opposite of compassion,
and compassion is the antidote to that [intention to harm].
Malice toward sentient beings is the opposite of loving-kindness;
loving-kindness is its antidote. Regard for possessions and livelihood is the opposite of generosity.

Generosity is that which serves as the antidote to its opposite. Receiving harm or misconduct from sentient beings and the abundance of duties to be performed constitute the opposite of indefatigability;
indefatigability is that which serves as the antidote to its opposite.

The application of improper means is the opposite of knowledge of the treatises; it is countered by knowledge of the treatises. Lack of gentleness and the failure to comply with the minds of others are the opposites of knowledge of the world.
The antidote to which is knowledge of the world (*lokajñatā*).
Negligence and laziness in the cultivation of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-bhāvanā*) are the opposites of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*);
the antidote to which is the possession of shame and dread of blame.
The state of being overwhelmed by the long-lasting, diverse, intense, and uninterrupted sufferings of saṃsāra is the obstacle to the acquisition of the power of fortitude;
its antidote is the acquisition of the power of fortitude.
Doubt, uncertainty, and hesitation regarding the Teacher are the obstacles to the service and worship of the Tathāgata.
That which serves as the counteragent to these is the service and worship of the Tathāgata.
Thus, first of all, their establishment occurs by way of the discordant factors and their counteragents.
What, then, is their summarized meaning?
In brief, the purity of intention and the purity of application are elucidated by these ten factors.
Among them, the purity of intention should be understood through the first three,
and the purity of application through the remaining ones.
A bodhisattva who has deep faith in awakening feels compassion for suffering beings;
feeling compassion, he thinks, "I must protect these beings," and thus cultivates loving-kindness.
For one whose mind is thus imbued with loving-kindness, there arises the relinquishment of everything, such that he becomes indifferent toward wealth and even his own life.
And being selfless in his application for their sake, he does not become weary;
and being unwearied, he becomes a knower of the treatises;
and being a knower of the treatises, as it is in the world—
He understands how it should be set in motion;
thus he becomes a knower of the world.
Furthermore, he himself feels shame and embarrassment regarding the manifestation of the afflictions.
Possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, he does not fall under the power of the afflictions and attains the empowerment of the strength of fortitude.
