Thus, with his aspirations fully realized, he has transcended the conduct and stages of a bodhisattva and has entered the conduct and stage of a Tathāgata. Furthermore,
because of the complete abandonment of the residual depravity (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the category of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), his basis (*āśraya*) becomes transformed.
And this transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) of his is unsurpassed.
All other transformations of the basis of Bodhisattvas, ending with the supreme dwelling (*paramavihāra*), should be understood as being surpassed.

In that regard, how is the distinction in knowledge (*jñānaviśeṣa*)—the difference in knowledge—to be understood between a Bodhisattva established on the stage of reaching the culmination (*niṣṭhāgamana-bhūmi*) and a Tathāgata?

In this case, the knowledge of a bodhisattva established on the stage of reaching the culmination should be understood as being like the sight of forms by one with clear vision when they are screened by a thin cloth;
whereas his knowledge regarding all that is to be known is like [vision] that is not screened by anything at all.
In this way, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is to be viewed;
it is like a painting complete with all its colors and hues, yet not fully refined by the final, most pure stroke of color.
In this way, the wisdom of that bodhisattva is to be viewed.
Just as [the eye] is perfectly purified, so should the gnosis of the Tathāgata be regarded.
Just as a man with sight perceives forms when the darkness is slight,
so it is for the Bodhisattva, as before.
Just as [vision] is entirely free from darkness, so should the gnosis of the Tathāgata be regarded.
Just as one with sight perceives forms from afar, so it is for the Bodhisattva as before; just as [one perceives them] when near, so it is for the Tathāgata as before.
Just as one with slight cataracts perceives forms, so it is for the Bodhisattva as before; just as one with perfectly pure vision [perceives them], so it is for the Tathāgata as before.
Just as the physical existence of one who is in the womb, so should the bodhisattva established on the stage of reaching the culmination be viewed.
Just as the physical existence of one born into the state of rebirth, so should the Tathāgata be viewed.
Just as the movement of the mind of an Arhat while in a dream, so should the bodhisattva established on the stage of reaching the culmination be viewed.
Just as the mental activity of that very person upon awakening is to be viewed, so should the [mental activity] of the Tathāgata be viewed.
Just as the nature of an impure lamp is to be viewed, so should the nature of the knowledge of a Bodhisattva established on the stage of reaching the culmination be viewed.
Just as the nature of a perfectly pure lamp is to be viewed, so should the nature of the knowledge of the Tathāgata be viewed.

Therefore, it should be understood that there is a great difference in knowledge, a difference in personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), and a difference in contemplation between [ordinary beings] and the Bodhisattvas who abide on the stage of reaching the culmination of the Tathāgata.
Having thus awakened to enlightenment, the Tathāgata performs all the Buddha-activities in all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
In that regard, what are the Buddha-activities?
In brief, these ten are the Tathāgata’s duties and tasks of a Tathāgata.
Each individual task of a Tathāgata brings about the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings.
There is nothing beyond this; there is nothing more than this.
What are the ten?

First, regarding his own state as a Great Being, he performs the primary function of a Tathāgata by generating conviction in that state of a Great Being which inspires clarity of mind from the very outset; and he accomplishes this through the primary and secondary marks.
The Tathāgata’s activity that consists of the application of instruction in all its aspects for all sentient beings— which he accomplishes through the four kinds of complete purity—
is the second Tathāgata-activity.
The capacity to perform all tasks for all sentient beings and the capacity to sever all doubts is the third Tathāgata-activity.

That which the Tathāgata accomplishes through the ten powers of a Tathāgata is as follows: for by means of these ten previously mentioned powers, the Tathāgata becomes capable of accomplishing every purpose for all sentient beings. And regarding those who ask him questions concerning the powers of a Tathāgata, the Tathāgata answers their questions exactly as those things have been known, seen, understood, and realized by the Tathāgata.
When questioned, he provides an explanation;
the subduing of all opponents' doctrines and the establishment of his own doctrine is the fourth task of the Tathāgata.

That which the Tathāgata accomplishes through the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*)—the state of an unafflicted mind toward those disciples who abide in the Tathāgata’s teaching and those who do not—is the fifth task of the Tathāgata.
That which the Tathāgata accomplishes through the foundations of mindfulness—that is, acting according to what he has spoken—is the sixth deed of a Tathāgata.
That which the Tathāgata accomplishes through the things that need no protection—that is, surveying the entire world day and night with the Buddha-eye—is the seventh deed of a Tathāgata.
That which the Tathāgata accomplishes through great compassion...

The eighth deed of a Tathāgata is the dwelling in all the activities for the sake of all sentient beings; that which the Tathāgata accomplishes through the nature of non-forgetfulness (*asammoṣadharmatā*). The ninth deed of a Tathāgata is the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consisting in the accordance with the conduct and dwelling of the Tathāgata as it truly is;

that which the Tathāgata accomplishes by the total eradication of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), having completely avoided those phenomena that are associated with disadvantage, as well as those that are neither associated with advantage nor associated with disadvantage.
Furthermore, the explanation, exposition, and clarification of those teachings that are connected with the goal is the tenth deed of a Tathāgata;

this is that which the Tathāgata accomplishes through his knowledge of the excellence of all aspects. For it is in this way that the Tathāgata, performing the ten deeds of a Tathāgata by means of these one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), carries out the entire work of a Buddha.
Furthermore, in terms of its detailed classification, it is not easy to calculate the extent of this very work of a Buddha, even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
This is called the dwelling of the Tathāgata, the stage of the Tathāgata, and the foundation.
Why is that?

Relying upon this and established in this, bodhisattvas— who desire its form— train in the bodhisattva trainings; and even having attained that [realization], by relying upon this very thing and being established in this, they accomplish all the aims of all sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called "establishment.
Furthermore, all these qualities of a Buddha are exceedingly conducive to performing the welfare of others and are manifested through the performance of the welfare of others by the Tathāgatas.
It is not so for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
therefore, these alone are called their "unshared" (āveṇika) qualities.
Furthermore, there are those Buddha-qualities which are not found at all among Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas in any respect whatsoever.
Namely: great compassion, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the eradication of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and the knowledge of all excellent aspects.
Even those qualities that are perceived [in others] are not complete in all their aspects;
however, in the case of the Tathāgata, all are perceived, and they are complete in all aspects, far more transcendent, and far more sublime.
Therefore, they are called "unique" (āveṇika) to him; and the meaning of "unique" should be understood as the sense of exclusivity.
Thus, this is the complete path of training for bodhisattvas.
And the path of training and its fruit have been revealed.

For the sake of explaining every aspect of the entire path of training for all bodhisattvas and the fruit of that path of training, this Bodhisattvabhūmi serves as the foundation; it is indeed called the "Matrix of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka" (Bodhisattvapiṭakamātṛkā) and is also called the "Compendium of the Mahāyāna" (Mahāyānasaṃgraha).
It is called the "Explanation of the Oath of Non-destruction," and it is also called the "Root of the Purity of Unobstructed Knowledge.
Whoever from this world— including its gods, humans, and asuras— whether being a god or a human, a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa...
Having generated firm resolve toward this bodhisattva stage, one will hear it, take it up, retain it,
or apply oneself to it through the mode of cultivation; or one will explain it in detail to others, and finally, having even had it written down,
one will retain it and offer worship and honor to it.

In brief, as much as the mass of merit for the act of hearing and so forth has been described, set forth, revealed, and elucidated by the Blessed One regarding that sūtra which is included within the entire Bodhisattva-piṭaka, such a mass of merit should be expected for this [sūtra].
Why is that?
For in this Bodhisattva stage, the introductory headings and detailed explanations of the entire Bodhisattva-piṭaka have been summarized and proclaimed.

Furthermore, as long as the Dharma and Vinaya revealed in detail within this Bodhisattva stage remain widespread through teaching, recitation, and the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharma-pratipatti), it will endure and attain great increase and expansion; for that long, counterfeit teachings will not become prevalent.
They will come about for the sake of the disappearance of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Furthermore, because counterfeits of the True Dharma will become abundant, this True Dharma—which is endowed with the actual reality—will consequently disappear.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, "The Foundation," in the section on the Finality of the Basis within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
And the Bodhisattvabhūmi is completed.
This is the work of the venerable master Ārya Asaṅga.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
